OE. been, beon, AS. beón to be, beóm I am; akin to OHG. bim, pim, G. bin, I am, Gael. & Ir. bu was, W. bod to be, Lith. bu-ti, O. Slav. by-ti, to be, L. fu-i I have been, fu-turus about to be, fo-re to be about to be, and perh to fieri to become, Gr. to be born, to be, Skr. bh to be. This verb is defective, and the parts lacking are supplied by verbs from other roots, is, was, which have no radical connection with be. The various forms, am, are, is, was, were, etc., are considered grammatically as parts of the verb "to be", which, with its conjugational forms, is often called the substantive verb. OE. blase, AS. blæse, blase; akin to OHG. blass whitish, G. blass pale, MHG. blas torch, Icel. blys torch; perh. fr. the same root as E. blast. Cf. Blast, Blush, Blink. | OE. blasen to blow; perh. confused with blast and blaze a flame, OE. blase. Cf. Blaze, v. i., and see Blast.

OE. blason, blasoun, shield, fr. F. blason coat of arms, OF. shield, from the root of AS. blæse blaze, i. e., luster, splendor, MHG. blas torch See Blaze, n. | From blazon, n.; confused with 4th blaze: cf. F. blasonner.
OE. blakien, blechen, v. t. & v. i., AS. blacian, bl, to grow pale; akin to Icel. bleikja, Sw. bleka, Dan. blege, D. bleeken, G. bleichen, AS. blac pale. See Bleak, a.

OE. blac, bleyke, bleche, AS. blac, bl, pale, wan; akin to Icel. bleikr, Sw. blek, Dan. bleg, OS. bl, D. bleek, OHG. pleih, G. bleich; all from the root of AS. blican to shine; akin to OHG. blichen to shine; cf. L. flagrare to burn, Gr. to burn, shine, Skr. bhraj to shine, and E. flame. Bleach, Blink, Flame. | From Bleak, a., cf. Blay.
See Blear, v. | OE. bleren; cf. Dan. plire to blink, Sw. plira to twinkle, wink, LG. plieren; perh. from the same root as E. blink. See Blink, and cf. Blur.
OE. bleten, AS. bl; akin to D. blaten, bleeten, OHG. blazan, plazan; prob. of imitative origin.
Prov. E. bleb, bleib, blob, bubble, blister. This word belongs to the root of blub, blubber, blabber, and perh. blow to puff.
OE. bleden, AS. bl, fr. bl blood; akin to Sw. blöda, Dan. blöde, D. bloeden, G. bluten. See Blood.

OE. blemissen, blemishen, OF. blemir, blesmir, to strike, injure, soil, F. blêmir to grow pale, fr. OF. bleme, blesme, pale, wan, F. blême, prob. fr. Icel blaman the livid color of a wound, fr. blar blue; akin to E. blue. OF. blemir properly signifies to beat one (black and) blue, and to render blue or dirty. See Blue.

OE. blenchen to blench, elude, deceive, AS. blencan to deceive; akin to Icel. blekkja to impose upon. Prop. a causative of blink to make to wink, to deceive. See Blink, and cf. 3d Blanch. | See 1st Blanch.

OE. blenden, blanden, AS. blandan to blend, mix; akin to Goth. blandan to mix, Icel. blanda, Sw. blanda, Dan. blande, OHG. blantan to mis; to unknown origin. | AS. blendan, from blind blind. See Blind, a.
G., fr. blenden to blind, dazzle, deceive, fr. blind blind. So called either in allusion to its dazzling luster; or (Dana) because, though often resembling galena, it yields no lead. Cf. Sphalerite.
So called from Blenheim House, the seat of the duke of Marlborough, in England.
L. blennius, blendius, blendea, Gr. , fr. slime, mucus.
D., fr. bles a white spot on the forehead + bok buck.
OE. blessien, bletsen, AS. bletsian, bledsian, bloedsian, fr. bl blood; prob. originally to consecrate by sprinkling with blood. See Blood.
AS. bletsung. See Bless, v. t.
F. blet, blette, a., soft from over ripeness.

Perh. contr. from AS. blicettan to glitter, fr. the same root as E. bleak. The meaning "to blight" comes in that case from to glitter, hence, to be white or pale, grow pale, make pale, bleach. Cf. Bleach, Bleak.
OE. blinnen, AS. blinnan; pref. be- + linnan to cease. | AS. blinn.
AS.; akin to D., G., OS., Sw., & Dan. blind, Icel. blindr, Goth. blinds; of uncertain origin.
OE. blindfolden, blindfelden, blindfellen; AS. blind blind + prob. fellan, fyllan, to fell, strike down.

OE. blenken; akin to dan. blinke, Sw. blinka, G. blinken to shine, glance, wink, twinkle, D. blinken to shine; and prob. to D. blikken to glance, twinkle, G. blicken to look, glance, AS. blican to shine, E. bleak. sq. root98. See Bleak; cf. 1st Blench. | OE. blink. See Blink, v. i.
OE. blis, blisse, AS. blis, bli, fr. bli blithe. See Blithe.
For blithesome: but cf. also Icel. bl of a goat at heat.
OE.; akin to OD. bluyster, fr. the same root as blast, bladder, blow. See Blow to eject wind.
AS. bli blithe, kind; akin to Goth. blei kind, Icel. bli mild, gentle, Dan. & Sw. blid gentle, D. blijd blithe, OHG. blidi kind, blithe.
Cf. Blaze to flash. Formerly, in local use, a rattling volley; cf. "to blaze away" to fire away.
Cf. Icel. blotna to become soft, blautr soft, wet, Sw. blöt soft, blöta to soak; akin to G. bloss bare, and AS. bleát wretched; or perh. fr. root of Eng. 5th blow. Cf. Blote.

OE. blok; cf. F. bloc (fr. OHG.), D. & Dan. blok, Sw. & G. block, OHG. bloch. There is also an OHG. bloch, biloh; bi by + the same root as that of E. lock. Cf. Block, v. t., Blockade, and see Lock. | Cf. F. bloquer, fr. bloc block. See Block, n.
Cf. It. bloccata. See Block, v. t.
OF. blanquet whitish, dim. of blanc white. Cf. Blanket.
F., fair, light, of uncertain origin; cf. AS. blonden-feax gray-haired, old, prop. blended-haired, as a mixture of white and brown or black. See Blend, v. t.
F., fair, light, of uncertain origin; cf. AS. blonden-feax gray-haired, old, prop. blended-haired, as a mixture of white and brown or black. See Blend, v. t.  | F.
OF. blanquet whitish, dim. of blanc white. Cf. Blanket.
OE. blod, blood, AS. bl; akin to D. bloed, OHG. bluot, G. blut, Goth, bl, Sw. & Dan. blod; prob. fr. the same root as E. blow to bloom. See Blow to bloom.
Blood + Prov. E. bolter to mat in tufts. Cf. Balter.
From the color of the flower.
AS. bl; bl blood + l to let.
Blood + shot, p. p. of shoot to variegate.
AS. bl; bl blood, + wite wite, fine.
AS. bl; bl blood, + wite wite, fine.

OE. blome, fr. Icel. bl, bl; akin to Sw. blom, Goth. bl, OS. bl, D. bloem, OHG. bluomo, bluoma, G. blume; fr. the same root as AS. bl to blow, blossom. See Blow to bloom, and cf. Blossom. | AS. bl a mass or lump, isenes bl a lump or wedge of iron.
From Mrs. Bloomer, an American, who sought to introduce this style of dress.
Perh. a variant of blare, v. i.; or cf. Gael. & Ir. blor a loud noise.
OE. blosme, blostme, AS. bl, bl, blossom; akin to D. bloesem, L. fios, and E. flower; from the root of E. blow to blossom. See Blow to blossom, and cf. Bloom a blossom. | AS. bl. See Blossom, n.
Cf. Dan. plette. See 3d Blot. | Cf. Icel. blettr, Dan. plet. | Cf. Dan. blot bare, naked, Sw. blott, d. bloot, G. bloss, and perh. E. bloat.
Cf. OE. blacche in blacchepot blacking pot, akin to black, as bleach is akin to bleak. See Black, a., or cf. Blot a spot.
Cf. Sw. blöt-fisk soaked fish, fr. blöta to soak. See 1st Bloat.

OE. blowen, AS. bl to blossom; akin to OS. bl, D. bloeijen, OHG. pluojan, MHG. bl, G. blühen, L. florere to flourish, OIr. blath blossom. Cf. Blow to puff, Flourish. | OE. blaw, blowe; cf. OHG. bliuwan, pliuwan, to beat, G. bläuen, Goth. bliggwan. | OE. blawen, blowen, AS. bl to blow, as wind; akin to OHG. pl, G. blähen, to blow up, swell, L. flare to blow, Gr. to spout out, and to E. bladder, blast, inflate, etc., and perh. blow to bloom.
From Blow to blossom: cf. Growth.
Prob. from the same root as blush.
Cf. Ir. blocan a little block, Gael. plocan a mallet, W. plocyn, dim. of ploc block; or perh. connected with E. blow a stroke. Cf. Block, Blow a stroke.
OE. bla, blo, blew, blue, Sw. bl, D. blauw, OHG. bl, G. blau; but influenced in form by F. bleu, from OHG. blao.
F. bluet, bleuet, dim. of bleu blue. See Blue, a.
Cf. OD. blaf flat, broad, blaffaert one with a broad face, also, a boaster; or G. verblüffen to confuse, LG. bluffen to frighten; to unknown origin.
OE. blunderen, blondren, to stir, confuse, blunder; perh. allied to blend to mix, to confound by mixture.
Either fr. blunder + D. bus tube, box, akin to G. büchse box, gun, E. box; or corrupted fr. D. donderbus (literally) thunder box, gun, musket.
Cf. Prov. G. bludde a dull or blunt knife, Dan. blunde to sleep, Sw. & Icel. blunda; or perh. akin to E. blind.
Prob. of same origin as blear. See Blear.
OE. bluschen to shine, look, turn red, AS. blyscan to glow; akin to blysa a torch, abl to blush, D. blozen, Dan. blusse to blaze, blush.
Cf. W. bw, an interj. of threatening or frightening; n., terror, fear, dread.
L. boa a kind of water serpent. Perh. fr. bos an ox.
Gr. , fr. Heb. bn sons of thunder. -- an appellation given by Christ to two of his disciples (James and John). See Mark iii. 17.
OE. bar, bor, bore, AS. bar; akin to OHG. p, MHG. b, G. bär, boar (but not bär bear), and perh. Russ. borov' boar.
OE. bord, AS. bord board, shipboard; akin to bred plank, Icel. bor board, side of a ship, Goth. f footstool, D. bord board, G. brett, bort. See def. 8. sq. root92. | F. aborder. See Abord, v. t.

OE. bosten, boosten, v., bost, boost, n., noise, boasting; cf. G. bausen, bauschen, to swell, pusten, Dan. puste, Sw. pusta, to blow, Sw. pösa to swell; or W. bostio to boast, bost boast, Gael. bosd. But these last may be from English. | Of uncertain etymology.
OE. boot, bat, AS. bat; akin to Icel. batr, Sw. båt, Dan. baad, D.& G. boot. Cf. Bateau.
L. boatus, fr. boare to roar.

An onomatopoetic word, expressing quick, jerky motion; OE. bob bunch, bobben to strike, mock, deceive. Cf. Prov. Eng. bob, n., a ball, an engine beam, bunch, blast, trick, taunt, scoff; as, a v., to dance, to courtesy, to disappoint, OF. bober to mock. | OE. bobben. See Bob, n.
OF. bobance, F. bombance, boasting, pageantry, fr. L. bombus a humming, buzzing.
Prob. an Anglo-Indian form of Hindi bap re O thou father! (a very disrespectful address).
F. bobine; of uncertain origin; cf. L. bombus a humming, from the noise it makes, or Ir. & Gael. baban tassel, or E. bob.
G. bockbier; bock a buck + bier beer; -- said to be so named from its tendency to cause the drinker to caper like a goat.
AS. b; b book + land land.

OE. bodien, AS. bodian to announce, tell from bod command; akin to Icel. bo to announce, Sw. båda to announce, portend. sq. root89. See Bid. | AS. boda; akin to OFries. boda, AS. bodo, OHG. boto. See Bode, v. t. | See Abide.
This is properly the plural of body, Oe. bodise a pair of bodies, equiv. to a bodice. Cf. Corset, and see Body.
OE. boydekyn dagger; of uncertain origin; cf. W. bidog hanger, short sword, Ir. bideog, Gael. biodag.
Prob. of Celtic origin: cf. Bordrage.
OE. bodi, AS. bodig; akin to OHG. botah. sq. root257. Cf. Bodice.
L. Boeotia, Gr. , noted for its moist, thick atmosphere, and the dullness and stupidity of its inhabitants.
Ir. & Gael. bog soft, tender, moist: cf. Ir. bogach bog, moor, marsh, Gael. bogan quagmire.
Scot. and North Eng. bogle, bogill, bugill, specter; as a verb, to terrify, fr. W. bwgwl threatening, fear, bwg, bwgan, specter, hobgoblin. Cf. Bug.
From Wu-i, pronounced by the Chinese bu-i, the name of the hills where this kind of tea is grown.

OE. boilen, OF. boilir, builir, F. bouillir, fr. L. bullire to be in a bubbling motion, from bulla bubble; akin to Gr. , Lith. bumbuls. Cf. Bull an edict, Budge, v., and Ebullition. | Influenced by boil, v. See Beal, Bile.
F., bow wood. So called because used for bows by the Western Indians.
OF. boiste, F. boîte, from the same root as E. box.
OE. boistous; of uncertain origin; cf. W. bwyst wild, savage, wildness, ferocity, bwystus ferocious.
OE. bald, bold, AS. bald, beald; akin to Icel. ballr, OHG. bald, MHG. balt, D. boud, Goth. bal boldness, It. baldo. In Ger. there remains only bald, adv. soon. Cf. Bawd, n.

OE. bole, fr. Icel. bolr; akin to Sw. bål, Dan. bul, trunk, stem of a tree, G. bohle a thick plank or board; cf. LG. boll round. Cf. Bulge. | Etym. doubtful. | Gr. a clod or lump of earth: cf. F. bol, and also L. bolus morsel. Cf. Bolus.
L., fr. Gr. missile, arrow, fr. to throw.
OE. bolle boll, bowl, AS. bolla. See Bowl a vessel.
Cf. Bole the stem of a tree, and Pollard.
Cf. Bole stem of a tree, and Poll, v. t.
OE. bolnen, bollen; cf. Dan. bulne. Cf. Bulge.
AS. bolster; akin to Icel. b, Sw. & Dan. bolster, OHG. bolstar, polstar, G. polster; from the same root as E. bole stem, bowl hollow vessel. Cf. Bulge, Poltroon.

AS. bolt; akin to Icel. bolti, Dan. bolt, D. bout, OHG. bolz, G. bolz, bolzen; of uncertain origin. | From Bolt, v. i. | OE. bolten, boulten, OF. buleter, F. bluter, fr. Ll. buletare, buratare, cf. F. bure coarse woolen stuff; fr. L. burrus red. See Borrel, and cf. Bultel.
L. bolus bit, morsel; cf. G. lump of earth. See Bole, n., clay.
F. bombe bombshell, fr. L. bombus a humming or buzzing noise, Gr. . | Cf. Boom.
F. bombarde, LL. bombarda, fr. L. bombus + -ard. Cf. Bumper, and see Bomb. | OE. bombarde, fr. F. bombarde.
OF. bombace cotton, LL. bombax cotton, bombasium a doublet of cotton; hence, padding, wadding, fustian. See Bombazine.
F. bombasin, LL. bombacinium, bambacinium, L. bombycinus silken, bombycinum a silk or cotton texture, fr. bombyx silk, silkworm, Gr. . Cf. Bombast, Bombycinous.
L. bombyx silk, silkworm: cf. F. bombique.
LL. bombilare, for L. bombitare. See Bomb, n.
F. bon good + vivant, p. pr. of vivre to live.
OE., also bonere, OF. bonnaire, Cotgr., abbrev. of debonnaire. See Debonair.
Sp., prop. calm., fair weather, prosperity, fr. L. bonus good.
F. bonbon, fr. bon bon very good, a superlative by reduplication, fr. bon good.
The same word as band. Cf. Band, Bend. | OE. bond, bonde, peasant, serf, AS. bonda
F. bonduc, fr. Ar. bunduq hazel nut, filbert nut.
OE. bon, ban, AS. ban; akin to Icel. bein, Sw. ben, Dan. & D. been, G. bein bone, leg; cf. Icel. beinn straight. | F. bornoyer to look at with one eye, to sight, fr. borgne one-eyed.
OE. bonefire, banefire, orig. a fire of bones; bone + fire; but cf. also Prov. E. bun a dry stalk.
F. bon good + grâce grace, charm.
From the sleek, jolly landlord in Farquhar's comedy of "The Beaux' Stratagem."
L. bonus good + -fy: cf. F. bonifier.
Senses 1 and 2 fr. 1st Bone, sense 3 fr. 3d Bone.
Sp. & Pg. bonito, fr. Ar. bainit and bainith.
F. bon, fem. bonne, good + bouche mouth.
OE. bonet, OF. bonet, bonete. F. bonnet fr. LL. bonneta, bonetum; orig. the name of a stuff, and of unknown origin.
F. bonne et belle, good and beautiful. Cf. Bellibone.
OE. boni, prob. fr. F. bon, fem. bonne, good, fr. L. bonus good. See Bounty, and cf. Bonus, Boon.
Ir. bainne, baine, milk + clabar mud, mire.
D. bont a sort of skin or fur, prop. variegated + bok buck.
Pg. bonzo, fr. Japan bozu a Buddhist priest: cf. F. bonze.
Sp. bobe dunce, idiot; cf. L. balbus stammering, E. barbarous.
L. Bootes, Gr. herdsman, fr. , gen. , ox, cow.

OE. book, bok, AS. b; akin to Goth. b a letter, in pl. book, writing, Icel. b, Sw. bok, Dan. bog, OS. b, D. boek, OHG. puoh, G. buch; and fr. AS. b, b, beech; because the ancient Saxons and Germans in general wrote runes on pieces of beechen board. Cf. Beech.
AS. b; b book + land land.
Ir. buachail cowherd; bo cow + giolla boy.

D. boom tree, pole, beam, bar. See Beam. | Of imitative origin; cf. OE. bommen to hum, D. bommen to drum, sound as an empty barrel, also W. bwmp a hollow sound; aderyn y bwmp, the bird of the hollow sound, i. e., the bittern. Cf. Bum, Bump, v. i., Bomb, v. i.

OE. bone, boin, a petition, fr. Icel. b; akin to Sw. & Dan. b, AS. b, and perh. to E. ban; but influenced by F. bon good, fr. L. bonus. Ban, Bounty. | F. bon. See Boon, n. | Scot. boon, bune, been, Gael. & Ir. bunach coarse tow, fr. bun root, stubble.
D. boer farmer, boor; akin to AS. geb countryman, G. bauer; fr. the root of AS. b to inhabit, and akin to E. bower, be. Cf. Neighbor, Boer, and Big to build.
AS. bos, bosig; akin to Icel. bass, Sw. bås, Dan. baas, stall, G. banse, Goth. bansts barn, Skr. bhasas stall. *252.
OE. | OE. bote, OF. bote, F. botte, LL. botta; of uncertain origin.
L. Bootes, Gr. herdsman, fr. , gen. , ox, cow.

OE. bothe; cf. Icel. b, Dan. & Sw. bod, MHG. buode, G. bude, baude; from the same root as AS. b to dwell, E. boor, bower, be; cf. Bohem. bauda, Pol. buda, Russ. budka, Lith. buda, W. bwth, pl. bythod, Gael. buth, Ir. both.

Cf. Icel. b exchange, barter, Sw. byte barter, booty, Dan. bytte; akin to D. buit booty, G. beute, and fr. Icel. byta, Sw. byta, Dan. bytte, to distribute, exchange. The Scandinavian word was influenced in English by boot profit.
D. buizen; akin to G. bausen, and perh. fr. D. buis tube, channel, bus box, jar.
Sp. borracha a leather bottle for wine, borracho drunk, fr. borra a lamb.
OE. borage (cf. F. bourrache, It. borraggine, borrace, LL. borago, borrago, LGr. ), fr. LL. borra, F. bourre, hair of beasts, flock; so called from its hairy leaves.
OE. boras, fr. F. borax, earlier spelt borras; cf. LL. borax, Sp. borraj; all fr. Ar. b, fr. Pers. b.
F. borborygme, fr. Gr. , fr. to rumble in the bowels.
Bordar (or perh. bord a board) + service.
LL. bordarius, fr. borda a cottage; of uncertain origin.
F. bordel, orig. a little hut, OF. borde hut, cabin, of German origin, and akin to E. board,n.See. Board, n.
F. bordel, orig. a little hut, OF. borde hut, cabin, of German origin, and akin to E. board,n.See. Board, n.

OE. bordure, F. bordure, fr. border to border, fr. bord a border; of German origin; cf. MHG. borte border, trimming, G. borte trimming, ribbon; akin to E. board in sense 8. See Board, n., and cf. Bordure.
Bordar (or perh. bord a board) + land.
Bordar (or perh. bord a board) + lode leading.
Bordar (or perh. bord a board) + man.
Perh. from OE. bord, for border + raging. Cf. Bodrage.
Perh. from OE. bord, for border + raging. Cf. Bodrage.

OE. borien, AS. borian; akin to Icel. bora, Dan. bore, D. boren, OHG. por, G. bohren, L. forare, Gr. to plow, Zend bar. sq. root91. | Icel. bara wave: cf. G. empor upwards, OHG. bor height, burren to lift, perh. allied to AS. beran, E. 1st bear. sq. root92.
L. borealis: cf. F. boréal. See Boreas.
Named after Von Born, a mineralogist.

OE. burgh, burw, boru, port, town, burrow, AS. burh, burg; akin to Icel., Sw., & Dan. borg, OS. & D. burg, OHG. puruc, purc, MHG. burc, G. burg, Goth. baúrgs; and from the root of AS. beorgan to hide, save, defend, G. bergen; or perh. from that of AS. beorg hill, mountain. Bury, v. t., and cf. Burrow, Burg, Bury, n., Burgess, Iceberg, Borrow, Harbor, Hauberk. | See Borrow.
OF. burel a kind of coarse woolen cloth, fr. F. bure drugget. See Bureau. Rustic and common people dressed in this cloth, which was prob. so called from its color. | Prob. from Borrel, n.
OE. borwen, AS. borgian, fr. borg, borh, pledge; akin to D. borg, G. borg; prob. fr. root of AS. beorgan to protect. Borough.
OE. borsolder; prob. fr. AS. borg, gen. borges, pledge + ealdor elder. See Borrow, and Elder, a.
Ar. b, Pers. b: cf. F. bosan.
OF. boscage grove, F. bocage, fr. LL. boscus, buscus, thicket, wood. See 1st Bush.
Cf. G. posse joke, trifle; It. bozzo a rough stone, bozzetto a rough sketch, s-bozzo a rough draught, sketch. | Turk. | Cf. G. böschung a slope.
F. bosquet a little wood, dim. fr. LL. boscus. See Boscage, and cf. Bouquet.
AS. b; akin to D. bozem, Fries. b, OHG. puosum, G. busen, and prob. E. bough.
L. Bosporus, G. , lit., ox-ford, the ox's or heifer's ford, on account of Io's passage here as a heifer; fr. ox, heifer + ford.
F. bosquet a little wood, dim. fr. LL. boscus. See Boscage, and cf. Bouquet.

OE. boce, bose, boche, OF. boce, boche, bosse, F. bosse, of G. origin; cf. OHG. bozo tuft, bunch, OHG. bozan, MHG. bôzen, to beat. See Beat, and cf. Botch a swelling. | OE. bocen, fr. OF. bocier. See the preceding word. | D. baas master.
F. bossage, fr. bosse. See Boss a stud.
Dim. fr. Prov. E. boss in boss-calf, buss-calf, for boose-calf, prop., a calf kept in the stall. See 1st Boose.
F. botanique, a. & n., fr. Gr. botanic, fr. herb, plant, fr. to feed, graze.
It. bottarga, bottarica; or Sp. botarga; a kind of large sausages, a sort of wide breeches: cf. F. boutargue.
Same as Boss a stud. For senses 2 & 3 cf. D. botsen to beat, akin to E. beat. | See Botch, n.
Old form of boot; -- used in composition. See 1st Boot.

OE. bothe, ba, fr. Icel. ba; akin to Dan. baade, Sw. båda, Goth. baj, OHG. beid, b, G. & D. beide, also AS. begen, ba, b, Goth. bai, and Gr. , L. ambo, Lith. abà, OSlav. oba, Skr. ubha. sq. root310. Cf. Amb-.
Cf. Ir. buaidhirt trouble, buaidhrim I vex.
Gr. pit + something poured in. Formed like parenchyma.
Pg. botoque stopple. So called because they wear a wooden plug in the pierced lower lip.
Cf. Gael. botus belly worm, boiteag maggot.

OE. bote, botelle, OF. botel, bouteille, F. bouteille, fr. LL. buticula, dim. of butis, buttis, butta, flask. Cf. Butt a cask. | OE. botel, OF. botel, dim. of F. botte; cf. OHG. bozo bunch. See Boss stud.

OE. botum, botme, AS. botm; akin to OS. bodom, D. bodem, OHG. podam, G. boden, Icel. botn, Sw. botten, Dan. bund (for budn ), L. fundus (for fudnus), Gr.budhna (for bhudhna), and Ir. bonn sole of the foot, W. bon stem, base. Cf. 4th Found, Fund, n. | OE. botme, perh. corrupt. for button. See Button.
From 1st Bottom in sense 8: cf.D. bodemerij. Cf. Bummery.
F. boutonné, fr. boutonner to bud, button.
F. boutonné, fr. boutonner to bud, button.
F., morsels, mouthfuls, fr. bouche mouth.
F., fr. bouder to pout, be sulky.
Named from Bougainville, the French navigator.
Variant of bulge. Cf. Bowge. | F. bouche mouth, victuals.
Cf. F. bougette sack, bag. Cf. Budget.
OE. bogh, AS. bog, boh, bough, shoulder; akin to Icel. bogr shoulder, bow of a ship, Sw. bog, Dan. bov, OHG. buog, G. bug, and to Gr.bahu (for bhaghu) arm. sq. root88, 251. Cf. Bow of a ship.
Cf. Dan. bugt bend, turning, Icel. bug. Cf. Bight, Bout, and see Bow to bend.
F. bougie wax candle, bougie, fr. Bougie, Bugia, a town of North Africa, from which these candles were first imported into Europe.
Cf. Sw. bullra to roar, rattle, Dan. buldre, dial. Sw. bullersteen larger kind of pebbles; perh. akin to E. bellow.
F. boulevard, boulevart, fr. G. bollwerk. See Bulwark.
OE. bunsen; cf. D. bonzen to strike, bounce, bons blow, LG. bunsen to knock; all prob. of imitative origin.

OE. bounde, bunne, OF. bonne, bonde, bodne, F. borne, fr. LL. bodina, bodena, bonna; prob. of Celtic origin; cf. Arm. bonn boundary, limit, and boden, bod, a tuft or cluster of trees, by which a boundary or limit could be marked. Cf. Bourne. | F. bondir to leap, OF. bondir, bundir, to leap, resound, fr. L. bombitare to buzz, hum, fr. bombus a humming, buzzing. See Bomb. | Past p. of OE. bounen to prepare, fr. boun ready, prepared, fr. Icel. bü, p. p. of büaboor and bower. See Bond, a., and cf. Busk, v.
From Bound a limit; cf. LL. bonnarium piece of land with fixed limits.
OE. bounte goodness, kindness, F. bonté, fr. L. bonitas, fr. bonus good, for older duonus; cf. Skr. duvas honor, respect.
F. bouquet bunch, bunch of flowers, trees, feathers, for bousquet, bosquet, thicket, a little wood, dim. of LL. boscus. See Bush thicket, and cf. Bosket, Busket.
From the castle and seigniory of Bourbon in central France.
F. bourde fib, lie, OF. borde, bourde, jest, joke.
F., fr. L. burdo mule, esp. one used for carrying litters. Cf. Sp. muleta a young she mule; also, crutch, prop. | F. See Burden a refrain.

From a French type founder named Bourgeois, or fr. F. bourgeois of the middle class; hence applied to an intermediate size of type between brevier and long primer: cf. G. bourgeois, borgis. Cf. Burgess. | F., fr. bourg town; of German origin. See Burgess.
OE. burjoun a bud, burjounen to bud, F. bourgeon a bud, bourgeonner to bud; cf. OHG. burjan to raise.

OE. burne, borne, AS. burna; akin to OS. brunno spring, G. born, brunnen, OHG. prunno, Goth. brunna, Icel. brunnr, and perh. to Gr. burn, v., because the source of a stream seems to issue forth bubbling and boiling from the earth. Cf. Torrent, and see Burn, v. | F. borne. See Bound a limit.

OE. burne, borne, AS. burna; akin to OS. brunno spring, G. born, brunnen, OHG. prunno, Goth. brunna, Icel. brunnr, and perh. to Gr. burn, v., because the source of a stream seems to issue forth bubbling and boiling from the earth. Cf. Torrent, and see Burn, v. | F. borne. See Bound a limit.
Named after Count Bournon, a minerologist.
F. bourse purse, exchange, LL. bursa, fr. Gr.Purse, Burse.
A different spelling and application of bought bend.
F., fr. bouter to thrust. See Butt.
F.; bouter to thrust, put + feu fire.
LL. bovata, fr. bos, bovis, ox.
LL. bovinus, fr.L. bos, bovis, ox, cow: cf. F. bovine. See Cow.

OE. bowen, bogen, bugen, AS. bugan (generally v.i.); akin to D. buigen, OHG. biogan, G. biegen, beugen, Icel. boginn bent, beygja to bend, Sw. böja, Dan. böie, bugne, Coth. biugan; also to L. fugere to flee, Gr. bhuj to bend. sq. root88. Cf. Fugitive. | OE. bowe, boge, AS. boga, fr. AS. bü to bend; akin to D. boog, G. bogen, Icel. bogi. See Bow, v. t. | Icel. bogr shoulder, bow of a ship. See Bough.
OE. bouel, bouele, OF. boel, boele, F. boyau, fr. L. botellus a small sausage, in LL. also intestine, dim. of L. botulus sausage.
From G.T.Bowen, who analyzed it in 1822.

From Bow, v. & n. | G. bauer a peasant. So called from the figure sometimes used for the knave in cards. See Boor. | OE. bour, bur, room, dwelling, AS. bur, fr. the root of AS. buan to dwell; akin to Icel. bur chamber, storehouse, Sw. bur cage, Dan. buur, OHG. pur room, G. bauer cage, bauer a peasant. *97 | From Bough, cf. Brancher.
OE. bolle, AS. bolla; akin to Icel. bolli, Dan. bolle, G. bolle, and perh. to E. boil a tumor. Cf. Boll. | F. boule, fr. L. bulla bubble, stud. Cf. Bull an edict, Bill a writing.
Cf. Sw. bullra to roar, rattle, Dan. buldre, dial. Sw. bullersteen larger kind of pebbles; perh. akin to E. bellow.
Cf. D. boelijn, Icel. böglïnabovline; properly the line attached to the shoulder or side of the sail. See Bow (of a ship), and Line.
Bow + sprit; akin to D.boegspriet; boeg bow of a ship + spriet, E. sprit, also Sw. bogspröt, G. bugspriet.
From Bow, like lawyer from law.

As. box, L. buxus, fr. Gr. Box a case. | As. box a small case or vessel with a cover; akin to OHG. buhsa box, G. büchse; fr. L. buxus boxwood, anything made of boxwood. See Pyx, and cf. Box a tree, Bushel. | Cf.Dan. baske to slap, bask slap, blow. Cf. Pash. | Cf.Sp. boxar, now spelt bojar.
Cf. D. boef, Fries. boi, boy; akin to G. bube, Icel. bofi rouge.
F. boyau gut, a long and narrow place, and (of trenches) a branch. See Bowel.
From Captain Boycott, a land agent in Mayo, Ireland, so treated in 1880.
D. boeijer; -- so called because these vessels were employed for laying the boeijen, or buoys: cf. F. boyer. See Buoy.
D. brabbelen to talk confusedly. Blab, Babble.
L. bracatus wearing breeches, fr. bracae breeches.
F. bracelet, dim. of OF. bracel armlet, prop. little arm, dim. of bras arm, fr. L. bracchium. See Brace,n.
OE. brache a kind of scenting hound or setting dog, OF. brache, braque, fr. OHG. braccho, G. bracke; possibly akin to E. fragrant, fr. L. fragrare to smell.
L. brachialis (bracch-), from bracchium (bracch-) arm: cf. F. brachial.
L. brachiatus (bracch-) with boughs or branches like arms, from brackium (bracch-) arm.
NL., from L. brachium (bracch-) arm + NL. ganoidei.
NL., fr. L. brachiolum (bracch-), dim. of brachium (bracch-) arm.
L. Brachmanae, pl., Gr. Defn: See Brahman. [Obs.
Incorrect for brachistochrone, fr. Gr. brachistochrone.

NL., fr. Gr. (Zoöl.) Defn: A group of decapod Crustacea, including the common crabs, characterized by a small and short abdomen, which is bent up beneath the large cephalo-thorax. [Also spelt Brachyoura.
Cf.D. braak, Dan. bræk, a breaking, Sw. & Isel. brak a crackling, creaking. Cf. Breach. | D. brak, adj., salt; cf. LG. wrak refuse, G. brack.
OE. braken, AS. bracce. See 2d Brake, n.
Cf.OF. braguette codpiece, F. brayette, Sp. bragueta, also a projecting mold in architecture; dim. fr.L. bracae breeches; cf. also, OF. bracon beam, prop, support; of unknown origin. Cf. Breeches.
L., a thin plate of metal or wood, gold foil.
Cf.L. bracteatus covered with gold plate.
L. bracteola, dim. of bractea. See Bractea.

Cf.OE. brod, Dan. braad prick, sting, brodde ice spur, frost nail, Sw. brodd frost nail, Icel. broddr any pointed piece of iron or stell; akin to AS. brord point, spire of grass, and perh. to E. bristle. See Bristle, n.

OE. braggen to resound, blow, boast (cf. F. braguer to lead a merry life, flaunt, boast, OF. brague merriment), from Icel. braka to creak, brak noise, fr. the same root as E. break; properly then, to make a noise, boast. 95. | See Brag, v. i.
From Braggadocchio, a boastful character in Spenser's "Faërie Queene."
OF. bragard flaunting, vain, bragging. See Brag, v. i.
OE. braket, bragot, fr. W. bragawd, bragod, fr. brag malt.
Bengalese, a wor Defn: A modern reforming theistic sect among the Hindos. [Written also Brahma-samaj.

OE. braiden, breiden, to pull, reach, braid, AS. bregdan to move to and fro, to weave; akin. to Icel. breg, D. breiden to knit, OS. bregdan to weave, OHG. brettan to brandish. Cf. Broid. | Cf.Icel. breg to move quickly. | AS. bræd, bred, deceit; akin to Icel. brag trick, AS. bredan, bregdan, to braid, knit, (hence) to knit a net, to draw into a net, i.e., to deceive. See Braid, v. t.
OE. brayle furling rope, OF. braiol a band placed around the breeches, fr.F. braies, pl., breeches, fr.L. braca, bracae, breeches, a Gallic word; cf. Arm. bragez. Cf. Breeches.
OE. brain, brein, AS. bragen, brægen; akin to LG. brägen, bregen, D. brein, and perh. to Gr. 95.
So called from its iridescent colors. | F. | F. braiser, fr. braise coals.
Cf.W. braith variegated, Ir. breath, breagh, fine, comely.
So called from its iridescent colors. | F.

OE. brake fern; cf. AS. bracce fern, LG. brake willow bush, Da. bregne fern, G. brach fallow; prob. orig. the growth on rough, broken ground, fr. the root of E. break. See Break, v. t., cf. Bracken, and 2d Brake, n. | OE. brake; cf. LG. brake an instrument for breaking flax, G. breche, fr. the root of E. break. See Break, v. t., and cf. Breach.
OE. brembil, AS.brbramal), fr. the same root as E. broom, As. br. See Broom.
OE. bren, bran, OF. bren, F. bran, from Celtic; cf. Armor. brenn, Ir. bran, bran, chaff.
OE. braunche, F. branche, fr. LL. branca claw of a bird or beast of prey; cf. Armor. brank branch, bough.

OE. brand, brond, AS. brand brond brand, sword, from byrnan, beornan, to burn; akin to D., Dan., Sw., & G. brand brand, Icel. brandr a brand, blade of a sword. sq. root32. See Burn, v. t., and cf. Brandish.
Prob. fr. 1st brand + goose: cf. Sw. brandgås. Cf. Brant.
OE. braundisen, F. brandir, fr. brand a sword, fr. OHG. brant brand. See Brand, n.
From older brandywine, brandwine, fr. D. brandewijn, fr. p. p. of branden to burn, distill + wijn wine, akin to G. branntwein. See Brand.
Prov. E. brangled confused, entangled, Scot. brangle to shake, menace; probably a variant of wrangle, confused with brawl.
Prov. of Celtic origin; cf. L. brance, brace, the Gallic name of a particularly white kind of corn. | Cf. Gael. brangus, brangas, a sort of pillory, Ir. brancas halter, or D. pranger fetter.
Cf. Gael. brangus, brangas, a sort of pillory, Ir. brancas halter, or D. pranger fetter.
F. branc-ursine, branch-ursine, fr. LL. branca claw + L. ursinus belonging to a bear (fr. ursus bear), i .e., bear's claw, because its leaves resemble the claws of a bear. Cf. Branch.
Scot. branlie fr. brand. | See Brand.
Cf.Brand goose, Brent, Brenicle. | See Brent. | AS. brant; akin to Dan. brat, Icel. brattr, steep.
For brand-fox; cf. G. brandfuchs, Sw. bradräf. So called from its yellowish brown and somewhat black color. See Brand.
Cf. Gael. bras or G. barsch harsh, sharp, tart, impetuous, D. barsch, Sw. & Dan. barsk. | Cf. Amer. bresk, brusk, fragile, brittle. | See Brash brittle.
OE. brasiere, F. braise live coals. See Brass. | F. brasier, braisíer, fr. braise live coals. See Brass.
OE. bras, bres, AS. bræs; akin to Icel. bras cement, solder, brasa to harden by fire, and to E. braze, brazen. Cf. 1st & 2d Braze.
F. brassard, fr. bras arm. See Brace, n.
Perh. a transposition of barse; but cf. LG. brasse the bream, G. brassen Cf. Bream.
OE. bratt coarse garnment, AS. bratt cloak, fr. the Celtic; cf. W. brat clout, rag, Gael. brat cloak, apron, raf, Ir. brat cloak; properly then, a child's bib or clout; hence, a child.
G., fr. It. viola da braccio viola held on the arm.
Sp. bravada, bravata, boast, brag: cf. F. bravade. See Brave.
F. brave, It. or Sp. bravo, (orig.) fierce, wild, savage, prob. from. L. barbarus. See Barbarous, and cf. Bravo.
I. See Brave, a. | It. See Brave.
It., (properly) bravery, spirit, from bravo. See Brave.
OF. braon fleshy part, muscle, fr. HG. br flesh, G. braten roast meat; akin to Icel. br flesh, food of beasts, AS. brbr to roast, G. braten, and possibly to E. breed.
Cf. AS. breac rheum, broc sickness, Ir. bracha corruption. Jamieson.

OE. brayen, OF. breier, F. broyer to pound, grind, fr. OHG. brehhan to break. See Break. | OE brayen, F. braire to bray, OF. braire to cry, fr. LL. bragire to whinny; perh. fr. the Celtic and akin to E. break; or perh. of imitative origin. | OE. braye, brey, brew, eyebrow, brow of a hill, hill, bank, Scot. bra, brae, bray, fr. AS. br eyebrow, influenced by the allied Icel. br eyebrow, bank, also akin to AS. brBrow.
F. braser to solder, fr. Icel. brasa to harden by fire. Cf. Brass. | AS. bræsian, fr. bræs brass. See Brass.
OE. brasen, AS. bræsen. See Brass.
OE. brasiere, F. braise live coals. See Brass. | F. brasier, braisíer, fr. braise live coals. See Brass.

OE. brasil, LL. brasile (cf. Pg. & Sp. brasil, Pr. bresil, Pr. bresil); perh. from Sp. or Pg. brasa a live coal (cf. Braze, Brasier); or Ar. vars plant for dyeing red or yellow. This name was given to the wood from its color; and it is said that King Emanuel, of Portugal, gave the name Brazil to the country in South America on account of its producing this wood.
Cf. Pg. & Sp. brasilete, It. brasiletto.
OE. breke, breche, AS. brice, gebrice, gebrece (in comp.), fr. brecan to break; akin to Dan. bræk, MHG. breche, gap, breach. See Break, and cf. Brake (the instrument), Brack a break
AS. brædan to make broad, to spread. See Broad, a. | AS. breád; akin to OFries. brad, OS. br, D. brood, G. brod, brot, Icel. brau, Sw. & Dan. bröd. The root is probably that of E. brew. Brew.
OE. brede, breede, whence later bredette, AS. brbrad broad. See Broad, a.

OE. breken, AS. brecan; akin to OS. brekan, D. breken, OHG. brehhan, G. brechen, Icel.braka to creak, Sw. braka, bräkka to crack, Dan. brække to break, Goth. brikan to break, L. frangere. Cf. Bray to pound, Breach, Fragile. | See Break, v. t., and cf. Brake (the instrument), Breach, Brack a crack.
OE. breme, brem, F. brême, OF. bresme, of German origin; cf. OHG. brahsema, brahsina, OLG. bressemo, G. brassen. Cf. Brasse. | Cf. Broom, and G. ein schiff brennen.
OE. brest, breost, As. breóst; akin to Icel. brj, Sw. bröst, Dan. bryst, Goth. brusts, OS. briost, D. borst, G. brust.
OE. breth, breeth, AS. br odor, scent, breath; cf. OHG. bradam steam, vapor, breath, G. brodem, and possibly E. Brawn, and Breed.
It., breach, pebble, fragments of stone, fr. F. brèche; of German origin. See Breach.
OE. brech, brek, AS. brek, pl. of broc breech, breeches; akin to Icel. brok breeches, ODan. brog, D. broek, G. bruch; cf. L. bracae, braccae, which is of Celtic origin. Cf. Brail.
OE. breden, AS. bredan to nourish, cherish, keep warm, from brod brood; akin to D. broeden to brood, OHG. bruoten, G. brüten. See Brood.

OE. brese, AS. briósa; perh. akin to OHG. brimissa, G. breme, bremse, D. brems, which are akin to G. brummen to growl, buzz, grumble, L. fremere to murmur; cf. G. brausen, Sw. brusa, Dan. bruse, to roar, rush. | F. brise; akin to It. brezza breeze, Sp. briza, brisa, a breeze from northeast, Pg. briza northeast wind; of uncertain origin; cf. F. bise, Pr. bisa, OHG. bisa, north wind, Arm. biz northeast wind. | F. braise cinders, live coals. See Brasier.

OE. brese, AS. briósa; perh. akin to OHG. brimissa, G. breme, bremse, D. brems, which are akin to G. brummen to growl, buzz, grumble, L. fremere to murmur; cf. G. brausen, Sw. brusa, Dan. bruse, to roar, rush.
OE. breme, brime, fierce, impetuous, glorious, AS. breme, br, famous. Cf. Brim, a.
OF. brenage; cf. LL. brennagium, brenagium. See Bran.
AS. brant; akin to Dan. brat, Icel. brattr, steep. | Cf. Brant.
OE. also brerdful, fr. brerd top, brim, AS. brerd.
OE. bretasce, bretage, parapet, OF. bretesche wooden tower, F. bretèche, LL. breteschia, bertresca, prob. fr. OHG. bret, G. brett board; akin to E. board. See Board, n., and cf. Bartizan.
AS. Bretwalda, br, a powerful ruler.
It. & (in sense 2) LL. breve, fr. L. brevis short. See Brief.
F. brevet, LL. brevetum, fr. L. brevis short. See Brief.
F. bréviarie, L. breviarium summary, abridgment, neut. noun fr. breviarius abridged, fr. brevis short. See Brief, and cf. Brevier.
L. breviatus, p.p. of breviare to shorten, brevis short.
Prob. from being originally used in printing a breviary. See Breviary.
L. brevis short + pes, pedis, foot: cf. F. brévipède.
L. brevis short + penna wing: cf. F. brévipenne.
L. brevis short + E. rostral, rostrate.
L. brevis short + E. rostral, rostrate.
L. brevitas, fr. brevis short: cf. F. brièvité. See Brief.

OE. brewen, AS. breówan; akin to D. brouwen, OHG. priuwan, MHG. briuwen, br, G. brauen, Icel. brugga, Sw. brygga, Dan. brygge, and perh. to L. defrutum must boiled down, Gr. to prepare by heat. sq. root93. Cf. Broth, Bread.
OE. brewis, brouwys, browesse, brewet, OF. brouet, -s being the OF. ending of the nom. sing. and acc. pl.; dim. of OHG. brod. sq. root93. See Broth, and cf. Brose.
OE. brere, brer, AS. brer, brær; cf. Ir. briar prickle, thorn, brier, pin, Gael. preas bush, brier, W. prys, prysg.
F. bribe a lump of bread, scraps, leavings of meals (that are generally given to a beggar), LL. briba scrap of bread; cf. OF. briber, brifer, to eat gluttonously, to beg, and OHG. bilibi food.
OE. brybery rascality, OF. briberie. See Bribe, n.
OE. brik, F. brique; of Ger. origin; cf. AS. brice a breaking, fragment, Prov. E. brique piece, brique de pain, equiv. to AS. hlafes brice, fr. the root of E. break. See Break.
OE. brekil, brokel, bruchel, fr. AS. brecan, E. break. Cf. Brittle.
From Bride. Cf. Bridal, n. | OE. bridale, brudale, AS. br brideale, bridal feast. See Bride, and Ale, 2.

OE. bride, brid, brude, brud, burd, AS. br; akin to OFries. breid, OSax. br, D. bruid, OHG. pr, br, G. braut, Icel. br, Sw. & Dan. brud, Goth. br33s; cf. Armor. pried spouse, W. priawd a married person.

OE. bridegome, brudgume, AS. br (akin to OS. br, D. bruidegom, bruigom, OHG. pr, MHG. briutegome, G. bräutigam); AS. br bride + guma man, akin to Goth. guma, Icel. gumi, OHG. gomo, L. homo; the insertion of r being caused by confusion with groom. See Bride, and cf. Groom, Homage.

OE. brig, brigge, brug, brugge, AS. brycg, bricg; akin to Fries. bregge, D. brug, OHG. bruccu, G. brücke, Icel. bryggja pier, bridge, Sw. brygga, Dan. brygge, and prob. Icel. br bridge, Sw. & Dan. bro bridge, pavement, and possibly to E. brow.
OE. bridel, AS. bridel; akin to OHG. britil, brittil, D. breidel, and possibly to E. braid. Cf. Bridoon.
F. bridon, from bride; of German origin. See Bridle, n.
OE. bref, F. brief, bref, fr. L. brevis; akin to Gr. barh to tear. Cf. Breve. | See Brief, a., and cf. Breve.
OE. brere, brer, AS. brer, brær; cf. Ir. briar prickle, thorn, brier, pin, Gael. preas bush, brier, W. prys, prysg.
F. brigade, fr. It. brigata troop, crew, brigade, originally, a contending troop, fr. briga trouble, quarrel. See Brigand.

F. brigand, OF. brigant light-armed soldier, fr. LL. brigans light-armed soldier (cf. It. brigante.) fr. brigare to strive, contend, fr. briga quarrel; prob. of German origin, and akin to E. break; cf. Goth. brikan to break, brakja strife. Cf. Brigue.
F. brigandine (cf. It. brigantina), fr. OF. brigant. See Brigand.
F. brigantin, fr. It. brigantino, originally, a practical vessel. See Brigand, and cf. Brig
OE. briht, AS. beorht, briht; akin to OS. berht, OHG. beraht, Icel. bjartr, Goth. baírhts. sq. root94.
From Dr. Bright of London, who first described it.
LL. brigosus, It. brigoso. See Brigue, n.
F. brigue, fr. LL. briga quarrel. See Brigand. | F. briguer. See Brigue, n.
Cf. Corn. brilli mackerel, fr. brith streaked, speckled.

F. brillant, p. pr. of briller to shine or sparkle (cf. Pr. & Sp. brillar, It. brillare), fr. L. beryllus a precious stone of sea-green color, Prov. It. brill. See Beryl. | F. brillant. See Brilliant, a.
CF. G. brille spectacles, D. bril, fr. L. berillus. See Brilliant.

OE. brim, brimme, AS. brymme edge, border; akin to Icel. barmr, Sw. bräm, Dan. bræmme, G. brame, bräme. Possibly the same word as AS. brim surge, sea, and properly meaning, the line of surf at the border of the sea, and akin to L. fremere to roar, murmur. Cf. Breeze a fly.
OE. brimston, bremston, bernston, brenston; cf. Icel. brennistein. See Burn, v. t., and Stone.
Cf. Icel. bröndottr brindled, fr. brandr brand; and OE. bernen, brinnen, to burn. See Brand, Burn.
AS. bryne a burning, salt liquor, brine, fr. brinnan, brynnan, to burn. See Burn.
OE. bringen, AS. bringan; akin to OS. brengian, D. brengen, Fries. brenga, OHG. bringan, G. bringen, Goth. briggan.
Dan. brink edge, verge; akin to Sw. brink declivity, hill, Icel. brekka; cf. LG. brink a grassy hill, W. bryn hill, bryncyn hillock.
Cf. W. brysg, fr. brys haste, Gael. briosg quick, lively, Ir. broisg a start, leap, jerk.

OE. bruskette, OF. bruschet, F. bréchet, brichet; prob. of Celtic origin; cf. W. brysced the breast of a slain animal, brisket, Corn. vrys breast, Armor. brusk, bruched, the front of the chest, Gael. brisgein the cartilaginous part of a bone.

OE. bristel, brustel, AS. bristl, byrst; akin to D. borstel, OHG. burst, G. borste, Icel. burst, Sw. borst, and to Skr. bh edge, point, and prob, L. fastigium extremity, Gr. brush, burr, perh. to brad. sq. root96.
L. Britannicus, fr. Britannia Great Britain.
OE. britel, brutel, AS. bryttian to dispense, fr. breótan to break; akin to Icel. brytja, Sw. bryta, Dan. bryde. Cf. Brickle.
Russ. britshka; cf. Pol. bryczka, dim. of bryka freight wagon.
OE. broche, F. broche, fr. LL. brocca; prob. of Celtic origin; cf. W. proc thrust, stab, Gael. brog awl. Cf. Brooch. | F. brocher, fr. broche. See Broach, n.
OE. brod, brad, AS. brad; akin to OS. bred, D. breed, G. breit, Icel. brei, Sw. & Dan. bred, Goth. braids. Cf. Breadth.
Cf. Gael. brog, E. brog, n.
From Brobdingnag, a country of giants in "Gulliver's Travels."
Sp. brocado (cf. It. broccato, F. brocart), fr. LL. brocare *prick, to figure (textile fabrics), to emboss (linen), to stitch. See Broach.
Perh. fr. Brocardica, Brocardicorum opus, a collection of ecclesiastical canons by Burkhard, Bishop of Worms, called, by the Italians and French, Brocard.
F. brocatelle, fr. It. brocatello: cf. Sp. brocatel. See Brocade.
It. broccoli, pl. of broccolo sprout, cabbage sprout, dim. of brocco splinter. See Broach, n.
From Brochant de Villiers, a French mineralogist.
F., fr. brocher to stitch. See Broach, v. t.
AS. broc, fr. W. broch; akin to Ir. & Gael. broc, Corn. & Armor. broch; cf. Ir. & Gael. breac speckled. | See Brocket.
OE. broket, F. broquart fallow deer a year old, fr. the same root as E. broach, meaning point (hence tine of a horn).
F. brodequin, OE. brossequin, fr. OD. broseken, brosekin, dim. of broos buskin, prob. fr. LL. byrsa leather, Gr. Buskin.
Dim. of Prov. E. brog to broggle. Cf. Brog, n.

OE. broiden, brouden, F. broder, confused with E. braid; F. broder is either the same word as border to border (see Border), or perh. of Celtic origin; cf. W. brathu to sting, stab, Ir. & Gael. brod goad, prickle, OE. brod a goad; and also Icel. broddr a spike, a sting, AS. brord a point.

F. brouiller to disorder, from LL. brogilus, broilus, brolium, thicket, wood, park; of uncertain origin; cf. W. brog a swelling out, OHG. proil marsh, G. brühl, MHG. brogen to rise. The meaning tumult, confusion, comes apparently from tangled undergrowth, thicket, and this possibly from the meaning to grow, rise, sprout. | OE. broilen, OF. bruillir, fr. bruir to broil, burn; of Ger. origin; cf. MHG. brüejen, G. brühen, to scald, akin to E. brood.
OE. brocour, from a word akin to broken, bruken, to use, enjoy, possess, digest, fr. AS. br to use, enjoy; cf. Fries. broker, F. brocanteur. See Brook, v. t.
Named after Olaf Bromel, a Swedish botanist.
From Bromley Hill, near Alston, Cumberland, England.
G. brompikrin; brom bromine + pikrinsäure picric acid.
F. bronze, fr. It. bronzo brown, fr. OHG. br, G. braun. See Brown, a. | Cf. F. bronzer. See Bronze, n.
See Broach, n. | imp. & p. p. Brooched (.
OE. brod, AS. brod; akin to D. broed, OHG. bruot, G. brut, and also to G. brühe broth, MHG. brüeje, and perh. to E. brawn, breath. Cf. Breed, v. t.

OE. brok, broke, brook, AS. broc; akin to D. broek, LG. brok, marshy ground, OHG. pruoh, G. bruch marsh; prob. fr. the root of E. break, so as that it signifies water breaking through the earth, a spring or brook, as well as a marsh. See Break, v. t. | OE. broken, bruken, to use, enjoy, digest, AS. br; akin to D. gebruiken to use, OHG. pr, G. brauchen, gebrauchen, Icel. br, Goth. br, and L. frui, to enjoy. Cf. Fruit, Broker.
Named from the English mineralogist, H.J.Brooke.
OE. brom, brome, AS. brom; akin to LG. bram, D. brem, OHG. bramo broom, thornbrombeere blackberry. Cf. Bramble, n.
CF. Gael. brothas. Cf. Brewis, Broth.
AS. bro; akin to OHG. brod, brot; cf. Ir. broth, Gael. brot. *93. Cf. Brewis, Brew.

OE. brothel, brodel, brethel, a prostitute, a worthless fellow, fr. AS. beró to ruin, destroy; cf. AS. breótan to break, and E. brittle. The term brothel house was confused with bordel brothel. CF. Bordel.

OE. brother, AS. bro; akin to OS. brothar, D. broeder, OHG. pruodar, G. bruder, Icel. bro, Sw. & Dan. broder, Goth. bro, Ir. brathair, W. brawd, pl. brodyr, Lith. brolis, Lett. brahlis, Russ. brat', Pol. & Serv. brat, OSlav. brat, L. frater, Skr. bhrat, Zend. bratar brother, Gr. Brothers; in the solemn style, Brethren, OE. pl. brether, bretheren, AS. dat. sing. bre, nom. pl. bro, bro. sq. root258. Cf. Frair, Fraternal.

OE. browe, bruwe, AS. br; akin to AS. br, breáw, eyelid, OFries. bre, D. braauw, Icel. bra, br, OHG. prawa, G. braue, OSlav. br, Russ. brove, Ir. brai, Ir. & Gael. abhra, Armor. abrant, Gr. bhr. Cf. Bray a bank, Bridge.
OE. brun, broun, AS. br; akin to D. bruin, OHG. br, Icel. br, Sw. brun, Dan. bruun, G. braun, Lith. brunas, Skr. babhru. *93, 253. Cf. Bruin, Beaver, Burnish, Brunette.
So called from its supposed tawny or swarthy color.

OF. brost, broust, sprout, shoot, F. brout browse, browsewood, prob. fr. OHG. burst, G. borste, bristle; cf. also Armor. brousta to browse. See Bristle, n., Brush, n. | For broust, OF. brouster, bruster, F. brouter. See Browse, n., and cf. Brut.
Cf. F. brucine, fr. James Bruce, a Scottish traveler.
Named after Dr. A.Bruce of New York.
D. bruin brown. In the epic poem of "Reynard the Fox" the bear is so called from his color. See Brown, a.
OE. brusen, brisen, brosen, bresen, AS. br or fr. OF. bruiser, bruisier, bruser, to break, shiver, perh. from OHG. brochison. Cf. Break, v. t.
OE. bruit, brut, noise, bruit, F. bruit, fr. LL. brugitus; cf. L. rugire to roar; perh. influenced by the source of E. bray to make a harsh noise, Armor. brud bruit.
L. brumalis, fr. bruma winter: cf. F. brumal.
F. brume winter season, mist, L. bruma winter.
Birmingham (formerly Bromwycham), Eng., "the great mart and manufactory of gilt toys, cheap jewelry," etc.
F. brunet, brunette, brownish, dim. of brun, brune, brown, fr. OHG. br. See Brown, a.
F. brugnon (cf. It. brugna, prugna), fr. L. prunum. See Prune, n.
G. Braunschweiger grün, first made at Brunswick, in Germany.
OE. brunt, bront, fr. Icel. bruna to rush; cf. Icel. brenna to burn. Cf. Burn, v. t.

OE. brusche, OF. broche, broce, brosse, brushwood, F. brosse brush, LL. brustia, bruscia, fr. OHG. brusta, brust, bristle, G. borste bristle, bürste brush. See Bristle, n., and cf. Browse. | OE. bruschen; cf. F. brosser. See Brush, n.
From George J.Brush, an American mineralogist.
F. brusque, from It. brusco brusque, tart, sour, perh. fr. L. (vitis) labrusca wild (vine); or cf. OHG. bruttisc grim, fr. brutti terror.
OE. brustlien and brastlien, AS. brastlian, fr. berstan to burst, akin to G. prasseln to crackle. See Burst, v. i.
F. brouter, OF. brouster. See Browse, n.
NL., neuter pl., fr. L. brutus heavy, stupid.
Cf. F. brutal. See Brute, a.
F. brut, nasc., brute, fem., raw, rough, rude, brutish, L. brutus stupid, irrational: cf. It. & Sp. bruto. | For bruit.
Cf. F. bubale. See Buffalo, n.
Cf. D. bobbel, Dan. boble, Sw. bubbla. Cf. Blob, n. | Cf. D. bobbelen, Dan. boble. See Bubble, n.
Cf. Prov. G. bübbi, or It. poppa, Pr. popa, OF. poupe, a woman's breast. | A corruption of brother.
L. bucca cheek: cf. F. buccal.
F. boucanier, fr. boucaner to smoke or broil meat and fish, to hunt wild beasts for their skins, boucan a smoking place for meat or fish, gridiron for smoking: a word of American origin.
L. bucina a crooked horn or trumpet.
L., a trumpeter, fr. bucinare to sound the trumpet.
L., a trumpet, a trumpet shell.
So called from Bucholz, a German chemist.

Akin to LG. büke, Dan. byg, Sw. byk, G. bauche: cf. It. bucato, Prov. Sp. bugada, F. buée. | OE. bouken; akin to LG. büken, Dan. byge, Sw. byka, G. bauchen, beuchen; cf. OF. buer. Cf. the preceding noun. | OE. buk, bucke, AS. bucca, bua, he-goat; akin to D. bok, OHG. pocch, G. bock, Ir. boc, W. bwch, Corn. byk; cf. Zend b, Skr. bukka. *256. Cf. Butcher, n. | See Beech, n.
OE. boket; cf. AS. buc pitcher, or Corn. buket tub.

OE. bocle buckle, boss of a shield, OF. bocle, F. boucle, boss of a shield, ring, fr. L. buccula a little cheek or mouth, dim. of bucca cheek; this boss or knob resembling a cheek. | OE. boclen, F. boucler. See Buckle, n.
OE. bocler, OF. bocler, F. bouclier, a shield with a boss, from OF. bocle, boucle, boss. See Buckle, n.
In the language of the Calabar coast, buckra means "demon, a powerful and superior being." J.L.Wilson.

OE. bokeram, bougeren, OF. boqueran, F. bougran, MHG. buckeram, LL. buchiranus, boquerannus, fr. MHG. boc, G. bock, goat (as being made of goat's hair), or fr. F. bouracan, by transposing the letter r. See Buck, Barracan.
Buck a beech tree + wheat; akin to D. boekweit, G. buchweizen.
L. bucolicus, Gr. kal to drive: cf. F. bucolique. See Cow the animal. | L. Bucolicôn poëma.

OE. budde; cf. D. bot, G. butze, butz, the core of a fruit, bud, LG. butte in hagebutte, hainbutte, a hip of the dog-rose, or OF. boton, F. bouton, bud, button, OF. boter to bud, push; all akin to E. beat. See Button.
Skr. buddha wise, sage, fr. budh to know.
Prov. E., to cleanse ore, also a vessel for this purpose; cf. G. butteln to shake.
From Bude, in Cornwall, the residence of Sir G.Gurney, the inventor.

F. bouger to stir, move (akin to Pr. bojar, bolegar, to stir, move, It. bulicare to boil, bubble), fr. L. bullire. See Boil, v. i. | See Budge, v. | OE. bouge bag, OF. boge, bouge, fr. L. bulga a leathern bag or knapsack; a Gallic word; cf. OIr. bolc, Gael. bolg. Cf. Budge, n.
OE. bogett, bouget, F. bougette bag, wallet, dim. of OF. boge, bouge, leather bag. See Budge, n., and cf. Bouget.
OE. buff, buffe, buff, buffalo, F. buffle buffalo. See Buffalo. | OF. bufer to cuff, buffet. See Buffet a blow. | See Buffet. | Of uncertain etymol.
Sp. bufalo (cf. It. bufalo, F. buffle), fr. L. bubalus, bufalus, a kind of African stag or gazelle; also, the buffalo or wild ox, fr. Gr. Cow the animal, and cf. Buff the color, and Bubale.
Prop a striker. See Buffet a blow.

F. buffet, LL. bufetum; of uncertain origin; perh. fr. the same source as E. buffet a blow, the root meaning to puff, hence (cf. puffed up) the idea of ostentation or display. | OE. buffet, boffet, OF. buffet a slap in the face, a pair of bellows, fr. buffe blow, cf. F. bouffer to blow, puff; prob. akin to E. puff. For the meaning slap, blow, cf. F. soufflet a slap, souffler to blow. See Puff, v. i., and cf. Buffet sidebroad, Buffoon | OE. buffeten, OF. buffeter. See the preceding noun.
So called from resembling buff Defn: A sort of coarse stuff; as, buffin gowns. [Obs.
OE., from F. buffle. See Buffalo.

F. bouffon (cf. It. buffone, buffo, buffa, puff of wind, vanity, nonsense, trick), fr. bouffer to puff out, because the buffoons puffed out their cheeks for the amusement of the spectators. See Buffet a blow.
L. bufo toad: cf. F. bufonite.
OE. bugge, fr. W. bwg, bwgan, hobgoblin, scarecrow, bugbear. Cf. Bogey, Boggle.

F. bougre, fr. LL. Bulgarus, a Bulgarian, and also a heretic; because the inhabitants of Bulgaria were infected with heresy. Those guilty of the crime of buggery were called heretics, because in the eyes of their adversaries there was nothing more heinous than heresy, and it was therefore thought that the origin of such a vice could only be owing to heretics.
OF. bougrerie, bogrerie, heresy. See Bugger.

OE. bugle buffalo, buffalo's horn, OF. bugle, fr. L. buculus a young bullock, steer, dim. of bos ox. See Cow the animal. | See Bugle a wild ox. | LL. bugulus a woman's ornament: cf. G. bügel a bent piece of metal or wood, fr. the same root as G. biegen to bend, E. bow to bend. | From Bugle a bead. | F. bugle; cf. It. bugola, L. bugillo.
From A.Ch.Boule, a French carver in wood.
From A.Ch.Boule, a French carver in wood.
OE. bur a whetstone for scythes.

OE. bulden, bilden, AS. byldan to build, fr. bold house; cf. Icel. bol farm, abode, Dan. bol small farm, OSw. bol, böle, house, dwelling, fr. root of Icel. b to dwell; akin to E. be, bower, boor. sq. root97.
L. bulbosus: cf. F. bulbeux. See Bulb, n.
L. bulbulus, dim. of bulbus. See Bulb, n.

OE. bulge a swelling; cf. AS. belgan to swell, OSw. bulgja, Icel. bolginn swollen, OHG. belgan to swell, G. bulge leathern sack, Skr. b to be large, strong; the root meaning to swell. Cf. Bilge, Belly, Billow, Bouge, n.
OE. bulke, bolke, heap; cf. Dan. bulk lump, clod, OSw. bolk crowd, mass, Icel. b to be bulky. Cf. Boll, n., Bile a boil, Bulge, n. | Icel. balkr a beam, partition. Cf. Balk, n. & v.
See Bulk part of a building.

OE. bule, bul, bole; akin to D. bul, G. bulle, Icel. boli, Lith. bullus, Lett. bollis, Russ. vol'; prob. fr. the root of AS. bellan, E. bellow. | OE. bulle, fr. L. bulla bubble, stud, knob, LL., a seal or stamp: cf. F. bulle. Cf. Bull a writing, Bowl a ball, Boil, v. i.
L. bulla bubble. See Bull an edict.
OE. bolas, bolace, OF. beloce; of Celtic origin; cf. Arm. bolos, polos, Gael. bulaistear.
LL. bullarium: cf. F. bullairie. See Bull an edict. | Cf. Boilary.
Native Australian name, from its cry.
Bull large, having a large head + nail.
F. boulet, dim. of boule ball. See Bull an edict, and cf. Boulet.
F. bulletin, fr. It. bullettino, dim. of bulletta, dim. of bulla, bolla, an edict of the pope, from L. bulla bubble. See Bull an edict.
Cf. G. bofist, AS. wulfes fist puffball, E. fizz, foist.
Cf. G. bofist, AS. wulfes fist puffball, E. fizz, foist.

Cf. OE. bullyon a hook used for fastening the dress, a button, stud, an embossed ornament of various kinds, e.g., on the cover of a book, on bridles or poitrels, for purses, for breeches and doublets, LL. bullio the swelling of boiling water, a mass of gold or silver, fr. L. bulla boss, stud, bubble (see Bull an edict), or perh. corrupted fr. billon base coin, LL. billio bullion. Cf. Billon, Billet a stick.
Cf. bully,n.& v., and rag to scold, rail. Cf. Ballarag.
F. bulliste. See Bull an edict.
L. bullire, bullitum, to boil. See Boil, v. i.
AS. bulluc a young bull. See Bull.
Cf. LG. bullerjaan, bullerbäk, bullerbrook, a blusterer, D. bulderaar a bluster, bulderen to bluster; prob. of imitative origin; or cf. MHG. buole lover, G. buhle.
OE. bulrysche, bolroysche; of uncertain origin, perh. fr. bole stem + rush.
LL. bultellus. See Bolt to sift.
Akin to D. bolwerk, G. bollwerk, Sw. bolwerk, Dan. bolvärk, bulvärk, rampart; akin to G. bohle plank, and werk work, defense. See Bole stem, and Work, n., and cf. Boulevard.
Contr. fr. bottom in this sense. | See Boom, v. i., to roar.
OE. bumblen to make a humming noise (dim. of bum, v.i.) + bee. Cf. Humblebee.
From bum the buttocks, on account of its clumsy form; or fr. D. bun a box for holding fish in a boat.
Cf. W. pwmp round mass, pwmpiaw to thump, bang, and E. bum, v.i., boom to roar. | From Bump to strike, to thump. | See Boom to roar.
A corruption of bumbard, bombard, a large drinking vessel.

The same word as bumkin, which Cotgrave defines thus: "Bumkin, Fr. chicambault, the luffe-block, a long and thick piece of wood, whereunto the fore-sayle and sprit-sayle are fastened, when a ship goes by the winde." Hence, a clumsy man may easily have been compared to such a block of wood; cf. OD. boomken a little tree. See Boom a pole.

Scot. bun, bunn, OE. bunne, bonne; fr. Celtic; cf. Ir. bunna, Gael. bonnach, or OF. bugne tumor, Prov. F. bugne a kind of pancake; akin to OHG. bungo bulb, MHG. bunge, Prov. E. bung heap, cluster, bunny a small swelling.
Akin to OSw. & Dan. bunke heap, Icel. bunki heap, pile, bunga tumor, protuberance; cf. W. pwng cluster. Cf. Bunk.
Buncombe a country of North Carolina.
Pers. bandar a landing place, pier.
G., from bund (akin to E. bond) confederacy + rath council, prob. akin to E. read.
OE. bundel, AS. byndel; akin to D. bondel, bundel, G. bündel, dim. of bund bundle, fr. the root of E. bind. See Bind.
Cf. W. bwng orfice, bunghole, Ir. buinne tap, spout, OGael. buine.
Prob. a diminutive from, akin to bang; cf. Prov. G. bungen to beat, bang, OSw. bunga. See Bang.
Cf. Prov. E. bunny a small swelling, fr. OF. bugne, It. bugna, bugnone. See Bun.
Cf. OSw. bunke heap, also boaring, flooring. Cf. Bunch.
Scot. bunker, bunkart, a bench, or low chest, serving for a seat. Cf. Bunk, Bank, Bench.
Sf. Sp. banco bank, banca a sort of game at cards. Cf. Bank (in the commercial sense).
Buncombe a country of North Carolina.

Scot. bun, bunn, OE. bunne, bonne; fr. Celtic; cf. Ir. bunna, Gael. bonnach, or OF. bugne tumor, Prov. F. bugne a kind of pancake; akin to OHG. bungo bulb, MHG. bunge, Prov. E. bung heap, cluster, bunny a small swelling.
Cf. Sw. bunt bundle, Dan. bundt, G. bund, E. bundle.
Prov. E. bunting sifting flour, OE. bonten to sift, hence prob. the material used for that purpose.
Scot. buntlin, corn-buntlin, OE. bunting, buntyle; of unknown origin. | Prov. E. bunting sifting flour, OE. bonten to sift, hence prob. the material used for that purpose.
Cf. Prov. E. bunny a small swelling, fr. OF. bugne, It. bugna, bugnone. See Bun.
D. boei buoy, fetter, fr. OF. boie, buie, chain, fetter, F. bouée a buoy, from L. boia. "Boiae genus vinculorum tam ferreae quam ligneae." Festus. So called because chained to its place.

OE. burre burdock; cf. Dan. borre, OSw. borra, burdock, thistle; perh. akin to E. bristle (burr- for burz-), or perh. to F. bourre hair, wool, stuff; also, according to Cotgrave, "the downe, or hairie coat, wherewith divers herbes, fruits, and flowers, are covered," fr. L. burrae trifles, LL. reburrus rough.
F. barbote, fr. barbe beard. See 1st Barb.
F. bourdelais, prob. fr. bordelais. See Bordelais.

OE. burden, burthen, birthen, birden, AS. byredhen; akin to Icel. byredhi, Dan. byrde, Sw. börda, G. bürde, OHG. burdi, Goth. baúr, fr. the root of E. bear, AS. beran, Goth. bairan. *92. See 1st Bear. | OE. burdoun the bass in music, F. bourdon; cf. LL. burdo drone, a long organ pipe, a staff, a mule. Prob. of imitative origin. Cf. Bourdon. | See Burdon.

F. bureau a writing table, desk, office, OF., drugget, with which a writing table was often covered, equiv. to F. bure, and fr. OF. buire dark brown, the stuff being named from its color, fr. L. burrus red, fr. Gr. Fire, n., and cf. Borel, n.
F., can, cruet, dim. of buire flagon.
AS. burh, burg, cf. LL. burgus. See 1st Borough.
From Burg: cf. F. bourgage, LL. burgagium.
OE. burgeis, OF. burgeis, fr. burcfortified town, town, F. bourg village, fr. LL. burgus fort, city; from the German; cf. MHG. burc, G. burg. See 1st Borough, and cf. 2d Bourgeois.
G. burggraf; burg fortress + graf count: cf. D. burggraaf, F. burgrave. See Margrave.
Burgh + F. brèche, equiv. to E. breach.
From burgh; akin to D. burger, G. bürger, Dan. borger, Sw. borgare. See Burgh.
OE. burg town, F. bourg, fr. LL. burgus (of German origin) + OF. lere thief, fr. L. latro. See Borough, and Larceny.
D. burgemeester; burg borough + meester master; akin to G. burgemeister, bürgermeister. See 1st Borough, and Master.
F. bouruignotte, because the Burgundians, F. Bouruignons, first used it.
Prov. E. burgood yeast, perh. fr. W. burym yeast + cawl cabbage, gruel.
OE. buriel, buriels, grave, tomb, AS. byrgels, fr. byrgan to bury, and akin to OS. burgisli sepulcher.
F. burin, cf. It. burino, bulino; prob. from OHG. bora borer, boron to bore, G. bohren. See 1st Bore.
From one Burke of Edinburgh, who committed the crime in 1829.
OE. burle stuffing, or a knot in cloth; cf. F. bourlet, bourrelet, OF. bourel, a wreath or a roll of cloth, linen, or leather, stuffed with flocks, etc., dim. of bourre. *92. See Bur.
F. burlesque, fr. It. burlesco, fr. burla jest, mockery, perh. for burrula, dim. of L. burrae trifles. See Bur.
It., dim. of burla mockery. See Burlesque, a.
OE. burlich strong, excellent; perh. orig. fit for a lady's bower, hence handsome, manly, stout. Cf. Bower.

OE. bernen, brennen, v.t., early confused with beornen, birnen, v.i., AS. bærnan, bernan, v.t., birnan, v.i.; akin to OS. brinnan, OFries. barna, berna, OHG. brinnan, brennan, G. brennen, OD. bernen, D. branden, Dan. brænde, Sw. bränna, brinna, Icel. brenna, Goth. brinnan, brannjan (in comp.), and possibly to E. fervent. | See 1st Bourn.
OE. burnet burnet; also, brownish (the plant perh. being named from its color), fr. F. brunet, dim. of brun brown; cf. OF. brunete a sort of flower. See Brunette.
OE. burnischen, burnissen, burnen, OF. burnir, brunir, to make brown, polish, F. brunir, fr. F. brun brown, fr. OHG. br; cf. MHG. briunen to make brown, polish. See Brown, a.
Ar. burnus a kind of high-crowned cap: cf. F. bournous, burnous, Sp. al-bornoz, a sort of upper garment, with a hood attached.
Ar. burnus a kind of high-crowned cap: cf. F. bournous, burnous, Sp. al-bornoz, a sort of upper garment, with a hood attached.

OE. burre burdock; cf. Dan. borre, OSw. borra, burdock, thistle; perh. akin to E. bristle (burr- for burz-), or perh. to F. bourre hair, wool, stuff; also, according to Cotgrave, "the downe, or hairie coat, wherewith divers herbes, fruits, and flowers, are covered," fr. L. burrae trifles, LL. reburrus rough. | See Bur.
Cf. OF. burel reddish (cf. Borel, n.), or F. beurré butter pear, fr. beurre butter. Cf. Butter.
From its reddish color. See 1st Burrel.
Either from annoying the enemy like a burrel fly, or, less probably, fr. F. bourreler to sting, torture.
Perh. from AS. burg, burh, hill + -ock.
LL. bursarius, fr. bursa purse. See Burse, and cf. Purser.
G., ultimately fr. LL. bursa. See Burse.
LL. bursa, or F. bourse. See Bourse, and cf. Bursch, Purse.

OE. bersten, bresten, AS. berstan (pers. sing. berste, imp. sing. bærst, imp. pl. burston, p.p. borsten); akin to D. bersten, G. bersten, OHG. brestan, OS. brestan, Icel. bresta, Sw. brista, Dan. briste. Cf. Brast, Break.
Cf. OE. & Prov. E. bort to press or indent anything.

Cf. F. cannibale. Columbus, in a letter to the Spanish monarchs written in Oct., 1498, mentions that the people of Hayti lived in great fear of the Caribales (equivalent to E. Caribbees.), the inhabitants of the smaller Antilles; which form of the name was afterward changed into NL. Canibales, in order to express more forcibly their character by a word intelligible through a Latin root "propter rabiem caninam anthropophagorum gentis." OE. , dailien; cf. Icel. pylja to talk, G. dallen, dalen, dahlen, to trifle, talk nonsense, OSw. tule a droll or funny man; or AS. dol foolish, E. dull.
OE. dame mistress, lady; also, mother, dam. See Dame. | Akin to OLG., D., & Dan. dam, G. & Sw. damm, Icel. dammr, and AS. fordemman to stop up, Goth. Faúrdammjan.
OF. damage, domage, F. dommage, fr. assumed LL. damnaticum, from L. damnum damage. See Damn. | Cf. OF. damagier, domagier. See Damage, n.
OF. damage + F. faisant doing, p. pr. See Feasible.
L. Damascenus of Damascus, fr. Damascus the city, Gr. . See Damask, and cf. Damaskeen, Damaskin, Damson.
From the city Damascus, L. Damascus, Gr. , Heb. Dammesq, Ar. Daemeshq; cf. Heb. d'meseq damask; cf. It. damasco, Sp. damasco, F. damas. Cf. Damascene, DamassÉ.
Cf. F. damasquin, adj., It. damaschino, Sp. damasquino. See Damaskeen.
F. damassé, fr. damas. See Damask.

F. dame, LL. domna, fr. L. domina mistress, lady, fem. of dominus master, ruler, lord; akin to domare to tame, subdue. See Tame, and cf. Dam mother, Dan, Danger, Dangeon, Dungeon, Dominie, Don, n., Duenna.
OE. damnen dap), OF. damner, dampner, F. damner, fr. L. damnare, damnatum, to condemn, fr. damnum damage, a fine, penalty. Cf. Condemn, Damage.
L. damnabilis, fr. damnare: cf. F. damnable. See Damn.
F. damnation, L. damnatio, fr. damnare. See Damn.
L. damnatorius, fr. damnator a condemner.
L. damnificus; damnum damage, loss + facere to make. See Damn.
LL. damnificare, fr. L. damnificus: cf. OF. damnefier. See Damnific.
Akin to LG., D., & Dan. damp vapor, steam, fog, G. dampf, Icel. dampi, Sw. damb dust, and to MNG. dimpfen to smoke, imp. dampf. | OE. dampen to choke, suffocate. See Damp, n.

OE. damosel, damesel, damisel, damsel, fr. OF. damoisele, damisele, gentlewoman, F. demoiselle young lady; cf. OF. damoisel young nobleman, F. damoiseau; fr. LL. domicella, dominicella, fem., domicellus, dominicellus, masc., dim. fr. L. domina, dominus. See Dame, and cf. Demoiselle, Doncella.
OE. damasin the Damascus plum, fr. L. Damascenus. See Damascene.
OE. dan, danz, OF. danz (prop. only nom.), dan, master, fr. L. dominus. See Dame. | Etymol. uncertain.
From the mythical Danaides, who were condemned to fill with water a vessel full of holes.
F. danser, fr. OHG. dans to draw; akin to dinsan to draw, Goth. apinsan, and prob. from the same root (meaning to stretch) as E. thin. See Thin. | F. danse, of German origin. See Dance, v. i.
Cf. F. danché dancetté, dent tooth.
F. dent de lion lion's tooth, fr. L. dens tooth + leo lion. See Tooth, n., and Lion.
Cf. G. dändeln to trifly, dandle, OD. & Prov. G. danten, G. tand trifly, prattle; Scot. dandill, dander, to go about idly, to trifly.
Prob. from W. toncrust, peel, skin + AS. dr dirty, draffy, or W. drwg bad: cf. AS. tan a letter, an eruption. sq. root240.
Cf. F. dandin, ninny, silly fellow, dandiner to waddle, to play the fool; prob. allied to E. dandle. Senses 2&3 are of uncertain etymol.
AS. danegeld. See Dane, and Geld, n.
AS. danegeld. See Dane, and Geld, n.

OE. danger, daunger, power, arrogance, refusal, difficulty, fr. OF. dagier, dongier (with same meaning), F. danger danger, fr. an assumed LL. dominiarium power, authority, from L. dominium power, property. See Dungeon, Domain, Dame.
OE., haughty, difficult, dangerous, fr. OF. dangereus, F. dangereux. See Danger.
Akin to Dan. dangle, dial. Sw. dangla, Dan. dingle, Sw. dingla, Icel. dingla; perh. from E. ding.
Cf. dial, Sw. dank a moist place in a field, Icel. dökk pit, pool; possibly akin to E. damp or to daggle dew.
L., a laurel tree, from Gr. .
L., daps a feast + ferre to bear.
OE. daper; prob. fr. D. dapper brave, valiant; akin to G. tapfer brave, OHG. taphar heavy, weighty, OSlav. dobrû good, Russ. dobrui. Cf. Deft.
Cf. Icel. depill a spot, a dot, a dog with spots over the eyes, dapi a pool, and E. dimple.
From L. Dardania, poetic name of Troy.

OE. I dar, dear, I dare, imp. dorste, durste, AS. ic dear I dare, imp. dorste. inf. durran; akin to OS. gidar, gidorsta, gidurran, OHG. tar, torsta, turran, Goth. gadar, gadaúrsta, Gr. tharsei^n, tharrei^n, to be bold, tharsy`s bold, Skr. Dhrsh to be bold. sq. root70. | OE. darien, to lie hidden, be timid. | See Dace.
OE. dark, derk, deork, AS. dearc, deorc; cf. Gael. & Ir. dorch, dorcha, dark, black, dusky.
OE. derling, deorling, AS. deórling; deóre dear + -ling. See Dear, and -ling.
NL. Named after Dr. William Darlington, a botanist of West Chester, Penn.
OE. derne, prob. of Celtic origin; cf. W. darnio to piece, break in pieces, W. & Arm. to E. tear. Cf. Tear, v. t.

OE. darnel, dernel, of uncertain origin; cf. dial. F. darnelle, Sw. dår-repe; perh. named from a supposed intoxicating quality of the plant, and akin to Sw. dåra to infatuate, OD. door foolish, G. thor fool, and Ee. dizzy.

OF. deraisnier to explain, defend, to maintain in legal action by proof and reasonings, LL. derationare; de- + rationare to discourse, contend in law, fr. L. ratio reason, in LL., legal cause. Cf. Arraign, and see Reason.

OF. deraisnier to explain, defend, to maintain in legal action by proof and reasonings, LL. derationare; de- + rationare to discourse, contend in law, fr. L. ratio reason, in LL., legal cause. Cf. Arraign, and see Reason.
OF. darrein, darrain, fr. an assumed LL. deretranus; L. de + retro back, backward.
OF. dart, of German origin; cf. OHG. tart javelin, dart, AS. dara, daro, Sw. dart dagger, Icel. darra dart.
From the name of Charles Darwin, an English scientist.
OE. dasewen, daswen; cf. AS. dysegian to be foolish.
Of. Scand. origin; cf. Dan daske to beat, strike, Sw. & Icel. daska, Dan. & Sw. dask blow.
Prob. from Icel. dæstr exhausted. breathless, p. p. of dæsa to groan, lose one's breath; cf. dasask to become exhausted, and E. daze.
NL., from Gr. hairy, shaggy + , , a child.
Gr. thick, shaggy + tail: cf. F. dasyure.

F. datte, L. dactylus, fr. Gr. , prob. not the same word as finger, but of Semitic origin. | F. date, LL. data, fr. L. datus given, p.p. of dare to give; akin to Gr. , OSlaw. dati, Skr. da. Cf. Datum, Dose, Dato, Die. | Cf. F. dater. See 2d Date.
L. dativus appropriate to giving, fr. dare to give. See 2d Date. | L. dativus.
From. Gr. to divide + -lite; in allusion to the granular structure of a massive variety.
NL.; cf. Skr. dhatt, Per. & Ar. tat, Tat.

OE. dauben to smear, OF. dauber to plaster, fr. L. dealbare to whitewash, plaster; de- + albare to whiten, fr. albus white, perh. also confused with W. dwb plaster, dwbio to plaster, Ir. & OGael. dob plaster. See Alb, and cf. Dealbate.

OE. doughter, doghter, dohter, AS. dohtor, dohter; akin to OS. dohtar, D. dochter, G. tochter, Icel. d, Sw. dotter, Dan. dotter, datter, Goth. daúhtar,, OSlav. d, Russ. doche, Lith. dukt, Gr. , Zendughdhar, Skr. duhit; possibly originally, the milker, cf. Skr. duh to milk. sq. root68, 245.
OF. danter, F. dompter to tame, subdue, fr. L. domitare, v. intens. of domare to tame. See Tame.

F. dauphin, prop., a dolphin, from L. delphinus. See Dolphin. The name was given, for some reason unexplained, to Guigo, count of Vienne, in the 12th century, and was borne by succeeding counts of Vienne. In 1349, Dauphiny was bequeathed to Philippe de Valois, king of France, on condition that the heir of the crown should always hold the title of Dauphin de Viennois.
From the name of the original maker. Encyc. Dict.
Cf. F. davier forceps, davit, cooper's instrument, G. david davit; all probably from the proper name David.
Named after Sir Humphry Davy, the English chemist.
OE. dawe; akin to OHG. taha, MHG. tahe, tahele, G. dohle. Cf. Caddow. | OE. dawen. See Dawn. | Contr. fr. Adaw.
Prov. E. dauk to cut or pierce with a jerk; cf. OE. dalk a dimple. Cf. Ir. tolch, tollachd, tolladh, a hole, crevice, toll to bore, pierce, W. tyllu.
Named after J. W. Dawson of Montreal.
OE. day, dai,, dei, AS. dæg; akin to OS., D., Dan., & Sw. dag, G, tag, Icel. dagr, Goth. dags; cf. Skr. dah (for dhagh ) to burn. *69. Cf. Dawn.
From day in the sense of day fixed for trial.

OE. dasen, prob. from Icel. dasask to become weary, a reflexive verb; cf. Sw. dasa to lie idle, and OD. daesen to be foolish, insane, daes, dwaes, D. dwaas, foolish, insane, AS. dw, dysig, stupid. Dizzy, Doze.
OE. diakne, deakne, deken, AS. diacon, deacon, L. diaconus, fr. Gr. dean.
OE. ded, dead, deed, AS. deád; akin to OS. d, D. dood, G. todt, tot, Icel. dau, Sw. & Dan. död, Goth. daubs; prop. p. p. of an old verb meaning to die. See Die, and cf. Death.
From Dead; cf. AS. d to kill, put to death. See Dead, a.

OE. def, deaf, deef, AS. deáf; akin to D. doof, G. taub, Icel. daufr, Dan. döv, Sw. döf, Goth. daubs, and prob. to E. dumb (the original sense being, dull as applied to one of the senses), and perh. to Gr. toben to rage. Cf. Dumb.

OE. del, deel, part, AS. d; akin to OS. d, D. & Dan. deel, G. theil, teil, Icel. deild, Sw. del, Goth. dails. Dole. | OE. delen, AS. d, fr. d share; akin to OS. d, D. deelen, G. theilen, teilen, Icel. deila, Sw. dela, Dan. dele, Goth. dailjan. See Deal, n.
L. dealbatus, p. p. of dealbare. See Daub.
From deal a long, narrow plank.
L. deambulare, deambulatum; de- + ambulare to walk.
Cf. LL. deambulator a traveler. | L. deambulatorium.

OE. dene, deene, OF. deien, dien, F. doyen, eldest of a corporation, a dean, L. decanus the chief of ten, one set over ten persons, e. g., over soldiers or over monks, from decem ten. See Ten, and cf. Decemvir.
OE. dere, deore, AS. deóre; akin to OS. diuri, D. duur, OHG. tiuri, G. theuer, teuer, Icel. d, Dan. & Sw. dyr. Cf. Darling, Dearth.
AS. derne, dyrne, dierne, hidden, secret. Cf. Derne.
OE. derthe, fr. dere. See Dear.
OE. deth, dea, AS. deá; akin to OS. d, D. dood, G. tod, Icel. dau, Sw. & Dan. död, Goth. daupus; from a verb meaning to die. See Die, v. i., and cf. Dead.
L. deauratus, p. p. of deaurare to gild; de- + aurum gold.
L. debacchatus, p. p. of debacchari to rage; de- + bacchari to rage like a bacchant.
F. débâcle, fr. débâcler to unbar, break loose; pref. dé- (prob. = L. dis) + bâcler to bolt, fr. L. baculum a stick.
F. débarquer; pref. dé- (L. dis-) + barque. See Bark the vessel, and cf. Disbark.
Pref. de- + base. See Base, a., and cf. Abase.
OF. debatre, F. débattre; L. de + batuere to beat. See Batter, v. t., and cf. Abate. | F. débat, fr. débattre. See Debate, v. t.

F. débaucher, prob. originally, to entice away from the workshop; pref. dé- (L. dis- or de) + OF. bauche, bauge, hut, cf. F. bauge lair of a wild boar; prob. from G. or Icel., cf. Icel. balkr. See Balk, n. | Cf. F. débauche.
F. dé, n., properly p. p. of débaucher. See Debauch, v. t.
F. de of + beige the natural color of wool.
L. debellatus, p. p. of debellare to subdue; de- + bellum war.
L. debentur they are due, fr. debere to owe; cf. F. debentur. So called because these receipts began with the words Debentur mihi.
L. debilis: cf. F. débile. See Debility.
L. debilitatus, p. p. of debilitare to debilitate, fr. debilis. See Debility.
L. debilitas, fr. debilis weak, prob. fr. de- + habilis able: cf. F. débilité. See Able, a.
L. debitum what is due, debt, from debere to owe: cf. F. débit. See Debt.
OE. debonere, OF. de bon aire, debonaire, of good descent or lineage, excellent, debonair, F. débonnaire debonair; de of (L. de) + bon good (L. bonus) + aire. See Air, and Bounty, and cf. Bonair.
F. déboucher; pref. dé- (L. dis- or de) + boucher to stop up, fr. bouche mouth, fr. L. bucca the cheek. Cf. Disembogue.
F., fr. pref. dé- (L. dis) + briser to break, shatter; perh. of Celtic origin.
Cf. OF. debruisier to shatter, break. Cf. Bruise.
OE. dette, F. dette, LL. debita, fr. L. debitus owed, p. p. of debere to owe, prop., to have on loan; de- + habere to have. See Habit, and cf. Debit, Due.
OE. dettur, dettour, OF. detor, detur, detour, F. débiteur, fr. L. debitor, fr. debere to owe. See Debt.
Pref. dé- + L. bullire to boil.
From the inventor, Debus, a French optician + -scope.
F. début, prop., the first cast or throw at play, fr. but aim, mark. See Butt an end.
F., p. pr. of débuter to have the first throw, to make one's début. See Début.
F., p. pr. of débuter to have the first throw, to make one's début. See Début.
NL., fr. Gr. de`ka ten + ke`ras a horn.

Gr. deka`chordos tenstringed; de`ka ten + chordj` a string.

F. décade, L. decas, -adis, fr. Gr. Ten.
LL. decadentia; L. de- + cadere to fall: cf. F. décadence. See Decay.
LL. decadentia; L. de- + cadere to fall: cf. F. décadence. See Decay.
