F. décagramme; Gr. gramme. See Gram.
Pref. deca- + Gr. 'e`dra a seat, a base, fr. 'e`zesthai to sit: cf. F. décaèdre.
F. décalitre; Gr. litre. See Liter.
F. décalitre; Gr. litre. See Liter.
F. décalogue, L. decalogus, fr. Gr. Ten.
F. décamètre; Gr. mètre. See Meter.
F. décamètre; Gr. mètre. See Meter.
F. décamper; pref. dé- (L. dis) + camp camp. See Camp.
F. décanter (cf. It. decantare), prop., to pour off from the edge of a vessel; pref. dé- (L. de) + OF. cant (It. canto) edge, border, end. See Cant an edge.
LL. decapitatus, p. p. of decapitare; L. de- + caput head. See Chief.
L. décastère; Gr. stère a stere.
Pref. deca- + syllabic: cf. F. décasyllabique, décasyllable.
OF. decaeir, dechaer, decheoir, F. déchoir, to decline, fall, become less; L. de- + cadere to fall. See Chance.
OE. deses, deces, F. décès, fr. L. decessus departure, death, fr. decedere to depart, die; de- + cedere to withdraw. See Cease, Cede.
L. decedens, p. pr. of decedere.
OF. deceit, des, decept (cf. deceite, de), fr. L. deceptus deception, fr. decipere. See Deceive.
OE. deceveir, F. décevoir, fr. L. decipere to catch, insnare, deceive; de- + capere to take, catch. See Capable, and cf. Deceit, Deception.
F. décembre, from L. December, fr. decem ten; this being the tenth month among the early Romans, who began the year in March. See Ten.
L. decem ten + root of findere to cleave.
L., fr. decem ten + vir a man.
L. decentia, fr. decens: cf. F. décence. See Decent.
L. decennium a period of ten years; decem ten + annus a year.

L. decens, decentis, p. pr. of decere to be fitting or becoming; akin to decus glory, honor, ornament, Gr. d to grant, to give; and perh. akin to E. attire, tire: cf. F. décent. Cf. Decorate, Decorum, Deig.
F. déception, L. deceptio, fr. decipere, deceptum. See Deceive.
L. decerpere; de- + carpere to pluck.
L. decerptus, p. p. of decerpere.
L. decertatio, fr. decertare, decertatum; de- + certare to contend.
L. decessio, fr. decedere to depart. See Decease, n.
L. decidere; de- + caedere to cut, cut off; prob. akin to E. shed, v.: cf. F. décider. Cf. Decision.
NL., fr. L. deciduus. See Deciduous.
L. deciduus, fr. dec to fall off; de- + cadere to fall. See Chance.
F. décigramme; pref. déci- tenth (fr. L. decimus) + gramme.
F. décigramme; pref. déci- tenth (fr. L. decimus) + gramme.
F. décil, fr. L. decem tendecile.
F. décil, fr. L. decem tendecile.
F. décilitre; pref. déci- tenth (L. decimus) + litre. See Liter.
F. décilitre; pref. déci- tenth (L. decimus) + litre. See Liter.
L. decem ten + the ending of million.
F. décimal (cf. LL. decimalis), fr. L. decimus tenth, fr. decem ten. See Ten, and cf. Dime.
L. decimatus, p. p. of decimare to decimate (in senses 1 & 2), fr. decimus tenth. See Decimal.
F. décimètre; pref. déci- tenth (fr. L. decimus) + mètre. See Meter.
F. décimètre; pref. déci- tenth (fr. L. decimus) + mètre. See Meter.
Prop., in sixteenth; fr. L. decimus tenth + sextus sixth.
Pref. de- + cipher. Formed in imitation of F. déchiffrer. See Cipher.
L. decipiens, p. pr. of decipere. See Deceive.
NL., fr. L. decipere to deceive.
L. decisio, fr. decidere, decisum: cf. F. décision. See Decide.
F. décistère; pref. déci- tenth (fr. L. decimus) + stère a stere.
D. dekken to cover; akin to E. thatch. See Thatch. | D. dek. See Deck, v.
L. declamare; de- + clamare to cry out: cf. F. déclamer. See Claim.
L. declamatio, from declamare: cf. F. déclamation. See Declaim.
Cf. F. déclarant, p. pr. of déclarer.
F. déclaration, fr. L. declaratio, fr. declarare. See Declare.
L. declarativus, fr. declarare: cf. F. déclaratif.
F. déclarer, from L. declarare; de + clarare to make clear, clarus, clear, bright. See Clear.
Apparently corrupted fr. F. déclinaison, fr. L. declinatio, fr. declinare. See Decline, and cf. Declination.
L. declinatus, p. p. of declinare. See Decline.
L. declinatio a bending aside, an avoiding: cf. F. déclination a decadence. See Declension.
LL. declinatorius, fr. L. declinare: cf. F. déclinatoire.

OE. declinen to bend down, lower, sink, decline (a noun), F. décliner to decline, refuse, fr. L. declinare to turn aside, inflect (a part of speech), avoid; de- + clinare to incline; akin to E. lean. See Lean, v. i. | F. déclin. See Decline, v. i.
L. declivitas, fr. declivis sloping, downhill; de + clivus a slope, a hill; akin to clinare to incline: cf. F. déclivité. See Decline.
L. decoctus, p. p. of decoquere to boil down; de- + coquere to cook, boil. See Cook to decoct.
L. decollatus, p. p. of decollare to behead; de- + collum neck.
F., p. p. of décolleter to bare the neck and shoulders; dé- + collet collar, fr. L. collum neck.
Cf. F. décolorer, L. decolorare. Cf. Discolor.
L. decoloratus, p. p. of decolorare.
Pref. de- (in sense 3 intensive) + composition: cf. F. décomposition. Cf. Decomposition.
Pref. de- (intens. in sense 1) + compound, v. t. | Pref. de- (intens.) + compound, a.
L. decoramentum. See Decorate, v. t.
L. decoratus, p. p. of decorare, fr. decus ornament; akin to decere to be becoming. See Decent.
L. dec, fr. decor comeliness, beauty; akin to decere. See Decent, and cf. Decorum.
L. decorticatus, p. p. of decorticare to bark; de- + cortex bark.
L. dec, fr. dec. See Decorous.
Pref. de- + coy; orig., to quiet, soothe, caress, entice. See Coy.

OE. decrecen, fr. OF. decreistre, F. décroître, or from the OF. noun (see Decrease, n.), fr. L. decrescere to grow less; de + crescere to grow. See Crescent, and cf. Increase. | OE. decrees, OF. decreis, fr. decreistre. See Decrease, v.
OE. decre, F. décret, fr. L. decretum, neut. decretus, p. p. of decernere to decide; de- + cernere to decide. See Certain, and cf. Decreet, Decretal.
L. decrementum, fr. decrescere. See Decrease.
L. decrepitus, perhaps orig., noised out, noiseless, applied to old people, who creep about quietly; de- + crepare to make a noise, rattle: cf. F. décrépit. See Crepitate.
L. decrescens, p. pr. of decrescere. See Decrease.
L. decretalis, fr. decretum. See Decree. | LL. decretale, neut. of L. decretalis. See Decretal, a.
From L. decrescere, decretum. See Decrease.
LL. decretista, fr. decretum: cf. F. décrétiste. See Decree, n.
From L. decretum. See Decree, n.
L. decretorius, from decretum. See Decree.
F. décrue, n., decrease, and décru, p. p. of décroître. See Decrease, and cf. Accrue.
F. décrier, OF. descrier; pref. des- (L. dis-) + crier to cry. See Cry, and cf. Descry.
From L. decubare; de- + cubare. See Decumbent.
NL., fr. L. de- + cubare, to lie down: cf. F. décubitus.
L. decumanus of the tenth, and by metonymy, large, fr. decem ten.
L. decumbens, -entis, p. pr. of decumbere; de- + cumbere (only in comp.), cubare to lie down.
F. décuple, L. decuplus, fr. decem ten.
L. decurio, decurionis, fr. decuria a squad of ten, fr. decem ten.
L. decurrens, -entis, p. pr. of decurrere to run down; de- + currere to run: cf. F. décurrent.
L. decursio, fr. decurrere. See Decurrent.
L. decussatus, p. p. of decussare to cross like an X, fr. decussis (orig. equiv. to decem asses) the number ten, which the Romans represented by X.
L. dedecoratus, p. p. of dedecorare to disgrace. See Decorate.
L. dedicatus, p. p. of dedicare to affirm, to dedicate; de- + dicare to declare, dedicate; akin to dicere to say. See Diction.
L. dedimus we have given, fr. dare to give. So called because the writ began, Dedimus potestatem, etc.
L. deditio, fr. dedere to give away, surrender; de- + dare to give.
L. dedolens, p. pr. of dedolere to give over grieving; de- + dolere to grieve.
L. deducere; de- + ducere to lead, draw. See Duke, and cf. Deduct.
L. deductus, p. p. of deducere to deduct. See Deduce.
AS. d; akin to OS. dad, D. & Dan. daad, G. thai, Sw. dåd, Goth. d; fr. the root of do. See Do, v. t.

OE. dippen, duppen, AS. dyppan; akin to Dan. dyppe, Sw. doppa, and to AS. d to baptize, OS. d, D. doopen, G. taufen, Sw. döpa, Goth. daupjan, Lith. dubus deep, hollow, OSlav. dupl hollow, and to E. dive. Cf. Deep, Dive.

OE. dulte, prop. p. p. of dullen to dull. See Dull.

F., fr. L. dos, dotis, dowry. See Dower, and cf. Dote dowry. | Cf. AS. dott small spot, speck; of uncertain origin.
L. dotalis, fr. dos, dotis, dowry: cf. F. dotal. See Dot dowry.
LL. dotatio, fr. L. dotare to endow, fr. dos, dotis, dower: cf. F. dotation. See Dot dowry.

See Dot dowry. | OE. doten; akin to OD. doten, D. dutten, to doze, Icel. dotta to nod from sleep, MHG. t to keep still: cf. F. doter, OF. radoter (to dote, rave, talk idly or senselessly), which are from the same source.
Cf. Dottard. | From Dote, v. i.
From Douay, or Douai, a town in France.

OE. doble, duble, double, OF. doble, duble, double, F. double, fr. L. duplus, fr. the root of duo two, and perh. that of plenus full; akin to Gr. Two, and Full, and cf. Diploma, Duple. | OE. doblen, dublen, doublen, F. doubler, fr. L. duplare, fr. duplus. See Double, a.
F. double double + entendre to mean. This is a barbarous compound of French words. The true French equivalent is double entente.
In sense 3, OF. doublet; in sense 4, F. doublet, dim. of double double. See Double, a.
F. doublon, Sp. doblon. See Double, a., and cf. Dupion.
OE. duten, douten, OF. duter, doter, douter, F. douter, fr. L. dubitare; akin to dubius doubtful. See Dubious. | OE. dute, doute, F. doute, fr. douter to doubt. See Doubt, v. i.
OF. doutable, L. dubitabilis, from dubitare. Cf. Dubitable.
F. doux, masc., douce, fem., sweet, fr. L. duleis sweet.
F. les douze pairs the twelve peers of France, renowned in romantic fiction.
F. doucet sweet, dim. of doux. See Douce.
F., fr. doux sweet. See Douce.
F., fr. It. doccia, fr. docciare to flow, pour, fr. an assumed LL. ductiare, fr. L. ducere, ductum, to lead, conduct (water). See Duct.
From aouck, for duck. See Duck, v. t.

OE. dagh, dogh, dow, AS. dah; akin to D. deeg, G. teig, Icel. deig, Sw. deg, Dan. deig, Goth. daigs; also, to Goth. deigan to knead, L. fingere to form, shape, Skr. dih to smear; cf. Gr. Feign, Figure, Dairy, Duff.

OE. duhti, dohti, douhti, brave, valiant, fit, useful, AS, dyhtig; akin to G. tüchtig, Dan. dygtig, Sw. dygdig virtuous, and fr. AS. dugan to avail, be of use, be strong, akin to D. deugen, OHG. tugan, G. taugen, Icel. & Sw. duga, Dan. due, Goth. dugan, but of uncertain origin; cf. Skr. duh to milk, give milk, draw out, or Gr. Defn: Able; strong; valiant; redoubtable; as, a doughty hero. Sir Thopas wex [grew
Gr. Defn: A government by slaves. [Written also dulocracy.
Cf. Dowse, and OD. donsen to strike with the fist on the back, Sw. dunsa to fall down violently and noisily; perh. akin to E. din. | AS. dwæscan. (Skeat.)
OE. dove, duve, douve, AS. d; akin to OS. d, D. duif, OHG. t, G. taube, Icel. d, Sw. dufva, Dan. due, Goth. d; perh. from the root of E. dive.
From Dr. Dover, an English physician.
OF. douagiere, fr. douage dower. See Dower.
Scot. dawdie slovenly, daw, da sluggard, drab, Prov. E. dowd flat, dead.
Cf. G. döbel peg, F. douelle state of a cask, surface of an arch, douille socket, little pipe, cartridge.
F. douaire, LL. dotarium, from L. dotare to endow, portion, fr. dos dower; akin to Gr. dare to give. See 1st Date, and cf. Dot dowry, Dotation.
Prob. fr. Doullens, a town of Picardy, in France, formerly celebrated for this manufacture.
Cf. OF. douille soft. Cf. Ductile.

Akin to LG. dune, dun, Icel. d, Sw. dun, Dan. duun, G. daune, cf. D. dons; perh. akin to E. dust. | OE. dun, doun, AS. d; of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. d hill, fortified hill, Gael. dun heap, hillock, hill, W. din a fortified hill or mount; akin to E. town. See Town, and cf. Down, adv. & prep., Dune. | For older adown, AS. ad, ad, prop., from or off the hill. See 3d Down, and cf. Adown, and cf. Adown. | From Down, adv.
AS. ad. See Down, adv., and - ward.
AS. ad. See Down, adv., and - ward.
Contr. from dowery; cf. LL. dotarium. See Dower.
F. doucet sweet, dim. of doux. See Douce.
LL. doxologia, Gr. doxologie. See Dogma, and Legend.
Prob. akin to daze, dizzy: cf. Icel. d to doze, Dan. döse to make dull, heavy, or drowsy, dös dullness, drowsiness, dösig drowsy, AS. dw dull, stupid, foolish. Dizzy.
OE. doseine, dosein, OF. doseine, F. douzaine, fr. douze twelve, fr. L. duodecim; duo two + decem ten. See Two, Ten, and cf. Duodecimal.

AS. drabbe dregs, lees; akin to D. drab, drabbe, dregs, G. treber; for sense 1, cf. also Gael. drabag a slattern, drabach slovenly. Cf. Draff. | F. drap cloth: LL. drappus, trapus, perh. orig., a firm, solid stuff, cf. F. draper to drape, also to full cloth; prob. of German origin; cf. Icel. drepa to beat, strike, AS. drepan, G. treffen; perh. akin to E. drub. Cf. Drape, Trappings.
From L. draco dragon, in allusion to the terms dragon's head and dragon's tail.
Cf. D. draf the sediment of ale, Icel. draf draff, husks. Cf. 1st Drab. | The same word as draught. OE. draught, draht, fr. AS. dragan to draw. See Draw, and cf. Draught.

See 3d Dredge. | OE. draggen; akin to Sw. dragga to search with a grapnel, fr. dragg grapnel, fr. draga to draw, the same word as E. draw. Draw. | See Drag, v. t., and cf. Dray a cart, and 1st Dredge.
From F. dragoman, or Sp. dragoman, or It. dragomanno; all fr. LGr. tarjuman, from the same source as E. targum. Cf. Drogman, Truchman.
F. dragon, L. draco, fr. Gr. dar to see), and so called from its terrible eyes. Cf. Drake a dragon, Dragoon.
F., fr. dragon dragoon, because Louis XIV., in persecuting the Protestants of his kingdom, quartered dragoons upon them.
F. dragon dragon, dragoon, fr. L. draco dragon, also, a cohort's standard (with a dragon on it). The name was given from the sense standard. See Dragon.
AS. drehnigean to drain, strain; perh. akin to E. draw.

Akin to LG. drake, OHG. antrache, anetrecho, G. enterich, Icel. andriki, Dan. andrik, OSw. andrak, andrage, masc., and fr. AS. ened, fem., duck; akin to D. eend, G. ente, Icel. önd, Dan. and, Sw. and, Lith. antis, L. anas, Gr. ati a water fowl. rich. Cf. Gulaund. | AS. draca dragon, L. draco. See Dragon. | Cf. F. dravik, W. drewg, darnel, cockle, etc.
OF. drame, F. drachme, L. drachma, drachm, drachma, fr. Gr. Drachm, Drachma.
F. draper, fr. drap cloth. See 3d Drab.
The same as draft, the spelling with gh indicating an older pronunciation. See Draft, n., Draw.
From Skr. Dravi, the name of the southern portion of the peninsula of India.

OE. dra, drahen, draien, drawen, AS. dragan; akin to Icel. & Sw. draga, Dan. drage to draw, carry, and prob. to OS. dragan to bear, carry, D. dragen, G. tragen, Goth. dragan; cf. Skr. dhraj to move along, glide; and perh. akin to Skr. dhar to hold, bear. Drag, Dray a cart, 1st Dredge.
From the name of a bullying braggart character in the play by George Villiers called "The Rehearsal."
Prob. fr. draw: cf. D. dralen to linger, tarry, Icel. dralla to loiter. See Draw, and cf. Draggle.
AS. dræge a dragnet, fr. dragan. . See Draw, and cf. 2d Drag, 1st Dredge.
AS. dr, in comp.; akin to OS. dradan, OHG. tratan, both only in comp.
Akin to OS. | Cf. AS. dr, dr, to rejoice. See Dream, n.
OE. dreori, dreri, AS. dreórig, sad; akin to G. traurig, and prob. to AS. dreósan to fall, Goth. driusan. Cf. Dross, Drear, Drizzle, Drowse.

F. drège, dreige, fish net, from a word akin to E. draw; cf. D. dreg, dregge, small anchor, dregnet dragnet. Draw. | OE. dragge, F. dragée, dredge, also, sugar plum; cf. Prov. dragea, It. treggea; corrupted fr. LL. tragemata, pl., sweetmeats, Gr. Defn: A mixture of oats and barley. [Obs.
AS. dreógan to bear, endure, complete.
Prob. from Icel. dregg; akin to Sw. drägg, cf. Icel. & Sw. draga to draw. Cf. Draw.
NL. Named after Dreyssen, a Belgian physician.

AS. drencan to give to drink, to drench, the causal of drincan to drink; akin to D. drenken, Sw. dränka, G. tränken. See Drink. | AS. drenc. See Drench, v. t. | AS. dreng warrior, soldier, akin to Icel. drengr.

OF. drecier to make straight, raise, set up, prepare, arrange, F. dresser. (assumed) LL. directiare, fr. L. dirigere, directum, to direct; dis- + regere to rule. See Right, and cf. Address, Adroit, Direct, Dirge.
Freq. of drib, which is a variant of drip.
From drive; akin to LG. & D. drift a driving, Icel. drift snowdrift, Dan. drift, impulse, drove, herd, pasture, common, G. trift pasturage, drove. See Drive.

D. drillen to bore, drill (soldiers); probably akin to AS. pyrlian, pyrelian, to pierce. See Thrill. | Cf. Trill to trickle, Trickle, Dribble, and W. rhillio to put in a row, drill. | Cf. Mandrill. | Usually in pl.
G. drillich, fr. L. trilix having three threads, fr. the of tres three + licium a thread of the warm. See Three, and cf. Twill.
AS. drincan; akin to OS. drinkan, D. drinken, G. trinken, Icel. drekka, Sw. dricka, Dan. drikke, Goth. drigkan. Cf. Drench, Drunken, Drown.
Akin to LG. drippen, Dan. dryppe, from a noun. See Drop.
AS. drifan; akin to OS. driban, D. drijven, OHG. triban, G. treiben, Icel. drifa, Goth. dreiban. Cf. Drift, Drove.
Cf. OE. dravelen, drabelen, drevelen, drivelen, to slaver, and E. drabble. Cf. Drool.
Prop. freq. of AS. dreósan to fall. See Dreary.
D. druilen to mope. | D. druil sluggard. Cf. Droll.

F. drôle; cf. G. & D. drollig, LG. drullig, D. drol a thick and short person, a droll, Sw. troll a magical appearance, demon, trolla to use magic arts, enchant, Dan. trold elf, imp, Icel. tröll giant, magician, evil spirit, monster. If this is the origin, cf. Trull.
F. dromadaire, LL. dromedarius, fr. L. dromas (sc. camelus), fr. Gr. dram to run.
OF. dromont, L. dromo, fr. Gr.Dromedary.
OF. dromont, L. dromo, fr. Gr.Dromedary.

OE. drane a dronebee, AS. dran; akin to OS. dran, OHG. treno, G. drohne, Dan. drone, cf. Gr. Drone, v. i. | Cf. (for sense 1) D. dreunen, G. dröhnen, Icel. drynja to roar, drynr a roaring, Sw. dröna to bellow, drone, Dan. dröne, Goth. drunjus sound, Gr. dhran to sound. Cf. Drone, n.
Icel. dr; akin to E. drop. See Drop.

OE. drope, AS. dropa; akin to OS. dropo, D. drop, OHG. tropo, G. tropfen, Icel. dropi, Sw. droppe; and Fr. AS. dreópan to drip, drop; akin to OS. driopan, D. druipen, OHG. triofan, G. triefen, Icel. drj. Cf. Drip, Droop. | OE. droppen, AS. dropan, v. i. See Drop, n.
AS. drop-m; dropa drop + m portion. Cf. Piecemeal.
AS. drop-m; dropa drop + m portion. Cf. Piecemeal.
OE. dropsie, dropesie, OF. idropisie, F. hydropisie, L. hydropisis, fr. Gr. Water, and cf. Hydropsy.
Russ. drojki, dim. of drogi a kind of carriage, prop. pl. of droga shaft or pole of a carriage.
AS. dros, fr. dreósan to fall. See Dreary.
OE. droght, drougth, dru, AS. druga, from drugian to dry. See Dry, and cf. Drouth, which shows the original final sound.
Cf. Scot. drum, dram, melancholy, Icel prumr a moper, W. trwm heavy, sad.
AS. draf, fr. drifan to drive. See Drive.
AS. dr dirty; cf. D. droef, G. trübe, Goth. dr to trouble.
OE. drunen, drounen, earlier drunknen, druncnien, AS. druncnian to be drowned, sink, become drunk, fr. druncen drunken. See Drunken, Drink.
AS. dr, dr, to sink, become slow or inactive; cf. OD. droosen to be sleepy, fall asleep, LG. dr, druusken, to slumber, fall down with a noise; prob, akin to AS. dreósan to fall. See Dreary.
Cf. Prov. E. drab to beat, Icel. & Sw. drabba to hit, beat, Dan. dræbe to slay, and perh. OE. drepen to strike, kill, AS. drepan to strike, G. & D. freffen to hit, touch, Icel. drepa to strike, kill.
OE. druggen; prob not akin to E. drag, v. t., but fr. Celtic; cf. Ir. drugaire a slave or drudge.
See 1st Drudge. | F. drogue, prob. fr. D. droog; akin to E. dry; thus orig., dry substance, hers, plants, or wares. See Dry. | Cf. F. droguer.
F. droguet, prop. dim. of drogue trash, stuff, perh, the same word as drogue drug, but cf. also W. drwg evil, bad, Ir. & Gael. droch, Arm. droug, drouk. See 3d Drug.
F. droguiste, fr. drogue. See 3d Drug.
L. Druides; of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. & Gael. draoi, druidh, magician, Druid, W. derwydd Druid.

Cf. D. trom, trommel, LG. trumme, G. trommel, Dan. tromme, Sw. trumma, OHG. trumba a trumpet, Icel. pruma a clap of thunder, and as a verb, to thunder, Dan. drum a booming sound, drumme to boom; prob. partly at least of imitative origin; perh. akin to E. trum, or trumpet.
Gael. druim the ridge of a hill.
From Thomas Drummond, a British naval officer.
OE. dronke, drunke, dronken, drunken, AS. druncen. Orig. the same as drunken, p. p. of drink. See Drink.
AS. druncen, prop., that has drunk, p. p. of drincan, taken as active. See Drink, v. i., and cf. Drunk.
Cf. G. druse bonny, crystallized piece of ore, Bohem. druza. Cf. Dross.
OE. dru, druye, drie, AS. dryge; akin to LG. dröge, D. droog, OHG. trucchan, G. trocken, Icel. draugr a dry log. Cf. Drought, Drouth, 3d Drug. | AS. drygan; cf. drugian to grow dry. See Dry, a.
L. dryas, pl. dryades, Gr. Tree.
L. dualis, fr. duo two. See Two.

AS. dubban to strike, beat ("dubbade his sunu . . . to ridere." AS. Chron. an 1086); akin to Icel. dubba; cf. OF. adouber (prob. fr. Icel.) a chevalier, Icel. dubba til riddara. | Cf. Ir. dób mire, stream, W. dwvr water.
L. dubietas, fr. dubius. See Dubious.
L. dubius, dubiosus, fr. duo two. See Two, and cf. Doubt.
L. dubitatus, p. p. of dubitare. See Doubt.
F. ducat, It. ducato, LL. ducatus, fr. dux leader or commander. See Duke.
F. or Sp. ducaton, fr. ducat.
F. duché, OF. duchée, (assumed) LL. ducitas, fr. L. dux. See Duke.

Cf. Dan. dukke, Sw. docka, OHG. doccha, G. docke. Cf. Doxy. | D. doek cloth, canvas, or Icel. d cloth; akin to OHG. tuoh, G. tuch, Sw. duk, Dan. dug. | OE. duken, douken, to dive; akin to D. duiken, OHG. t, MHG. tucken, tücken, t, G. tuchen. Cf. 5th Duck. | OE. duke, doke. See Duck, v. t.
L. ductus a leading, conducting, conduit, fr. ducere, ductum, to lead. See Duke, and cf. Douche.
L. ductilis, fr. ducere to lead: cf. F. ductile. See Duct.
L. ductio, fr. ducere to lead.
In Suffolk, Eng., to shiver, shake, tremble; also written dodder. | From Duds.
Scot. dud rag, pl. duds clothing of inferior quality.
OF. deu, F. dû, p. p. of devoir to owe, fr. L. debere. See Debt, Habit, and cf. Duty.
It. duello, fr. L. duellum, orig., a contest between two, which passed into the common form bellum war, fr. duo two: cf. F. duel. See Bellicose, Two, and cf. Duello.
Sp. dueña, doña, fr. L. domina. See Dame.
It ., dim. fr. duetto a duet.
It., fr. It & L. duo two. See Two.
D. duffel, from Duffel, a town not far from Antwerp.

F. duc, fr. L. dux, ducis, leader, commander, fr. ducere to lead; akin to AS. teón to draw; cf. AS. heretoga (here army) an army leader, general, G. herzog duke. See Tue, and cf. Doge, Duchess, Ducat, Duct, Adduce, Deduct.
NL., fr. L. dulcis sweet + amarus bitter.
OF. doucet, dim. of dous sweet, F. doux, L. dulcis; akin to Gr. Doucet.
L. dulcis sweet + fluere to flow.
L. dulcis sweet + -fy: cf. F. dulcifier.
L. dulcis sweet + loqui to speak.
It. dolcemele,r Sp. dulcemele, fr. L. dulcis sweet + melos song, melody, Gr. doulcemele. See Dulcet, and Melody.
Sp., from Dulcinea del Toboso the mistress of the affections of Don Quixote.
Cf. F. dulcite, fr. L. dulcis sweet.
L. dulcitudo, fr. dulcis sweet. Defn: Sweetness. [R.
L. dulcoratus, p. p. of dulcorare, fr. dulcor sweetness, fr. dulcis sweet.
AS. dol foolish; akin to gedwelan to err, D. dol mad, dwalen to wander, err, G. toll mad, Goth. dwals foolish, stupid, cf. Gr. dhvr to cause to fall. Cf. Dolt, Dwale, Dwell, Fraud.
Cf. Gael. duileasg; duille leaf + uisge water. Cf. Whisky.
AS. dumb; akin to D. dom stupid, dumb, Sw. dumb, Goth. dumbs; cf. Gr. Deaf, and cf. Dummy.
The first part is prob. of imitative origin. See Dor a beetle.
L. dumosus, fr. dumus a thornbush, a bramble.
L. dumosus, fr. dumus a thornbush, a bramble.

See Dumpling. | Cf. dial. Sw. dumpin melancholy, Dan.dump dull, low, D. dompig damp, G. dumpf damp, dull, gloomy, and E. damp, or rather perh. dump, v. t. Cf. Damp, or Dump, v. t. | OE. dumpen to throw down, fall down, cf. Icel. dumpa to thump, Dan. dumpe to fall suddenly, rush, dial. Sw. dimpa to fall down plump. Cf. Dump sadness.
Dimin. of dump an illshapen piece; cf. D. dompelen to plunge, dip, duck, Scot. to dump in to plunge into, and E. dump, v. t.
See Dune. | AS. dyne noise, dynian to make a noise, or fr. Icel. dynr, duna, noise, thunder, duna to thunder; the same word as E. din. Din. | AS. dunn. of Celtic origin; cf. W. dwn, Ir. & Gael. donn.
From Joannes Duns Scotus, a schoolman called the Subtle Doctor, who died in 1308. Originally in the phrase "a Duns man". See Note below.
Prov. Eng. also dunderpoll, from dunder, same as thunder.
The same word as down: cf. D. duin. See Down a bank of sand.
AS. dung; akin to G. dung, dünger, OHG. tunga, Sw. dynga; cf. Icel. dyngja heap, Dan. dynge, MHG. tunc underground dwelling place, orig., covered with dung. Cf. Dingy.

OE. donjoun highest tower of a castle, tower, prison, F. donjon tower or platform in the midst of a castle, turret, or closet on the top of a house, a keep of a castle, LL. domnio, the same word as LL. dominus lord. See Dame, Don, and cf. Dominion, Domain, Demesne, Danger, Donjon.
Prob. of Celtic origin; cf. Gael. dun hill (E. dune), and linne pool, pond, lake, E. lin.
From Dun to ask payment from.
It. duo, fr. L. duo two. See Duet.
L. duodecennis; duodecim twelve + annus year.
L. duodecim twelve + findere to cleave.
L. in duodecimo in twelfth, fr. duodecimus twelfth, fr. duodecim twelve. See Dozen.
L. duodenarius, fr. duodeni twelve each: cf. F. duodénaire.
NL., fr. duodeni twelve each: cf. F. duodenum. So called because its length is about twelve fingers' breadth.
Contr. fr. do up, that is, to lift up the latch. Cf. Don, Doff.

F., prob. from Prov. F. dupe, dube; of unknown origin; equiv. to F. huppe hoopoe, a foolish bird, easily caught. Cf. Armor. houpérik hoopoe, a man easily deceived. Cf. also Gull, Booby. | Cf. F. duper, fr. dupe. See Dupe, n.
F. doupion, It. doppione, fr. doppio double, L. duplus. See Double, and cf. Doubloon.
L., fr. duo two + plicare to fold. See Two, and Complex.
L. duplicatus, p. p. of duplicare to double, fr. duplex double, twofold. See Duplex.
F. duplicité, L. duplicitas, fr. duplex double. See Duplex.
G., fr. L. durus hard, firm, vigorous.
L., lit., hard mother. The membrane was called mater, or mother, because it was formerly thought to give rise to every membrane of the body.
L. durabilis, fr. durare to last: cf. F. durable. See Dure.
L., hardness, a hardened, i. e., ligneous, vine branch, fr. durare to harden. See Dure.
OF. durance duration, fr. L. durans, -antis, p. pr. durare to endure, last. See Dure, and cf. Durant.
F. durant, p. pr. of durer to last. Cf. Durance.
L., abl. case of the p. pr. of durare to last.
Hind. darbar, fr. Per dar house, court, hall of audience; dar door, gate + bar court, assembly.

L. durus; akin to Ir. & Gael. dur , stubborn, W. dir certain, sure, cf. Gr. Defn: Hard; harsh; severe; rough; toilsome. [R. | F. durer, L. durare to harden, be hardened, to endure, last, fr. durus hard. See Dure, a.
L. durus hard; -- so called because solid at ordinary temperatures.
OF. duresse, du, hardship, severity, L. duritia, durities, fr. durus hard. See Dure.
AS. dust; cf. LG. dust, D. duist meal dust, OD. doest, donst, and G. dunst vapor, OHG. tunist, dunist, a blowing, wind, Icel. dust dust, Dan. dyst mill dust; perh. akin to L. fumus smoke, E. fume. .

D. duitsch German; or G. deutsch, orig., popular, national, OD. dietsc, MHG. diutsch, tiutsch, OHG. diutisk, fr. diot, diota, a people, a nation; akin to AS. peód, OS. thiod, thioda, Goth. piuda; cf. Lith. tauta land, OIr. tuath people, Oscan touto. The English have applied the name especially to the Germanic people living nearest them, the Hollanders. Cf. Derrick, Teutonic.
L., fr. duo two + vir man.
D. duiker diver + bok a buck, lit., diver buck. So named from its habit of diving suddenly into the bush.
OE. dwale, dwole, deception, deadly nightshade, AS. dwala, dwola, error, doubt; akin to E. dull. See Dull, a.
Cf. D. dwingen to force, compel.
OE. dwergh, dwerf, dwarf, AS. dweorg, dweorh; akin to D. dwerg, MHG. twerc, G. zwerg, Icel. dvergr, Sw. & Dan. dverg; of unknown origin.

OE. dwellen, dwelien, to err, linger, AS. dwellan to deceive, hinder, delay, dwelian to err; akin to Icel. dvelja to delay, tarry, Sw. dväljas to dwell, Dan. dvæle to linger, and to E. dull. See Dull, and cf. Dwale.

From OE. dwinen to languish, waste away, AS. dwinan; akin to LG. dwinen, D. dwijnen to vanish, Icel. dvina to cease, dwindle, Sw. tvina; of uncertain origin. The suffix -le, preceded by d excrescent after n, is added to the root with a diminutive force.
L. dyas, dyadis, the number two. Gr. dyade. See two, and cf. Duad.
Gr. -meter: cf. F. dynamètre. Cf. Dynamometer.
Gr. durus hard, E. dure: cf. F. dynamique.
Gr. durus hard, E. dure: cf. F. dynamique.
L. dynastes, Gr. dynaste. See Dynamic.
Gr. Dynast. The name alludes to the immense size of some species.
L. dysenteria, Gr. in: cf. F. dysenterie. See Dys, and In.
L. dyspepsia, Gr. cook: cf. F. dyspepsie. See Dys-, and 3d Cook.

Cf. LG. fakk wearied, weary, vaak slumber, drowsiness, OFries. fai, equiv. to fach devoted to death, OS. f, OHG. feigi, G. feig, feige, cowardly, Icel. feigr fated to die, AS. f, Scot. faik, to fail, stop, lower the price; or perh. the same word as E. flag to droop.

L., a band: cf. It. fascia. See Fasces, and cf. Fess.

L. fasciculus, dim. of fascis. See Fasces.
F., fr. L. fascina a bundle of sticks, fr. fascis. See Fasces.
L. fascinum witchcraft, akin to fascinare. See Fascinate.
L. fasciola a little bandage. See Fascia.
OF. faschier, F. f, to anger, vex; cf. Pr. fasticar, fastigar, fr. L. fastidium dilike. See Fastidious.
OE. fasoun, facioun, shape, manner, F. facon, orig., a making, fr. L. factio a making, fr. facere to make. See Fact, Feat, and cf. Faction. | Cf. F. faconner.

AS. fæstan; akin to D. vasten, OHG. fasten, G. fasten, Icel. & Sw. fasta, Dan. faste, Goth. fastan to keep, observe, fast, and prob. to E. fast firm. | OE. faste, fast; cf. AS. f, OHG. fasta, G. faste. See Fast, v. i. | OE., firm, strong, not loose, AS. f; akin to OS. fast, D. vast, OHG. fasti, festi, G. fest, Isel. fastr, Sw. & Dan. fast, and perh. to E. fetter. OE. fader, AS. fæder; akin to OS. fadar, D. vader, OHG. fatar, G. vater, Icel. Fa Sw. & Dan. fader, OIr. athir, L. pater, Gr. pitr, perh. fr. Skr. pa protect. Papa, Paternal, Patriot, Potential, Pablum.

OE. faut, faute, F. faute (cf. It., Sp., & Pg. falta), fr. a verb meaning to want, fail, freq., fr. L. fallere to deceive. See Fail, and cf. Default.

NL.: cf. F. faune. See Faun.

L., contr. fr. favitor, fr. favere to be favorable: cf. F. fauteur. See Favor.

OF. favorit favored, F. favori, fem. favorite, p.p. of OF. favorir, cf. It. favorito, frm. favorita, fr. favorire to favor. See Favor.

OF. faon the young one of any beast, a fawn, F. faon a fawn, for fedon, fr. L. fetus. See Fetus. | Cf. F. faonner. | OE. fawnen, fainen, fagnien, to rejoice, welcome, flatter, AS. fægnian to rejoice; akin to Icel. fagna to rejoice, welcome. See Fain.
AS. feaxede haired, fr. feax hair. Cf. Paxwax.

F. fée. See Fate, and cf. Fairy. | OF. fei, F. foi. See Faith. | OE. feien, v.t. & i., AS. fegan to join, unite; akin to OS. fogian, D. voegen, OHG. fuogen, G. fügen, Sw. foga. See Fair, and cf. Fadge.
So called from the island Fayal.
Cf. Prov. E. feabe, theabe, thape.
Cf. G. fegen to sweep, Icel. fægia to cleanse, polish, E. fair, fay, to fit, fey to cleanse.

OE. faute, OF. fauté, fealté, feelé, feelteit, fr. L. fidelitas, fr. fidelis faithful. See Feal, and cf. Fidelity.

OE. fer, feer, fere, AS. f a coming suddenly upon, fear, danger; akin to D. vaar, OHG. fara danger, G. gefahr, Icel. far harm, mischief, plague, and to E. fare, peril. See Fare. | OE. feren, faeren, to frighten, to be afraid, AS. fFear, n.
F. faisable, fr. faire to make or do, fr. L. facere. See Fact, Feat.

OE. feste festival, holiday, feast, OF. feste festival, F. fête, fr. L. festum, pl. festa, fr. festus joyful, festal; of uncertain origin. Cf. Fair, n., Festal, F. | OE. festen, cf. OF. fester to rest from work, F. fêter to celebrate a holiday. See Feast, n.
OE. fet, OF. fet, fait, F. fait, factum, fr. L. facere, factum, to make or do. Cf. Fact, Feasible, Do. | F. fait made, shaped, fit, p.p. of faire to make or do. See Feat, n.
Cf. OF. faitis, faitice, fetis, well made, fine, L. facticius made by art.

OE. fether, AS. fe; akin to D. veder, OHG. fedara, G. feder, Icel. fjö, Sw. fjäder, Dan. fjæder, Gr. pattra wing, feathr, pat to fly, and prob. to L. penna feather, wing. sq. root76, 248. Cf. Pen a feather.

L. Februarius, orig., the month of expiation, because on the fifteenth of this month the great feast of expiation and purification was held, fr. februa, pl., the Roman festival or purification; akin to februare to purify, expiate.
L. fetialis belonging to the fetiales, the Roman priests who sanctioned treaties and demanded satisfaction from the enemy before a formal declaration of war.
L.fae burnt tartar or salt of tartar, dim. of faex, faecis, sediment, dregs: cf. F. fécule.

L. fecundus, from the root of fetus: cf. F. fécond. see Fetus.
L. fecundare, fr. fecundus. See Fecund.
L. fecunditas: cf. F. fécondité. See Fecund.
L. foedus league, treaty, compact; akin to fides faith: cf. F. fédéral. see Faith.
L. foederatus, p.p. of foederare to establish by treaty or league, fr. foedus. See Federal.
L. foeditas, fr. foedus foul, fikthy.

OE. fe, feh, feoh, cattle, property, money, fiet, AS. feoh cattle, property, money; the senses of "property, money," arising from cattle being used in early times as a medium of exchange or payment, property chiefly consisting of cattle; akin to OS. feuh cattle, property, D. vee cattle, OHG. fihu, fehu, G. vieh, Icel. f cattle, property, money, Goth. faíhu, L. pecus cattle, pecunia property. money, Skr. pa cattle, perh. orig., "a fastened or tethered animal," from a root signifying to bind, and perh. akin to E. fang, fair, a.; cf. OF. fie, flu, feu, fleu, fief, F. fief, from German, of the same origin. the sense fief is due to the French. Feud, Fief, Fellow, Pecuniary.
OE. feble, OF. feble, flebe, floibe, floible, foible, F. faible, L. flebilis to be wept over, lamentable, wretched, fr. flere to weep. Cf. Foible.
AS. f, fr. f food; akin to C. f, OFries f, f, D. voeden, OHG. fuottan, Icel. fæ, Sw. föda, Dan. föde. Food.
AS. f; akin to OS. gif to perceive, D. voelen to feel, OHG. fuolen, G. fühlen, Icel. falma to grope, and prob. to AS. folm paim of the hand, L. palma. Cf. Fumble, Palm.
Cf. OE. fesien to put to flight, AS. fesian, fysian, fysan, fr. fus, prompt, willing.
For sense 1, cf. F. visser to screw, vis screw, or 1st E. feaze, v.t.: for sense 2, see Feese.
OE. feinen, F. feindre (p. pr. feignant), fr. L. fingere; akin to L. figura figure,and E. dough. See Dough, and cf. Figure, Faint, Effigy, Fiction.
F. feint, p.p. of feindre to feign. See Feign. | F. feinte, fr. feint. See Feint, a.
G. feldspath; feld field + spath spar.
G. feldspath; feld field + spath spar.
AS. fela, feola; akin to G. viel, gr. Full, a.
L. felicitatus, p.p. of felicitare to felicitate, fr. felix, -icis, happy. See felicity. | Cf. F. féliciter.
OE. felicite, F. félicité, fr. L. felicitas, fr. felix, -icis, happy, fruitful; akin to fetus.
L. felinus, fr. feles, felis, cat, prob. orig., the fruitful: cf. F. félin. See Fetus.

OE. fel, OF. fel cruel, fierce, perfidious; cf. AS. fel (only in comp.) OF. fel, as a noun also accus. felon, is fr. LL. felo, of unknown origin; cf. Arm fall evil, Ir. feal, Arm. falloni treachery, Ir. & Gael. feall to betray; or cf. OHG. fillan to flay, torment, akin to E. fell skin. Cf. Felon. | Cf. L. fel gall, bile, or E. fell, a. | AS. fell; akin to D. vel, OHG. fel, G. fell, Icel. fell (in comp.), Goth fill in Þrutsfill leprosy, L. pellis skin, G. Film, Peel, Pell, n. | Icel. fell, fjally; akin to Sw. fjäll a ridge or chain of mountains, Dan. fjeld mountain, rock and prob. to G. fels rock, or perh. to feld field, E. field. | AS. fellan, a causative verb fr. feallan to fall; akin to D. vellen, G. fällen, Icel. fella, Sw. fälla, Dan. fælde. See Fall, v. i. | Cf. Gael. fill to fold, plait, Sw. fåll a hem.
Cf. AS. fealafor, and E. fieldfare.
L. fellifluus; fel gall + fluere to flow.

OE. feli, felwe, felow, AS. felg, felge; akin to D. velg, G. felge, OHG. felga felly (also, a harrow, but prob. a different word), Dan. felge.
LL. felo, E. felon + de of, concerning + se self.
OE., adj., cruel, n., villain, ruffian, traitor, whitlow, F. félon traitor, in OF. also, villain, fr. LL. felo. See Fell, a.
OE. felonie cruelty, OF. felonie, F. félonie treachery, malice. See Felon, n.
From G. feldstein, in analogy with E. felspar.
AS. felt; akin to D. vilt, G. filz, and possibly to Gr. pilus hair, pileus a felt cap or hat.
It. feluca (cf. Sp. faluca, Pg. falua), fr. Ar. fulk ship, or harraqah a sort of ship.
OE. femel, femal, F. femelle, fr. L. femella, dim. of femina woman. See Feminine.
OF. fumeraille part of a chimney. See Fume.
L. femininus, fr. femina woman; prob. akin to L. fetus, or to Gr. fæmme woman, maid: cf. F. féminin. See Fetus.
OF. femenie, feminie, the female sex, realm of women.
L. femur, femoris, thigh: cf. F. fémoral.

From Fend, v. t. & i., cf. Defender.
L. faeneratus, p.p. of faenerari lend on interest, fr. faenus interest.

From the Finians or Fenii, the old militia of Ireland, who were so called from Fin or Finn, Fionn, or Fingal, a popular hero of Irish traditional history.
AS. fenol, finol, from L. feniculum, faeniculum, dim. of fenum, faenum, hay: cf. F. fenouil. Cf. Fenugreek. Finochio.
AS. fynig musty, fynegean to become musty or filthy: cf. fennig fenny, muddy, dirty, fr. fen fen. Cf. Finew.
L. faenum Graecum, lit., Greek hay: cf. F. fenugrec. Cf. Fennel.
OE. feffen, OF. feffer, fieffer, F. fieffer, fr. fief fief; cf. LL. feoffare, fefare. See Fief.
OF. feoffement, fieffement; cf. LL. feoffamentum.
F., the iron of a lance, lance head.
L. ferax, -acis, fr. ferre to bear.
L., wild animals, fem. pl. of ferus wild.
L. ferus. See Fierce. | L. feralis, belonging to the dead.

LL. ferialis, fr. L. ferie holidays: cf. F. férial. See 5th Fair.
L. feriari to keep holiday, fr. ferie holidays.
OF. ferie, fr. L. ferie holidays. See 5th Fair.
L. ferinus, fr. ferus wild. See Fierce.
Per. Farangi, or Ar. Firanji, properly, a Frank.
AS. f sudden, unexpected. See Fear, n.

L. fermentum ferment (in senses 1 & 2), perh. for fervimentum, fr. fervere to be boiling hot, boil, ferment: cf. F. ferment. Cf. 1st Barm, Fervent. | L. fermentare, fermentatum: cf. F. fermenter. See Ferment, n.

L. ferox, -ocis, fierce: cf. F. féroce. See Ferocity.

F.; cf. OF. ferrant iron-gray, from L. ferrum iron.

F. furet, cf. LL. furo; prob. fr. L. fur thief (cf. Furtive); cf. Arm. fur wise, sly. | Cf. F. fureter. See Ferret, n. | Ital. foretto, dim. of fiore flower; or F. fleuret. Cf. Floret. | F. feret, dim. or fer iron, L. ferrum.
It. ferretto di Spagna, dim. of ferro iron, fr. L. ferrum.

L. ferrum iron + -ferous: cf. F. ferrifère.
L. ferruginus, ferrugineus, fr. ferrugo, - ginis, iron rust: cf. F. ferrugineux. See Ferrugo.
L., iron rust, fr. ferrum iron.

Formerly verrel, F. virole, fr. L. viriola little bracelet, dim. of viriae, pl., bracelets; prob. akin to viere to twist, weave, and E. withe. The spelling with f is due to confusion with L. ferrum iron.
L. ferruminatus, p.p. of ferruminare to cement, solder, fr. ferrumen cement, fr. ferrum iron.
OE. ferien to convey, AS. ferian, from faran to go; akin to Icel. ferja to ferry, Goth. farjan to sail. See Fare. | OE. feri; akin to Icel. ferja, Sw. färja, Dan. færge, G. fähre. See Ferry, v. t.
L. fertilis, fr. ferr to bear, produce: cf. F. fertile. See Bear to support.
L. ferula giant fennel (its stalks were used in punishing schoolboys), rod, whip, fr. ferire to strike; akin to OHG. berjan, Icel. berja. Cf. Ferule.
L. ferulaceus, fr. ferula rod: cf. F. férulacé.
L. ferula: cf. F. férule. See Ferula.
F. fervent, L. fervens, -entis. p.pr. of fervere o the boiling hot, to boil, glow.
L. fervescens, p.pr. of fervescere to become boiling hot, incho., fr. fervere. See Fervent.
L. fervidus, fr. fervere. See Fervent.
OF. fervor, fervour, F. ferveur, L. fervor, fr. fervere. See Fervent.
L. Fescenninus, fr. Fescennia, a city of Etruria.
OE. festu, OF. festu, F. fétu, fr. L. festuca stalk, straw.
OF. fesse, faisse, F. fasce, fr. L. fascia band. See Fascia.
OF. fesse, faisse, F. fasce, fr. L. fascia band. See Fascia.
L. festum holiday, feast. See feast.
OE. festern, fr. fester, n.; or fr. OF. festrir, fr. festre, n. See Fester, n. | OF. festre, L. fistula a sort of ulcer. Cf. Fistula.
L. festinatus, p.p. of festinare to hasten.
OF. festival, fr. L. festivum festive jollity, fr. festivus festive, gay. See Festive.
L. festivus, fr. festum holiday, feast. See feast, and cf. Festivous.
F. feston (cf. Sp. feston, It. festone), prob. fr. L. festum festival. See Feast.
L. festula stalk, straw. Cf. Fescue.

Cf. feat, F. fait, and It. fett slice, G. fetzen rag, Icel. fat garment. | OE. fetten, feten, AS. fetian; akin to AS. fæt a journey, and to E. foot; cf. G. fassen to seize. sq. root 77. See Foot, and cf. Fetch.

See feat. | See Foot. | F. See Feast. | Cf. F. fêter.

L. fetidus, foetidus, fr. fetere, foetere, to have an ill smell, to stink: cf. F. fétide.
F. fétiche, from Pg. feiti, adj., n., sorcery, charm, fr. L. facticius made by art, artifical, factitious. See Factitious.
OE. fetlak, fitlock, cf. Icel. fet pace, step, fit webbed foot of water birds, akin to E. foot. sq. root 77. See Foot.
AS. fetor, feter; akin to OS. feter, pl., OD. veter, OHG. fezzera, Icel. fjöturr, L. pedi, Gr. foot. sq. root 77. See Foot. | imp. & p.p. Fettered (n. Fettering.
OE. & Prov. E., to fettle (in sense 1), fettle, n., order, repair, preparation, dress; prob. akin to E. fit. See Fit, a.

L. fetus, foetus, a bringing forth, brood, offspring, young ones, cf. fetus fruitful, fructified, that is or was filled with young; akin to E. fawn a deer, fecundity, felicity, feminine, female, and prob. to do, or according to others, to be.
OE. feide, AS. f, fr. fah hostile; akin to OHG. f, G. fehde, Sw. fejd, D. feide; prob. akin to E. fiend. See Foe. | LL. feudum, feodum prob. of same origin as E. fief. See Fief, Fee.
LL. feudarius, fr. feudum. See 2d Feud.
F. feuille morte a dead leaf.
OE. feutre rest for a lance, OF. feutre, fautre, feltre, felt, cushion, rest for a lance, fr. LL. filtrum, feltrum; of German origin, and akin to E. felt. See Felt, and cf. Filter.
Either fr. G. fütterer feeder, or corrupted fr. OF. vautrier, vaultrier; fr. vaultre, viautre, a kind of hound, fr. L. vertragus, vertraga, a greyhound. The last is of Celtic origin.
OE. fever, fefer, AS. fefer, fefor, L. febris: cf. F. fièvre. Cf. Febrile.
AS. feferfuge, fr. L. febrifugia. See fever, Fugitive, and cf. Febrifuge.
OE. fewe, feawe, AS. feá, pl. feáwe; akin to OS. fah, OHG. f*, Icel. far, Sw. få, pl., Dan. faa, pl., Goth. faus, L. paucus, cf. Gr. Paucity.
AS. f, Icel. feigr, OHG. feigi. | See Fay faith. | Cf. Feague.
F., fr. the town of Fez in Morocco.
L., let it be done, 3d pers. sing., subj. pres., fr. fieri, used as pass. of facere to make. Cf. Be.

L. fibra a fiber + E. vascular.

From Fidge; cf. OE. fiken to fidget, to flatter, Icel. fika to hasten, Sw. fika to hunt after, AS. befician to deceive. Cf. Fickle.

OE. fi; cf. D. fif. G. pfui, Icel. f, Sw. & Dan. fy, F. fi, L. fi, phy.

Prob. fr. or akin to flank.

L. funereus, fr. fentus a funeral.
L. funestus, fr. funus a funeral, destruction: cf. F. funeste.
NL., fr. L. fungus mushroom: cf. F. fongie.

LL. (res) fungibiles, probably fr. L. fungi to discharge. "A barbarous term, supposed to have originated in the use of the words functionem recipere in the Digeste." Bouvier. "Called fungibiles, quia una alterius vice fungitur." John Taylor (1755). Cf. Function.
L. fungus mushroom: cf. F. fungique, fongique.

L. funiculus, dim. of funis cord, rope: cf. F. funicule funicle (in sense 2). Cf. Funambulo.
L., a little cord. See Funicle.
OE. funke a little fire; akin to Prov. E. funk touchwood, G. funke spark, and perh. to Goth. f fire.
OE. funel, fonel, prob. through OF. fr, L. fundibulum, infundibulum, funnel, fr. infundere to pour in; in in + fundere to pour; cf. Armor. founil funnel, W. ffynel air hole, chimney. See Fuse, v. t.

OE. furre, OF. forre, fuerre, sheatth, case, of German origin; cf. OHG. fuotar lining, case, G. futter; akin to Icel. f lining, Goth. f, scabbard; cf. Skr. p vessel, dish. The German and Icel. words also have the sense, fodder, but this was probably a different word originally. Cf. Fodder food, Fother, v. t., Forel, n.
L. furax, -racis thievish, from fur thief.
Prov. F. farbala, equiv. to F. falbala, It. falbalà.
OE. forbischen, OF. forbir, furbir, fourbir, F. fourbir, fr. OHG. furban to clean. See -ish.
L. furcifer yoke bearer, scoundrel; furca fork, yoke, fork-shaped instrument of punishment + ferre to bear.
L., a forked prop, dim. of furca a fork.
NL., dim. of L. furca a fork.
L. furibundus, fr. furere to rage.
L. furiosus, fr. furia rage, fury: cf. F. furieux. See Fury.
Contr. fr. furdle, fr. fardel bundle: cf. F. ferler to furl, OF. fardeler to pack. See Furdle, Fardel, and cf. Farl.
OE. furlong, furlang, AS. furlang, furlung, prop., the length of a furrow; furh furrow + lang long. See Furrow, and Long, a.
Prob. fr. D. verlof, fr. a prefix akin to E. for + the root of E. lief, and akin to Dan. forlov, Sw. förlof, G. verlaub permission. See Life, a.
OE. fornais, forneis, OF. fornaise, F. fournaise, from L. fornax; akin to furnus oven, and prob. to E. forceps.

OF. furnir, fornir, to furnish, finish, F. fournir; akin to Pr. formir, furmir, fromir, to accomplish, satisfy, fr. OHG. frumjan to further, execute, do, akin to E. frame. See Frame, v. t., and - ish.
F. fourniture. See Furnish, v. t.
OE. forow, forgh, furgh, AS. furh; akin to D. voor, OHG. furuh, G. furche, Dan. fure, Sw. f, Icel. for drain, L. porca ridge between two furrows. | From Furrow, n.; cf. AS. fyrian.
A comparative of forth; OE. further, forther, AS. fur, far; akin to G. fürder. See Forth, adv. | OE. furthren, forthren, AS. fyredhran, fyredhrian. See Further, adv.
L. furtivus, fr. furtum theft, fr. fur thief, akin to ferre to bear: cf. F. furtif. See Fertile.
L. furunculus a petty thief, a boil, dim. of fur thief: cf. F. furoncle.
L. fur. | L. furia, fr. furere to rage: cf. F. furie. Cf. Furor.
F., the spindle tree; also, charcoal made from it.
F. fusarolle, fr. It. fusaruolo, fr. fuso spindle, shaft of a column. See Fusee a conical wheel.
L. fuscare, fuscatum, to make dark, fr. fuscus dark.
L. fusus, p. p. of fundere to pour, melt, cast. See Foundo to cast, and cf. Futile. | For fusee, fusil. See 2d Fusil.
See 2d Fusil, and cf. Fuse, n. | Etymol. uncertain. | F. fusée a spindleful, fusee, LL. fusata, fr. fusare to use a spindle, L. fusus spindle.
F. fusible. See Fuse, v. t.
L. fusus spindle + -form: cf. F. fusiforme.

L. fusilis molten, fluid, fr. fundere, fusum, to pour, cast. See Fuse, v. t. | F. fusil, LL. fosile a steel for kindling fire, from L. focus hearth, fireplace, in LLL. fire. See Focus, and cf. Fusee a firelock. | See 3d Fusee.
F. fusillade, cf. It. fucilata. See Fusil a firelock.
L. fusio, fr. fundere, fusum to pour, melt: cf. F. fusion. See Fuse, v. t., aud cf, Foison.
AS. f to hasten, fr. f ready, prompt, quick; akin to OS. f, OHG. funs, Icel. fuss willing; prob. from the root of E. find.
OF. fust, F. f, fr. L. fustis stick staff. | OF. fust cask, F. f cask, taste or smell of the caak, fustiness, cf. sentir le f to taste of the cask. See 1st Fust.
F. fustet (cf. Sp. & Pg. fustete), LL. fustetus, fr. L. fustis stick, in LL., tree, See 1st Fust, and cf. Fustic.
OE. fustan, fustian, OF. fustaine, F. futaine, It. fustagno, fr. LL. fustaneum, fustanum; cf. Pr. fustani, Sp. fustan. So called from Fustat, i. e., Cairo, where it was made.
F. fustoc, Sp. fustoc. Cf. Fustet.
L. fustigare, fr. fustis stick. See 1st Fust.
Fusty + lug someting heavy, to be drawn or carried.
Fusty + lug someting heavy, to be drawn or carried.
L. fusura, fr. fundere, fusum. See Fuse, v. t.
L. futilis that easily pours out, that easily lets loose, vain, worthless, from the root of fundere to pour out: cf. F. futile. See Fuse, v. t.
F. futur, L. futurus, used as fut. p. of esse to be, but from the same root as E. be. See Be, v. i. | Cf. F. futur. See Future, a.
Cf. Prov. E. fuzzy that ravels (of silk or cotton), D. voos spongy, fungous, G. faser filament. E. feaze to untwist.
Cf. LG. fuseln to drink common liquor, fr. fusel bad liquor.
Prov. fr. AS. fy, fierf, feówerf. See Four, and Foot, n.
AS.; akin to E. fare, v. i.
AS.; akin to E. fare, v. i.

Cf. Gaff. | OE. gabbe gabble, mocking, fr. Icel. gabb mocking, mockery, or OF. gab, gabe; perh. akin to E. gape, or gob. Cf. Gab, v. i., Gibber. | OE. gabben to jest, lie, mock, deceive, fr. Icel. gabba to mock, or OF. gaber. See 2d Gab, and cf. Gabble.

Sp. gabardina; cf. It. gavardina, OF. galvardine, calvardine, gavardine, galeverdine; perh. akin to Sp. & OF. gaban a sort of cloak or coat for rainy weather, F. caban great coat with a hood and sleeves, It. gabbano and perh. to E. cabin.
Freq. of gab. See Gab, v. i.
F. gabelle, LL. gabella, gabulum, gablum; of uncertain origin. Cf.Gavel tribute.

Sp. gabardina; cf. It. gavardina, OF. galvardine, calvardine, gavardine, galeverdine; perh. akin to Sp. & OF. gaban a sort of cloak or coat for rainy weather, F. caban great coat with a hood and sleeves, It. gabbano and perh. to E. cabin.
F., from It. gabbione a large cage, gabion, from gabbia cage, L. cavea. See Cage.

OE. gable, gabil, F. gable, fr. LL. gabalum front of a building, prob. of German or Scand. origin; cf. OHG. gibil, G. giebel gable, Icel. gafl, Goth. gibla pinnacle; perh. akin to Gr. cephalic, or to G. gabel fork, AS. geafl, E. gaffle, L. gabalus a kind of gallows.
Icel. gapi a rash, reckless man. Cf. Gafe.
OE. gad, Icel. gaddr goad, sting; akin to Sw. gadd sting, Goth. gazds, G. gerte switch. See Yard a measure. | Prob. fr. gad, n., and orig. meaning to drive about.
Gad, n. + -ling. | See Gad, v. i.
NL. gadus cod + -oid: cf. F. gadoïde gadoid, Gr. gade.
Named after Gadolin, a Russian chemist.
Gael. Gàidhealach, Gaelach, from Gàidheal, Gael, a Scotch Highlander. | Gael. Gaelig, Gàilig.
OE. gaffe, F. gaffe an iron hook with which seamen pull great fishes into their ships; cf. Ir. gaf, gafa hook; perh. akin to G. gabel fork, Skr. gabhasti. CF. Gaffle, Gable.
Possibly contr. fr. godfather; but prob. fr. gramfer for grandfather. Cf. Gammer.
Cf. AS. geafl fork, LG., D., Sw., & Dan. gaffel, G. gabel, W. gafl, Ir. & Gael. gabhal. Cf. Gaff.
Prob. fr. W. cegio to choke or strangle, fr. ceg mouth, opening, entrance.
L. gagates. See Jet a black mineral.

F. gage, LL. gadium, wadium; of German origin; cf. Goth. wadi, OHG. wetti, weti, akin to E. wed. See Wed, and cf. Wage, n. | So called because an English family named Gage imported the greengage from France, in the last century. | Cf. F. gager. See Gage, n., a pledge.
Of imitative origin; cf. D. gaggelen, gagelen, G. gackeln, gackern, MHG. g, E. giggle, cackle. | Cf. Gaggle v. i.
Named after Gahn, a Swedish chemist.

Cf. W. gan a mortise. | OE. gein, gain, good, near, quick; cf. Icel. gegn ready, serviceable, and gegn, adv., against, opposite. CF. Ahain. | OE. gain, gein, ga, gain, advantage, Icel. gagn; akin to Sw. gagn, Dan. gavn, cf. Goth. gageigan to gain. The word was prob. influenced by F. gain gain, OF. gaain. Cf. Gain, v. t. | From gain, n. but. prob. influenced by F. gagner to earn, gain, OF. gaaignier to cultivate, OHG. weidin, weidinen to pasture, hunt, fr. weida pasturage, G. weide, akin to Icel. vei hunting, AS. wa, cf. L. venari to hunt, E. venison. See Gain, n., profit.
CF. F. gagnable. See Gain, v. t.
OF. gaignage pasturage, crop, F. gaignage pasturage. See Gain, v. t.
F. gagner to gain + pain bread.
OE. geinseien, ageinseien. See Again, and Say to utter.
F. guêtre, cf. Armor. gweltren; or perh. of German origin, and akin to E. wear, v.
F. gala show, pomp, fr. It. gala finery, gala; of German origin. See Gallant.
Gr. -meter: cf. F. galactomètre. Cf. Lactometer.
OE. galingale, OF. galingal, garingal, F. galanga (cf. Sp. galanga), prob. fr. Ar. khalanj.

F. galaxie, L. galaxias, fr. Gr. lac. CF. Lacteal.
L. galbanum, Gr. klekb'n: cf. F. galbanum.
L. galbanum, Gr. klekb'n: cf. F. galbanum.

Prob. of Scand.. origin; cf. Dan. gal furious, Icel. galinn, cf. Icel. gala to sing, AS. galan to sing, Icel. galdr song, witchcraft, AS. galdor charm, sorcery, E. nightingale; also, Icel. gjla gust of wind, gola breeze. Cf. Yell. | OE. gal. See Gale wind. | AS. galan. See 1st Gale. | AS. gagel, akin to D. gagel. | Cf. Gabel.

L. galena lead ore, dross that remains after melting lead: cf. F. galène sulphide of lead ore, antidote to prison, stillness of the sea, calm, tranquility.
L. galericulum, dim. of galerum a hat or cap, fr. galea helmet.
L. galerum a hat, cap: cf. F. galérite.
Cf. Sp. Galiciano, Gallego, fr. L. Gallaecus, Gallaicus, fr. Gallaeci a people in Western Spain.
L. Galilaeus, fr. Galilaea Galilee, Gr. galiléen.
Supposed to have been so termed in allusion to the scriptural "Galilee of the Gentiles." cf. OF. galilée.
OE. galiote, F. galiote. See Galley.
F. galipot; cf. OF. garipot the wild pine or pitch tree.

OE. galle, gal, AS. gealla; akin to D. gal, OS. & OHG. galla, Icel. gall, SW. galla, Dan. galde, L. fel, Gr. yellow. Yellow, and cf. Choler | F. galle, noix de galle, fr. L. galla. | OE. gallen; cf. F. galer to scratch, rub, gale scurf, scab, G. galle a disease in horses' feet, an excrescence under the tongue of horses; of uncertain origin. Cf. Gall gallnut.

F. gallant, prop. p. pr. of OF. galer to rejoice, akin to OF. gale amusement, It. gala ornament; of German origin; cf. OHG. geil merry, luxuriant, wanton, G. geil lascivious, akin to AS. g wanton, wicked, OS. g merry, Goth. gailjan to make to rejoice, or perh. akin to E. weal. See Gala, Galloon.
Cf. F. gallate. See Gall gallnut.
F. galéasse, galéace; cf. It. galeazza, Sp. galeaza; LL. galea a galley. See Galley.
Sp. galeon, cf. F. galion; fr. LL. galeo, galio. See Galley.
F. galerie, It. galleria, fr. LL. galeria gallery, perh. orig., a festal hall, banquetting hall; cf. OF. galerie a rejoicing, fr. galer to rejoice. Cf. Gallant, a.
Prob. so called because the numerous legs along the sides move rhythmically like the oars of a galley.
L. galliambus a song used by the priests of Cybele; Gallus (a name applied to these priests) + iambus
OE., fr. F. gaillard, perh. of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. & Gael. galach valiant, or AS. gagol, geagl, wanton, lascivious. | F. gaillarde, cf. Sp. gallarda. See Galliard, a.
From Gallium. | From Gall the excrescence. | L. Gallicus belonging to the Gauls, fr. Galli the Gauls, Gallia Gaul, now France: cf. F. gallique.
Prob. corrupted fr. It. Grechesco Grecian, a name which seems to have been given in Venice, and to have been afterwards confused with Gascony, as if they came from Gascony.
F. galimafrée a sort of ragout or mixed hash of different meats.
L. gallinaceus, fr. gallina hen, fr. gallus cock.
NL., fr. L. gallina a hen, gallus a cock.
L. gallinula chicken, dim. of gallina hen: cf. F. gallinule.
Prob. fr. OD. gleypot, the first part of which is possibly akin to E. glad. See Glad, and Pot.
Prob. fr. Pg. galeota; cf. E. galiot, galley.
OF galon, jalon, LL. galo, galona, fr. galum a liquid measure; cf. F. jale large bowl. Cf. Gill a measure.
From F. or Sp. galon. See Gala.

OE. galopen, F. galoper, of German origin; cf. assumed Goth. ga-hlaupan to run, OHG. giloufen, AS. gehleápan to leap, dance, fr. root of E. leap, and a prefix; or cf. OFlem. walop a gallop. See Leap, and cf. 1st Wallop. | Cf. F. galop. See Gallop, v. i., and cf. Galop.
F. galopin. See Gallop, v. i.

OE. galwes, pl., AS. galga, gealga, gallows, cross; akin to D. galg gallows, OS. & OHG. galgo, G. galgen, Icel. galgi, Sw. & Dan. galge, Goth. galga a cross. Etymologically and historically considered, gallows is a noun in the plural number, but it is used as a singular, and hence is preceded by a; as, a gallows.
OE. galoche, galache, galage, shoe, F. galoche galoche, perh. altered fr. L. gallica a Gallic shoe, or fr. LL. calopedia wooden shoe, or shoe with a wooden sole, Gr. 1. A clog or patten. [Obs.
Scot. gelore, gilore, galore, fr. Gael. gu leòr, enough; gu- to, also an adverbial prefix + leòr, leòir, enough; or fr. Ir. goleor, the same word.
OE. galoche, galache, galage, shoe, F. galoche galoche, perh. altered fr. L. gallica a Gallic shoe, or fr. LL. calopedia wooden shoe, or shoe with a wooden sole, Gr. 1. A clog or patten. [Obs.
From Galvani, a professor of physiology at Bologna, on account of his connection (about 1780) with the discovery of dynamical or current electricity: cf. F. galvanique.
From Galvani: cf. F. galvanisme. See Galvanic.
From Gama, a cluster of the Maldive Islands.
I. or Sp. gamba leg. See Gambol, n.
OF. gambeson, gambaison, fr. gambais, wambais, of German origin: cf. MHG. wambeis, G. wams doublet, fr. OHG. wamba, stomach. See Womb.
F. gambit, cf. It. gambitto gambit, a tripping up. See Gambol, n.

OE. gambolde, gambaulde, F. gambade, gambol, fr. It. gambata kick, fr. L. gamba leg, akin to F. jambe, OF. also, gambe, fr. L. gamba, hoof or perh. joint: cf. Gr. cam crooked; perh. akin to E. chamber: cf.F. gambiller to kick about. Cf. Jamb, n., Gammon ham, Gambadoes.
OF. gambe, jambe leg, F. jambe. Cf. Cambrel, Chambrel, and see Gambol. n.

Cf. W. cam crooked, and E. gambol, n. | OE. game, gamen, AS. gamen, gomen, play, sport; akin to OS., OHG., & Icel. gaman, Dan. gammen mirth, merriment, OSw. gamman joy. Cf. Gammon a game, Backgammon, Gamble v. i. | OE. gamen, game, to rejoice, AS. gamenian to play. See Game, n.
Possibly contr. fr. godmother; but prob. fr. grammer for grandmother. Cf. Gaffer.
OF. gambon, F. jambon, fr. OF. gambe leg, F. jambe. See Gambol, n., and cf. Ham. | See 2d Game. | Etymol. unknown.
F. gamme + ut the name of a musical note. F. gamme is fr. the name of the Greek letter Gamma, and Ut.
Cf. F. ganche, n., also Sp. & Pg. gancho hook, It. gancio.
AS. gandra, ganra, akin to Prov. G. gander, ganter, and E. goose, gannet. See Goose.

AS. gangan, akin to OS. & OHG. gangan, Icel. ganga, Goth. gaggan; cf. Lith. to walk, Skr. ja leg. sq. root48. CF. Go. | Icel. gangr a going, gang, akin to AS., D., G., & Dan. gang a going, Goth. gaggs street, way. See Gang, v. i.
L. ganglion a sort of swelling or excrescence, a tumor under the skin, Gr. ganglion.
F. gangrène, L. gangraena, fr. Gr. gras, gar, to devour, and E. voracious, also canker, n., in sense 3. | Cf. F. gangréner.
F. gangue, fr. G. gang a metallic vein, a passage. See Gang, n.
OE. gant, AS. ganet, ganot, a sea fowl, a fen duck; akin to D. gent gander, OHG. ganazzo. See Gander, Goose.
Sp. gansa, ganso, goose; of Gothic origin. See Gannet, Goose.
OE. gap; cf. Icel. gap an empty space, Sw. gap mouth, breach, abyss, Dan. gab mouth, opening, AS. geap expanse; as adj., wide, spacious. See Gape.
OE. gapen, AS. geapan to open; akin to D. gapen to gape, G. gaffen, Icel. & Sw. gapa, Dan. gabe; cf. Skr. jabh to snap at, open the mouth. Cf. Gaby, Gap.
Prob. AS. gar dart, spear, lance. The name is applied to the fish on account of its long and slender body and pointed head. Cf. Goad, Gore, v. | Of Scand. origin. See Gear, n.

OF. garbe looks, countenance, grace, ornament, fr. OHG. garawi, garwi, ornament, dress. akin to E. gear. See Gear, n. | F. gerbe, OF. also garbe, OHG. garba, G. garbe; cf. Skr. grbh to seize, E. grab.

OE. also garbash, perh. orig., that which is purged or cleansed away; cf. OF. garber to make fine, neat, OHG. garawan to make ready, prepare, akin to E. garb dress; or perh. for garbleage, fr. garble; or cf. OF. garbage tax on sheaves, E. garb sheaf.

Formerly, to pick out, sort, OF. grabeler, for garbeler to examine precisely, garble spices, fr. LL. garbellare to sift; cf. Sp. garbillar to sift, garbillo a coarse sieve, L. cribellum, dim. of cribrum sieve, akin to cernere to separate, sift (cf. E. Discern); or perh. rather from Ar. gharbal, gharbil, sieve.
OF. garbouil; cf. Sp. garbullo, It. garbuglio; of uncertain origin; the last part is perh. fr. L. bullire to boil, E. boil.
OE. gardin, OF. gardin, jardin, F. jardin, of German origin; cf. OHG. garto, G. garten; akin to AS. geard. See Yard an inclosure.
F. gare l'eau beware of the water.
From Gargantua, an allegorical hero of Rabelais.
F. gargarisme, L. gargarisma. See Gargarize.
F. gargarizare, fr. Gr. Defn: To gargle; to rinse or wash, as the mouth and throat. [Obs.
OE. garget, gargate, throat, OF. gargate. Cf. Gorge. The etymol. of senses 2, 3, & 4 is not certain.
F. gargouiller to dabble, paddle, gargle. Cf. Gargoyle, Gurgle.
OE. garguilie, gargouille, cf. Sp. gárgola, prob. fr. the same source as F. gorge throat, influenced by L. gargarizare to gargle. See Gorge and cf. Gargle, Gargarize.
Cf. OE. gauren to stare; of uncertain origin. Cf. gairish.
OE. garland, gerlond, OF. garlande, F. guirlande; of uncertain origin; cf. OHG. wiara, wiera, crown, pure gold, MHG. wieren to adorn.
OE. garlek, AS. garleác; gar spear, lance + leác leek. See Gar, n., and Leek.
OE. garnement, OF. garnement, garniment, fr. garnir to garnish. See Garnish.
OE. garner, gerner, greiner, OF. gernier, grenier, F. grenier, fr. L. granarium, fr. granum. See 1st Grain, and cf. Granary.

OE. gernet, grenat, OF. grenet,grenat, F. grenat, LL. granatus, fr. L. granatum pomegranate, granatus having many grains or seeds, fr. granum grain, seed. So called from its resemblance in color and shape to the grains or seeds of the pomegranate. See Grain, and cf. Grenade, Pomegranate. | Etymol. unknown.
Named after the French geologist Garnier.

OE. garnischen, garnissen, OF. garnir to provide, strengthen, prepare, garnish, warn, F. garnir to provide, furnish, garnish, -- of German origin; cf. OHG. warnon to provide, equip; akin to G. wahren to watch, E. aware, ware, wary, and cf. also E. warn. See Wary, -ish, and cf. Garment, Garrison.
Cf. OF. garnissement protection, guarantee, warning.
F. garniture. See Garnish, v. t.
Gael. garrán, gearrán, gelding, work horse, hack.

OE. garite, garette, watchtower, place of lookout, OF. garite, also meaning, a place of refuge, F. guérite a place of refuge, donjon, sentinel box, fr. OF. garir to preserve, save, defend, F. guérir to cure; of German origin; cf. OHG. werian to protect, defend, hinder, G. wehren, akin to Goth. warjan to hinder, and akin to E. weir, or perhaps to wary. See Weir, and cf. Guerite.

OE. gaderen, AS. gaderian, gadrian, fr. gador, geador, together, fr. gæd fellowship; akin to E. good, D. gaderen to collect, G. gatte husband, MHG. gate, also companion, Goth. gadiliggs a sister's son. sq. root29. See Good, and cf. Together.

OF. gaugier, F. jauger, cf. OF. gauge gauge, measuring rod, F. jauge; of uncertain origin; perh. fr. an assumed L. qualificare to determine the qualities of a thing (see Qualify); but cf. also F. jalon a measuring stake in surveying, and E. gallon. | Written also gage.

OE. gentil, F. gentil noble, pretty, graceful, fr. L. gentilis of the same clan or race, fr. gens, gentis, tribe, clan, race, orig. that which belongs together by birth, fr. the root of genere, gignere, to beget; hence gentle, properly, of birth or family, that is, of good or noble birth. See Gender, and cf. Genteel, Gentil, Gentile, Gentoo, Jaunty.
Generally in the United States in the plural form.

OE. german, germain, F. germain, fr. L. germanus full, own (said of brothers and sisters who have the same parents); akin to germen germ. Cf. Germ, Germane. | L. Germanus, prob. of Celtis origin. | L. Germanus. See German, n.

OE. gigawe, gugawe, gewgaude, prob. the same word as OE. givegove gewgaw, apparently a reduplicated form fr. AS. gifan to give; cf. also F. joujou plaything, and E. gaud, n. See Give, and cf. Giffgaff.
Icel. geysir, fr. geysa to rush furiously, fr. gj to gush. Cf. Gush.

OE. gossomer, gossummer, gosesomer, perh. for goose summer, from its downy appearance, or perh. for God's summer, cf. G. mariengarr gossamer, properly Mary's yarn, in allusion to the Virgin Mary. Perhaps the E. word alluded to a legend that the gossamer was the remnant of the Virgin Mary's winding sheet, which dropped from her when she was taken up to heaven. For the use of summer in the sense of film or threads, cf. G. Mädchensommer, Altweibersommer, fliegender Sommer, all meaning, gossamer.

D. abberdaan, labberdaan; or a French form, cf. OF. habordeau, from the name of a Basque district, cf. F. Labourd, adj. Labourdin. The l was misunderstood as the French article.

F. habile, L. habilis. See Able, Habit.

OE. habit, abit fr. habit fr. L. habitus state, appearance, dress, fr. habere to have, be in a condition; prob. akin to E. have. See Have, and cf. OE. haceney, hacenay; cf. F. haquenée a pacing horse, an ambling nag, OF. also haquenée, Sp. hacanea, OSp. facanea, D. hakkenei, also OF. haque horse, Sp. haca, OSp. faca; perh akin to E. hack to cut, and orig. meaning, a jolting horse. Cf. Hack a horse, Nag.

F. hagard; of German origin, and prop. meaning, of the hegde or woods, wild, untamed. See Hedge, 1st Haw, and -ard. | See Haggard, a. | See 1st Haw, Hedge, and Yard an inclosed space.

Freq. of Scot. hag, E. hack. See Hack to cut.

OE. | OE. hailen, AS. haqalian. | OE. hailen, heilen, Icel. heil hale, sound, used in greeting. See Hale sound. | See Hail, v. t.

F. hallebarde; of German origin; cf. MHG. helmbarte, G. hellebarte; prob. orig., an ax to split a helmet, fr. G. barte a broad ax (orig. from the same source as E. beard; cf. Icel. bar, a kind of ax, skegg beard, skeggia a kind of halberd) + helm helmet; but cf. also MNG. helm, halm, handle, and E. helve. See Beard, Helmet.
Written also heil, Icel. heill; akin to E. whole. See Whole. | OE. halen, halien; cf. AS. holian, to acquire, get. See Haul.
AS. healf, half, half; as a noun, half, side, part; akin to OS., OFries., & D. half, G. halb, Sw. half, Dan. halv, Icel. halfr, Goth. halbs. Cf. Halve, Behalf. | AS. healf. See Half, a.
OE. halfendele. See Half, and Deal.
OE. hali holy + but, butte, flounder; akin to D. bot, G. butte; cf. D. heilbot, G. heilbutt. So named as being eaten on holidays. See Holy, Holiday.
AS. haligd holiness, sacrament, sanctuary, relics; halig holy + -d, E. -dom. See Holy.
L. halitus breath, vapor, fr. halare to breathe: cf. F. halitueux.
OE. halle, hal, AS. heal, heall; akin to D. hal, OS. & OHG. halla, G. halle, Icel. hölt, and prob. from a root meaning, to hide, conceal, cover. See Hell, Helmet.
Perh. fr. ah + lo; cf. AS. eala, G. halloh, F. haler to set (a dog) on. Cf. Hollo, interj. | OE. halow. See Halloo, n.
OE. halowen, halwien, halgien, AS. halgian, fr. halig holy. See Holy.
L. hallucinatus, alucinatus, p. p. of hallucinari, alucinari, to wander in mind, talk idly, dream.
L. halos, acc. halo, Gr. volvere, and E. voluble.
AS. heals; akin to D., G., & Goth. hals. See Collar.
Formerly alt, It. alto, G. halt, fr. halten to hold. See Hold. | AS. healt; akin to OS., Dan., & Sw. halt, Icel. haltr, halltr, Goth. halts, OHG. halz. | OE. halten, AS. healtian. See Halt, a.
OE. halter, helter, helfter, AS. hælftre; akin to G. halfter, D. halfter, halster, and also to E. helve. See Helve.
OE., fr. AS. halga. See Holy.

L. Hamadryas, -adis, Gr. hamadryade. See Same, and Tree.
OE. hamelen to mutilate, AS. hamelian; akin to OHG. hamal to mutilate, hamal mutilated, ham mutilated, Icel. hamla to mutilate. Cf.Ham to fetter.

OWE. hamelet, OF. hamelet, dim. of hamel, F. hameau, LL. hamellum, a dim. of German origin; cf. G. heim home. sq. root220. See Home.
OE. hamer, AS. hamer, hamor; akin to D. hamer, G. & Dan. hammer, Sw. hammare, Icel. hamarr, hammer, crag, and perh. to Gr. a stone.
Prob. fr. D. hemel heaven, canopy, tester (akin to G. himmel, and perh. also to E. heaven) + E. cloth; or perh. a corruption of hamper cloth.

A word of Indian origin: cf. Sp. hamaca. Columbus, in the Narrative of his first voyage, says: "A great many Indians in canoes came to the ship to-day for the purpose of bartering their cotton, and hamacas, or nets, in which they sleep."
Contr. fr. hanaper. | OE. hamperen, hampren, prob. of the same origin as E. hamble. | See Hamper to shackle.
L. hamulus, dim. of hamus a hook.
LL. hanaperium a large vase, fr. hanaus vase, bowl, cup (whence F. hanap); of German origin; cf. ONG. hnapf, G. napf, akin to AS. hnæp cup, bowl. Cf. Hamper, Nappy, n.
AS. hand, hond; akin to D., G., & Sw. hand, OHG. hant, Dan. haand, Icel. hönd, Goth. handus, and perh. to Goth. hinpan to seize (in comp.). Cf. Hunt.
Hand + book; cf. AS. handb, or G. handbuch.

G. handfest; hand hand + fest strong. See Fast.
From hand in cap; -- perh. in reference to an old mode of setting a bargain by taking pieces of money from a cap.
For handcraft, influenced by handiwork; AS. handcræft.
OE. handiwerc, AS. handgeweorc; hand hand + geweorc work; prefix ge- + weorc. See Work.
OE. handlen, AS. handian; akin to D. handelen to trade, G. handeln. See Hand. | AS. handle. See Hand.

Hand + -some. It at first meant, dexterous; cf. D. handzaam dexterous, ready, limber, manageable, and E. handy.
OE. hendi, AS. hendig (in comp.), fr. hand hand; akin to D. handig, Goth. handugs clever, wise.

OE. hangen, hangien, v. t. & i., AS. hangian, v. i., fr. h, v. t. (imp. heng, p. p. hongen); akin to OS. hang, v. i. D. hangen, v. t. & i., G. hangen, v. i, hängen, v. t, Isel hanga, v. i., Goth. hahan, v. t. (imp. haíhah), hahan, v. i. (imp. hahaida), and perh. to L. cunctari to delay. sq. root37.
Cf. Dan. hank handle, Sw. hank a band or tie, Icel. hanki hasp, clasp, hönk, hangr, hank, coil, skein, G. henkel, henk, handle; ar prob. akin to E. hang. See Hang. | OE. hanken.

F. harangue: cf. Sp. arenda, It. aringa; lit., a speech before a multitude or on the hustings, It. aringo arena, hustings, pulpit; all fr. OHG. hring ring, anything round, ring of people, G. ring. See Ring. | Cf. F. haranguer, It. aringare.
F. harasser; cf. OF. harace a basket made of cords, harace, harasse,a very heavy and large shield; or harer to set (a dog) on.
OE. herbergeour, OF. herbergeor one who provides lodging, fr. herbergier to provide lodging, F. héberger, OF. herberge lodging, inn, F. auberge; of German origin. See Harbor.

OE herbor, herberwe, herberge, Icel. herbergi (cf. OHG. heriberga), orig., a shelter for soldiers; herr army + bjarga to save, help, defend; akin to AS. here army, G. heer, OHG. heri, Goth. harjis, and AS. beorgan to save, shelter, defend, G. bergen. See Harry, 2d Bury, and cf. Harbinger. | OE. herberen, herberwen, herbergen; cf. Icel. herbergja. See Harbor, n.

OE. heard, AS. heard; akin to OS. & D. heard, G. hart, OHG. harti, Icel. har, Dan. haard, Sw. hård, Goth. hardus, Gr.,, strength, and also to E. -ard, as in coward, drunkard, -crat, -cracy in autocrat, democracy; cf. Skr. kratu strength, to do, make. Gf.Hardy. | OE. harde, AS. hearde.

OE.harlot, herlot, a vagabond, OF. harlot, herlot, arlot; cf. Pr. arlot, Sp. arlote, It. arlotto; of uncertain origin.
OE.harm, hearm, AS.hearm; akin to OS. harm, G. harm grief, Icel. harmr, Dan. harme, Sw. harm; cf. OSlav. & Russ. sram' shame, Skr. crama toil, fatigue. | OE. harmen, AS. hearmian. See Harm, n.
F. harmattan, prob. of Arabic origin.
L. harmonicus, Gr. harmonique. See Harmony.
Fem. fr. L. harmonicus harmonic. See Harmonic, n.

OE. harneis, harnes, OF.harneis, F. harnais, harnois; of Celtic origin; cf. Armor. harnez old iron, armor, W. haiarn iron, Armor. houarn, Ir. iarann, Gael. iarunn. Gf. Iron. | OE. harneisen; cf. F. harnacher, OF. harneschier.

F. harpon, LL. harpo, perh. of Ger. origin, fr. the harp; cf. F. harper to take and grasp strongly, harpe a dog's claw, harpin boathook (the sense of hook coming from the shape of the harp); but cf. also Gr. harpy. Cf. Harp.
OF. harpechorde, in which the harpe is of German origin. See Harp, and Chord.
F. harpie, L. harpyia, Gr. Rapacious.

OE. | OE. harowen, harwen; cf. Dan. harve. See Harrow, n. | OF. harau, haro; fr. OHG. hara, hera, herot, or fr. OS. herod hither, akin to E. here. | See Harry.

OF. harwen, herien, her, AS. hergisn to act as an army, to ravage, plunder, fr. here army; akin to G. here army; akin to G. heer, Icel. herr, Goth. harjis, and Lith. karas war. Gf. Harbor, Herald, Heriot.
OE. harsk; akin to G. harsch, Dan. harsk rancid, Sw. härsk; from the same source as E. hard. See Hard, a.
OE.hart, hert, heort, AS. heort, heorot; akin to D. hert, OHG. hiruz, hirz, G. hirsch, Icel. hjörtr, Dan. & Sw. hjort, L. cervus, and prob. to Gr.Horn.

Cf. hare,v. t., and scare, v. t.
OE. harvest, hervest, AS. hærfest autumn; akin to LG. harfst, D. herfst, OHG. herbist, G. herbst, and prob. to L. carpere to pluck, Gr. Carpet.
Cf. OF. harier to harass, or E. harry, v. t.
Formerly hachey, hachee, F. hachis, hacher to hash; of German origin; cf. G. hippe sickle, OHG. hippa, for happia. Cf. Hatchet. | From Hash, n.: cf. F. hacher to hash.
F. hâtelettes broil, for hastelettes, fr. F. haste spit; cf. L. hasta spear, and also OHG. harst gridiron.
OE. hasp, hesp, AS. hæpse; akin to G. haspe, häspe, Sw. & Dan. haspe, Icel. hespa. | AS. hæpsian.
Scot. hassock, hassik, a besom, anything bushy, a large, round turf used as a seat, OE. hassok sedgy ground, W. hesgog sedgy, hesg sedge, rushes; cf. Ir. seisg, and E. sedge.
L. hastatus, fr. hasta spear. Cf. Gad, n.
L. hastatus, fr. hasta spear. Cf. Gad, n.

OE. hast; akin to D. haast, G., Dan., Sw., & OFries. hast, cf. OF. haste, F. hâte (of German origin); all perh. fr. the root of E. hate in a earlier sense of, to pursue. See Hate. | OE. hasten; akin to G. hasten, D. haasten, Dan. haste, Sw. hasta, OF. haster, F. hâter. See Haste, n.
OF. hastif. See Haste, n., and cf. Hastif.
Akin to D. haastig, G., Sw., & Dan. hastig. See Haste, n.
AS. hæt, hætt; akin to Dan. hat, Sw. hatt, Icel. hattr a hat, höttr hood, D. hoed hat, G. hut, OHG. huot, and prob. to L. cassis helmet. Hood.

As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not. Jer. xvii. 11. For the hens do not sit upon the eggs; but by keeping them in a certain equal heat they [the husbandmen | OE. hacche, AS. hæc, cf. haca the bar of a door, D. hek gate, Sw. häck coop, rack, Dan. hekke manger, rack. OE. hechele, hekele; akin to D. hekel, G. hechel, Dan. hegle, Sw. häkla, and prob. to E. hook. See Hook, and cf. Hackle, Heckle. | OE. hechelen, hekelen; akin to D. hekelen, G. hecheln, Dan. hegle, Sw. häkla. See Hatchel, n.
F. hachette, dim. of hache Hatch, Hash.

OE. haten, hatien, AS. hatian; akin to OS. hatan, hat to be hostile to, D. haten to hate, OHG. hazz, hazz, G. hassen, Icel. & Sw. hata, Dan. hade, Goth. hatan, hatian. . Cf. Hate, n., Heinous. | OE. hate, hete, AS. hete; akin to D. haat, G. hass, Icel. hatr, SW. hat, Dan. had, Goth. hatis. Cf. Hate, v.

Prov. E., to entangle; cf. LG. verhaddern, verheddern, verhiddern.
Turk., fr. Ar. knatt a writing + sherif noble.
OF. hauberc, halberc, F.haubert, OHG. halsberc; hals neck + bergan to protect, G. bergen; akin to AS. healsbeorg, Icel. halsbjörg. See Collar, and Bury, v. t.
Named after Von Hauer, of Vienna.
OE. hautein, F. hautain, fr. haut high, OF. also halt, fr. L. altus. See Altitude.

OE. halen, halien, F. geholian to acquire, get, D. halen to fetch, pull, draw, OHG. hol, hal, G. holen, Dan. hale to haul, Sw. hala, and to L. calare to call, summon, Gr. Hale, v. t., Claim. Class, Council, Ecclesiastic.
OE. halm, AS. healm; akin to D., G., Dan., & Sw. halm, Icel. halmr, L. calamus reed, cane, stalk, Gr. Excel, Culminate, Culm, Shawm, Calamus.
OF. hault, F. haut. See Haughty.
F. hanche, of German origin; cf. OD. hancke, hencke, and also OHG. ancha; prob. not akin to E. ankle.
F. hanter; of uncertain origin, perh. from an assumed LL. ambitare to go about, fr. L. ambire (see Ambition); or cf. Icel. heimta to demand, regain, akin to heim home (see Home). sq. root36.
L. hauriens, p. pr. of haurire to breathe.
NL., fr. haustellum, fr. L. haurire, haustum, to draw water, to swallow. See Exhaust.
LL., a well, fr. L. haurire, haustum, to drink.
F. hautbois, lit., high wood; haut high + bois wood. So called on account of its high tone. See Haughty, Bush; and cf. Oboe.
F., fr. haut high. See Haughty.

OE. haven, habben, AS. habben (imperf. hæfde, p. p. gehæfd); akin to OS. hebbian, D. hebben, OFries, hebba, OHG. hab, G. haben, Icel. hafa, Sw. hafva, Dan. have, Goth. haban, and prob. to L. habere, whence F. avoir. Cf. Able, Avoirdupois, Binnacle, Habit.
From Havelock, an English general distinguished in India in the rebellion of 1857.

AS. hæfene; akin to D. & LG. haven, G. hafen, MNG. habe, Dan. havn, Icel. höfn, Sw. hamn; akin to E. have, and hence orig., a holder; or to heave (see Heave); or akin to AS. hæf sea, Icel. & Sw. haf, Dan. hav, which is perh. akin to E. heave.
D. haver; akin to G. haber. | Etymol. uncertain.
F. havresac, G. habersack, sack for oats. See 2d Haver, and Sack a bag.
OE. havour, a corruption of OF. aveir, avoir, a having, of same origin as E. aver a work horse. The h is due to confusion with E. have.
W. hafog devastation, havoc; or, if this be itself fr. E. havoc, cf. OE. havot, or AS. hafoc hawk, which is a cruel or rapacious bird, or F. hai, voux! a cry to hounds. | See Havoc, n.

OE. hawe, AS. haga; akin to D. haag headge, G. hag, hecke, Icel. hagi pasture, Sw. hage, Dan. have garden. Haggard, Ha- ha, Haugh, Hedge. | Etymol. uncertain. | Cf. ha an interjection of wonder, surprise, or hesitation. | Written also hoi.

OE. hauk (prob. fr. Icel.), havek, AS. hafoc, heafoc; akin to D. havik, OHG. habuh, G. habicht, Icel. haukr, Sw. hök, Dan. hög, prob. from the root of E. heave. | W. hochi. | W. hoch. | Akin to D. hauker a hawker, G. höken, höcken, to higgle, to retail, höke, höker, a higgler, huckster. See Huckster.
Orig. a hawse hole, or hole in the ship; cf. Icel. hals, hals, neck, part of the bows of a ship, AS. heals neck. See Collar, and cf. Halse to embrace.
From F. hausser to hausserée towpath, towing, F. haussière hawser), LL. altiare, fr. L. altus high. See Haughty.
AS. hagaborn, hæg. See Haw a hedge, and Thorn.

AS. hege: cf. F. haie, of German origin. See Haw a hedge, Hedge. | OE. hei, AS. h; akin to D. kooi, OHG. hewi, houwi, G. heu, Dan. & Sw. hö, Icel. hey, ha, Goth. hawi grass, fr. the root of E. hew. See Hew to cut.
See Hay hedge, and Bote, and cf. Hedgebote.

F. hazard, Sp. azar an unforeseen disaster or accident, an unfortunate card or throw at dice, prob. fr. Ar. zahr, zar, a die, which, with the article al the, would give azzahr, azzar. | Cf. F. hazarder. See Hazard, n.

OE. hord, AS. hord; akin to OS. hord, G. hort, Icel. hodd, Goth. huzd; prob. from the root of E. hide to conceal, and of L. custos guard, E. custody. See Hide to conceal. | AS. hordian.
From OF. hourd, hourt, barrier, palisade, of German or Dutch origin; cf. D. horde hurdle, fence, G. horde, hürde; akin to E. hurdle. sq. root16. See Hurdle.

So called from Hochheim, in Germany. |  AS. h the heel; prob. akin to Icel. hasinn hock sinew, Dan. hasc, G. hechse, hächse, LG. hacke, D.hak; also to L. coxa hip (cf. Cuisses), Skr. kaksha armpit. sq. root12. Cf. Heel.
