From the same source as hog; prob. orig., a sheep clipped the first year. See Hog.
Icel. haugr hill, mound; akin to E. high. See High.
D. okshoofd; akin to Sw. oxhufvud, Dan. oxehoved, G. oxhoft; apparently meaning orig., ox head, but it is not known why this name was given. Cf. Ox, Head.
OE. hoydon a lout, rustic, OD. heyden a heathen, gypsy, vagabond, D. heiden, fr. OD. heyde heath, D. heide. See Heathen, Heath.
OE. hoise, hyse, OD. hyssen, D. hijshen; akin to LG. hissen, Dan. hisse, Sw. hissa.
Gf. W. hoetian to dally, dandle.
Gr. 'olka`s, -a`dos, a ship which is towed, a ship of burden, fr. 'e`lkein to draw. Gf. Hulk.
D. hol hole, hollow. See Hole. | OE. haldan, D. houden, OHG. hoten, Icel. halda, Dan. holde, Sw. hålla, Goth. haldan to feed, tend (the cattle); of unknown origin. Gf. Avast, Halt, Hod.

OE. hol, hole, AS. hol, hole, cavern, from hol, a., hollow; akin to D. hol, OHG. hol, G. hohl, Dan.huul hollow, hul hole, Sw. hål, Icel. hola; prob. from the root of AS. helan to conceal. See Hele, Hell, and cf. Hold of a ship. | AS. holian. See Hole, n.
F. hola; ho ho + là there, fr. L. illac that way, there. Cf. Hollo.
See Halloo, and cf. Holla. | See Hollo, intery., and cf. Halloo.
OE. holow, holgh, holf, AS. holh a hollow, hole. Cf. Hole. | See Hollo.
OE holi, holin, AS. holen, holegn; akin to D. & G. hulst, OHG. huls hulis, W. celyn, Armor. kelen, Gael. cuilionn, Ir. cuileann. Cf. 1st Holm, Hulver.
OE. holihoc; holi holy + hoc mallow, AS. hoc; cf. W. hocys mallows, hocys bendigaid hollyhock, lit., blessed mallow. Prob. so named because brought from the Holy Land. See Holy.

OE., prob. from AS. holen holly; as the holly is also called holm. See Holly. | AS. holm, usually meaning, sea, water; akin to Icel. holmr, holmr, an island, Dan. holm, Sw. holme, G. holm, and prob. to E. hill. Cf. Hill.
L. holocaustum, Gr. "o'los whole + kaysto`s burnt, fr. kai`ein to burn (cf. Caustic): cf. F. holocauste.
L.holographus entirely autograph, Gr. "olo`grafos; "o`los whole + gra`fein to write: cf. F. holographe, olographe.
NL., fr. Gr. "o`los whole + sto`ma, - atos, mouth.
D. holster; skin to AS. heolstor den, cave, fr.helan to conceal, and to Icel. hulstr case, Goth.hulistr covering, veil, huljan to cover. sq. root17. See Hele to cover, Hell, and cf. Housing, Houss.

OE. holi, hali, AS.halig, fr. hæl health, salvation, happiness, fr. hal whole, well; akin to OS. h, D. & G.heilig, OHG. heilac, Dan. hellig, Sw. helig, Icel. heilagr. See Whole, and cf. Halibut, Halidom, Hallow, Hollyhock.

OF.homage, homenage, F. hommage, LL. hominaticum, homenaticum, from L. homo a man, LL. also, a client, servant, vassal; akin to L. humus earth, Gr.groom in bridegroom. Cf. Bridegroom, Human. | Cf. OF. hommager.
F., fr. L. homicidium, fr. homicida a man slayer; homo man + caedere to cut, kill. See Homage, and cf. Concise, Shed, v. t.
LL. homilia, Gr. homélie. See Same.

Gr. homogène. See Same, and Kin.
Gr. "omo`grafos with the same letters; "omo`s the same + gra`fein to write.

OE. honest, onest, OF. honeste, oneste, F. honnête, L. honestus, fr. honos, honor, honor. See Honor. | L. honestare to clothe or adorn with honor: cf. F. honester. See Honest, a.
OE. honeste, oneste, honor, OF. honesté, onesté (cf. F. honnêteté), L. honestas. See Honest, a.

See 1st Hoop. | So called from its note.
So called from its cry; cf. L. upupa, Gr. hop, F. huppe; cf. also G. wiedenhopf, OHG. wituhopfo, lit., wood hopper.
So called from its cry; cf. L. upupa, Gr. hop, F. huppe; cf. also G. wiedenhopf, OHG. wituhopfo, lit., wood hopper.
OE. hoten, houten, huten; cf. OSw. huta, Sw. huta ut to take one up sharply, fr. Sw. hut interj., begone! cf. also W. hwt off! off with it! away! hoot!

Cf. Icel. hop a small bay or inlet. | AS., akin to D. hoop, hope, Sw. hopp, Dan. haab, MHG. hoffe. Hope in forlorn hope is different word. See Forlorn hope, under Forlorn. | AS. hopian; akin to D. hopen, Sw. hopp, Dan. haabe, G. hoffen. See 2nd Hope.
Named after Professor Hope, of Edinburgh.

G., fr. horn horn + blende blende.
AS. hyrnet; akin to OHG. hornaz, hornuz, G. horniss; perh. akin to E. horn, and named from the sound it makes as if blowing the horn; but more prob. akin to D. horzel, Lith. szirszone, L. crabo.
A dim. fr. Sp. horno oven, L. furnus. See Furnace.
OE. horologe, orloge, timepiece, OF. horloge, orloge, oriloge, F. horloge, L. horologium, fr. Gr. Hour, and Logic.

L. horrisonus; horrere to be horrible + sonus a sound.

Gr. hoshi'ah nnasave now, save, we pray, hoshia' to save (Hiphil, a causative form, of yasha') + na, a particle.

F., fr. L. hospitium hospitality, a place where strangers are entertained, fr. hospes stranger, guest. See Host a landlord.
Cf. OF. hospitable, LL. hospitare to receive as a guest. See Host a landlord.

OF. hospital, ospital, F. hôpital, LL. hospitale (or perh. E. hospital is directly from the Late Latin), from L. hospitalis relating to a guest, hospitalia apartments for guests, fr. hospes guest. See Host a landlord, and cf. Hostel, Hotel, Spital. | L. hospitalis: cf. OF. hospital.
F. hospitalier. See Hospital, and cf. Hostler.
L. hospitatus, p.p. of hospitari to be a guest, fr. hospes guest.

Host a landlord. | OE. host, ost, OF. hoste, oste, F. hôte, from L. hospes a stranger who is treated as a guest, he who treats another as his guest, a hostl prob. fr. hostis stranger, enemy (akin to E. guest a visitor) + potis able; akin to Skr. pati master, lord. See Host an army, Possible, and cf. Hospitable, Hotel.

OE. hostage, OF. hostage, ostage, F. ôtage, LL. hostaticus, ostaticum, for hospitaticum, fr. L. hospes guest, host. The first meaning is, the state of a guest, hospitality; hence, the state of a hostage (treated as a guest); and both these meanings occur in Old French. See Host a landlord.
OE. hostel, ostel, OF. hostel, ostel, LL. hospitale, hospitalis, fr. L. hospitalis. See Hospital, and cf. Hotel.
OE. hostelrie, hostelrye, ostelrie, OF. hostelerie, fr. hostel. See Hostel.
OE. hostesse, ostesse. See Host a landlord.
L. hostilis, from hostis enemy: cf. F. hostile. See Host an army.
OE. hosteler, osteler, innkeeper, OF. hostelier, F. hôtelier. See Hostel, and cf. Hospitaler, Hosteler.
OE. hosterie, osterie, OF. hosterie. See Host a landlord.
OE. hot, hat, AS. hat; akin to OS. het, D. heet, OHG. heiz, G. heiss, Icel. heitr, Sw. het, Dan. heed, hed; cf. Goth. heito fever, hais torch. Cf. Heat.
F. hochepot, fr. hocher to shake + pot pot; both of Dutch or German origin; cf. OD. hutspot hotchpotch, D. hotsen, hutsen, to shake. See Hustle, and Pot, and cf. Hodgepodge.
F. hochepot, fr. hocher to shake + pot pot; both of Dutch or German origin; cf. OD. hutspot hotchpotch, D. hotsen, hutsen, to shake. See Hustle, and Pot, and cf. Hodgepodge.
Hot + cockle, cockle being perh. corrupt. fr. knuckle. Cf. F. main chaude (lit., hot hand) hotcockles.
F. hôtel, OF. hostel. See Hostel.
D. Hottentot; -- so called from hot and tot, two syllables of frequent occurrence in their language. Wedgwood.

AS. h the heel; prob. akin to Icel. hasinn hock sinew, Dan. hasc, G. hechse, hächse, LG. hacke, D.hak; also to L. coxa hip (cf. Cuisses), Skr. kaksha armpit. sq. root12. Cf. Heel. | Cf. D. hak. Cf. Hack.

OE. hound, hund, dog, AS. hund; akin to OS. & OFries. hund, D. hond, G. hund, OHG. hunt, Icel. hundr, Dan. & Sw. hund, Goth. hunds, and prob. to Lith. sz, Ir. & Gael. cu, L. canis, Gr. çvan. sq. root229. Cf. Canine, Cynic, Kennel.
OE. hour, our, hore, ure, OF. hore, ore, ure, F. heure, L. hora, fr. Gr. Year, and cf. Horologe, Horoscope.
Per. huri, hura, hur; akin to Ar. hur, pl. of ahwar beautiful-eyed, black-eyed.
A translation of L. Horae (Gr. Hour.

OE. hous, hus, AS. h; akin to OS. & OFries. h, D. huis, OHG. h, G. haus, Icel. h, Sw. hus, Dan. huus, Goth. gudh, house of God, temple; and prob. to E. hide to conceal. See Hide, and cf. Hoard, Husband, Hussy, Husting. | AS. h.
OE. huscarle. See House, and Carl.
OE. housel, husel, AS. h; akin to Icel. h, Goth. hunsl a sacrifice. | AS. h.
From House. In some of its senses this word has been confused with the following word. | From Houss.
F. housse, LL. hulcia, fr. OHG. hulst; akin to E. holster. See Holster, and cf. 2d Housing.

Etymol. doubtful. | OE. hoveren, and hoven, prob. orig., to abide, linger, and fr. AS. hof house; cf. OFries. hovia to receive into one's house. See Hovel.

OE. how, hou, hu, hwu, AS. h, from the same root as hwa, hwæt, who, what, pron. interrog.; akin to OS. hwow, D. hoe, cf. G. wie how, Goth. hwe wherewith, hwaiwa how. sq. root182. See Who, and cf. Why.
Scot., also houdy- wife. Of uncertain origin; cf. OSw. jordgumma; or perh. fr. E. how d'ye.
G. haubitze, formerly hauffnitz, Bohem. haufnice, orig., a sling.
OE. houlen, hulen; akin to D. huilen, MHG. hiulen, hiuweln, OHG. hiuwilon to exult, h owl, Dan. hyle to howl.

D. heu, or Flem. hui. | D. hui. Cf. Ahoy.
Cf. Whoobub, Whoop, Hoop, v. i.
See Hawk to offer for sale, Huckster.
Perh. orig., peddler's wares; cf. LG. hukkebak pickback. Cf. Huckster.
Perh. dim. of Prov. E. hucka hook, and so named from its round shape. See Hook.

Cf. OE. hoderen, hodren, to cover, keep, warm; perh. akin to OE. huden, hiden, to hide, E. hide, and orig. meaning, to get together for protection in a safe place. Cf. Hide to conceal.
OE. hew, heow, color, shape, form, AS. hiw, heow; akin to Sw. hy skin, complexion, Goth. hiwi form, appearance. | OE. hue, huer, to hoot, shout, prob. fr. OF. hu an exclamation.
Cf. OE. hoove to puff up, blow; prob. of imitative origin.
Prob. of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. sidde paa huk to squat, Sw. huka sig to squat, Icel. h. Cf. Huckster.
OE. huge, hoge, OF. ahuge, ahoge.
Scot. huggrie-muggrie; Prov. E. hugger to lie in ambush, mug mist, muggard sullen.
F., properly a dim. of Hugues. The name is probably derived from the Christian name (Huguenot) of some person conspicuous as a reformer.
Native name; -- so called from its cry.
OF. huque, LL. huca; cf. D. huik.

OE. hulfere; prob. akin to E. holly.

Prob. a dim. of hump. See Hump.

Cf. L. humorosus, umorosus, moist. See Humor.
Cf. D. homp a lump, LG. hump heap, hill, stump, possibly akin to E. heap. Cf. Hunch.
NL. Humulus, the genus including the hop.
L. Hunni, also Chunni, and Chuni; cf. AS. H, H, OHG. H, G. Hunnen.

OE. prechen, OF. preechier, F. prêcher, fr. L. praedicare to cry in public, to proclaim; prae before + dicare to make known, dicere to say; or perhaps from (assumed) LL. praedictare. See Diction, and cf. Predicate, Predict. | Cf. F. prêche, fr. prêcher. See Preach, v.
Cf. OF. preeschierre, prescheur, F. prêcheur, L. praedicator.
LL. praeambulum, from L. praeambulus walking before, fr. praeambulare to walk before; prae before + ambulare to walk: cf. F. préambule. See Amble.
F. prébende (cf. It. & Sp. prebenda), from L. praebenda, from L. praebere to hold forth, afford, contr. fr. praehibere; prae before + habere to have, hold. See Habit, and cf. Provender.
LL. praebendarius: cf. F. prébendaire. See Prebend.
LL. praebendatus, p. p. of praebendari.
L. precans, -antis, p. pr. of precari to pray.

L. precativus, precatorius, fr. precari to pray. See Precarious.
L. precativus, precatorius, fr. precari to pray. See Precarious.
F. précation, L. praecautio, fr. praecavere, praecautum, to guard against beforehand; prae before + cavere be on one's guard. See Pre-, and Caution. | Cf. F. précautionner.
L. praecedere, praecessum; prae before + cedere to go, to be in motion: cf. F. préceder. See Pre-, and Cede.
L. praecedens, -entis, p. pr. of praecedere: cf. F. précédent. See Precede.
L. praecellentia, from praecellens, p. pr. of praecellere to excel, surpass: cf. OF. precellence.
L. praecellentia, from praecellens, p. pr. of praecellere to excel, surpass: cf. OF. precellence.
L. praecentor, fr. praecinere to sing before; prae before + canere to sing. See Chant.
L. praeceptum, from praecipere to take beforehand, to instruct, teach; prae before + capere to take: cf. F. précepte. See Pre-, and Capacious.
L. praeceptor, fr. praecipere to teach: cf. F. précepteur. See Precept.
LL. praeceptoria an estate assigned to a preceptor, from L. praeceptor a commander, ruler, teacher, in LL., procurator, administrator among the Knights Templars. See Preceptor.
L. praecedere, praecessum, to go before: cf. F. précession. See Precede.
LL. praecinctum, fr. L. praecingere, praecinctum, to gird about, to encompass; prae before + cingere to gird, surround. See Pre-, and Cincture.
OF. precious, precius, precios, F. précieux, L. pretiosus, fr. pretium price, worth, value. See Price.
F. précipice, L. praecipitium, fr. praeceps, - cipitis, headlong; prae before + caput, capitis, the head. See Pre-, and Chief.
L. praecipiens, p. pr. See Precept.
L. praecipitans, -antis, p. pr. of praecipitare: cf. F. précipitant. See Precipitate.
L. praecipitatus, p. p. of praecipitare to precipitate, fr. praeceps headlong. See Precipice. | NL. praecipitatum: cf. F. précipité.
L. praeceps, -cipitis: cf. OF. precipiteux. See Precipice.
L. praecisus cut off, brief, concise, p. p. of praecidere to cut off in front, to cut off; prae before + caedere to cut: cf. F. précis. Cf. Concise.
Cf. F. précision, L. praecisio a cutting off. See Precise.
L. praecludere, praeclusum; prae before + claudere to shut. See Close, v.

L. praecogitatus, p. p. of praecogitare. See Pre-, and Cogitate.
L. praecognitio, fr. praecognoscere to foreknow. See Pre-, and Cognition.
L. praeconium a crying out in public, fr. praeco, -onis, a crier, a herald: cf. F. préconisation.
Pref. pre- + L. cor, cordis, heart: cf. F. précordial.
L. praecursor, fr. praecurrere to run before; prae before + currere to run. See Course.
L. praedatio, fr. praedari to plunder.
L. praedatorius, fr. praedari to plunder, fr. praeda prey. See Prey.

L. praedecessor; prae before + decessor one who withdraws from the province he has governed, a retiring officer (with reference to his successor), a predecessor, fr. decedere: cf. F. prédécesseur. See Decease.
L. praedestinatus, p. p. of praedestinare to predestine; prae before + destinare to determine. See Destine. | Cf. Predestine.
Pref. pre- + determine: cf. F. prédéterminer.
L. praedium a farm, estate: cf. F. prédial.
Cf. F. prédicable, L. praedicabilis praiseworthy. See Predicate.
Cf. F. prédicament, L. praedicamentum. See Predicate.
L. praedicans, -antis, p. pr. of praedicare. See Predicate.
L. praedicatus, p. p. of praedicare to cry in public, to proclaim. See Preach. | L. praedicatum, neut. of praedicatus, p. p. praedicare: cf. F. prédicat. See Predicate, v. t. | L. praedicatus, p. p.
L. praedictus, p. p. of praedicere to predict; prae before + dicere to say, tell. See Diction, and cf. Preach.
Pref. pre- + L. dilectus, p. p. diligere to prefer: cf. F. prédilection. See Diligent.
Pref. pre- + dispose: cf. F. prédisposer.

Pref. pre- + dominate: cf. F. prédominer.
F. pré\'82minence, L. praeeminentia. See Preëminent.
L. praeminens, -entis, p. pr. praeminere to be prominent, to surpass: cf. F. pré\'82minent. See Pre-, and Eminent.
Pref. pre- + emption: cf. F. préemption. See Redeem.
AS. preón a clasp, bodkin; akin to D. priem punch, bodkin, awl, G. pfriem, Icel. prjonn a knitting needle, pin, Dan. preen a bodkin, punch. | See Preen, n.; or cf. Prune.
F. préface; cf. Sp. prefacio, prefacion, It. prefazio, prefazione; all fr. L. praefatio, fr. praefari to speak or say beforehand; prae before + fari, fatus, to speak. See Fate.
L. praefectus, fr. praefectus, p. p. of praeficere to set over; prae before + facere to make: cf. F. préfet.
F. préférer, L. praeferre; prae before + ferre to bear or carry. See 1st Bear.
Cf. L. praefidens overconfident. See Pre-, and Confident.
L. praefiguratus, p. p. See Prefigure.
F. préfigurer, or L. praefigurare, praefiguratum; prae before + figurare to figure. See Figure, and cf. Prefigurate.
L. praefinire; prae before + finire to limit, determine: cf. F. préfiner.
L. praefixus, p. p. of praefigere to fix or fasten before; prae before + figere to fix: cf. F. préfix fixed beforehand, determined, préfixer to prefix. See Fix. | Cf. F. préfixe.
Pref. pre- + L. flos, floris, flower.
L. praeformare. See Pre-, and Form.
L. praefulgens, p. pr. of praefulgere to shine forth. See Pre-, and Fulgent.
L. praegnans, -antis; prae before + genere, gignere, to beget: cf. F. prégnant. See Gender, 2d Kin. | F. prenant taking. Cf. Pregnable.
L. praegravatus, p. p. of praegravare to be heavy upon, fr. praegravis very heavy.
L. praegustans, p. pr. of praegustare to taste beforehand; prae before + gustare to taste.
L. prehensus, p. p. of prehendere to lay hold of, seize; pre- (equiv. to prae before) + hendere (in comp.), akin to E. get: cf. F. préhensile. See Get, and cf. Prison, Prize, n.
L. prehensio; cf. F. préhension. See Prehensile.
So called from the German Colonel Prehn, who first found it.
Pref. pre + judge: cf. F. préjuger. Cf. Prejudicate, Prejudice.
L. praejudicatus, p. p. of praejudicare to prejudge; prae before + judicare to judge. See Judge. | Cf. Prejudge.
F. préjudice, L. praejudicium; prae before + judicium judgment. See Prejudicate, Judicial. | Cf. F. préjudicier. See Prejudice, n.
L. praejudicialis belonging to a preceding judgment: cf. F. préjudiciel.
LL. praelatia. See Prelate; cf. Prelaty.
F. prélat, LL. praelatus, fr. L. praelatus, used as p. p. of praeferre to prefer, but from a different root. See Elate.
L. praelatio: cf. F. prélation. See Prelate, and cf. Prefer.
L. praelectus, p. p. of praelegere to read before. See Pre-, and Lection.
L. praelibatio, fr. praelibare to taste beforehand: cf. F. prelibation.
Pref. pre + L. liminaris belonging to a threshold, fr. limen, liminis, threshold, entrance: cf. F. préliminaire. Cf. Limit.
F. prélude (cf. It. preludio, LL. praeludium), fr. L. prae before + ludus play. See Prelude, v. t. | L. praeludere, praelusum; prae before + ludere to play: cf. F. préluder. See Ludicrous.
L. praematurus; prae before + maturus ripe. See Mature.
L. praemeditatus, p. p. of praemeditari; prae before + meditari to meditate. See Meditate. | L. praemeditatus, p. p.
F. prémices, L. primitiae. See Primitia.
F. premier, fr. L. primarius of the first rank, principal, fr. primus the first. See Primary, Prime, a.
L. praemiosus, fr. praemium a premium.
F. prémisse, fr. L. praemissus, p. p. of praemittere to send before; prae before + mittere to send. See Mission. | From L. praemissus, p. p., or E. premise, n. See Premise, n.
L. praemium, originally, what one has got before or better than others; prae before + emere to take, buy. See Redeem.
Pref. pre- + monish: cf. L. praemonere.
L. praemonstratus, p. p. of praemonstrare; prae before + monstrate to show.
F.prémontré, fr. Prémontré, fr. L. pratum monstratum.
L. praemorsus, p. p. of praemordere to bite off; prae before + mordere to bite.
L. praemunitus, p. p. of praemunire to fortify in front; prae before + munire to fortify.
F. prendre to take, fr. L. prehendere to take.
L. praenominatus, p. p. of praenominare to give the prenomen to, to prenominate, fr. praenomen prenomen.
L. praenoscere to foreknow; prae before + noscere, notum, to know.
L. praenotare; prae before + notare to note.
L. praenotio: cf. F. prénotion. See Prenostic.
L. prensatio, from prensare, prehensare, v. freq. from prehendere to seize.
L. praenunciatio, fr. praenunciare to announce beforehand. See Pre-, and Announce.
L. praeoccupatus, p. p. of praeoccupare to preoccupy. See Preoccupy.
Cf. F. préoccuper. See Preoccupate, Occupy.
Pref. pre + ordain: cf. L. praeordinare.
L. praeordinatus, p. p. See Preordain.

L. praepollens, p. p. of praepollere to surpass in power; prae before + pollere to be powerful. | NL. See Pre-, Pollex.
L. praeponderans, -antis: cf. F. prépondérant. See Preponderate.
L. praeponderatus, p. p. of praeponderare; prae before + ponderare to weigh, fr., pondus, ponderis, a weight. See Ponder.
F. préposer; pref. pré- (L. prae before) + poser. See Pose.
L. praepositio, fr. praeponere to place before; prae before + ponere to put, place: cf. F. préposition. See Position, and cf. Provost.
L. praepositura. See Preposition, and cf. Provost.
L. praeposterus; prae before + posterus coming after, latter. See Posterior.
L. praepotens. See Pre-, and Potent.

F. prérogative, from L. praerogativa precedence in voting, preference, privilege, fr. praerogativus that is asked before others for his opinion, that votes before or first, fr. praerogare to ask before another; prae before + rogare to ask. See Rogation.
F. présage, L. praesagium, from praesagire. See Presage, v. t.  | F. présager, L. praesagire: prae before + sagire to perceive acutely or sharply. See Sagacious.
L. an elder, fr. Gr. Priest.
L. presbyterium, Gr. Presbyter, and cf. Presbyterium.
F. prescience, L. praescientia. See Prescient.
L. praesciens, -entis, p. pr. of praescire to foreknow; prae before + scire to know: cf. F. prescient. See Science.
L. praescindere to cut off in front; prae before + scindere to cut asunder: cf. F. prescinder.
L. praescius; prae before + scius knowing, fr. scire to know.
L. praescribere, praescriptum; prae before + scriebe to write. See Scribe.
L. praescriptus, p. p. of praescribere: cf. F. prescrit. See Prescribe. | L. praescriptum: cf. OF. prescript.
F. prescription, L. praescriptio,an inscription, preface, precept, demurrer, prescription (in sense 3), fr. praescribere. See Prescribe.
L. praescriptivus of a demurrer or legal exception.
F. présence, L. praesentia. See Present.
L. praesensio, fr. praesentire to perceive beforehand. See Presentient.

F. présent, L. praesens,-entis, that is before one, in sight or at hand, p. p. of praeesse to be before; prae before + esse to be. See Essence. | Cf. F. présent. See Present, a. | F. présenter, L. praesentare, fr. praesens, a. See Present, a. | F. présent .
L. praesentatio a showing, representation: cf. F. présentation.
F. présenté, p. p. See Present, v. t.
L. praesentiens, p. pr. of praesentire to perceive beforehand; prae before + sentire to feel.
L. praesens, -entis, present + facere to make.
Pref. pre- + sentiment: cf. F. pressentiment. See Presentient.
F. préserver, from L. prae before + servare to save, preserve; cf. L. praeservare to observe beforehand. See Serve.
L. praesidere; prae before + sedere to sit: cf. F. présider. See Sit.
F. président, L. praesidens, -entis, p. pr. of praesidere. See Preside.
L. praesidialis and praesidiarius, fr. praesidium a presiding over, defense, guard. See Preside.
L. praesidialis and praesidiarius, fr. praesidium a presiding over, defense, guard. See Preside. | L. praesidiarium.
L. praesignificare; prae before + significare to signify.

Corrupt. fr. prest ready money advanced, a loan; hence, earnest money given soldiers on entering service. See Prest, n. | For prest, confused with press. | F. presser, fr. L. pressare to press, fr. premere, pressum, to press. Cf. Print, v. | F. presse. See 4th Press.
L. pressio: cf. F. pression. See 4th Press.
L. presssus pressed (p. p. of premere) + rostrum beak: cf. F. pressirostre. See 4th Press.
OF., fr. L. pressura, fr. premere. See 4th Press.

OF. prest, F. prêt, fr. L. praestus ready. Cf. Presto. | OF. prest, F. prêt, fr. OF. prester to lend, F. prêter, fr. L. praestare to stand before, to become surety for, to fulfill, offer, supply; prae before + stare to stand. See Pre-, and Stand, and cf. Press to force into service.
L. praestatio a performing, paying, fr. praestare: cf. F. prestation.
NL., fr. Gr. 1. A meteor or exhalation formerly supposed to be thrown from the clouds with such violence that by collision it is set on fire. [Obs. | OF. prestre. See Priest.
L. praesto ready + digitus finger: cf. F. prestidigitateur.
F., fr. L. praestigum delusion, illusion, praestigae deceptions, jugglers' tricks, prob. fr. prae before + the root of stinguere to extinguish, originally, to prick. See Stick, v.
L. praestigiare to deceive by juggling tricks, fr. praestigae. See Prestige.
LL. praestimonium, fr. L. praestare to furnish, supply: cf. F. prestimonie. See Prest, n.
It. or Sp. presto quick, quickly. See Prest, a.
L. praestrictio a binding fast, fr. praestringere. See Pre-, and Stringent.
L. praesultor; prae before + salire to dance.
F. présumer, L. praesumere, praesumptum; prae before + sumere to take. See Assume, Redeem.
L. praesumptio: cf. F. présomption, OF. also presumpcion. See Presume.
L. praesumptuosus: cf. F. présomptueux, OF. also presumptuous. See Presumption.
Pref. pre- + suppose: cf. F. présupposer.
Pref. pre- + supposition: cf. F. présupposition.
LL. praetensus, for L. praetentus, p. p. of praetendere. See Pretend, and cf. Tension.
OE. pretenden to lay claim to, F. prétendre, L. praetendere, praetentum, to stretch forward, pretend, simulate, assert; prae before + tendere to stretch. See Tend, v. t.

Cf. F. prétention. See Pretend, Tension.
Pref. pre- + tentative: cf. L. praetentare to try beforehand.
L. praeter past, beyond, originally a compar. of prae before. See For, prep.
L. praeteriens, p. pr. See Preterit.
L. praeteritus, p. p. of praeterire to go or pass by; praeter beyond, by + ire to go: cf. F. prétérit. See Issue.
L. praeterlapsus, p. p. of praeterlabi to glide by. See Preter-, Lapse.
L. praetermittere, praetermissum; praeter beyond + mittere to send. See Mission.
L. praetervectio, fr. praetervehere to carry beyond. See Invection.
F. prétexte, L. praetextum, fr. praetextus, p. p. of praetexere to weave before, allege as an excuse; prae before + texere to weave. See Text.
L. praetor, for praeitor, fr. praeire to go before; prae before + ire to go. See Issue.

OE. prati, AS. prættig, prætig, crafty, sly, akin to præt, prætt, deceit, trickery, Icel. prettugr tricky, prettr a trick; probably fr. Latin, perhaps through Celtic; cf. W. praith act, deed, practice, LL. practica execution, practice, plot. See Practice.
F. prévaloir, OF. prevaleir, L. praevalere; prae before + valere to be strong, able, or worth. See Valiant.
L. praevalentia: cf. F. prévalence. See Prevail.
L. praevalens, -entis, p. pr. of praevalere. See Prevail.

F. prévenir, L. praevenire. See Prevent.
L. praevenire, praeventum; prae before + venire to come. See Come.
L. praevius going before, leading the way; prae before + via the way. See Voyage.
L. praevisus, p. p. of praevidere to foresee; prae before + videre to see. See Vision.
OF. preie, F. proie, L. praeda, probably for praeheda. See Prehensile, and cf. Depredate, Predatory. | OF. preier, preer, L. praedari, fr. praeda. See Prey, n.
Cornish, clayey ground, from pri clay.

L. priapismus, Gr. Priapus the god of procreation, the penis, Gr. priapisme.

AS. prica, pricca, pricu; akin to LG. prick, pricke, D. prik, Dan. prik, prikke, Sw. prick. Cf. Prick, v. | AS. prician; akin to LG. pricken, D. prikken, Dan. prikke, Sw. pricka. See Prick, n., and cf. Prink, Prig.

AS. pricele, pricle; akin to LG. prickel, D. prikkel. See Prick, n.

OE. prest, preost, AS. preóst, fr. L. presbyter, Gr. pristinus. Cf. Pristine, Presbyter.
See Privet. | OF. prim, prin, prime, first, principal. sharp, thin, piercing, fr. L. primus first. See Prime, a.

L., from abl. of primus first + abl. of facies appearance.

L. primarius, fr. primus first: cf. F. primaire. See Prime, a., and cf. Premier, Primero.
OE. primat, F. primat, L. primas, -atis one of the first, chief, fr. primus the first. See Prime, a.

L. primus first: cf. F. primine.
L., fr. primus first + parere to bring forth.

L. primitiae, pl., fr. primus first. Cf. Premices.
L. primitivus, fr. primus the first: cf. F. primitif. See Prime, a.
LL., fr. L. primus first + genitor a begetter.
LL., fr. L. primus first + genitura a begetting, birth, generation, fr. genere, gignere, to beget: cf. F. primogéniture, L. primogenitus firstborn. See Prime, a., and Genus, Kin.
L. primordialis, from primordium the first beginning; primus first + ordiri to begin a web, to begin: cf. F. primordial.
L. primordius first of all, fr. primordium.
OE. primerole, F. primerole, a derivative fr. LL. primula, from L. primus first. See Prime, a.
F., from L. princeps, -cipis, the first, chief; primus first + capere to take. See Prime, a., and Capacious.
F. princesse. See Prince, and cf. Princesse.
F., from L. principalis. See Prince.

L. principians, p. pr. of principiare to begin, fr. principium. See Principle.

Probably a nasalized form of prick. See Prick, v. t., and cf. Prig, Prank.

L. prior former, previous, better, superior; compar. corresponding to primus first, and pro for. See Former, and cf. Prime, a., and Pre-, Pro-. | OE. priour, OF. priour, prior, priur, F. prieur, from L. prior former, superior. See Prior, a.
Cf. F. priorité. See Prior, a.
Cf. LL. prioria. See Prior, n.

F., fr. L. prehensio, prensio, a seizing, arresting, fr. prehendre, prendere, to lay hold of, to seize. See Prehensile, and cf. Prize, n., Misprision.
L. pristinus, akin to prior: cf. F. pristin. See Prior, a.
Sp., fr. L. privatus. See Private.

L. privatus apart from the state, peculiar to an individual, private, properly p. p. of privare to bereave, deprive, originally, to separate, fr. privus single, private, perhaps originally, put forward (hence, alone, single) and akin to prae before. See Prior, a., and cf. Deprive, Privy, a.
L. privatio: cf. F. privation. See Private.
L. privativus: cf. F. privatif. See Private.
Cf. Scot. privie, Prov. E. prim-print, primwort. Prob. for primet, and perh. named from being cut and trimmed. See, Prim, a., and cf. Prime to prune, Prim, n., Prie, n.

It is said that Daly, the manager of a Dublin playhouse, laid a wager that a new word of no meaning should be the common talk and puzzle of the city in twenty-fours. In consequence of this the letters q u i z were chalked by him on all the walls of Dublin, with an effect that won the wager. Perhaps, however, originally a variant of whiz, and formerly the name of a popular game.
So called from the Law L. words quo warranto (by what authority), in the original Latin form of the writ. See Which, and Warrant.
OE. coite; cf. OF. coitier to spur, press, (assumed) LL. coctare, fr. L. coquere, coctum, to cook, burn, vex, harass, E. cook, also W. coete a quoit.
L., of whom, gen. pl. of qui who, akin to E. who. See the Note below.

F.; cf. Sp. rob, It. rob, robbo, Pg. robe, arrobe, Ar. rubb, robb, Per. rub. | OF. rober, of German origin; cf. OHG. roub, G. rauben, and OHG. roub robbing, booty, G. raub. sq. root114. See Reave,and cf. Robe.

Cf. OE. roilen to wander; possibly fr. OF. roeler to roll, equiv. to F. rouler. See Roll, v., and cf. Rile.
Probably fr. F. rustre boor, a clown, clownish, fr. L. rustucus rustic. See Rustic.

OF. roeler, roler, F. rouler, LL. rotulare, fr. L. royulus, rotula, a little wheel, dim. of rota wheel; akin to G. rad, and to Skr. ratha car, chariot. Cf. NL., dim. of rota wheel; cf. LL. rotella a little whell.

L., a little wheel; cf. It. rotula.

L. rotundus round + folium a leaf.
F., properly p.p. of rouer to break upon the wheel, fr. roue a wheel, L. rota. See Rotate, Rotary.

OE. rou, rou, row, rugh, ruh, AS. r; akin to LG. rug, D. rug, D. ruig, ruw, OHG. r, G. rauh, rauch; cf. Lith. raukas wrinkle, rukti to wrinkle. sq. root 18. Cf. Rug, n.

F., properly, a little wheel or ball. See Rouleau, Roll.

Cf. F. ronce bramble, brier, thorn, ranche a round, step, rack, or E. round.

From Roun. | OF. roond, roont, reond, F. rond, fr. L. rotundus, fr. rota wheel. See Rotary, and cf. Rotund, roundel, Rundlet.

Cf. AS. hrrufen, Goth. hr. Cf. Roop.

perhaps fr. or akin to reeve. | Cf. D. rooven to rob; akin to E. reave. See Reave Rob.

From Rout, or Row a brawl.

Cf. E. rough, OE. row, rowe.

From an assumed Old French dim. of robe See Rubbish.

NL. Rucervus, the genus, fr. NL. Rusa a certain genus of deer (Malay r deer) + Cervus.

Icel hrukkast to wrinkle, hrukka wrinkle, fold. | Icel. hrukka. Cf. Ruck, v. t. | Cf. Dan. ruge to brood, to hatch. | Cf. Ruck.

OE. scof; akin to OFries. schof, OHG. scoph, Icel. skaup, and perh. to E. shove. | Cf. Dan. skuffe to deceive, delude, Icel. skopa to scoff, OD. schoppen. See Scoff, n.
Akin to D. schelden, G. schelten, OHG. sceltan, Dan. skielde.

L. scomma a taunt, jeer, scoff, Gr. 1. A bufoon. [Obs.
D. schans, OD. schantse, perhaps from OF. esconse a hiding place, akin to esconser to hide, L. absconsus, p. p. of abscondere. See Abscond, and cf. Ensconce, Sconce a candlestick.
OE. scope, of Scand. origin; cf. Sw. skopa, akin to D. schop a shovel, G. schüppe, and also to E. shove. See Shovel. | OE. scopen. See Scoop, n.

OE. scorchen, probably akin to scorcnen; cf. Norw. skrokken shrunk up, skrekka, skrökka, to shrink, to become wrinkled up, dial. Sw. skråkkla to wrinkle (see Shrug); but perhaps influenced by OF. escorchier to strip the bark from, to flay, to skin, F. écorcher, LL. excorticare; L. ex from + cortex, -icis, bark (cf. Cork); because the skin falls off when scorched.
AS. scor twenty, fr. sceran, scieran, to shear, cut, divice; or rather the kindred Icel. skor incision, twenty, akin to Dan. skure a notch, Sw. skåra. See Shear.

OE. scorn, scarn, scharn, OF. escarn, escharn, eschar, of German origin; cf. OHG. skern mockery, skern to mock; but cf. also OF. escorner to mock. | OE. scornen, scarnen, schornen, OF. escarning, escharnir. See Scorn, n.

G. scorodit; -- so called in allusion to its smell under the blowpipe, from Gr. (Min.) Defn: A leek-green or brownish mineral occurring in orthorhombic crystals. It is a hydrous arseniate of iron. [Written also skorodite.
NL. Scorpaena, a typical genus (see Scorpene) + -oid.
F., fr. L. scorpio, scorpius, Gr. sharp.
Cf. It. scorsa a course, and E. discourse. | Written also scourse, and scoss.
L. scorator a fornicator, from scortari to fornicate, scortum a prostitute.

Cf. L. Skoti, pl., AS. Scotta, pl. Skottas, Sceottas. | Icel. skot; or OF. escot, F. écot, LL. scottum, scotum, from a kindred German word; akin to AS. scot, and E. shot, shoot; cf. AS. sceótan to shoot, to contribute. See Shoot, and cf. Shot.

Cf. Scottish. | Cf. Prov. E. scole a prop, and Walloon ascot a prop, ascoter to prop, F. accoter, also Armor. skoaz the shoulder, skoazia to shoulder up, to prop, to support, W. ysgwydd a shoulder, ysgwyddo to shoulder. Cf. Scoat. | Probably the same word as scutch; cf. Norw. skoka, skoko, a swingle for flax; perhaps akin to E. shake.
Cf. Prov. E. scote to plow up.
L., fr. Gr. skoti`a darkness, a sunken molding in the base of a pillar, so called from the dark shadow it casts, from sko`tos darkness. | L.

For older Scottis Scottish. See Scottish.
From Scot a Scotchman: cf. AS. Scyttisc, and E. Scotch, a., Scots, a.
Probably from Prov. E. & Scotch scunner, scouner, to loathe, to disgust, akin to AS. scunian to shun. See Shun.
Akin to LG. schüren, D. schuren, schueren, G. scheuern, Dan. skure; Sw. skura; all possibly fr. LL. escurare, fr. L. ex + curare to take care. Cf. Cure.

Icel. sk a small craft or cutter. | Icel. skuta to jut out. Cf. Scout to reject. | Icel. sk a taunt; cf. Icel. skuta to jut out, skota to shove, skj to shoot, to shove. See Shoot. | OF. escaute scout, spy, fr. escouter, escolter, to listen, to hear, F. écouter, fr. L. auscultare, to hear with attention, to listen to. See Auscultation.
OF. escouve, escouvette, broom, L. scopae, or cf. W. ysgubell, dim. of ysgub a broom.
Akin to Dan. skule; cf. Icel. skolla to skulk, LG. schulen to hide one's self, D. schuilen, G. schielen to squint, Dan. skele, Sw. skela, AS. sceolh squinting. Cf. Skulk.
Freq. of scrape. Cf. Scramble, Scrawl, v. t.
See Scramble: cf. OD. schraeffelen to scrape.
Cf. dial. Sw. skraka a great dry tree, a long, lean man, Gael. sgreagach dry, shriveled, rocky. See Shrink, and cf. Scrog, Shrag, n.
Freq. of Prov. E. scramb to rake together with the hands, or of scramp to snatch at. cf. Scrabble.
Cf. D. schransen to eat greedily, G. schranzen. Cf. Crunch, Scrunch.

Icel. skrapa; akin to Sw. skrapa, Dan. skrabe, D. schrapen, schrabben, G. schrappen, and prob. to E. sharp.
OE. scratten. Cf. Scratch. | Cf. AS. scritta an hermaphrodite, Ir. scrut a scrub, a low, mean person, Gael. sgrut, sgruit, an old, shriveled person.

OE. cracchen (perhaps influenced by OE. scratten to scratch); cf. OHG. chrazz, G. kratzen, OD. kratsen, kretsen, D. krassen, Sw. kratsa to scrape, kratta to rake, to scratch, Dan. kradse to scratch, to scrape, Icel. krota to engrave. Cf. Grate to rub.
Ir. scrath a turf, sgraith a turf, green sod; akin to Gael. sgrath, sgroth, the outer skin of anything, a turf, a green sod.
Cf. W. ysgräen, ysgräell, a sea swallow, Armor. skrav.
L. screare to hawk, spit out.
Cf. Icel. skrækja to screech. Cf. Creak, v., Screech.
Icel. skræma to scare, terrify; akin to Sw. skräma, Dan. skræmme. Cf. Screech.

Also formerly, scritch, OE. skriken, skrichen, schriken, of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. skrækja to shriek, to screech, skrija to titter, Sw. skrika to shriek, Dan. skrige; also Gael. sgreach, sgreuch, W. ysgrechio, Skr. kharj to creak. Cf. Shriek, v., Scream, v.
Prov. E., a shred, the border of a cap. See Shred. | See 1st Screed. For sense 2 cf. also Gael. sgread an outcry.
OE. scren, OF. escrein, escran, F. écran, of uncertain origin; cf. G. schirm a screen, OHG. scrim, scern a protection, shield, or G. schragen a trestle, a stack of wood, or G. schranne a railing.
OE. scrue, OF. escroue, escroe, female screw, F. écrou, L. scrobis a ditch, trench, in LL., the hole made by swine in rooting; cf. D. schroef a screw, G. schraube, Icel. skr.
L. scriba, fr. scribere to write; cf. Gr. scarify. Cf. Ascribe, Describe, Script, Scrivener, Scrutoire.
A corruption of skirmish. "Sore scrymmishe." Ld. Berners.
Cf. Dan. skrumpe, G. schrumpfen, D. krimpen. Cf. Shrimp, Shrine.
L. scrinium a case for books, letters, etc.: cf. OF. escrin, F. écrin. See Shrine. | Cf. Cringe.
OE. scrippe, probably of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. & OSw. skreppa, and also LL. scrippum, OF. esquerpe, escrepe, F. écharpe scarf. Cf. Scarp, Scarf a piece of dress. | From script.
OE. scrit, L. scriptum something written, fr. scribere, scriptum to write: cf. OF. escript, , F. écrit. See Scribe, and cf. Scrip a writing.
L. scriptorius, fr. scribere, scriptum to write.
L. scriptura, fr. scribere, scriptum, to write: cf. OF. escripture, escriture, F. écriture. See Scribe.
From older scrivein, OF. escrivain, F. écrivain, LL. scribanus, from L. scribere to write. See Scribe.
L. scrobiculus, dim. of scrobis a ditch or trench.
L. scrobiculus, dim. of scrobis a ditch or trench.

L. scrofulae, fr. scrofa a breeding sow, because swine were supposed to be subject to such a complaint, or by a fanciful comparison of the glandular swellings to little pigs; perhaps akin to Gr. scrofules. Cf. Scroyle.
Cf. Scrag, or Gael. sgrogag anything shriveled, from sgrag to compress, shrivel.

A dim. of OE. scroue, scrowe (whence E. escrow), OF. escroe, escroue, F. écrou entry in the jail book, LL. scroa scroll, probably of Teutonic origin; cf. OD. schroode a strip, shred, slip of paper, akin to E. shred. Cf. Shred, Escrow.
NL. So called because it was reputed to be remedy for scrofula.
Cf. OF. escrouselle a kind of vermin, escrouelles, pl., scrofula, F. écrouelles, fr. (assumed) LL. scrofulae. See Scrofula, and cf. Cruels.
OE. scrobben, probably of Dutch or Scand. origin; cf. Dan. sckrubbe, Sw. skrubba, D. schrobben, LG. schrubben.

L. scrupulus a small sharp or pointed stone, the twenty-fourth part of an ounce, a scruple, uneasiness, doubt, dim. of scrupus a rough or sharp stone, anxiety, uneasiness; perh. akin to Gr. kshura: cf. F. scrupule.
L. scrutinium, fr. scrutari to search carefuly, originally, to search even to the rags, fr. scruta trash, trumpery; perhaps akin to E. shred: cf. AS. scrudnian to make scrutiny.
From Scry, v. | OE. ascrie, fr. ascrien to cry out, fr. OF. escrier, F. s'écrier. See Ex-, and Cry.
Dan. skyde to shoot, shove, push, akin to skud shot, gunshot, a shoot, young bough, and to E. shoot. sq. root159. See Shoot.
Freq. of scud: cf. Scuttle to hurry.
It., a crown, a dollar, a shield, fr. L. scutum a shield. Cf. Scute.
Cf. D. schoft shoulder, Goth. skuft hair of the head. Cf. Scruff. | See Scuffle.
Freq. of scuff, v.i.; cf. Sw. skuffa to push, shove, skuff a push, Dan. skuffe a drawer, a shovel, and E. shuffle, shove. See Shove, and cf. Shuffle.
Cf. Dan. skugge to darken, a shade, SW. skugga to shade, a shade, Icel. skuggja to shade, skuggi a shade.
See 1st School. | Of uncertain origin; cf. Icel. skola to wash.

Probably originally, a place for washing dishes, and for swillery, fr. OE. swilen to wash, AS. swilian (see Swill to wash, to drink), but influenced either by Icel. skola, skyla, Dan. skylle, or by OF. escuelier a place for keeping dishes, fr. escuele a dish, F. écuelle, fr. L. scutella a salver, waiter (cf. Scuttle a basket); or perhaps the English word is immediately from the OF. escuelier; cf. OE. squyllare a dishwasher.
OF. escouillon (Cot.) a dishclout, apparently for escouvillon, F. écouvillon a swab; cf. also OF. souillon a servant employed for base offices. Cf. Scovel.
L. sculptor, fr. sculpere, sculptum, to carve; cf. scalpere to cut, carve, scratch, and Gr. sculpteur.
Of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. & Sw. skum, Icel. sk, LG. schum, D. schuim, OHG. sc, G. schaum; probably from a root meaning, to cover. sq. root158. Cf. Hide skin, Meerschaum, Skim, v., Sky.
Cf. OF. escumoire, F. écumoire. See Scum, and cf. Skimmer.
D. schop. | Contr. fr. American Indian mishcùp, fr. mishe-kuppi large, thick-scaled.
Contr. fr. Amer. Indian mishcuppauog, pl. of mishcup.
OF. escopir, escupir, to spit, perhaps for escospir, L. ex + conspuere to spit upon; pref. con- + spuere to spit. Cf. Spit, v.

AS. scurf, sceorf, or from Scand.; cf. Sw. skorf, Dan. skurv, Icel. skurfur, D. schurft, G. schorf; all akin to AS. scurf, and to AS. sceorfan to scrape, to gnaw, G. schürfen to scrape, and probably also to E. scrape. Cf. Scurvy.
L. scurrilis, fr. scurra a bufoon, jester: cf. F. scurrile.
From Scurf; cf. Scurvy, n. | Probably from the same source as scirbute, but influenced by scurf, scurfy, scurvy, adj.; cf. D. scheurbuik scurvy, G. scharbock, LL. scorbutus. Cf. Scorbute.
Cf. Icel. skott a fox's tail. sq. root 159.
LL. scutagium, from L. scutum a shield.

NL., fem. dim. of L. scutum.

L. scutella a dish, salver. Cf. Scuttle a basket.

Skillet. | For scuddle, fr. scud. | OF. escoutille, F. éscoutille, cf. Sp. escotilla; probably akin to Sp. escoter to cut a thing so as to make it fit, to hollow a garment about the neck, perhaps originally, to cut a bosom- shaped piece out, and of Teutonic origin; cf. D. schoot lap, bosom, G. schoss, Goth. skauts the hem of a garnment. Cf. Sheet an expanse.
AS. scylan to withdraw or remowe.
OE. sithe, AS. si\'ebe, sigthe; akin to Icel. sigthr a sickle, LG. segd, seged, seed, seid, OHG. segansa sickle, scythe, G. sense scythe, and to E. saw a cutting instrument. See Saw.
OE. see, AS. sæ; akin to D. zee, OS. & OHG. seo, G. see, OFries. se, Dan. sö, Sw. sjö, Icel. sær, Goth. saiws, and perhaps to L. saevus firce, savage. sq. root 151 a.
So called from a whistling sound which it makes.
Sea + (perhaps) Mall Mally, for Mary; hence, Prov. E. mally a hare.

OE. sele, AS. seolh; akin to OHG. selah, Dan. sæl, Sw. själ, Icel. selr. | OE. seel, OF. seel, F. sceau, fr. L. sigillum a little figure or image, a seal, dim. of signum a mark, sign, figure, or image. See Sign, n., and cf. Sigil. | OE. selen; cf. OF. seeler, seieler, F. sceller, LL. sigillare. See Seal a stamp.

See Saim. | OE. seem, seam, AS. seám; akin to D. zoom, OHG. soum, G. saum, LG. soom, Icel. saumr, Sw. & Dan. söm, and E. sew. sq. root 156. See Sew to fasten with thread. | AS. seám, LL. sauma, L. sagma a packsaddle, fr. Gr. Sumpter.
From older seamster, properly fem., AS. seámestre. See Seam.
F., fr. L. sedens, -entis, p.pr. of sedere to sit. See Sit.
OE.seeren, AS. seárian. See Sear, a. | F. serre a grasp, pressing, fr. L. sera. See Serry.
OE. serchen, cerchen, OF. cerchier, F. chercher, L. circare to go about, fr. L. circum, circa, around. See Circle. | Cf. OF. cerche. See Search, v. t.
OE. sesoun, F. saison, properly, the sowing time, fr. L. satio a sowing, a planting, fr. serere, satum, to sow, plant; akin to E. sow, v., to scatter, as seed.
OE. sete, Icel. sæti; akin to Sw. säte, Dan. sæde, MHG. saze, AS. set, setl, and E. sit. sq. root154. See Sit, and cf. Settle, n.
Cf. Dan. siv, Sw. säf, Icel. sef.
NL. sebaceus, from L. sebum tallow, grease.
L. sebum tallow: cf. F. sébacique.

L. secessio: cf. F. sécession. See Secede.
F. sec, properly, dry, L. siccua.

F. secrétaire (cf. Pr. secretari, Sp. & Pg. secretario, It. secretario, segretario) LL. secretarius, originally, a confidant, one intrusted with secrets, from L. secretum a secret. See Secret, a. & n.
L. secretus separated, secret, hidden, p. p. of secernere. See Secret, and cf. Discrete, Discreet.
L. secare, sectum, to cut. | F. secte, L. sects, fr. sequi to follew; often confused with L. secare, sectum, to cut. See Sue to follow, and cf. Sept, Suit, n.
L., fr. sectari, v. intens. fr. sequi to follow. See Sue to follow.
L. sectilis, fr. secare, sectum, to cut: cf. F. sectile. See Section.
L. sectio, fr. secare, sectum, to cut; akin to E. saw a cutting instrument: cf. F. section. See Saw, and cf. Scion, Dissect, Insect, Secant, Segment.
L., properly, a cutter, fr. secare, sectum, to cut: cf. F. secteur. See Section.
OE. secular, seculer. L. saecularis, fr. saeculum a race, generation, age, the times, the world; perhaps akin to E. soul: cf. F. séculier.
L. secundus following the course or current of wind of water. See Second, a.
L.secundatus, p. p. of secundare to direct faverably.
L. secundus second + genitura a begetting, generation.
L. securus; pref. se- without + cura care. See Cure care, and cf. Sure, a.
NL., from L. securis an ax + ferre to bear.

L. securitas: cf. F. sécurité. See Secure, and cf. Surety.
Said to be named from Sedan, in France, where it was first made, and whence it was introduced into England in the time of King Charles I.
L. sedatus, p. p. of sedare, sedatum, to allay, calm, causative of sedere to sit. See Sit.

L., they sat, fr. sedere to sit.

OE. segge, AS. secg; akin to LG. segge; -- probably named from its bladelike appearance, and akin to L. secare to cut, E. saw a cutting instrument; cf. Ir. seisg, W. hesg. Cf. Hassock, Saw the instrument.
F. sédiment, L. sedimentum a settling, fr. sedere to sit, to settle. See Sit.
OE. sedicioun, OF. sedition, F. sédition, fr. L. seditio, originally, a going aside; hence, an insurrectionary separation; pref. se-, sed-, aside + itio a going, fr. ire, itum, to go. Cf. Issue.
L. seducere, seductum; pref. se- aside + ducere to lead. See Duke.
L. seductio: cf. F. séduction. See Seduce.
L. sedulus, perhaps from sedere to sit, and so akin to E. sit.
NL., fr. L. sedere to sit; so called in allusion to the manner in which the plants attach themselves to rocks and walls.

OE. se, see, OF. se, sed, sied, fr. L. sedes a seat, or the kindred sedere to sit. See Sit, and cf. Siege. | OE. seen, sen, seon, As. seón; akin to OFries. sia, D. zien, OS. & OHG. sehan, G. sehen, Icel. sja, Sw. se, Dan. see, Goth. saíhwan, and probably to L. sequi to follow (and so originally meaning, to follow with the eyes). Gr. sac. Cf. Sight, Sun to follow.
OE. seed, sed, AS. s, fr. sawan to sow; akin to D. zaad seed, G. saat, Icel. sa, s, Goth. manas seed of men. world. See Sow to scatter seed, and cf. Colza.
AS. s; s seed + leáp basket.
AS. s; s seed + leáp basket.
OE, seken, AS. s, s; akin to OS. s, LG. söken, D. zoeken, OHG. suohhan, G. suchen, Icel. s, Sw. söka, Dan. söge, Goth. s, and E. sake. Cf. Beseech, Ransack, Sagacious, Sake, Soc.
F.siller, ciller, fr. cil an eyelash, L. cilium. | Cf. LG. sielen to lead off water, F. siller to run ahead, to make headway, E. sile, v.t. | AS. s, from s good, prosperous. See Silly.

OE. semen to seem, to become, befit, AS. s to satisfy, pacify; akin to Icel. s to honor, to bear with, conform to, s becoming, fit, s to beseem, to befit, sama to beseem, semja to arrange, settle, put right, Goth. samjan to please, and to E. same. The sense is probably due to the adj. seemly. sq. root191. See Same, a., and cf. Seemly.
Icel. s, fr. s becoming, fit; akin to samr same, E. same; the sense being properly, the same or like, hence, fitting. See Seem, v. i.
Probably a reduplication of saw, to express the alternate motion to and fro, as in the act of sawing.
OE. sethen, AS. seó; akin to D. sieden, OHG. siodan, G. sieden, Icel. sj, Sw. sjuda, Dan. syde, Goth. saubs a burnt offering. Cf. Sod, n., Sodden, Suds.
See Sedge. | Probably from the root of L. secare to cut.
Prov. E. saggard a seggar, seggard a sort of riding surtout, contr. fr. safeguard.
L. segmentum, fr. secare to cut, cut off: cf. F. segment. See Saw a cutting instrument.
L. segnitas, fr. segnis slow, sluggish.
L. segnitas, fr. segnis slow, sluggish.
L. segregatus, p. p. of segregare to separate; pref. se- aside + grex, gregis, a flock or herd. See Gregarious.
OF. seignor, F. seigneur, cf. It. signore, Sp. señor from an objective case of L. senier elder. See Senior.
OE. seignorie, OF. seigneurie, F. seigneurie; cf. It. signoria.
OE. seisen, saisen, OF. seisir, saisir, F. saisir, of Teutonic origin, and akin to E. set. The meaning is properly, to set, put, place, hence, to put in possession of. See Set, v. t.
F. séant, p. pr. of seoir to sit, L. sedere.
F. séant, p. pr. of seoir to sit, L. sedere.
L. sejungere; pref. se- aside + jungere to join. See Join.
NL., fr. L. selago, -inis, a kind of plant.
AS. selc, seldc; seld rare + c known. See Uncouth.
AS. seldan, seldon, seldum, fr. seld rare; akin to OFries. sielden, D. zelden, G. selten, OHG. seltan, Icel. sjaldan, Dan. sielden, Sw. sällan, Goth. sildaleiks marvelous.
L. selectus, p. p. of seligere to select; pref. se- aside + levere to gather. See Legend.
NL., from Gr. tellurium (from L. tellus the earth), being, as it were, a companion to it.
AS. self, seolf, sylf; akin to OS. self, OFries. self, D. zelf, G. selb, selber, selbst, Dan. selv. Sw. sjelf, Icel. sjalfr, Goth. silba. Cf. Selavage.
OF. seillon a measure of land, F. sillon a ridge, furrow, LL. selio a measure of land.

F. selle, L. sella, akin to sedere to sit. See Sit. | OE. sellen, sillen, AS. sellan, syllan, to give, to deliver; akin to OS. sellian, OFries. sella, OHG. sellen, Icel. selja to hand over, to sell, Sw. sälja to sell, Dan. s, Goth. saljan to offer a sacrifice; all from a noun akin to E. sale. Cf. Sale.
Seltzer water + the root of Gr.

AS. sendan; akin to OS. sendian, D. zenden, G. senden, OHG. senten, Icel. senda, Sw. sända, Dan. sende, Goth. sandjan, and to Goth. sinp a time (properly, a going), gasinpa companion, OHG. sind journey, AS. si, Icel. sinni a walk, journey, a time. W. hynt a way, journey, OIr. s. Cf. Sense.
OF. cendal (cf. Pr. & Sp. cendal, It. zendale), LL. cendallum, Gr. Defn: A light thin stuff of silk. [Written also cendal, and sendal.
L., groundsel, lit., an old man. So called in allusion to the hoary appearance of the pappus.

L. sensus, from sentire, sensum, to perceive, to feel, from the same root as E. send; cf. OHG. sin sense, mind, sinnan to go, to journey, G. sinnen to meditate, to think: cf. F. sens. For the change of meaning cf. See, v. t. See Send, and cf. Assent, Consent, Scent, v. t., Sentence, Sentient.

F., from L. sententia, for sentientia, from sentire to discern by the senses and the mind, to feel, to think. See Sense, n., and cf. Sentiensi.

L. sentina bilge water, hold of a ship, dregs: cf. F. sentine.

F. sentinelle (cf. It. sentinella); probably originally, a litle path, the sentinel's beat,, and a dim. of a word meaning, path; cf. F. sente path. L. semita; and OF. sentine, sentele, senteret, diminutive words. Cf. Sentry.
L. sentire to feel + E. section.
Probably from OF. senteret a little patch; cf. F. sentier path, and OF. sente. See Sentinel.
NL. sepalum, formed in imitation of NL. petalum, petal, to denote one of the divisions of the calyx: cf. F. sépale.

NL., fr. L. septum, saeptum, an inclosure, a partition, fr. sepire, saepire, to inclose.

L. septemfluus; septem seven + fluere to flow.

L. septentrio the northern regions, the north, fr. septentriones the seven stars near the north pole, called Charles's Wain, or the Great Bear, also those called the Little Bear; properly, the seven plow oxen; septem seven + trio, orig., a plow ox: cf. F. septentrion. | L. septentrionalis: cf. F. septentrional.
From L. septem seven, like duet, from L. duo.

L. sequens, -entis, p. pr. of sequi to follow. See Sue to follow.

L., one that hinders or impedes.
F. sequin, It. zecchino, from zecca the mint, fr. Ar. sekkah, sikkah, a die, a stamp. Cf. Zechin.
NL. So called by Dr. Endlicher in honor of Sequoyah, who invented the Cherokee alphabet.

It. serraglio, originally, an inclosure of palisades, afterwards also, a palace, seraglio (by confusion with Per. sera\'8ba a palace, an entirely different word), fr. serrare to shut, fr. LL. serra a bar for fastening doors, L. sera. See Serry, Series.
Per. sera\'8b, or saraï, a palace, a king's court, a seraglio, an inn. Cf. Caravansary.
Turk., fr. Per. ser head, chief + Ar. 'asker an army.
F. sérénade, It. serenata, probably fr. L. serenus serene (cf. Serene), misunderstood as a derivative fr. L. serus late. Cf. Soirée.
F., fr. L. serus servant, slave; akin to servare to protect, preserve, observe, and perhaps originally, a client, a man under one's protection. Cf. Serve, v. t.
F. serge, sarge, originally, a silken stuff, fr. L. serica, f. or neut. pl. of sericus silken. See Sericeous, Silk. | F. cierge.
F. sergent, fr. L. serviens, -entis, p. pr. of servire to serve. See Serve, and cf. Servant.
Cf. OF. sergentie, LL. sergentia. See Sergeant.
L. sericus silken, sericum Seric stuff, silk, fr. Sericus belonging to the Seres, Gr. Silk, Serge a woolen stuff.
L. series, fr. serere, sertum, to join or bind together; cf. Gr. sarit thread. Cf. Assert, Desert a solitude, Exert, Insert, Seraglio.
L. serius: cf. F. sérieux, LL. seriosus.

L. serpens, -entis, a serpent + - genous: cf. L. serpentigena.

NL., dim. fr. L. serta a garland.
L., akin to Gr. sara curd.
OE. servant, servaunt, F. servant, a & p. pr. of servir to serve, L. servire. See Serve, and cf. Sergeant.

OE. serven, servien, OF. & F. servir, fr. L. servire; akin to servus a servant or slave, servare to protect, preserve, observe; cf. Zend har to protect, haurva protecting. Cf. Conserve, Desert merit, Dessert, Observe, Serf, Sergeant.
Properly, the tree which bears serve, OE. serves, pl., service berries, AS. syrfe service tree; akin to L. sorbus. | OE. servise, OF. servise, service, F. service, from L. servitium. See Serve.

L., fr. servire to serve: cf. F. serviteur.
F., fr. Ar. saisaban, seiseban, a kind of tree, fr. Per. sisaban seed of cinquefoil.
L., one half more, one and a half.
L. sesquialter once and a half; sesqui- + alter other: cf. F. sesquialtére.
L. sesquialter once and a half; sesqui- + alter other: cf. F. sesquialtére.

Prov. E. suss hogwash, soss a dirty mess, a puddle + E. pool a puddle; cf. Gael. ses a coarse mess.

It. sestetto, fr. sesto sixth, L. sextus, fr. sex six.
OE. setten, AS. setton; akin to OS. settian, OFries. setta, D. zetten, OHG. sezzen, G. setzen, Icel. setja, Sw. sätta, Dan. s, Goth. satjan; causative from the root of E. sit. Sit, and cf. Seize.
L. seta a bristle: cf. F. sétacé.
F. séton (cf. It. setone), from L. seta a thick, stiff hair, a bristle.
L. setosus, saetosus, from seta, saeta, bristle: cf. F. séteux.

OE. setel, setil, a seat, AS. setl: akin to OHG. sezzal, G. sessel, Goth. sitls, and E. sit. sq. root154. See Sit. | OE. setlen, AS. setlan. sq. root154. See Settle, n. In senses 7, 8, and 9 perhaps confused with OE. sahtlen to reconcile, AS. sahtlian, fr. saht reconciliation, sacon to contend, dispute. Cf. Sake.
L. setula, saetula, dim. of seta, saeta, bristle.

OE. seven, seoven, seofen, AS. seofon, seofan, seofen; akin to D. zeven, OS., Goth., & OHG. sibun, G. sieben, Icel. sjau, sjö, Sw. sju, Dan. syv, Lith. septyni, Russ. seme, W. saith, Gael. seachd, Ir. seacht, L. septem, Gr. saptan. sq. root305. Cf. Hebdomad, Heptagon, September.
OE. seventene, AS. seofontyne, i. e., seven- ten. Cf. Seventy.
From Seventeen: cf. AS. seofonteóedha, seofonteogeedha.
AS. hund-seofontig. See Seven, and Ten, and cf. Seventeen, Sixty.
OF. sevrer, severer, to separate, F. sevrer to wean, fr. L. separare. See Separate, and cf. Several.
OF., fr. LL. separalis, fr. L. separ separate, different. See Sever, Separate.
L. severus; perhaps akin to Gr. swikns innocent, chaste: cf. F. sévère. Cf. Asseverate, Persevere.
Prob. corrupted fr. ciborium. Oxf. Gloss.
L. sevocare, sevocatum, to call aside.

OE. See Sewer household officer. | See Sue to follow. | OE. sewen, sowen, AS. siówian, siwian; akin to OHG. siuwan, Icel. s, Sw. sy, Dan. sye, Goth. siujan, Lith. siuti, Russ, shite, L. ssuere, Gr. siv. sq. root156. Cf. Seam a suture, Suture. | sq. root151 b. See Sewer a drain.

OF. sewiere, seuwiere, ultimately fr. L. ex out + a derivative of aqua water; cf. OF. essevour a drain, essever, esseuwer, essiaver, to cause to flow, to drain, to flow, LL. exaquatorium a channel through which water runs off. Cf. Ewer, Aquarium. | Cf. OE. assewer, and asseour, OF. asseour, F. asseoir to seat, to set, L. assidere to sit by; ad + sedere to sit (cf. Sit); or cf. OE. sew pottage, sauce, boiled meat, AS. seáw juice, Skr. su to press out.
L. sexagenarius, fr. sexageni sixty each, akin to sexaginta sixty, sex six: cf. sexagénaire. See Six.
L., fem. of sexagesimus sixtieth, fr. sexaginta sixty.
L. sexangulus sexangular; sex six + angulus angle: cf. F. sexangle. Cf. Hexangular.

Sex- + root of L. findere to split: cf. F. sexfide.

L. sexta, fem. of sextus sixtt, fr. sex six: cf. F. sexte.
L. sextus sixth, fr. sex six: cf. It. sestina.
L. sextans, -antis, the sixth part of an as, fr. sextus sixth, sex six. See Six.
L. sextarius the sixth part of a measure, weight, etc., fr. sextus sixth, sex six. | For sextonry.
F. sextil, fr. L. sextus the sixth, from sex six. See Six. | Cf. F. aspect sextil.
Formed (in imitation of million) fr. L. sextus sixth, sex six: cf. F. sextilion.
L. sextus-decimus the sixteenth; sextus the sixth (fr. sex six) + decimus the tenth, from decem ten. See - mo.
Formed (in imitation of quadruple) fr. L. sextus sixth: cf. F. sextuple.
L. sexualis, fr. sexus sex: cf. F. sexuel.
It. sforzando, p. pr., and sforzato, p. p. of sforzare to force.
It. sforzando, p. pr., and sforzato, p. p. of sforzare to force.
OE. shabbe, AS. sc. See Scab. | See Scab, 3.
Cf. D. sabel, and G. säbel.
See Shab, n., Scabby, and Scab.
Turk. tshaprak, whence F. chabraque, G. shabracke.
Prov. E., to shake, to shed. See Shake. | Cf. Scot. shag refuse of barley or oats.
AS. sceadda a kind of fish, akin to Prov. G. schade; cf. Ir. & Gael. sgadan a herring, W. ysgadan herrings; all perhaps akin to E. skate a fish.
Said to be so called from a Captain Shaddock, who first brought this fruit from the East Indies.
OE. shade, shadewe, schadewe, AS. sceadu, scead; akin to OS. skado, D. schaduw, OHG. scato, (gen. scatewes), G. schatten, Goth. skadus, Ir. & Gael. sgath, and probably to Gr. Shadow, Shed a hat.
Originally the same word as shade. sq. root162. See Shade. | OE. shadowen, AS. sceadwian. See adow, n.
OE. shaft, schaft, AS. sceaft; akin to D. schacht, OHG. scaft, G. schaft, Dan. & Sw. skaft handle, haft, Icel. skapt, and probably to L. scapus, Gr. Scape, Scepter, Shave.
AS. sceacga a bush of hair; akin to Icel. skegg the beard, Sw. skägg, Dan. skj. Cf. Schock of hair.
F. chagrin, It. zigrino, fr. Turk. saghri the back of a horse or other beast of burden, shagreen. Cf. Chagrin.
Per. shah a king, sovereign, prince. Cf. Checkmate, Chess, Pasha.
Cf. AS. sceolh squinting, Icel. skjagr wry, oblique, Dan. skele to squint.
OE. shaken, schaken, AS. scacan, sceacan; akin to Icel. & Sw. skaka, OS. skakan, to depart, to flee. sq. root161. Cf. Shock, v.
Hung. csákó: cf. F. shako, schako.
AS. scealy, scalu. See Scalme, and cf. Shell.

OE. shal, schal, imp. sholde, scholde, AS. scal, sceal, I am obliged, imp. scolde, sceolde, inf. sculan; akin to OS. skulan, pres. skal, imp. skolda, D. zullen, pres. zal, imp. zoude, zou, OHG. solan, scolan, pres. scal, sol. imp. scolta, solta, G. sollen, pres. soll, imp. sollte, Icel. skulu, pres. skal, imp. skyldi, SW. skola, pres. skall, imp. skulle, Dan. skulle, pres. skal, imp. skulde, Goth. skulan, pres. skal, imp. skulda, and to AS. scyld guilt, G. schuld guilt, fault, debt, and perhaps to L. scelus crime.
F. chalon, from Châlons, in France, where it was first made.
F. chaloupe, probably from D. sloep. Cf. Sloop.
OF. eschalote (for escalone), F. échalote. See Scallion, and cf. Eschalot.
OE. schalowe, probably originally, sloping or shelving; cf. Icel. skjalgr wry, squinting, AS. sceolh, D. & G. scheel, OHG. schelah. Cf. Shelve to slope, Shoal shallow.
Originally the same word as shame, hence, a disgrace, a trick. See Shame, n.

OE. schamel a bench, stool, AS. scamel, sceamol, a bench, form, stool, fr. L. scamellum, dim. of scamnum a bench, stool. | Cf. OD. schampelen to slip, schampen to slip away, escape. Cf. Scamble, Scamper.

OE. shame, schame, AS. scamu, sceamu; akin to OS. & OHG. scama, G. scham, Icel. skömm, shkamm, Sw. & Dan. skam, D. & G. schande, Goth. skanda shame, skaman sik to be ashamed; perhaps from a root skam meaning to cover, and akin to the root (kam) of G. hemd shirt, E. chemise. Cf. Sham. | AS. scamian, sceamian. See Shame, n.
For shamefast; AS. scamf. See Shame, n., and Fast firm.
F. chamious a chamois, shammy leather. See Chamois.
Hind. champna to press, to squeeze.
L. seamrog, seamar, trefoil, white clover, white honeysuckle; akin to Gael. seamrag.
OE. shanke, schanke, schonke, AS. scanca, sceanca, sconca, sceonca; akin to D. schonk a bone, G. schenkel thigh, shank, schinken ham, OHG. scincha shank, Dan. & Sw. skank. sq. root161. Cf. Skink, v.
Said to be fr. Ir. sean old + tig. a house.

OE. shapen, schapen, AS. sceapian. The p. p. shapen is from the strong verb, AS. scieppan, scyppan, sceppan, p. p. sceapen. Cf. -ship.

Of uncertain origin; perhaps through OF. fr. carcharus a kind of dogfish, Gr. Shark, v. t.&i.); cf. Corn. scarceas. | Of uncertain origin; perhaps fr. shark, n., or perhaps related to E. shear (as hearken to hear), and originally meaning, to clip off. Cf. Shirk.
OE. sharp, scharp, scarp, AS. scearp; akin to OS. skarp, LG. scharp, D. scherp, G. scharf, Dan. & Sw. skarp, Icel. skarpr. Cf. Escarp, Scrape, Scorpion.
