Skr. castra an order or command, a sacred book, fr. cas to order, instruct, govern. Cf. Sastra.
OE. schateren, scateren, to scatter, to dash, AS. scateran; cf. D. schateren to crack, to make a great noise, OD. schetteren to scatter, to burst, to crack. Cf. Scatter.

OE. shaven, schaven, AS. scafan, sceafan; akin to D. schaven, G. schaben, Icel. skafa, Sw. skafva, Dan. skave, Goth. scaban, Russ. kopate to dig, Gr. scabere to scratch, to scrape. Cf. Scab, Shaft, Shape. | AS. scafa, sceafa, a sort of knife. See Shave, v. t.
OE. schawe, scha, thicket, grove, AS. scaga; akin to Dan. skov, Sw. skog, Icel. sk.
Per. & Hind. shal: cf. F. châle.
OE. shalmie, OF. chalemie; cf. F. chalumeau shawm, chaume haulm, stalk; all fr. L. calamus a reed, reed pipe. See Haulm, and cf. Calumet.

OE. she, sche, scheo, scho, AS. seó, fem. of the definite article, originally a demonstrative pronoun; cf. OS. siu, D. zij, G. sie, OHG. siu, si, si, Icel. su, sja, Goth. si she, so, fem. article, Russ. siia, fem., this, Gr. sa, sya. The possessive her or hers, and the objective her, are from a different root. See Her.
From AS. scadan, sceádan, to separate, divide. See Shed, v. t.
OE. sheef, shef, schef, AS. sceáf; akin to D. schoof, OHG. scoub, G. schaub, Icel. skauf a fox's brush, and E. shove. See Shove.

OE. sheren, scheren, to shear, cut, shave, AS. sceran, scieran, scyran; akin to D. & G. scheren, Icel. skera, Dan. ski, Gr. Jeer, Score, Shard, Share, Sheer to turn aside. | AS. sceara. See Shear, v. t.
Formerly used also in the singular. See Shear, n.,1.
Shear + water; cf. G. wassersherer; -- so called from its running lightly along the surface of the water.
Cf. dial. G. scheid, schaid, schaiden.

OE. schethe, AS. scæedh, sceáedh, sceedh; akin to OS. skeedhia, D. scheede, G. scheide, OHG. sceida, Sw. skida, Dan. skede, Icel. skeiedhir, pl., and to E. shed, v.t., originally meaning, to separate, to part. See Shed.
Akin to OD. schijve orb, disk, wheel, D. schiff, G. scheibe, Icel. skifa a shaving, slice; cf. Gr. Shift, v., Shive. | See Sheaf of straw.
Of Irish origin; cf. Ir. seapa a shop.

The same word as shade. See Shade. | OE. scheden, sch, to pour, to part, AS. scadan, sceádan, to pert, to separate; akin to OS. sk, OFries. skscheiden, OHG. sceidan, Goth. skaidan, and probably to Lith. skëdu I part, separate, L. scindere to cleave, to split, Gr. chid, and perch. also to L. caedere to cut. sq. root159. Cf. Chisel, Concise, Schism, Sheading, Sheath, Shide.
Icel. skj a shelter, a cover; akin to Dan. & Sw. skjul.

OE. sehene, AS. sciéne, sc, sc, splendid, beautiful; akin to OFries. sk, sk, OS. sc, D. schoon, G. schön, OHG. sc, Goth, skanus, and E. shew; the original meaning being probably, visible, worth seeing. It is not akin to E. shine. See Shew, v. t.
OE. shep, scheep, AS. sc, sceáp; akin to OFries. sk, LG. & D. schaap, G. schaf, OHG. scaf, Skr. chaga. sq. root295. Cf. Sheepherd.
So called because of the fancied resemblance of its head and front teeth to those of a sheep.

OE. shere, skere, pure, bright, Icel. sk; akin to skirr, AS. scir, OS. skiri, MHG. schir, G. schier, Dan. sk, Sw. skär, Goth. skeirs clear, and E. shine. sq. root157. See Shine, v. i. | See Shear. | D. sheren to shear, cut, withdraw, warp. See Shear.

OE. shete, schete, AS. sc, sc, fr. sceát a projecting corner, a fold in a garment (akin to D. schoot sheet, bosom, lap, G. schoss bosom, lap, flap of a coat, Icel. skaut, Goth. skauts the hem of a garment); originally, that which shoots out, from the root of AS. sceótan to shoot. sq. root159. See Shoot, v. t.
OE. scheten to shoot, AS. sceótan; cf. OE. shoot anchor. See Shoot, v. t.
Ar. sheikh, shaykh, a venerable old man, a chief, fr. shakha to grow or be old.
Heb. shegel, fr. shagal to weigh.
Heb Talmud shekinah, fr. shakan to inhabit.
OE., fr. sheld a shield, probably in allusion to the ornamentation of shields. See Shield.
Perhaps for sheld dapple. Cf. Sheldrake.
Perhaps for sheld dapple. Cf. Sheldrake.
OE. shelfe, schelfe, AS. scylfe; akin to G. schelfe, Icel. skjalf. In senses 2 & 3, perhaps a different word (cf. Shelve, v. i.).
OE. shelle, schelle, AS. scell, scyll; akin to D. shel, Icel. skel, Goth. skalja a tile, and E. skill. Cf. Scale of fishes, Shale, Skill.
Shell + lac a resinous substance; cf. D. shellak, G. schellack.
Shell + lac a resinous substance; cf. D. shellak, G. schellack.
Cf. OE. scheltrun, shiltroun, schelltrome, scheldtrome, a guard, squadron, AS. scildtruma a troop of men with shields; scild shield + truma a band of men. See Shield, n.
Perhapss originally from the same source as shallow, but influenced by shelf a ledge, a platform.
AS. scendan to disgrace, bring to shame, from sceand, sceond, disgrace, dishonor, shame; akin to G. schande, Goth. skanda. See Shame, n.
OE. schepherde, schephirde, AS. sceáphyrde; sceáp sheep + hyrde, hirde, heorde, a herd, a guardian. See Sheep, and Herd.
NL. So called from John Shepherd, an English botanist.
Ar. sherbet, shorbet, sharbat, properly, one drink or sip, a draught, beverage, from shariba to drink. Cf. Sorbet, Sirup, Shrub a drink.
Ar. sherif noble, holy, n., a prince.
Ar. sherif noble, holy, n., a prince.
OE. shereve, AS. scir-ger; scir a shire + ger a reeve. See Shire, and Reeve, and cf. Shrievalty.
So called from Xeres, a Spanish town near Cadiz, x in Spanish having been formerly pronounced like sh in English.
Cf. Sp. zaraquelles wide breeches or overalls.
Ar. shi'aia follower of the sect of Ali, fr. shi'at, shi'ah, a multitude following one another in pursuit of the same object, the sect of Ali, fr. sha'a to follow.
Heb. shibboleth an ear of corn, or a stream, a flood.
OE. shide, schide, AS. scide; akin to OHG. scit, G. scheit, Icel. ski, and E. shed, v.t.

OE. sheld, scheld, AS. scield, scild, sceld, scyld; akin to OS. scild, OFries. skeld, D. & G. schild, OHG. scilt, Icel. skjöldr, Sw. sköld, Dan. skiold, Goth. skildus; of uncertain origin. Cf. Sheldrake. | AS. scidan, scyldan. See Shield, n.

OE. shiften, schiften, to divide, change, remove. AS. sciftan to divide; akin to LG. & D. schiften to divide, distinguish, part Icel. skipta to divide, to part, to shift, to change, Dan skifte, Sw. skifta, and probably to Icel. skifa to cut into slices, as n., a slice, and to E. shive, sheave, n., shiver, n. | Cf. Icel skipti. See Shift, v. t.
Ar. shi'aia follower of the sect of Ali, fr. shi'at, shi'ah, a multitude following one another in pursuit of the same object, the sect of Ali, fr. sha'a to follow.
OE. shilling, schilling, AS. scilling; akin to D. schelling, OS. & OHG. scilling, G. schilling, Sw. & Dan. skilling, Icel. skillingr, Goth. skilliggs, and perh. to OHG. scellan to sound, G. schallen.
Heb. shiloh, literally, quiet, rest, fr. shalah to rest.

OE. schimeren, AS. scimerian; akin to scimian, sciman, to glitter, D. schemeren, G. schimmern, Dan. skimre, Sw. skimra, AS. scima a light, brightness, Icel. skima, Goth. skeima a torch, a lantern, and E. shine. sq. root157. See Shine, v. i.
OE. shine, schine, AS. scina; akin to D. scheen, OHG. scina, G. schiene, schienbein, Dan. skinnebeen, Sw. skenben. Cf. Chine.

OE. shinen, schinen, AS. scinan; akin to D. schijnen, OFries. skina, OS. & OHG. scinan, G. scheinen, Icel.skina, Sw. skina, Dan. skinne, Goth. skeinan, and perh. to Gr. Sheer pure, and Shimmer. | AS. scin. See Shine, v. i.
Prob. from Norw. singl, singling, coarse gravel, small round stones. | OE.
OF. cengle a girth, F. sangle, fr. L. cingulum a girdle, fr. cingere to gird. Cf. Cincture, Cingle, Surcingle.
Chin. shin god + tao way, doctrine.
Chin. shin god + tao way, doctrine.
Cf. Gael. sinteag a skip, a bound.
AS. scipe. | OE. ship, schip, AS. scip; akin to OFries. skip, OS. scip, D. schip, G. schiff, OHG. scif, Dan. skib, Sw. skeep, Icel. & Goth. skip; of unknown origin. Cf. Equip, Skiff, Skipper.
See Ship, n., and cf. Skipper.
AS. scire, scir, a division, province, county. Cf. Sheriff.
Probably the same word as shark. See Shark, v. t.

OE. schirte, sherte, schurte; akin to Icel. skyrta, Dan. skiorte, Sw. skjorta, Dan. skiört a petticoat, D. schort a petticoat, an argon, G. schurz, schürze, an argon; all probably from the root of E. short, as being originally a short garment. See Short, and cf. Skirt.

OE. schivere, fr. shive; cf. G. schifer a splinter, slate, OHG. scivere a splinter, Dan. & Sw. skifer a slate. See Shive, and cf. Skever. | OE. schiveren, scheveren; cf. OD. scheveren. See Shiver a fragment. | OE. chiveren, cheveren; of uncertain origin. This word seems to have been confused with shiver to shatter.

AS. scolu, sceolu, a company, multitude, crowd, akin to OS. skola; probably originally, a division, and akin to Icel. skilja to part, divide. See Skill, and cf. School. of fishes. | Cf. Shallow; or cf. G. scholle a clod, glebe, OHG. scollo, scolla, prob. akin to E. shoal a multitude.

OE. schokke; cf. OD schocke, G. schock a heap, quantity, threescore, MHG. schoc, Sw. skok, and also G. hocke a heap of hay, Lith. kugis. | Cf. D. schok a bounce, jolt, or leap, OHG. scoc a swing, MHG. schoc, Icel. skykkjun tremuously, F. choc a shock, collision, a dashing or striking against, Sp. choque, It. ciocco a log. sq. root161. Cf. Shock to shake. | OE. schokken; cf. D. schokken, F. choquer, Sp. chocar. sq. root161. Cf. Chuck to strike, Jog, Shake, Shock a striking, Shog, n. & v. | Cf. Shag.
Perhaps fr. Shed, v. t.; as meaning originally, waste stuff shedor thrown off.
AS. scade, fr. sceádan. See Shed, v. t.
OE. sho, scho, AS. sc, sceóh; akin to OFries. sk, OS. sk, D. schoe, schoen, G. schuh, OHG. scuoh, Icel. sk, Dan. & Sw. sko, Goth. sk; of unknown origin. | AS. sc, sce. See Shoe, n.
See Shock a striking. | Cf. W. ysgogi to wag, to stir. Cf. Jog.
Chin. tsiang kiÜn commander in chief.
Cf. G. scheuchen to scare, drive away.
Cf. Shock a bundle of sheaves.

F. chute. See Chute. Confused with shoot to let fly. | OE. shotien, schotien, AS. scotian, v. i., sceótan; akin to D. schieten, G. schie, OHG. sciozan, Icel. skj, Sw. skjuta, Dan. skyde; cf. Skr. skund to jump. sq. root159. Cf. Scot a contribution, Scout to reject, Scud, Scuttle, v. i., Shot, Sheet, Shut, Shuttle, Skittish, Skittles.
OE. shoppe, schoppe, AS. sceoppa a treasury, a storehouse, stall, booth; akin to scypen a shed, LG. schup a shed, G. schoppen, schuppen, a shed, a coachhouse, OHG. scopf.
Shop + lift. See Lift to steal.

OE. schore; akin to LG. schore, D. schoor, OD. schoore, Icel. skor, and perhaps to E. shear, as being a piece cut off. | OE. schoren. See Shore a prop. | OE. schore, AS. score, probably fr. scieran, and so meaning properly, that which is shorn off, edge; akin to OD. schoore, schoor. See Shear, v. t.
OE. short, schort, AS. scort, sceort; akin to OHG. scurz, Icel. skorta to be short of, to lack, and perhaps to E. shear, v. t. Cf. Shirt. | AS. sceortian.

AS. scot, sceot, fr. sceótan to shoot; akin to D. sschot, Icel. skot. sq. root159. See Scot a share, Shoot, v. t., and cf. Shot a shooting. | OE. shot, schot, AS. gesceot a missile; akin to D. schot a shot, shoot, G. schuss, geschoss a missile, Icel. skot a throwing, a javelin, and E. shoot, v.t. sq. root159. See Shoot, and cf. Shot a share.
AS. sceóta a darting fish, a trout, fr. sceótan. See Shoot, v. t.
Properly p. p. of shoot; AS. scoten, sceoten, p. p. of sceótan.
OE. sholde, shulde, scholde, schulde, AS. scolde, sceolde. See Shall.
OE. shulder, shuldre, schutder, AS. sculdor; akin to D. schoulder, G. schulter, OHG. scultarra, Dan. skulder, Sw. skuldra.
OE. shouten, of unknown origin; perhaps akin to shoot; cf. Icel. sk, sk, a taunt.

OE. shoven, AS. scofian, fr. sc; akin to OFries. sk, D. schuiven, G. schieben, OHG. scioban, Icel. sk, sk, Sw. skuffa, Dan. skuffe, Goth. afskiuban to put away, cast away; cf. Skr. kshubh to become agitated, to quake, Lith. skubrus quick, skubinti to hasten. sq. root160. Cf. Sheaf a bundle of stalks, Scoop, Scuffle.
OE. shovele, schovele, AS. scoft, sceoft; akin to D. schoffel, G. schaufel, OHG. sc, Dan. skovl, Sw. skofvel, skyffel, and to E. shove. sq. root160. See Shove, v. t.

OE. schowen, shewen, schewen, shawen, AS. sceáwian, to look, see, view; akin to OS. scaw, OFries. skawia, D. schouwen, OHG. scouw, G. schauen, Dan. skue, Sw. sk, Icel. sko, Goth. usskawjan to waken, skuggwa a mirror, Icel. skuggy shade, shadow, L. cavere to be on one's guard, Gr. kavi wise. Cf. Caution, Scavenger, Sheen. | Written also shew. | Formerly written also shew.
OE. shour, schour, AS. se; akin to D. schoer, G. schauer, OHG. sc, Icel. sk, Sw. skur, Goth. sk a storm of wind; of uncertain origin.

OE. shrede, schrede, AS. screáde; akin to OD. schroode, G. schrot a piece cut off, Icel. skrjothr a shred, and to E. shroud. Cf. Screed, Scroll, Scrutiny. | OE. shreden, schreden, AS. screádian; akin to OD. schrooden, OHG. scr, G. schroten. See Shred, n.
OE. shrewe, schrewe. Cf. Shrewd. | See Shrew, a. | See Shrew, a., and cf. Beshrew.
Originally the p. p. of shrew, v.t.
OE. shriken, originallythe same word as E. screech. See Screech, and cf. Screak.
Contr. from sheriffalty. See Shrieve, n. Sheriff.
Contr. from OE. shereve. See Sheriff.
OE. shrift, schrift, AS. scrift, fr. scrifan to shrive. See Shrive.
Akin to Icel. skrikja a shrieker, the shrike, and E. shriek; cf. AS. scric a thrush. See Shriek, v. i.

OE. shril, schril; akin to LG. schrell, G. schrill. See Shrill,v. i. | OE. schrillen, akin to G. schrillen; cf. AS. scralletan to resound loudly, Icel. skrölta to jolt, Sw. skrälla to shrill, Norw. skryla, skr. Cf. Skirl.

Cf. AS. scrimman to dry up, wither, MHG. schrimpfen to shrink, G. schrumpfen, Dan. skrumpe, skrumpes, Da. & Sw. skrumpen shriveled. Cf. Scrimp, Shrink, Shrivel. | OE. shrimp; -- probably so named from its shriveled appearance. See Shrimp, v.
OE. schrin, AS. scrin, from L. scrinium a case, chest, box.
OE. shrinken, schrinken, AS. scrincan; akin to OD. schrincken, and probably to Sw. skrynka a wrinkle, skrynkla to wrinkle, to rumple, and E. shrimp, n. & v., scrimp. CF. Shrimp.
OE. shriven, schriven, AS. scrivan to shrive, to impose penance or punishment; akin to OFries. skriva to impose punishment; cf. OS. biskriban to be troubled. Cf. Shrift, Shrovetide.
Probably akin to shrimp, shrink; cf. dial. AS. screpa to pine away, Norw. skrypa to waste, skryp, skryv, transitory, frail, Sw. skröpling feeble, Dan. skröbelig, Icel. skrj brittle, frail.

OE. shroud, shrud, schrud, AS. scr a garment, clothing; akin to Icel. skru the shrouds of a ship, furniture of a church, a kind of stuff, Sw. skrud dress, attire, and E. shred. See Shred, and cf. Shrood. | Cf. AS. scr. See Shroud, n.
From shrive to take a confession (OE. imp. shrof, AS. scraf) + tide.
Ar. shirb, shurb, a drink, beverage, fr. shariba to drink. Cf. Sirup, Sherbet. | OE. schrob, AS. scrob, scrobb; akin to Norw. skrubba the dwarf cornel tree.
Probably akin to shrink, p. p. shrunk; cf. Dan. skrugge, skrukke, to stoop, dial. Sw. skrukka, skruga, to crouch.
Perhaps akin to G. shote a husk, pod, shell.
OE. shoderen, schuderen; akin to LG. schuddern, D. schudden to shake, OS. skuddian, G. schaudern to shudder, schütteln to shake, schütten to pour, to shed, OHG. scutten, scuten, to shake.
Originally the same word as scuffle, and properly a freq. of shove. See Shove, and Scuffle.
OE. shunien, schunien, schonien, AS. scunian, sceonian; cf. D. schuinen to slepe, schuin oblique, sloping, Icel. skunda, skynda, to hasten. Cf. Schooner, Scoundrel, Shunt.
Prov. E., to move from, to put off, fr. OE. shunten, schunten, schounten; cf. D. schuinte a slant, slope, Icel. skunda to hasten. Cf. Shun. | Cf. D. schuinte slant, slope, declivity. See Shunt, v. t.

OE. shutten, schutten, shetten, schitten, AS. scyttan to shut or lock up (akin to D. schutten, G. schützen to protect), properly, to fasten with a bolt or bar shot across, fr. AS. sceótan to shoot. sq. root159. See Shoot.

Also shittle, OE. schitel, scytyl, schetyl; cf. OE. schitel a bolt of a door, AS. scyttes; all from AS. sceótan to shoot; akin to Dan. skyttel, skytte, shuttle, dial. Sw. skyttel, sköttel. sq. root159. See Shoot, and cf. Shittle, Skittles.
OE. schey, skey, sceouh, AS. sceóh; akin to Dan. sky, Sw. skygg, D. schuw, MHG. schiech, G. scheu, OHG. sciuhen to be or make timid. Cf. Eschew. | From Shy, a.
L., if any one (the first words of the notice in Latin).
AS. sibb alliance, gesib a relative. sq. root289. See Gossip.
L. sibilans, -antis, p. pr. of sibilare to hiss: cf. F. sibilant.
L. siccatus, p. p. of siccare to dry, fr. siecus dry.
L. siccificus; siccus dry + facere to make. See -fy.
F. six, fr. L. sex six. See Six.
OE. sek, sik, ill, AS. seóc; akin to OS. siok, seoc, OFries. siak, D. ziek, G. siech, OHG. sioh, Icel. sj, Sw. sjuk, Dan. syg, Goth. siuks ill, siukan to be ill.
AS. sicerian. | OE. siker; cf. OS. sikur, LG. seker, D. zeker, Dan. sikker, OHG. sihhur, G. sicher; all fr. L. securus. See Secure, Sure.
OE. sikel, AS. sicol; akin to D. sikkel, G. sichel, OHG. sihhila, Dan. segel, segl, L. secula, fr. secare to cut; or perhaps from L. secula. See Saw a cutting instrument.
F., fr. L. silcus, Heb. shegel. See Shekel.
AS. side; akin to D. zijde, G. seite, OHG. sita, Icel. si, Dan. side, Sw. sida; cf. AS. sid large, spacious, Icel. si long, hanging.
OE. sideling, fr. side side. See Side, and cf. Sidelong, Headlong.
L. sideratus, p. p. of siderari to be blasted by a constellation, fr. sidus, sideris, a constellation.
L. sidereus, from sidus, sideris, a constellation, a star. Cf. Sideral, Consider, Desire.

OE. sege, OF. siege, F. siège a seat, a siege; cf. It. seggia, seggio, zedio, a seat, asseggio, assedio, a siege, F. assiéger to besiege, It. & LL. assediare, L. obsidium a siege, besieging; all ultimately fr. L. sedere to sit. See Sit, and cf. See, n.
It. terra di Siena, fr. Siena in Italy.
Sp., properly, a saw, fr. L. serra a saw. See Serrate.
Sp., probably fr. L. sessitare to sit much or long, v. freq. of sedere, sessum, to sit. See Sit.
F., abbrev. from seigneur. Cf. Monsieur, Seignior.
OE. sive, AS. sife; akin to D. zeef, zift, OHG. sib, G. sieb. sq. root151a. Cf. Sift.
AS. siftan, from sife sieve. sq. root151a. See Sieve.
Akin to AS. sigan to fall. sq. root151a. See Sink, v. t.
OE. sighen, si; cf. also OE. siken, AS. sican, and OE. sighten, si, sichten, AS. siccettan; all, perhaps, of imitative origin. | OE. sigh; cf. OE. sik. See Sigh, v. i.
OE. sight, si, siht, AS. siht, gesiht, gesih, gesieh, gesyh; akin to D. gezicht, G. sicht, gesicht, Dan. sigte, Sw. sigt, from the root of E. see. See See, v. t.
L. sigillum. See Seal a stamp.
L., from sigillum a seal. See Sigil. | NL., fem sing. fr. L. sigillum a seal.
L. sigillatus adorned with little images.
L. sigillum a seal: cf. OF. sigillatif.

F. signe, L. signum; cf. AS. segen, segn, a sign, standard, banner, also fr. L. signum. Cf. Ensign, Resign, Seal a stamp, Signal, Signet. | OE. seinen to bless, originally, to make the sign of the cross over; in this sense fr. ASS. segnian (from segn, n.), or OF. seignier, F. signer, to mark, to sign (in sense 3), fr. L. signare to mark, set a mark upon, from signum. See Sign, n.
F., fr. LL. signale, fr. L. signum. See Sign, n. | From signal, n.: cf. F. signalé.
L. signatus, p. p. See Sign, v. t.
L. signatio. See Sign, v. t.
F. (cf. It. signatura, segnatura, Sp. & LL. signatura), from L. signare, signatum. See Sign, v. t.
OF. signet a signet, F., a bookmark, dim. of signe. See Sign, n., and cf. Sennet.
L., from signum sign + ferre to bear.
L. significans, -antis, p. pr. of significare. See Signify.
L. significatus, p. p. of significare. See Signify.
L., (he) has signified, perf. ind. of significare to signify.
F. signifier, L. significare; signum a sign + - ficare (in comp.) to make. See Sign, n., and -fy.
AS. sic. Cf. Sig. | See Sick.
OE. siker; cf. OS. sikur, LG. seker, D. zeker, Dan. sikker, OHG. sihhur, G. sicher; all fr. L. securus. See Secure, Sure.
Akin to Sw. sila to strain, sil sieve, G. sielen to draw away or lead off water. sq. root151a. See Silt. | Icel. sild herring; akin to Sw. sill, Dan. sild. Cf. Sill the young of a herring.
F., fr. L. silentium. See Silent.
NL., fr. L. Silenus, the attendant of Bacchus.
L. silens, -entis, p. pr. of silere to be silent; akin to Goth. ana-silan.
L. silentiarius: cf. F. silenciaire. See Silence.
L. Silenus the tutor and attendant of Bacchus.
F.; -- so called from Etienne de Silhoutte, a French minister of finance in 1759, whise diversion it was to make such portraits on the walls of his apartments.
NL., from L. silex, silics, a flint.
L. siliceus, fr. silex, silicis, a flint.
L. silex, silicis, a flint: cf. F. silicique.
L. silex, silicis, a flint + -fy: cf. F. silicifier.
L. silicula, dim. of siliqua a pod or husk: cf. F. silicule.
NL. siliculosus, fr. L. silicula: cf. F. siliculeux. See Silicle.
L. siligineus, fr. siligo, -inis, fine and very white wheat.
L. siliqua a pod or husk, a very small weight or measure: cf. F. silique.

OE. silk, selk, AS. seolc, seoloc; akin to Icel. silki, SW. & Dan. silke; prob. through Slavic from an Oriental source; cf. Lith. szilkai, Russ. shelk', and also L. sericum Seric stuff, silk. Cf. Sericeous. Serge a woolen stuff.
OE. sille, sylle, AS. syl, syll; akin to G. schwelle, OHG. swelli, Icel. syll, svill, Sw. syll, Dan. syld, Goth. gasuljan to lay a foundation, to found. | Cf. Thill. | Cf. 4th Sile.
Cf. sile to strain, and bub liquor, also Prov. E. sillibauk.
After Benjamin Siliman, an American meneralogist.

OE. seely, sely, AS. s, ges, happy, good, fr. s, s, good, happy, s good fortune, happines; akin to OS. salig, a, good, happy, D. zalig blessed, G. selig, OHG. salig, Icel. s, Sw. säll, Dan. salig, Goth. s good, kind, and perh. also to L. sollus whole, entire, Gr. sarva. Cf. Seel, n.
Prov. E. silly-hew; cf. AS. sælig happy, good, and hufe a cap, hood. See Silly, a.

OE. silte gravel, fr. silen to drain, E. sile; probably of Scand. origin; cf. Sw. sila, prob. akin to AS. seón to filter, sigan to fall, sink, cause to sink, G. seihen to strain, to filter, OHG. sihan, Icel.sia, Skr. sic to pour; cf. Gr. Sig, Sile.
L. silurus a sort of river fish, Gr. silure.
From L. Silures, a people who anciently inhabited a part of England and Wales.
L. silva, less correctly sylva, a wood or grove, perh. akin to Gr. "y`lh; cf. L. Silvanus Silvanus the god of woods: cf. F. sylvain silvan. Cf. Savage.
L. silva a forest, Sp. selva.

OE. silver, selver, seolver, AS. seolfor, siolfur, siolufr, silofr, sylofr; akin to OS. silubar, OFries. selover, D. zilver, LG. sulver, OHG. silabar, silbar, G. silber, Icel. silfr, Sw. silfver, Dan. sölv, Goth. silubr, Russ. serebro, Lith. sidabras; of unknown origin.
F. similaire, fr. L. similis like, similar. See Same, a., and cf. Simulate.
F. similitude, L. similitudo, from similis similar. See Similar.
F., fr. L. similus similar + F. or gold, L. aurum. Cf. Semilor.
Prov. E. also simper; -- an onomatopoetic word.
OF. simenel cake or bread of wheat flour, LL. simenellus wheat bread, fr. L. simila the finest wheat flour. Cf. Semolina.
F. simonie, LL. simonia, fr. Simon Magus, who wished to purchase the power of conferring the Holy Spirit. Acts viii.
Ar. sam, fr. samma to poison. Cf. Samiel.
Ar. sam, fr. samma to poison. Cf. Samiel.
Cf. Norw. semper fine, smart, dial. Dan. semper, simper, affected, coy, prudish, OSw. semper one who affectedly refrains from eating, Sw. sipp finical, prim, LG. sipp.

F., fr. L. simplus, or simplex, gen. simplicis. The first part of the Latin words is probably akin to E. same, and the sense, one, one and the same; cf. L. semel once, singuli one to each, single. Cg. Single, a., Same, a., and for the last part of the word cf. Double, Complex. | F. See Simple, a.
F. simplicité, L. simplicitas. See Simple.
Cf. F. simplifier, LL. simplificare. See Simple, and -fy.
Cf. L. simulator, F. simulateur. See Simulate.
L. simulatus, p. p. of simulare to simulate; akin to simul at the same time, together, similis like. See Similar, and cf. Dissemble, Semblance.
LL. simultim at the same time, fr. L. simul. See Simulate.
L. simultas a hostile encounter, drudge, originally, a (hostile) coming together, fr. simul together: cf. OF. simulté.

OE. sinne, AS. synn, syn; akin to D. zonde, OS. sundia, OHG. sunta, G. sünde, Icel., Dan. & Sw. synd, L. sons, sontis, guilty, perhaps originally from the p. pr. of the verb signifying, to be, and meaning, the one who it is. Cf. Authentic, Sooth. | OE. sinnen, singen, sinegen, AS. syngian. See Sin, n.
L. sinapi, sinapis, mustard, Gr. sinapine.
So called because obtained by the action of alkalies on sinapine.

For sins, contr. fr. OE. sithens, sithenes, formed by an adverbial ending (cf. Besides) from OE. sithen, also shortened into sithe, sin, AS. si, sy, seo, afterward, then, since, after; properly, after that; fr. sisi afterward, since, OHG. sid, G. seit since, Goth. seipus late, ni sei no longer) + instrumental of the demonstrative and article. See That.
L. sincerus, of uncertain origin; the first part perhaps akin to sin- in singuli (see Single), and the second to cernere to separate (cf. Discern): cf. F. sincère.
L., half a head; semihalf + caput the head.
L., a kind of fine Indian cotton stuff, Gr. 1. A wrapper. [Obs.

LL. sinus a sine, L. sinus bosom, used in translating the Ar. jaib, properly, bosom, but probably read by mistake (the consonants being the same) for an original jiba sine, from Skr. jiva bowstring, chord of an arc, sine. | L.
L. sine without + cura care, LL., a cure. See Cure.
OE. sinewe, senewe, AS. sinu, seonu; akin to D. zenuw, OHG. senawa, G. sehne, Icel. sin, Sw. sena, Dan. sene; cf. Skr. snava. sq. root290.
AS. singan; akin to D. zingen, OS. & OHG. singan, G. singen, Icel. syngja, Sw. sjunga, Dan. synge, Goth. siggwan, and perhaps to E. say, v.t., or cf. Gr. Singe, Song.

OE. sengen, AS. sengan in besengan (akin to D. zengen, G. sengen), originally, to cause to sing, fr. AS. singan to sing, in allusion to the singing or hissing sound often produced when a substance is singed, or slightly burned. See Sing.
L. singulus, a dim. from the root in simplex simple; cf. OE. & OF. sengle, fr. L. singulus. See Simple, and cf. Singular.
OE. singuler, F. singulier, fr. L. singularius, singularis, fr. singulus single. See Single, a.
Accented on the middle syllable by the older poets, as Shakespeare, Milton, Dryden.
L. sinistra the left hand + ad tp.
L.sinistrorsus, sinistroversus, turned toward the left side; sinister left + vertere, vortere, versum, vorsum, to turn.
OE. sinken, AS. sincan; akin to D. zinken, OS. sincan, G. sinken, Icel. sökkva, Dan. synke, Sw. sjunka, Goth. siggan, and probably to E. silt. Cf. Silt.
From L. Sinae, an Oriental people mentioned by Ptolemy, or Ar. Sin China or the Chinese + Gr. theologue: cf. F. sinologue.
F., fr. LL. sinopis. See Sinople a mineral.
L. sinuatus, p. p. of sinuare to wind, bend, fr. sinus a bend.
L. sinuosus, fr. sinus a bent surface, a curve: cf. F. sinueux. See Sinus.
L., a bent surface, a curve, the folds or bosom of a garment, etc., a bay. Cf. Sine, n.
OE. sippen; akin to OD. sippen, and AS. s to sip, suck up, drink. See Sup, v. t.
L. sipho a siphon + -oid: cf. F. vase siphoïde.
NL., fr. L. sipho, -onis, siphon + ferre to bear.
L. siphunculus, sipunculus, dim. of sipho. See Siphon.
NL., from Sipunculus, the typical genus. See Siphuncle.

OE. sire, F. sire, contr. from the nominative L. senior an elder, elderly person, compar. of senex,senis, an aged person; akin to Gr. sana, Goth. sineigs old, sinista eldest, Ir. & Gael. sean old, W. hen. Cf. Seignior, Senate, Seneschal, Senior, Senor, Signor, Sire, Sirrah.
Hind. & Per. sarkar a superintendant, overseer, chief; Per. sar the head + kar action, work.
Hind. & Per. sardar a chief, general; sar the head, top + dar holding, possessing.
F. sire, originally, an older person. See Sir.
L., fr. Gr. (Med.) (a) A sunstroke. (b) The act of exposing to a sun bath. [Obs.
A corruption of surloin. Not so called because this cut of beaf was once jocosely knighted (dubbed Sir Loin) by an English king, as according to a popular story.
It. sirocco, scirocco, Ar. shorug, fr. sharq the rising of the sun, the east, fr, sharaca to rise as the sun. Cf. Saracen.
Probably from Icel. sira, fr. F. sire. See Sir.
F. sirop (cf. It. siroppo, Sp. jarabe, jarope, LL. siruppus, syrupus), fr. Ar. sharab a drink, wine, coffee, sirup. Cf. Sherbet.

F. sirvente, fr. Pr. sirventes, sirventesc, originally, the poem of, or concerning, a sirvent, fr. sirvent, properly, serving, n., one who serves (e. g., as a soldier), fr. servir to serve, L. servire.
Dan. sisgen; cf. Sw. siska, G. zeisig, D. sijsje; of Slav. origin; cf. Pol. czy.
Of imitative origin; cf. D. sissen, G. zischen.
L. sistere to bring to a stand, to stop.

OE. sister, fr. Icel. systir; also suster, from AS. sweostor, sweoster, swuster, akin to OFries. sweester, suster, LG. süster, suster, D. zuster, OS. & OHG. swestar, G. schwester, Icel. systir, Sw. syster, Dan. söster, Goth. swistar, Lith. ses, Russ. sestra, Pol. siostra, L. soror, Skr. svasr. sq. root298. Cf. Cousin.

OE. sitten, AS. sittan; akin to OS. sittian, OFries. sitta, D. zitten, G. sitzen, OHG. sizzen, Icel. sitja, SW. sitta, Dan. sidde, Goth. sitan, Russ. sidiete, L. sedere, Gr. sad. sq. root154. Cf. Assess,Assize, Cathedral, Chair, Dissident, Excise, Insidious, Possess, Reside, Sanhedrim, Seance, Seat, n., Sedate, 4th Sell, Siege, Session, Set, v. t., Sizar, Size, Subsidy.
L. situs, fr. sinere, situm, to let, p. p. situs placed, lying, situate: cf. F. site. Cf. Position.
NL., fr. Gr. (Med.) Defn: A version to food; refusal to take nourishment. [Written also sitiophobia.
LL. situatus, from situare to place, fr. L. situs situation, site. See Site.
LL. situatus, from situare to place, fr. L. situs situation, site. See Site.

AS. six, seox, siex; akin to OFries. sex, D. zes, OS. & OHG. sehs, G. sechs, Icel., Sw., & Dan. sex, Goth. saíhs, Lith. szeszi, Russ. sheste, Gael. & Ir. se, W. chwech, L. sex, Gr. shesh, Skr. shash. sq. root304. Cf. Hexagon, Hexameter, Samite, Senary, Sextant, Sice.
AS. sixt, sixt. See Six, and Ten, and cf. Sixty.
From Six: cf. AS. sixta, siexta.
AS. siextig; akin to G. sechzig, Goth. saíhs tigjus. See Six, Ten, and cf. Sixteen.

See Sice, and Sise. | OIt. sisa glue used by painters, shortened fr. assisa, fr. assidere, p. p. assiso, to make to sit, to seat, to place, L. assidere to sit down; ad + sidere to sit down, akin to sedere to sit. See Sit, v. i., and cf. Assize, Size bulk. | Abbrev. from assize. See Assize, and cf. Size glue.
Perhaps originally, a companion in winding thread (see Skein), or a companion in arms, from skain a sword (see Skean).
D. schaats. Cf. Scatches. | Icel. skata; cf. Prov. G. schatten, meer-schatten, L. squatus, squatina, and E. shad.
Ir sgian; akin to Gael. sgian, W. ysgien a large knife, a scimiter.
Dan. ski; Icel. ski a billet of wood. See Skid.
Prov. E., also a stump of a branch, a wooden peg; cf. Icel. sk a wood, Sw. skog. Cf. Shaw.
OE. skeyne, OF. escaigne, F. écagne, probably of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. sgainne, Gael. sgeinnidh thread, small twine; or perhaps the English word is immediately from Celtic.
Cf. Prov. E. skelp to kick severely, to move rapidly; Gael. sgealp, n., a slap with the palm of the hand, v., to strike with the palm of the hand.
Icel. skeppa a measure, bushel; cf. Gael. sgeap a basket, a beehive.
Gr. skeptiko`s thoughtful, reflective, fr. ske`ptesqai to look carefully or about, to view, consider: cf. L. scepticus, F. sceptique. See Scope. | Written also sceptic, sceptical.
Of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. sker, Sw. skär, Dan. ski. Cf. Scar a bank.
D. schets, fr. It. schizzo a sketch, a splash (whence also F. esquisse; cf. Esquisse.); cf. It. schizzare to splash, to sketch. | Cf D. schetsen, It. schizzare. See Sketch, n.
Cf. D. scheef. Dan. ski, Sw. skef, Icel. skeifr, G. schief, also E. shy, a. & v. i. | See Skew, adv.
Probably of Scand, origin; cf. Sw. & Dan. skifer a slate. Cf. Shuver a fragment.
Icel. ski a billet of wood. See Shide.
F. esquif, fr. OHG. skif, G. schiff. See Ship.

Icel. skil a distinction, discernment; akin to skilja to separate, divide, distinguish, Sw. skilja,. skille to separate, skiel reason, right, justice, Sw. skäl reason, Lith. skelli to cleave. Cf. Shell, Shoal, a multitude.
OF. escuelette, dim. of escuelle a porringer, F. ecuelle, fr. L. scutella, dim. of scutra, scuta, a dish. Cf. Scuttle a basket.
Cf. Sheeling. | Sw. & Dan. See Shilling.
Cf. Sw. skymma to darken. sq. root158. See Scum.
Etymol. uncertain. Perhaps the name of some notorius scold.
Icel. skinn; akin to Sw. skinn, Dan. skind, AS. scinn, G. schined to skin.

L. scincus, Gr. [Written also scink. | Icel. skenja; akin to Sw. skäka, Dan. skienke, AS. scencan, D. & G. schenken. As. scencan is usually derived from sceonc, sceanc, shank, a hollow bone being supposed to have been used to draw off liquor from a cask. sq. root161. See Shank, and cf. Nunchion.

See Skep. | OE. skippen, of uncertain origin; cf. Icel. skopa run, skoppa to spin like a top, OSw. & dial. Sw. skimmpa to run, skimpa, skompa, to hop, skip; or Ir. sgiob to snatch, Gael. sgiab to start or move suddenly, to snatch, W. ysgipio to snatch.
D. schipper. See Shipper, and Ship.
Cf. Icel. skip, E. skipper. See Ship.
Of Scand. origin, and originally the same word as E. shrill.

OE. skirmishen, scarmishen, OF. escremir, eskermir, to fence, fight, F. escrimer, of German origin; cf. OHG. scirmen to protect, defend, G. schirmen, OHG. scirm, scerm, protection, shield, G. schirm; perhaps akin to Gr. Scaramouch, Scrimmage. | OE. scarmishe, scrymishe. See Skirmish, v. i.
A corrupted form equivalent to sugarwort.
OE. skyrt, of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. skyrta a shirt, Sw. skört a skirt, skjorta a shirt. See Shirt.

Prov. E. skitto slide, as adj., hasty, precipitate, of Scand. origin, and akin to E. shoot, v.t.; cf. Icel. skyti, skytja, skytta, a marksman, shooter, skjota to shoot, skuta a taunt. sq. root159. See Shoot.
Of Scand. origin. sq. root159. See Shoot, v. t., and cf. Shuttle, Skit, v. t.
Cf. Icel. skifa a shaving, slice, E. shive, sheave.

Of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. skulke to spare or save one's self, to play the truant, Sw. skolka to be at leisure, to shirk, Icel. skolla. Cf. Scowl. | Cf. Icel. skollr, skolli, a fox, and E. skulk, v.i.
See School a multitude. | OE. skulle, sculle, scolle; akin to Scot. skull, skoll, a bowl, Sw. skalle skull, skal a shell, and E. scale; cf. G. hirnschale, Dan. hierneskal. Cf. Scale of a balance.
Contr. from the Abenaki (American Indian) seganku.
Icel. sk; akin to Sw. skuta, Dan. skude, D. schuit, Lg. schüte, and E. schoot, v.t.
From Skuttertid, in Norway, whence it is ibtained.
OE. skie a cloud, Icel. sk; akin to Sw. & Dan. sky; cf. AS. sc, sc, shadow, Icel. skuggi; probably from the same root as E. scum. sq. root158. See Scum, and cf. Hide skin, Obscure.

OE. slabbe, of uncertain origin; perhaps originally meaning, a smooth piece, and akin to slape, Icel. sleipr slippery, and E. slip, v. i. | Cf. Gael. & Ir. slaib mud, mire left on a river strand, and E. slop puddle.
OE. slaberen; akin to LG. & D. slabbern, G. schlabbern, LG. & D. slabben, G. schlabben, Icel. slafra. Cf. Slaver, Slobber, Slubber. | See 1st Slab.

Cf. Slag. | Icel. slakki a slope on a mountain edge. | OE. slak, AS. sleac; akin to OS. slak, OHG. slah, Prov. G. schlack, Icel. slakr, Sw. slak; cf. Skr. srsj to let loose, to throw. Cf. Slake. | See Slack, a.
Sw. slagg, or LG. slacke, whence G. schlacke; originally, perhaps, the splinters struck off from the metal by hammering. See Slay, v. t.
OE. slaken to render slack, to slake, AS. sleacian, fr. sleac slack. See Slack, v. & a.
Of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. slamra, slambra, sl, Norw. slemba, slemma, dial. Sw. slämma.
Cf. G. schlampe, schlamp, dim. schlämpchen; schlampen to dangle, to be slovenly in one's dress.
Cf. G. schlampe, schlamp, dim. schlämpchen; schlampen to dangle, to be slovenly in one's dress.
OE. sclandere, OF. esclandre, esclandle, escandre, F. esclandre, fr. L. scandalum, Gr. skand to spring, leap. See Scan, and cf. Scandal.

Cf. Sling. | Said to be of Gypsy origin; but probably from Scand., and akin to E. sling; cf. Norw. sleng a slinging, an invention, device, slengja to sling, to cast, slengja kjeften (literally, to sling the jaw) to use abusive language, to use slang, slenjeord (ord = word) an insulting word, a new word that has no just reason for being.
OE. slenten to slope, slide; cf. Sw. slinta to slide. | Cf. dial. Sw. slant. See Slant, v. i.
OE. slappe; akin to LG. slappe, G. schlappe; probably of imitative origin. | Cf. LG. slap, G. schlapp. See Slap, n.
Icel. sleipr slippery; akin to E. slip.
OE. slaschen, of uncertain origin; cf. OF. esclachier to break, esclechier, esclichier, to break, and E. slate, slice, slit, v. t.
Cf. Sw. slaska to dabble in water. Cf. Slush.
CF. Slot a bar. | OE. slatten; cf. Icel. sletta to slap, to dab.

OE. slat, OF. esclat a shiver, splinter, F. éclat, fr. OF. esclater to shiver, to chip, F. éclater, fr. OHG. sliezen to tear, slit, split, fr. slizan to slit, G. schleissen. See Slit, v. t., and cf. Eclat. | Cf. AS. slæting a privilege of hunting.
See Slat a strip of board.
E. slat to throw or dash about.
OE. slautir, slaughter, slaghter, Icel. slatr slain flesh, modified by OE. slaught, slaht, slaughter, fr. AS. sleaht a stroke, blow; both from the root of E. slay. See Slay, v. t., and cf. Onslaught.

A word originally meaning, intelligible, and used to contrast the people so called with foreigners who spoke languages unintelligible to the Slavs; akin to OSlav. slovo a word, slava fame, Skr. çru to hear. Cf. Loud.

Cf. F. esclave, D. slaaf, Dan. slave, sclave, Sw. slaf, all fr. G. sklave, MHG. also slave, from the national name of the Slavonians, or Sclavonians (in LL. Slavi or Sclavi), who were frequently made slaves by the Germans. See Slav.
D. sla, contr. fr. salade, OD. salaet, salad. See Salad.

OE. slan, sl, sleen, slee, AS. sleán to strike, beat, slay; akin to OFries. sla, D. slaan, OS. & OHG. slahan, G. schlagen, Icel. sla, Dan. slaae, Sw. sl, Goth. slahan; perhaps akin to L. lacerare to tear to pieces, Gr. lacerate. Cf. Slaughter, Sledge a hammer, Sley.
Cf. Dan. slöif, a knot loop, Sw. slejf, G. schleife a knot, silding knot, and E. slip, v.i.
Cf. G. schleissig worn out, threadbare, from schleissen to slit, split, decay, or E. leasy.
Akin to D. slede, G. schlitten, OHG. slito, Icel. sle, Sw. släde, Dan. sl, and E. slide, v. See Slide, and cf. Sledge a vehicle, Sleigh.
Perhaps from sleds, pl. of sled, confused with sledge a hammer. See Sled, n. | AS. slecge,from sleán to strike, beat. See Slay, v. t.
OE. slik; akin to Icel. slikr, and OE. sliken to glide, slide, G. schleichen, OHG. slihhan, D. slik, slijk, mud, slime, and E. slink. Cf. Slick, Slink.

OE. slepen, AS. sl; akin to OFries. sl, OS. slapan, D. slapen, OHG. slafan, G. schlafen, Goth. sl, and G. schlaff slack, loose, and L. labi to glide, slide, labare to totter. Cf. Lapse. | AS. sl; akin to OFries. sl, OS. slap, D. slaap, OHG. slaf, G. schlaf, Goth. sl. See Sleep, v. i.
Cf. Norw. sleip a sleeper (a timber), as adj., slippery, smooth. See Slape.
OE. sleet; akin to MHG. sl, sl hailstone, G. schlosse; of uncertain origin.
OE. sleeve, sleve, AS. sl, sl; akin to sl to put on, to clothe; cf. OD. sloove the turning up of anything, sloven to turn up one's sleeves, sleve a sleeve, G. schlaube a husk, pod.
Cf. D. & LG. slede, slee, Icel. sle. See Sled.
OE. sleighte, sleihte, sleithe, Icel. sl (for sl) slyness, cunning, fr. sl (for sl) sly, cunning. See Sly.
OE. slendre, sclendre, fr. OD. slinder thin, slender, perhaps through a French form; cf. OD. slinderen, slidderen, to creep; perh. akin to E. slide.
Icel. sloedh. See Slot a track.
AS. sl, fr. sleán to strike. See Slay, v. t.
OE. slice, sclice, OF. esclice, from esclicier, esclichier, to break to pieces, of German origin; cf. OHG. slizan to split, slit, tear, G. schleissen to slit. See Slit, v. t.
AS. sliderian. See Slide, v. t. | AS. slidor. See Slide, v. t.
AS. slidor. See Slide, v. t.
AS. slidor. See Slide, v. t.
OE. sliden, AS. slidan; akin to MHG. sliten, also to AS. slidor slippery, E. sled, Lith. slidus slippery. Cf. Sled. | AS. slide.

Cf. D. slechten to level, to demolish. | OE. sli, sleght, probably from OD. slicht, slecht, simple, plain, D. slecht; akin to OFries. sliucht, G. schlecht, schlicht, OHG. sleht smooth, simple, Icel. sl smooth, Sw. slät, Goth. slaíhts; or uncertain origin.
Formerly, bad, worthless, weak, slight, awry, fr. D. slim; akin to G. schlimm, MHG. slimp oblique, awry; of uncertain origin. The meaning of the English word seems to have been influenced by slender.
OE. slim, AS. slim; akin to D. slijm, G. schleim, MHG. slimen to make smooth, Icel. slim slime, Dan. sliim; cf. L. limare to file, polish, levis smooth, Gr. limus mud.

OE. slinge; akin to OD. slinge, D. slinger, OHG. slinga; cf. OF. eslingue, of German origin. See Sling, v. t. | AS. slingan; akin to D. slingeren, G. schlingen, to wind, to twist, to creep, OHG. slingan to wind, to twist, to move to and fro, Icel. slyngva, slöngva, to sling, Sw. slunga, Dan. slynge, Lith. slinkti to creep. | Cf. G. schlingen to swallow.
AS. slincan; probably akin to G. schleichen, E. sleek. See Sleek, a.

OE. slippen; akin to LG. & D. slippen, MHG. slipfen (cf. Dan. slippe, Sw. slippa, Icel. sleppa), and fr. OE. slipen, AS. slipan (in comp.), akin to G. schleifen to slide, glide, drag, whet, OHG. slifan to slide, glide, make smooth, Icel. slipa to whet; cf. also AS. sl, Goth. sliupan, OS. slopian, OHG. sliofan, G. schliefen, schl, which seem to come from a somewhat different root form. Cf. Slope, n. | AS. slipe, slip.

OE. slitten, fr. sliten, AS. stitan to tear; akin to D. slijten to wear out, G. schleissen to slit, split, OHG. slizan to split, tear, wear out, Icel. stita to break, tear, wear out, Sw. slita, Dan. slide. Cf. Eclat, Slate, n., Slice. | AS. slite.
Cf. G. schlittern, LG. schliddern. See Slide.
Cf. Slip. | OE. sliven to split, cleave, AS. slifan.
OE. slo, AS. sla; akin to D. slee, G. schlehe, OHG. sl$ha, Dan. slaaen, Sw. sl, perhaps originally, that which blunts the teeth, or sets them on edge (cf. Slow); cf. Lith. sliwa a plum, Russ. sliva.
Gael. sluagh-ghairm, i.e., an army cry; sluagh army + gairm a call, calling.
D. sloep, of uncertain origin. Cf. Shallop.

OE. sloppe a pool; akin to As. sloppe, slyppe, the sloppy droppings of a cow; cf. AS. sl to slip, and E. slip, v.i. Cf. Cowslip. | AS. slop a frock or over-garment, fr. sl to slip, to slide; akin to Icel sloppr a thin garment; cf. OHG. slouf a garment. Cf. Slip, v. i.
Formed (like abode fr. abide) from OE. slipen. See Slip, v. i.

LG. & D. slot a lock, from a verb meaning to close., to shut, D. sluiten; akin to G. schliessen, OHG. sliozan, OFries. sl, and probably to L. claudere. Cf. Close, Sluice. | See Slot a bar. | Cf. Icel. sl, and E. sleuth.
OE. slouthe, sleuthe, AS. sl, fr. slaw slow. See Slow.
See Slot a track, and cf. Sleuthhound.
Cf. Icel. sla slouching felloew, and E. slack, slug, a lazy fellow.
OE. | OE. slugh, slouh; cf. MHG. sl the skin of a serpent, G. schlauch a skin, a leather bag or bottle.
D. slaf careless, negligent, a sloven; akin to LG. sluf slovenly.
OE. slow, slaw, AS. slaw; akin to OS. sl blunt, dull, D. sleeuw, slee, sour, OHG. sl blunt, dull, Icel. sl, sl, Dan. slöv, Sw. slö. Cf. Sloe, and Sloth.
AS. slawyrm; the first part is probably akin to sleán to strike, the reptile being supposed to be very poisonous. See Slay, v. t., and Worm.
Cf. Dan. slubbreto swallow, to sup up, D. slobberen to lap, to slabber. Cf. Slabber.
Slubber + Prov. E. gullion a wretch.
Prov. E. slew to turn round, Scot. to lean or incline to a side; cf. Icel. sn to turn, bend.
OE. slugge slothful, sluggen to be slothful; cf. LG. slukk low-spirited, sad, E. slack, slouch, D. slak, slek, a snail.
OF. escluse, F. écluse, LL. exclusa, sclusa, from L. excludere, exclusum, to shut out: cf. D. sluis sluice, from the Old French. See Exclude.
OE. slombren, slumberen, slumeren, AS. slumerian, fr. sluma slumber; akin to D. sluimeren to slumber, MHG. slummern, slumen, G. schlummern, Dan. slumre, Sw. slumra, Goth. slawan to be silent.

Cf. D. slomp a mass, heap, Dan. slump a quantity, and E. slump, v.t. | Cf. Lump; also Sw. slumpa to bargain for the lump. | Scot. slump a dull noise produced by something falling into a hole, a marsh, a swamp.
Cf. OE. sloor mud, clay, Icel. sl, slo, to trail or drag one's self along, D. sleuren, sloren, to train, to drag, to do negligently and slovenly, D. sloor, sloerie, a sluttish girl.
Cf. Sw. slaska to paddle in water, slask wet, filth.
OE. slutte; cf. OD. slodde a slut, Icel. slöttr a heavy, loglike fellow, slota to droop.
OE. sli, slegh, sleih, Icel sl, for sl; akin to Sw. slug, Dan. slu, LG. slou, G. schlau; probably to E. slay, v.t.; cf. G. verschlagen sly. See Slay, v. t., and cf. Sleight.

D. smak; akin to LG. smack, smak, Dan. smakke, G. schmacke, F. semaque. | OE. smak, AS. ssm taste, savor; akin to D. smaak, G. geschmack, OHG. smac; cf. Lith. smagus pleasant. Cf. Smack, v. i. | OE. smaken to taste, have a taste, -- from the noun; cf. AS. smecan taste; akin to D. smaken, G. schmecken, OHG. smechen to taste, smachschmatzen to smack the lips, to kiss with a sharp noise, MHG. smatzen, smackzeen), Icel smakka to taste, Sw. smaka, Dan. smage. See 2d Smack, n.
Small + F. ache smallage. See Ach parsley.
It. smalto, LL. smaltum; of Teutonic origin; cf. OHG. smalz grease, butter, G. schmalz grease, OHG. smelzan to melt, G. schmelzen. See Smelt, v. t., and cf. Amel, Enamel.
Cf. F. smaragdite; -- so called from its emerald-green color. See Smaragd.

OE. smarten, AS. smeortan; akin to D. smarten, smerten, G. schmerzen, OHG. smerzan, Dan. smerte, SW. smärta, D. smart, smert, a pain, G. schmerz, Ohg. smerzo, and probably to L. mordere to bite; cf. Gr. m to rub, crush. Cf. Morsel. | OE. smerte. See Smart, v. i.
Cf. Sw. smisk a blow, stroke, smiska to strike, dial. Sw. smaske to kiss with a noise, and E. smack a loud kiss, a slap.
OE. smach, smak. See Smack taste.
OE. smateren to make a noise; cf. Sw. smattra to clatter, to crackle, G. schmettern to dash, crash, to warble, quaver.

OE. smeren, smerien, AS. smierwan, smyrwan, fr. smeoru fat, grease; akin to D. smeren, OHG. smirwen, G. schmieren, Icel. smyrja to anoint. See Smear, n. | OE. smere,. smeoru fat, grease; akin to D. smeer, G. schmeer, OHG. smero, Icel. smjör, Sw. & Dan. smör butter, Goth. smaír fatness, smarna dung; cf. Lith. smarsas fat. Cf. Smirch.
Etymol. uncertain. | OE. sme, AS. sm. See Smooth.
OE. smellen, smillen, smullen; cf. LG. smellen, smelen, smölen, schmelen, to smoke, to reek, D. smeulen to smolder, and E. smolder. Cf. Smell, n. | OE. smel, smil, smul, smeol. See Smell, v. t.

AS. smelt, smylt; akin to Dan. smelt. | Of foreign origin; cf. Sw. smälta, D. smelten, Dan. smelte, Icel. smelta, G. schmelzen OHG. smelzan, smelzen; probably akin to Gr. Enamel, Melt, Mute, v. i., Smalt.
Akin to Sw. smickra to flatter, Dan. smigre, and perhaps to G. schmeicheln, and E. smile. Cf. Smicker, a. | AS. smicere tasteful, trim. See Smicker, v.

OE. smilen; akin to Dan. smile, Sw. smila, MHG. smielen, smieren, L. mirari to wonder at, Skr. smi to smile; and probably to E. smicker. sq. root173. Cf. Admire, Marvel, Smirk. | CF. Dan. smiil, Sw. smil. See Smile, v. i.
OE. smirken, ASS. smercian, smearcian; cf. MHG. smieren, smielen, to smile. See Smile, v. i.

AS. smitan to smite, to soil, pollute; akin to OFries. smita to smite, LG. smiten, D. smijten, G. schmeissen, OHG. smizan to smear, stroke, OSw. & dial. Sw. smita to smite, Dan. smiide to throw, Goth. bismeitan, to anoint, besmear; cf. Skr. m to be fat. The original sense seems to have been, to daub on, to smear. Cf. Smut.
AS. | AS. smi. See Smith, n.
AS. smi, fr. smi; akin to D. smidse, smids, OHG. smitta, G. schmiede, Icel. smi. See Smith, n.
CF. G. schmitz a stain, schmitzen besmear. See Smite, v. t.
Freq. fr. OE. smitten to befoul. See Smite, v. t.

AS. smoc; akin to OHG. smocho, Icel. smokkr, and from the root of AS. sm to creep, akin to G. schmiegen to cling to, press close. MHG. smiegen, Icel. smj to creep through, to put on a garment which has a hole to put the head through; cf. Lith. smukti to glide. Cf. Smug, Smuggle.
AS. smoca, fr. smeócan to smoke; akin to LG. & D. smook smoke, Dan. smög, G. schmauch, and perh. to Gr. smaugti to choke. | AS. smocian; akin to D. smoken, G. schmauchen, Dan. smöge. See Smoke, n.
OE. smolderen; cf. Prov. G. smölen, smelen, D. smeulen. Cf. Smell.
AS. smorian; akin to D. & LG. smoren, G. schmoren to stew. Cf. Smother.
OE. smothe, smethe, AS. smeedhe, smoeedte, where e, oe, come from an older o; cf. LG. smöde, smöe, smödig; of uncertain origin. | OE. smothen, smethen, AS. smeedhian; cf. LG. smöden. See Smooth, a.
OE. smotheren; akin to E. smoor. See Smoor. | OE. smorther. See Smother, v. t.
OE. smolderen; cf. Prov. G. smölen, smelen, D. smeulen. Cf. Smell.
Cf. Dan. smuds smut, E. smutch, or smoke.
Of. Scand. or Low German origin; cf. LG. smuck, G. schmuck, Dan. smuk, OSw. smuck, smöck, and E. smock, smuggle; cf. G. schmuck ornament. See Smock.

Of Low German or Scand. origin; cf. LG. smuggeln, D. smokkelen, G. schmuggeln, Dan. smugle, Sw. smyga to introduce or convey secretly, Dan. i smug secretly, D. smuigen to eat in secret, AS. smgan to creep. See Smock.

Akin to Sw. smuts, Dan. smuds, MHG. smuz, G. schmutz, D. smet a spot or stain, smoddig, smodsig, smodderig, dirty, smodderen to smut; and probably to E. smite. See Smite, v. t., and cf. Smitt, Smutch.
Prob. for smuts. See Smut, n.
Said to be corrupted fr. NL. syngnathus, fr. Gr. sy`n together + gna`qos jaw, because the jaws can be only slightly separated.
D. snavel a beak, bill, snout; akin to G. schnabel, OHG. snabul,. sneb, snebbe, OFries. snavel mouth, Dan. & Sw. snabel beak, bill, Lith. snapas, and to E. snap, v. See Snap, and cf. Neb.

Prov. E., n., a lump on a tree where a branch has been cut off; v., to cut off the twigs and small branches from a tree, of Celtic origin; cf. Gael. snaigh, snaidh, to cut down, to prune, to sharpen, p. p. snaighte, snaidhte, cut off, lopped, Ir. snaigh a hewing, cutting.
OE. snaile, AS. sn, snegel, sn; akin to G. schnecke, OHG. snecko, Dan. snegl, Icel. snigill.
AS. snaca; akin to LG. snake, schnake, Icel. snakr, sn, Dan. snog, Sw. snok; of uncertain origin.
So named from its snakelike neck.
LG. or D. snappen to snap up, to snatch; akin to G. schnappen, MHG. snaben, Dan. snappe, and to D. snavel beak, bill. Cf. Neb, Snaffle, n. | Cf. D. snap a snatching. See Snap, v. t.
D. snaphaan a gun, originally, the snapping cock of a gun. See Snap, and Hen.
Akin to LG. & OD. snarren, G. schnarren, E. snore. See Snore, and cf. Snarl to growl.

AS. sneara cord, a string; akin to D. snoer, G. schnur, OHG. snour a cord, snarahha a noose, Dan. snare, Sw. & Icel. snara, Goth. sn a basket; and probably also to E. needle. See Needle, and cf. Snarl to entangle.
Etymol. uncertain. | From Snare, v. t. | From Snar.
OE. snachen, snechen; akin to D. snakken to gasp, to long (for), to desire. Cf. Snack, n., Sneck.
Cf. AS. sni to cut, to mow, sn a bite, bit snip.
Cf. Icel. snei to cut into alices, sni to cut; akin to AS. besn, sni, G. schneiden, OHG. snidan, Goth. snei to cut, to reap, and E. snath, snithe.
OE. sniken, AS. snican to creep; akin to Dan. snige sig; cf. Icel. snikja to hanker after.
Cf. Icel. sneypa to dishonor, disgrace, chide, but also E. snip, and snub.
OE. sneren, Dan. sn to snarl or grin (like a dog); cf. Prov. E. sneer to grin, sner to snort, snert to sneer at. See Snore, v. i.
OE. snesen; of uncertain origin; cf. D. snuse to sniff, E. neese, and AS. fneósan.
AS. snell; akin to D. snel, G. schnell, OHG. snel, Icel. snjallr valiant.
Cf. G. schnitt that which is cut, fr. schneiden to cut, E. snath. | See Snot.
OE. snibben; cf. Dan. snibbe, and E. snub, v. t.
Prov. E. snick a notch; cf. Icel. snikka nick, cut.
Cf. D. snikken to sob, to sigh.
OE. sneven; akin to snivel, snuff; cf. Dan. snive to sniff. See Snuff, v. t.
See Snick a small cut. | See Sneak. | Cf. Sneak.
See Snig a kind of eel.
D. snippen; akin to G. schnippen.
OE. snipe; akin to D. snep, snip, LG. sneppe, snippe, G. schnepfe, Icel. snipa (in comp.), Dan. sneppe, Sw. snäppa a sanpiper, and possibly to E. snap. See Snap, Snaffle.
AS. sni to cut. See Snathe.
AS. sni to cut. See Snathe.
OE. snivelen, snevelen, snuvelen, freg. of sneven. See Sniff, and cf. Snuffle. | AS. snofel. Cf. Snivel, v. i.
Icel. snapr a dolt, impostor, charlatan. Cf. Snub.
See Snood. | Scot. snod to prune, put in order.
Prov. E. snook to search out, to follow by the scent; cf. Sw. snoka to lurk, LG. snöggen, snuckern, snökern, to snuffle, to smell about, to search for. | D. snoek.
Scot. snooze to sleep; cf. Dan. & Sw. snus snuff.

OE. snoren, AS. snora a snoring; akin to LG. snoren, snorken, snurken, to snore, D. snorken, G. schnarchen to snore, schnarren to rattle, MHG. snarren, Sw. snarka to snore, Icel. snarka to sputter, fizzle. Cf. Snarl to growl, Sneer, Snort. See Snoring.
OE. snorten; akin to snoren. See Snore.
AS. snot; akin to D. snot, LG. snotte, Dan. snot, and to E. snout. See Snout.

OE. snoute, probably of Scand, or Low German origin; cf. LG. snute, D. snuit, G. schnauze, Sw. snut, snyte, Dan. snude, Icel. sn to blow the nose; probably akin to E. snuff, v.t. Cf. Snite, Snot, Snuff.

LG. snaue, or D. snaauw, from LG. snau a snout, a beak. | OE. snow, snaw, AS. snaw; akin to D. sneeuw, OS. & OHG. sneo, G. schnee, Icel. snær, snjor, snajar, Sw. snö, Dan. snee, Goth. snaiws, Lith. snëgas, Russ. snieg', Ir. & Gael. sneachd, W. nyf, L. nix, nivis, Gr. acc. ni`fa, also AS. sniwan to snow, G. schneien, OHG. sniwan, Lith. snigti, L. ningit it snows, Gr. ni`fei, Zend snizh to snow; cf. Skr. snih to be wet or sticky. sq. root172.

Cf. D. snuiven to snort, to pant, G. schnauben, MHG. snuben, Prov. G. schnupfen, to sob, and E. snuff, v.t. | Cf. Icel. ssnubba to snub, chide, Sw. snubba, Icel. snubbottr snubbed, nipped, and E. snib.

Cf. G. schnuppe candle snuff, schnuppen to snuff a candle (see Snuff, v. t., to snuff a candle), or cf. Snub, v. t. | OE. snuffen. See Snuff of a candle Snuff to sniff. | Akin to D. snuffen, G. schnupfen, schnuppen, to snuff, schnupfen a cold in the head, schnuppen to snuff (air), also, to snuff (a candle). Cf. Sniff, Snout, Snub, v. i.
Freq. of snuff, v.i.; akin to LG. snuffeln, G. schnüffeln, D. snuffeln, Dan. snövle. Cf. Sniffle.
Prov. E. snug tight, handsome; cf. Icel. snöggr smooth, ODan. snög neat, Sw. snugg.

OE. so, sa, swa, AS. swa; akin to OFries, sa, s, D. zoo, OS. & OHG. s, G. so, Icel. sva, sv, svo, so, Sw. s, Dan. saa, Goth. swa so, sw as; cf. L. suus one's own, Skr. sva one's own, one's self. sq. root192. Cf. As, Custom, Ethic, Idiom, Such.
OE. soken, AS. socian to sioak, steep, fr. s, s, to suck. See Suck.
OE. sope, AS. sape; akin to D. zeep, G. seife, OHG. seifa, Icel. sapa, Sw. s, Dan. s, and perhaps to AS. sipan to drip, MHG. sifen, and L. sebum tallow. Cf. Saponaceous.

See Sop. | OE. sobben; akin to AS. seófian, siófian, to complain, bewail, seófung, siófung, sobbing, lamentation; cf. OHG. s, s, to sigh, MHG. siuften, siufzen, G. seufzen, MHG. s a sigh, properly, a drawing in of breath, from s to drink, OHG. s. Cf. Sup.
OE. sobre, F. sobre, from L. sobrius, probably from a prefix so- expressing separation + ebrius drunken. Cf. Ebriety.
L. sobrietas: cf. F. sobriété. See Sober.
F. sobriquet, OF. soubzbriquet, soubriquet, a chuck under the chin, hence, an affront, a nickname; of uncertain origin; cf. It. sottobecco a chuck under the chin.
AS. s the power of holding court, sway, domain, properly, the right of investigating or seeking; akin to E. sake, seek. Sake, Seek, and cf. Sac, and Soke.
F., fr. L. sociabilis, fr. sociare to associate, fr. socius a companion. See Social.
L. socialis, from socius a companion; akin to sequi to follow: cf. F. social. See Sue to follow.
L. sociatus, p. p. of sociare to associate, fr. socius companion.
L. societas, fr. socius a companion: cf. F. société. See Social.
F. soc, LL. soccus, perhaps of Celtic origin. | OE. sock, AS. socc, fr. L. soccus a kind of low- heeled, light shoe. Cf. Sucket.
OE. soket, a dim. through OF. fr. L. soccus. See Sock a covering for the foot.
F., fr. L. socculus, dim. of soccus. See Sock a covering for the foot. Cf. Zocco.
AS. socen, socn, searching, or the right of searching, the lord's court. See Soc.
Akin to LG. sode, D. zode, OD. sode, soode, OFries. satha, and E. seethe. So named from its sodden state in wet weather. See Seethe.
It., soda, in OIt., ashes used in making glass, fr. L. solida, fem. of solidus solid; solida having probably been a name of glasswort. See Solid.
L. sodalitas, fr. sodalis a comrade.
From Sodom. a country mentioned in the Bible: cf. F. sodomite.
Scot. sae, say, saye; cf. Icel. sar a large cask, Sw. s a tub.
Ar. soffah, from saffa to dispose in order: cf. F. sofa, It.sofà.
It. soffitta, soffitto, fr. soffiggere to hide, properly, to fix or fasten under, L. suffigere to fasten beneath or below; sub under, beneath + figere to fix, faste: cf. F. soffite.
OE. softe, AS. s, properly adv. of s, adj.; akin to OS. safto, adv., D. zacht, OHG. samfto, adv., semfti, adj., G. sanft, LG. sacht; of uncertain origin.
Corruption of Per. s one who burns, is ardent or zealous.
Cf. Icel. söggr damp, wet, or E. soak.

OF. saoler, saouler, to satiate, F. soûler, L. satullare, fr. satullus, dim. of satur sated. See Satire. | OE. soile, F. sol, fr. L. solum bottom, soil; but the word has probably been influenced in form by soil a miry place. Cf. Saloon, Soil a miry place, Sole of the foot. | OF. soil, souil, F. souille, from OF. soillier, F. souiller. See Soil to make dirty. | OE. soilen, OF. soillier, F. souiller, (assumed) LL. suculare, fr. L. sucula a little pig, dim. of sus a swine. See Sow, n. | See Soil to make dirty, Soil a miry place.
OF. soillure, F. souillure. See Soil to make dirty.
F., fr. soir evening, fr. L. serus late, serum late time. Cf. Serenade.

OE. sojornen, sojournen, OF. sojorner, sejorner, F. séjourner, fr. L. sub under, about + diurnus belonging to the day. See Journal, Diurnal. | Cf. OF. sujurn, sujur, sejor, F. séjour. See Sojourn, v. i.
It. solfa the gamut, from the syllables fa, sol.
L., fem. of solus. | Native name. | L.
OF. solas, ssoulaz, L. solacium, solatium, fr. solari to comfort, console. Cf. Console, v. t. | OF. solacier, soulacier, F. solacier, LL. solatiare. See Solace, n.
Icel. s; akin to Norw. sula.
Sp., fr. L. solanussc. ventus), from sol the sun.

OE. soler, AS. solere, L. solarium, from sol the sun. See Solar, a. | L. solaris, fr. sol the sun; akin to As. s, Icel. s, Goth. sauil, Lith. saule, W. haul,. sul, Skr. svar, perhaps to E. sun:F. solaire. Cf. Parasol. Sun.
F. solde. See Soldier, and cf. Sou.
OE. soudan, F. soudan, from the Arabic. See Sultan.
Formerly soder; F. soudure, OF. soudeure, fr. OF. & F. souder to solder, L. solidare to fasten, to make solid. See Solid, and cf. Sawder. | Formerlysoder. See Solder, n.

OE. souldier, soudiour, souder, OF. soldier, soldoier, soldeier, sodoier, soudoier, soudier, fr. L. solidus a piece of money (hence applied to the pay of a soldier), fr. solidus solid. See Solid, and cf. Sold, n.

F. sole, L. solea; -- so named from its flat shape. See Sole of the foot. | AS. sole, fr. L. soolea (or rather an assumed L. sola), akin to solumround, soil, sole of the foot. Cf. Exile, Saloon, Soil earth, Sole the fish. | L. solus, or OF. sol, F. seul (fr. L. solus; cf. L. sollus whole, entire. Cf. Desolate, Solemn, Solo, Sullen.

F. solécisme, L. soloecismus, Gr. soloikismo`s, fr. soloiki`zein to speak or write incorrectly, fr. so`loikos speaking incorrectly, from the corruption of the Attic dialect among the Athenian colonists of So`loi in Cilicia.
Gr. Defn: To commit a solecism. [R.

OE. solempne, OF. solempne, L. solemnis, solennis, sollemnis, sollennis; sollus all, entire + annus a year; properly, that takes place every year; -- used especially of religious solemnities. Cf. Silly, Annual.
L. solemnitas, solennitas: cf. F. solennité, solemnité, OF. also sollempnité.
It., from solfo brimstone, sulphur, L. sulfur, E. sulphur.
F. sollicier, L. sollicitare, solicitare, -atum, fr. sollicitus wholly (i. e., violently) moved; sollus whole + citus, p. p. of ciere to move, excite. See Solemn, Cite.
L. sollicitus, solicitus. See Solicit, v. t.
L. solidus, probably akin to sollus whole, entire, Gr. solide. Cf. Consolidate,Soda, Solder, Soldier, Solemn.
NL., fr. L. solidare to strengthen, unite; -- so called in allusion to its reputed healing qualities.
F. solidarité, fr. solide. See Solid.
L. solidatus, p. p. of solidare. See Solder.
NL., from L. solidus solid + ungula a hoof.
NL., from L. solifuga (better solipuga), a kind of venomous ant, or spider.
L. soliloquium; solus alone + loqui to speak. See Sole ly, and Loquacious.
Cf. F. solipède, It. solipede, Sp. solipedo; apparently fr. L. solus alone + pes, pedis, a foot; but probably fr. L. solidipes solid-footed, whole-hoofed. See Solid, and Pedal.
L. sol sun + sequi to follow.
L. solitarius, fr. solus alone: cf. F. solitaire. See Sole, a., and cf. Solitaire.
F., from L. solitudo, solus alone. See Sole, a.
F. soleretim. fr. OF. soler shoe.
F. solmisation, fr. solmiser to sol-fa; -- called from the musical notes sol, mi. See Sol-fa.
It., from L. solus alone. See Sole, a.
L. solstitium; sol the sun + sistere to cause to stand, akin to stare to stand: cf. F. solstice. See Solar, a., Stand, v. i.
L. solubilis, fr. solvere, solutum, to loosen, to dissolve: cf. F. soluble. See Solve, and cf. Solvable.
L. solutus, p.p. of solvere to loosen. See Solve.
OE. solucion, OF. solucion, F. solution, fr. L. solutio, fr. solvere, solutum, to loosen, dissolve. See Solve.
F. solvable. See Solve, and cf. Soluble, Solvible.
L. solvere, solutum; from a prefix so- expressing separation (cf. Sober) + luere to loosen; cf. OF. soldre, soudre. See Loose, and cf. Absolve.
L. solvendus to be loosened or dissolved, fr. solvere. See Solution.
L. solvens, p.pr. of solvere. See Solvable.
F. sombre; cf. Sp. sombra, shade, prob. from LL. subumbrare to put in the shade; L. sub under + umbra shade. See Umbrage.
F. sombre; cf. Sp. sombra, shade, prob. from LL. subumbrare to put in the shade; L. sub under + umbra shade. See Umbrage.
Sp., from sombra shade. See Sombre.
OE. som, sum, AS. sum; akin to OS., OFries., & OHG. sum, OD. som, D. sommig, Icel. sumr, Dan. somme (pl.), Sw. somlige (pl.), Goth. sums, and E. same. sq. root191. See Same, a., and cf. - some.

OE. sterre, AS. steorra; akin to OFries. stera, OS. sterro, D. ster, OHG. sterno, sterro, G. stern, Icel. stjarna, Sw. stjerna, Dan. stierne, Goth. staírno, Armor. & Corn. stern, L. stella, Gr. star; perhaps from a root meaning, to seater, Skr. st, L. sternere (cf. Stratum), and originally applied to the stars as beingstrewn over the sky, or as beingscatterers or spreaders of light. *296. Cf. Aster, Asteroid, Constellation, Disaster, Stellar.

So called (as conjectured by Blackstone) from being held in a room at the Exchequer where the chests containing certain Jewish comtracts and obligations called starrs (from the Heb. shetar, pron. shtar) were kept; or from the stars with which the ceiling is supposed to have been decorated.
OE. sterbord, AS. steórbord, i.e., steer board. See Steer, v. t., Board of a vessel, and cf. Larboard.

L. statuminatus, p.p. of statuminare to prop, fr. statumen a prop, fr. statuere to place.

From Staff, and corresponding to the pl. staves. See Staff. | From Stave, n., or Staff, n.
Cf. Dan. staae to stand, Sw. stå. *163.

OE. stede place, AS. stede; akin to LG. & D. stede, OS. stad, stedi, OHG. stat, G. statt, stätte, Icel. staedhr, Dan. sted, Sw. stad, Goth. sta, and E. stand. *163. See Stand, and cf. Staith, Stithy.

Cf. AS. stedig sterile, barren, stæ, steady (in gestæ), D. stedig, stadig, steeg, G. stätig, stetig. See Stead, n.

OE. stem, steem, vapor, flame, AS. steám vapor, smoke, odor; akin to D. stoom steam, perhaps originally, a pillar, or something rising like a pillar; cf. Gr. stand.

AS. st. See Stone. | AS. st to adorn with stones or gems. See Stone.

So called from the battle of Steinkirk, in 1692, on which occasion the French nobles had no time to arrange their lace neckcloths.

AS. stæppan; akin to OFries. steppa, D. stappen to step, stap a step, OHG. stepfen to step, G. stapfe a footstep, OHG. stapfo, G. stufe a step to step on; cf. Gr. Stamp, n. & a. | AS. stæpe. See Step, v. i.
AS. steóp-; akin to OFries. stiap-, stiep-, D. & G. stief-, OHG. stiuf-, Icel. stj, Sw. styf-, and to AS. astepan, asteópan, to deprive, bereave, as children of their parents, OHG. stiufen.
So named after the Archduke Stephan, mining director of Austria.
From Russ. stepe, through G. or F. steppe.
LL. stercoranista, fr. L. stercus, -oris, dung.
LL. stercorarium, from L. stercorarius belonging to dung.
L. stercoratio, from stercorare to dung.
NL. Sterculia, the typical genus, fr. L. Sterculius the deity that presided over manuring, from stercus dung. So called because one of the original species is fetid.
Gr. stereo`s solid. See Stare to gaze.
Stereo- + -type: cf. F. stéréotype. | Cf. F. stéréotyper.
F. stérile, L. sterilis, akin to Gr. stereo`s stiff, solid, stei^ros barren, stei^ra a cow that has not calved, Goth. stairo, fem., barren. See Stare to gaze.

OE. sterlynge, starling, for easterling, LL. esterlingus, probably from Easterling, once the popular name of German trades in England, whose money was of the purest quality: cf. MHG. sterlink a certain coin. Cf. East. "Certain merchants of Norwaie, Denmarke, and of others those parties, called Ostomanni, or (as in our vulgar language we tearme them), easterlings, because they lie east in respect of us." Holinshed. "In the time of . . . King Richard the First, monie coined in the east parts of Germanie began to be of especiall request in England for the puritie thereof, and was called Easterling monie, as all inhabitants of those parts were called Easterlings, and shortly after some of that countrie, skillful in mint matters and allaies, were sent for into this realme to bring the coine to perfection; which since that time was called of them sterling, for Easterling." Camden. "Four thousand pound of sterlings." R. of Gloucester.

AS. stearn a kind of bird. See Starling. | OE. sterne, sturne, AS. styrne; cf. D. stuurish stern, Sw. stursk refractory. *166. | Icel. stjorn a steering, or a doubtful AS. steórn. *166. See Steer, v. t.

Cf. Stow. | OE. stuven, OF. estuver, F. étuver, fr. OF. estuve, F. étuve, a sweating house, a room heated for a bath; probably of Teutonic origin, and akin to E. stove. See Stove, and cf. Stive to stew. | OE. stue, stuwe, OF. estuve. See Stew, v. t.

OE. stiward, AS. stiweard, stigweard, literally, a sty ward; stigu sty + weard warden, guardian, -- his first duty having been probably to attend to the domestic animals. *164. See Sty pen for swine, Ward.
NL. stibiatus, from L. stibium antimony.
Gr. sti`chos a row, line, akin to to go, march, E. sty, v.i.

OE. sticke, AS. sticca; akin to stician to stab, prick, pierce, G. stecken a stick, staff, OHG. steccho, Icel. stik a stick. See Stick, v. t.. | OE. stikien, v.t. & i., combined with steken, whence E. stuck), AS. stician, v.t. & i., and (assumed) stecan, v.t.; akin to OFries. steka, OS. stekan, OHG. stehhan, G. stechen, and to Gr. tij to be sharp. Cf. Distinguish, Etiquette, Extinct, Instigate, Instinct, Prestige, Stake, Steak, Stick, n., Stigma, Stimulate, Sting, Stitch in sewing, Style for or in writing.
Probably fr. OE. stightlen, sti, to dispose, arrange, govern, freq. of stihten, AS. stihtan: cf. G. stiften to found, to establish. | Cf. stick, v. t. & i.

OE. stif, AS. stif; akin to D. stijf, G. steif, Dan. stiv, Sw. styf, Icel. stifr, Lith. stipti to be stiff; cf. L. stipes a post, trunk of a tree, stipare to press, compress. Cf. Costive, Stifle, Stipulate, Stive to stuff.
From Stiff. | Freq. of OE. stif stiff; cf. Icel. stifla to dam up.

L. suburbium; sub under, below, near + urbs a city. See Urban.
LL. suburbicarius, equiv. to L. suburbanus: cf. F. suburbicaire. See Suburban.
LL. suburbicarius, equiv. to L. suburbanus: cf. F. suburbicaire. See Suburban.
Pref. sub- + L. venire to come. See Subvention.
