L. subvertere, subversum; sub under + vertere to turn: cf. F. subvertir. See Verse.
L. succus, sucus, juice: cf. F. succade a sugarbox. Cf. Sucket.
L. succedere, successum; sub under + cedere to go, to go along, approach, follow, succeed: cf. F. succéder. See Cede, and cf. Success.
LL., an accompanier in singing, fr. succinere to sing, to accompany; sub under, after + canere to sing.
L. successus: cf. F. succès. See Succeed.
L. successio: cf. F. succession. See Succeed.
OE. successour, OF. successur, successor, F. successeur, L. successor. See Succeed.
L. succiduus, fr. succidere to fall under.
L. succinum, sucinum, amber, from succus, sucus, juice, sap: cf. F. succinate.
L. succinctus, p.p. of succingere to gird below or from below, to tuck up; sub + cingere to gird. Cf. Cincture.
L. succisio, fr. succidere, succisum, to cut away below, sub under + caedere to cut.

OE. socouren, OF. sucurre, soucourre, secorre, F. secourir, L. succurrere, succursum, to run under, run to the aid of, help, succor; sub under + currere to run. See Current. | OE. socours, sucurs, OF. sucurs, socors, secors, F. secours, L. succursus, fr. L. succurrere. See Succor, v. t.
Narragansett Indian m'sickquatash corn boiled whole.
NL., fr. L. succubare to lie under; sub under + cubare to lie down; cf. L. succuba, succubo, one who lies under another.
L. sucula a winch, windlass, capstan.
L. succulentus, suculentus, fr. succus, sucus, juice; perhaps akin to E. suck: cf. F. succulent.
L. succumbere; sub under + cumbere (in comp.), akin to cubare to lie down. See Incumbent, Cubit.
Cf. F. succursale. See Succor, n. & v. t.
NL., literally, juice of the intestines.
L. succussare to jolt, v. intens. fr. succutere, succussum, to fling up from below, to toss up; sub under + quatere to shake.
L. succussio, from succutere: cf. F. succussion. See Succussation.

OE. such, sich, sech, sik, swich, swilch, swulch, swilc, swulc, AS. swelc, swilc, swylc; akin to OFries. selik, D. zulk, OS. sulic, OHG. sulih, solih, G. solch, Icel. slikr, OSw. salik, Sw. slik, Dan. slig, Goth. swaleiks; originally meaning, so shaped. *192. See So, Like, a., and cf. Which.
OE. suken, souken, AS. s, s; akin to D. zuigen, G. saugen, OHG. s, Icel. s, sj, Sw. suga, Dan. suge, L. sugere. Cf. Honeysuckle, Soak, Succulent, Suction.
OE. sokeling. See Suck, v. t.
L. sugere, suctum, to suck; cf. OF. suction. See Suck, v. t.
NL. sudamen, -inis, fr. sudare to sweat. See Sweat.
L. sudarium, fr. sudare to sweat. See Sweat.
L. sudatio, fr. sudare to sweat: cf. F. sudation.
L. sudatorius, fr. sudare to sweat: cf. F. sudatoire. See Sweat. | L. sudatorium.

OE. sodian, sodein, OF. sodain, sudain, F. soudain, L. subitaneus, fr. subitus sudden, that has come unexpectedly, p.p. of subire to come on, to steal upon; sub under, secretly + ire to go. See Issue, and cf. Subitaneous.
L. sudor sweat (akin to E. sweat) + facere to make.
L. sudor sweat + parere to produce.
Akin to sodden, seethe. See Seethe.

OE. suen, sewen, siwen, OF. sivre (pres.ind. 3d sing. il siut, suit, he follows, nous sevons we follow), LL. sequere, for L. sequi, secutus; akin to Gr. sac to accompany, and probably to E. see, v.t. See See, v. t., and cf. Consequence, Ensue, Execute, Obsequious, Pursue, Second, Sect in religion, Sequence, Suit.
OE. suet, dim. fr. OF. seu, suif, F. suif, L. sebum. Cf. Soap, Sebaceous.
OE. suffren, soffren, OF. sufrir, sofrir, F. souffrir, (assumed) LL. sofferire, for L. sufferre; sub under + ferre to bear, akin to E. bear. See Bear to support.
OE. suffrance, OF. sufrance, soufrance, F. souffrance, L. sufferentia, from sufferens, -entis, p.pr. of sufferre. See Suffer.
OE. suffisen, OF. soufire, F. suffire (cf. suffisant, p.pr.), L. sufficere to put under, to substitute, to avail for, to suffice; sub under + facere to make. See Fact.
L. sufficientia: cf. F. suffisance. See Suffice.
L. sufficiens, -entis, p.pr. of sufficere: cf. F. suffisant. See Suffice.
L. suffixus, p.p. of suffigere to fasten on, to affix; sub under + figere to fix: cf. F. suffixe. See Fix.
L. sufflaminatus, p.p. of sufflaminare to hold back by a clog, from sufflamen a clog.
L. sufflatus, p.p. of sufflare to blow up, inflate; sub under + flare to blow.
L. suffocatus, p.p. of suffocare to choke; sub under + fauces the throat. Cf. Faucal.
L. suffossio, from suffodere, suffossum, to dig under; sub under + fodere to dig.
F. suffragant, L. suffragans, p.pr. of suffragari to support with one's vote, to be favorable. See Suffrage. | F. suffragant: cf. LL. suffraganeus. See Suffragan, a.
L. suffragatus, p.p. of suffragari. See Suffragan, a.
F., fr. L. suffragium; perhaps originally, a broken piece, a potsherd, used in voting, and fr. sub under + the root of frangere to break. See Break.
L. suffraginosus diseased in the hock, fr. suffrago the pastern, or hock.
L., the hock, from sub under + frangere to break.
L. suffumigatus, p.p. of suffumigare to fumigate from below. See Sub-, and Fumigate.
L. suffusus, p.p. of suffundere to overspread; sub under + fundere to pour. See Fuse to melt.
From the name of a dynasty of Persian kings, Safi, Safavi; said to come from name Safi-ud-din of an ancestor of the family, confused with s pious. | Ar. & Per. s, wise, pious, devout.
OE. sugre, F. sucre (cf. It. zucchero, Sp. azúcar), fr. Ar. sukkar, assukkar, fr. Skr. çarkara sugar, gravel; cf. Per. shakar. Cf. Saccharine, Sucrose.
L. suggestus, p.p. of suggerere to put under, furnish, suggest; sub under + gerere to carry, to bring. See Jest.
L. suggillare, sugillare, suggillatum, sugillatum, literally, to beat black and blue.
L. sui of one's self (akin to suus one's own) + caedere to slay, to kill. Cf. So, adv., Homicide.
OF. souillage, soillage, fr. souiller, soiller. See Soil to stain, and cf. Sullage.
Cf. F. suer to sweat, L. sudare.
L. Suiones (a Teutonic tribe in what is now Sweeden) + E. Goth.
L. suus belinging to himself or to one's self.
OE. suite, F. suite, OF. suite, sieute, fr. suivre to follow, OF. sivre; perhaps influenced by L. secta. See Sue to follow, and cf. Sect, Suite.
NL., fr. Icel. s the gannet. See Solan goose.
L. sulcatus, p.p. of sulcare to furrow, fr. sulcus a furrow.
L. sulcatus, p.p. of sulcare to furrow, fr. sulcus a furrow.
For sulkenness, fr. AS. solcen slothful, remiss, in asolcen, besolcen, properly p.p. of sealcan in asealcan to be weak or slothful; of uncertain origin.
See Sulkiness, and cf. Sulky, n. | From Sulky, a.; -- so called from the owner's desire of riding alone.
AS. suluh, sulh, a plow; cf. OHG. suohili a little plow.
OE. solein, solain, lonely, sullen; through Old French fr. (assumed) LL. solanus solitary, fr. L. solus alone. See Sole, a.
L. sublevare to raise up. Cf. Sublevation.
Cf. Sullage, Suillage, or Sully, v. t.
OE. sulien, AS. sylian, fr. sol mire; akin to G. suhle mire, sich, sühlen to wallow, Sw. söla to bemire, Dan. söle, Goth. bisaulijan to defile.
NL. sulphas, sulphatis, fr. L. sulphur, sulfur, brimstone, sulphur: cf. F. sulfate.
Sulpho- + vinum wine: cf. F. sulfovinique.
L., better sulfur: cf. F. soufre.
Cf. F. sulfuration, L. sulphuratio, sulfuratio, a vein of sulphur.
L. sulphurosus, sulfurosus: cf. F. sulfureux.
So called after the parish of St. Sulpice in Paris, of which the founder, Jean Jacques Olier, was pastor in 1643.
F. sultan (cf. Sp. soldan, It. sultano, soldano), Ar. sultan sultan, dominion. Cf. Soldan.
OE. summe, somme, OF. sume, some, F. somme, L. summa, fr. summus highest, a superlative from sub under. See Sub-, and cf. Supreme. | Cf. F. sommer, LL. summare.
F. sumac, formerly sumach (cf. Sp. zumaque), fr. Ar. summaq.
F. sumac, formerly sumach (cf. Sp. zumaque), fr. Ar. summaq.
Cf. F. sommaire. See Sum. | F. sommaire, or L. summarium. See Summary, a.
Cf. F. sommation. See Sum, v. t.

From Sum, v. | F. sommier a rafter, the same word as sommier a beast of burden. See Sumpter. | OE. sumer, somer, AS. sumor, sumer; akin to OFries. sumur, D. zomer, OS. sumar, G. sommer, OHG. & Icel. sumar, Dan. sommer, Sw. sommar, W. haf, Zend hama, Skr. sama year. *292.
F. sommet, dim. of OF. som, sum, top, from L. summum, from summus highest. See Sum, n.
L. summitas, fr. summus highest: cf. F. sommité. See Sum, n.
OE. somonen, OF. sumundre, semondre, F. semondre, from (assumed) LL. summonêre, for L. summonere to give a hint; sub under + monere to admonish, to warn. See Monition, and cf. Submonish.
OE. somner, sompnour, OF. semoneor, F. semonneur. See Summon, v. t.
OE. somouns, OF. sumunse, semonse, semonce, F. semonce, semondre to summon, OF. p.p. semons. See Summon, v.
Cf. G. sumpf a sump in a mine, a swamp, akin to LG. sump, D. somp a swamp, Dan. & Sw. sump, and perhaps to E. swamp.
OF. sommetier the driver of a pack horse; akin to OF. & F. sommier a pack horse, L. sagmarius, fr. sagma a pack saddle, in LL., a load, Gr. saj, sañj, to hang on. Cf. Seam a weight, Summer a beam.
L. sumptio, fr. sumere, sumptum, to take.
L. sumptuarius, fr. sumptus expense, cost, fr. sumere, sumptum, to take, use, spend; sub under + emere to take, buy: cf. F. somptuaire. See Redeem.
L. sumptuosus, fr. sumptus expanse, cost: cf. F. somptueux. See Sumptuary.
OE. sunne, sonne, AS. sunne; akin to OFries. sunne, D. zon, OS. & OHG. sunna, G. sonne, Icel. sunna, Goth. sunna; perh. fr. same root as L. sol. *297. Cf. Solar, South.
AS. sunnandæg; sunne, gen. sunnan, the sun + dæg day; akin to D. zondag, G. sonntag; -- so called because this day was anciently dedicated to the sun, or to its worship. See Sun, and Day.

OE. sundren, AS. sundrain (in asundrain, gesundrain), from sundor asunder, separately, apart; akin to D. zonder, prep., without, G. sonder separate, as prep., without, sondern but, OHG. suntar separately, Icel. sundr asunder, Sw. & Dan. sönder, Goth. sundro alone, separately. | See Sunder, v. t., and cf. Asunder.
OE. sundry, sondry, AS. syndrig, fr. sundor asunder. See Sunder, v. t.
OE. soupen to drink, AS. s; akin to D. zuipen, G. saufen, OHG. s, Icel. s, Sw. supa, Dan. söbe. Cf. Sip, Sop, Soup, Supper. | See Supper.
L. super over, above; akin to Gr. sub under, and E. over. See Over, and cf. Hyper-, Sub-, Supra-, Sur-.
L. superabilis, from superare to go over, to surmount, fr. super above, over.
L. superabundare: cf. OF. superabonder. See Super-, and Abound.
L. superabundans, p.pr. of superabundare. See Superabound.
L. superaddere. See Super-, and Add.
Pref. super- + L. annus a year.
F. superbe, L. superbus, fr. super over. See Super-.
Super- + cargo: cf. Sp. sobrecargo. Cf. Surcharge.
Pref. super- + celestial: cf. L. supercaelestis.
L. supercilium an eyebrow. See Supercilious.
L. superciliosus, fr. supercilium an eyebrow, pride; super over, + cilium an eyelid; probably akin to celare to conceal. Cf. Conceal.
L. supercrescens, p.pr. of supercrescere; super above + crescere to grow.
L. supereminens, p.pr. of supereminere. See Super-, and Eminent.

L. supererogatus, p.p. of supererogare to spend or pay out over and above; super over, above + erogare to expend or pay out money from the public treasury after asking the consent of the people. See Super-, and Erogate, Rogation.
L. supererogatio a payment in addition.
Pref. super- + excellent: cf. L. superexcellens.
L. superfetare; super above, over + fetare to bring forth.
L. superficialis: cf. F. superficiel. See Superficies.
L., fr. super above, over + facies make, figure, shape. See Surface.
L. superfluens, p.pr. of superfluere to flow or run over. See Superfluous.
L. super above + fluitans, p.pr. of fluitare intensive fr. fluere to flow.
L. superfluité, L. superfluitas. See Superfluous.
L. superfluus overflowing; super over, above + fluere to flow. See Super-, and Fluent.
L. superincumbens, p.pr. of superincumbere. See Super-, and Incumbent.
Pref. super- + induce: cf. L. superinducere to draw over.
Pref. super- + infuse: cf. L. superinfundere, superinfusum, to pour over.
Pref. super- + inspect: cf. L. superinspicere, superinspectum.
L. superintendere. See Super-, and Intend.
L. superintendens, p.pr. See Superintend. | Cf. OF. superintendant, F. surintendant. Cf. Surintendant.
L., compar. of superus being above, fr. super above, over: cf. F. supérieur. See Super-, and cf. Supreme.
L. superjacens, p.pr. of superjacere; super above + jacere to lie.
L. superlativus, fr. superlatus excessive, used as p.p. of superiorferre, but from a different root: cf. F. superlatif. See Elate, Tolerate.
NL., from L. super over + G. nagel, a nail, as of the finger, or a corruption of L. super and ungulam claw.
L. supernus, from super above: cf. F. supernel. See Super-.
L. supernatanus, p.pr. of supernatare to swim above; super above + natare to swim.
Pref. super- + natural: cf. OF. supernaturel, F. surnaturel.
L. supernumerarius: cf. OF. supernuméraire, F. surnuméraire. See Super-, and Numerary, Number.
Pref. super- + ordination: cf. L. superordinatio.
L. superparticularis. See Super-, and Particular.
L. superpartiens; super over + partiens, p.pr. of partire to divide.
Pref. super- + L. plus more. See Surplus.
F. superposer. See Super-, and Pose.
Cf. F. superposition. See Super-, and Position.
Pref. super- + L. saliens p.pr. of salire to leap.
L. superscribere, superscriptum; super over + scribere to write. See Super-, and Scribe.
L. supersedere, supersessum, to sit above, be superior to, forbear, omit; super above + sedere to sit: cf. F. superséder. See Sit, and cf. Surcease.
L., suspend, set aside, stay, 2d pers. sing. present subjunctive of supersedere. See Supersede.
Pref. super- + sensible: cf. F. supersensible.

F. superstition, L. superstitio, originally, a standing still over or by a thing; hence, amazement, wonder, dread, especially of the divine or supernatural, fr. superstare to stand over; super over + stare to stand. See Super-, and Stand.
NL.: cf. L. supersternere, superstratum, to spread upon. See Super-, and Stratum.
L. superstructus, p.p. of superstruere to build upon; super over + struere to build. See Super-, and Structure.
Pref. super- + substantial: cf. F. supersubstantiel.
Pref. super- + terrene: cf. L. superterrenus.
L. supervacaneus, supervacuus; super over + vacuus empty.
L. supervenire, superventum, to come over, to come upon; super over + venire to come. See Super-, and Come, and cf. Overcome.
Pref. super- + L. visere to look at attentively, to view, surely, intens. from videre, visum, to see. Cf. Survise, and Survey.
L. supervolutus, p.p. of supervolvere to roll over; super over + volvere to roll.
L. supinare, supinatum, to bend or lay backward, fr. supinus supine: cf. F. supination. See Supine.

L. supinus, akin to sub under, super above. Cf. Sub-, Super-. | L. supinum (sc. verbum), from supinus bent or thrown backward, perhaps so called because, although furnished with substantive case endings, it rests or falls back, as it were, on the verb: cf. F. supin.
L. suppalpari to caress a little; sub under, a little + palpare to caress.
L. supparasitari; sub under, a little + parasitus a parasite.
Pref. sub- + L. pes, pedis, a foot: cf. L. suppedaneum a footstool.
L. suppeditatus, p.p. of suppeditare to supply.
OE. soper, super, OF. super, soper, F. souper; originally an infinitive, to sup, take a meal. See Soup, and cf. Sup to take supper.
F. supplanter, L. supplantare to trip up one's heels, to throw down; sub under + planta the sole of the foot, also, a sucker, slip, sprout. Cf. Plant, n.
Cf. F. supplantation, L. supplantatio hypocritical deceit.
OE. souple, F. souple, from L. supplex suppliant, perhaps originally, being the knees. Cf. Supplicate.
F. supplément, L. supplementum, fr. supplere to fill up. See Supply, v. t.
Cf. F. supplétif, LL. suppletivus, from L. supplere, suppletum, to fill up. See Supply.
Cf. F. supplétif, LL. suppletivus, from L. supplere, suppletum, to fill up. See Supply.
F., p.pr. of supplier to entreat, L. supplicare. See Supplicate, and cf. Supplicant.
L. supplicans, p.pr. See Supplicate, and cf. Suppliant.

L. supplicatus, p.p. of supplicare to supplicate; of uncertain origin, cf. supplex, supplicis, humbly begging or entreating; perhaps fr. sub under + a word akin to placare to reconcile, appease (cf. Placable), or fr. sub under + plicare to fold, whence the idea of bending the knees (cf. Ply, v. t.). Cf. Supple.
For older supploy, F. suppléer, OF. also supployer, (assumed) LL. suppletare, from L. supplere, suppletum; sub under + plere to fill, akin to plenus full. See Plenty.
F. supporter, L. supportare to carry on, to convey, in LL., to support, sustain; sub under + portare to carry. See Port demeanor. | F.
F. supposer; pref. sub- under + poser to place; -- corresponding in meaning to L. supponere, suppositum, to put under, to substitute, falsify, counterfeit. See Pose.
F. supposition, L. suppositio a placing under, a substitution, fr. supponere, suppositium, to put under, to substitute. The word has the meaning corresponding to suppose. See Sub-, and Position.
LL. suppositorium, fr. L. suppositorius that is placed underneath: cf. F. suppositoire. See Supposition.
L. suppressus, p.p. of supprimere to suppress; sub under + premere, pressum, to press. See Sub-, and Press.
L. suppuratus, p.p. of suppurare to suppurate, cause to suppurate; sub under + pus, puris, matter. See Pus.
L. supputatus, p.p. of supputare. See Suppute.
F. supputer, or L. supputare; sub under + putare to reckon.
L.; akin to super. See Super-.
L. supremus, superlative of superus that is above, upper, fr. super above: cf. F. suprême. See Super-, and cf. Sum.
F. sur over, above, contr. fr. L. super, supra. See Super-.
L. sura the calf of the leg: cf. F. sural.
F. solbatu, p.p., bruised (said of a horse's foot); sole a sole (of a horse's foot) + battu, p.p. of battre to beat.
F. sursis, from sursis, p.p. of surseoir to suspend, postpone, defer, in OF., to delay, refrain from, forbear, L. supersedere. Surcease is not connected with E. cease. See Supersede.
F. surcharger. See Sur-, and Charge, and cf. Overcharge, Supercharge, Supercargo. | F.
OE. sursengle, OF. sursangle. See Sur-, and Cingle, Shingles.
OE. surcote, OF. surcote. See Sur-, and Coat, and cf. Overcoat.
From F. surcroît increase, or surcrû, p.p. of surcroître to overgrow.
L. surculatus, p.p. of surculare to purne, from surculus a shoot, sprout. See Surcle.
CF. L. sucrulosus woody. See Surcle.
L. surdus deaf (whence the meaning, deaf to reason, irrational), perhaps akin to E. swart. Cf. Sordine.
OE. sur, OF. seür, F. sûr, L. securus; se aside, without + cura care. See Secure, and cf. Assure, Insure, Sicker sure.
OE. seurte, OF. seürté, F. sûreté. See Sure, Security.
Formerly spelled suffe, and probably the same word as E. sough.
F. See Sur-, and Face, and cf. Superficial.
OE. surfet, OF. surfait, sorfait, excess, arrogance, crime, fr. surfaire, sorfaire, to augment, exaggerate, F. surfaire to overcharge; sur over + faire to make, do, L. facere. See Sur-, and Fact.

L. surgere, surrectum, to raise, to rise; sub under + regere to direct: cf. OF. surgeon, sourgeon, fountain. See Regent, and cf. Insurrection, Sortie, Source. | Cf. F. surgir to cast anchor, to land. Cf. Surge, n.
OE. surgien, OF. surgien, contr. fr. chirurgien. See Chirurgeon.
OE. surgenrie, surgerie; cf. OF. cirurgie, F. chirurgie, L. chirurgia, Gr. Surgeon.
F. surikate, from the native name in South Africa.
F. surlonge; sur upon + longe loin. See Sur-, and Loin.
Probably from sir, and originally meaning, sirlike, i.e., proud. See Sir, and Like, a.
OF. surmise accusation, fr. surmettre, p.p. surmis, to impose, accuse; sur (see Sur-) + mettre to put, set, L. mittere to send. See Mission.
OE. sourmounten, OF. surmonter, sormonter, F. surmonter; sur over + monter to mount. See Sur-, and Mount, v. i.
F. surmulet; saur, saure, brownish yellow, red + mulet a mullet. See Sorrel, a., and Mullet.
Pref. sur + name; really a substitution for OE. sournoun, from F. surnom. See Sur-, and Noun, Name. | Cf. F. surnommer.
Cf. F. suroxyde. See Sur-, and Oxide.
F. surpasser; sur over + passer to pass. See Sur- , and Pass.
F. surplis, OF. surpeiz, LL. superpellicium; super over + pellicium, pelliceum, a robe of fur, L. pellicius made of skins. See Pelisse.
F., fr. sur over + plus more. See Sur-, and Plus, and cf. Superplus.
F. surprise, fr. surprendre, surpris; sur over + prendre to take, L. prehendere. See Sur-, and Prehensile. | From Surprise, n.: cf. F. surprendre, p.p. surpris.
OF. surcuidier to presume; sur over + cuidier to think, L. cogitare. See Sur-, and Cogitate.
OF. surcuidier to presume; sur over + cuidier to think, L. cogitare. See Sur-, and Cogitate.
OF. surrendre to deliver; sur over + rendre to render. See Sur-, and Render.
L. surreptio, or subreptio. Cf. Subreption.
L. surreptitius, or subreptitius, fr. surripere, subripere, to snatch away, to withdraw privily; sub- under + rapere to snatch. See Sub-, and Ravish.
L. surrogatus, p.p. of surrogare, subrogare, to put in another's place, to substitute; sub under + rogare to ask, ask for a vote, propose a law. See Rogation, and cf. Subrogate.
See Surrogate, n., and cf. Subrogation.

OF. suronder to overflow, LL. superundare; fr. L. super over + undare to rise in waves, overflow, fr. unda wave. The English sense is due to the influence of E. round. See Super-, and Undulate, and cf. Abound.
(Assumed) OF. sursaneüre. See Sur-, and Sane.
OF., fr. OF. & F. surseoir. See Surcease.
F. sursolide. See Sur-, and Solid.
F., fr. sur over + tout all.
Icel. surtarbrandr; svartr black + brandr a firebrand.

OE. suspecious; cf. L. suspiciosus. See Suspicion.
L. suspirare to breathe out, to sigh; sub under + spirare to breathe: cf. F. souspirer, OF. souspirer. | Cf. L. suspirium.

OE. sustenen, susteinen, OF. sustenir, sostenir, F. soutenir (the French prefix is properly fr. L. subtus below, fr. sub under), L. sustinere; pref. sus- (see Sub-) + tenere to hold. See Tenable, and cf. Sustenance.

OE. swappen to strike; cf. E. to strike a bargain; perh. akin to E. sweep. Cf. Swap a blow, Swap, v. i. | Cf. Swap, v. t. | Cf. G. schwapp, n., a slap, swap, schwapp, schwapps, interj., slap! smack! and E. swap, v.t. | See Swap, n.

Cf. Swerve. | OE. swarm, AS. swearm; akin to D. zwerm, G. schwarm, OHG. swaram, Icel. svarmr a tumult, Sw. svärm a swarm, Dan. sværm, and G. schwirren to whiz, to buzz, Skr. svar to sound, and perhaps to E. swear. *177. Cf. Swerve, Swirl.

OE. swelen to burn, AS. swelan; akin to G. schwelen to burn slowly, schwül sultry, Icel. svæla a thick smoke.

OE. swerien, AS. swerian; akin to D. zweren, OS. swerian, OHG. swerien, G. schwören, Icel. sverja, Sw. svärja, Dan. sværge, Icel. & Sw. svara to answer, Dan. svare, Dan. & Sw. svar an answer, Goth. swaran to swear, and perhaps to E. swarm. *177. Cf. Answer.

OE. sweten, AS. swætan, fr. swat, n., sweat; akin to OFries. & OS. swet, D. zweet, OHG. sweiz, G. schweiss, Icel. sviti, sveiti, Sw. svett, Dan. sved, L. sudor sweat, sudare to sweat, Gr. sveda sweat, svid to sweat. *178. Cf. Exude, Sudary, Sudorific. | Cf. OE. swot, AS. swat. See Sweat, v. i.

See Swelter, Swelt, v. i., and cf. Sultry.

OE. swerven, AS. sweorfan to wipe off, to file, to polish; akin to OFries. swerva to creep, D. zwerven to swerve, to rope, OS. swerban to wipe off, MHG. swerben to be whirled, OHG. swerban to wipe off, Icel. sverfa to file, Goth. swaírban (in comp.) to wipe, and perhaps to E. swarm. Cf. Swarm.

NL. Named after Gerard Van Sweiten, physician to Maria Theresa of Austria.
AS. swift; akin to swapan to sweep, swipu a whip; cf. swifan to move quickly, to revolve. See Swoop, v. i., and cf. Swivel, Squib.
Cf. D. zwelgen to swallow, E. swallow, v.t. | Cf. Prov. E. swig to leak out, AS. swijian to be silent, swican to evade, escape.

Sound an air bladder, a strait. | OE. swime dizziness, vertigo, AS. swima; akin to D. zwijm, Icel. svimi dizziness, svina to subside, svia to abate, G. schwindel dizziness, schwinden to disappear, to dwindle, OHG. swinan to dwindle. OE. swin, AS. swin; akin to OFries. & OS. swin, D. zwijn, G. schwein, OHG. swin, Icel. svin, Sw. svin, Dan. sviin, Goth. swein; originally a diminutive corresponding to E. sow. See Sow, n.
Swine + Prov. E. crue a coop.

OE. swingen, AS. swingan to scourge, to fly, to flutter; akin to G. schwingen to winnow, to swingle, oscillate, sich schwingen to leap, to soar, OHG. swingan to throw, to scourge, to soar, Sw. svinga to swing, to whirl, Dan. svinge. Cf. Swagger, Sway, Swinge, Swink.
So named from its swift flight and dark color, which give it an uncanny appearance.
OE. swengen, AS. swengan to shake, causative of swingan. See Swing.
AS. swingele whip, scourge. See Swing.
So named in allusion to its swinging. See Swingle, v. i., and cf. Swingtree.
AS. swincan, akin to swingan. See Swing. | As. swinc, geswinc.
From AS. swipian to whip, shake, whirl; akin to swapan to sweep. See Swoop.
Akin to Norw. svirla to whirl, freq. of sverra to whirl, Dan. svirre, G. schwirren to whiz, to buzz. *177. See Swarm, n.
F. Suisse, of German origin. Cf. Switzer.
Cf. OD. swick a scourage, a whip. Cf. Swink, Swing.
OE. swiven, fr. AS. swifan. See Swivel.
AS. swifan to move quickly, to remove; akin to Icel. sveifla to whirl, shake, svifa to ramble, to turn. See Swoop, and cf. Swift a reel, Swift, a.
OE. swounen, swoghenen, for swo, fr. swo to sigh deeply, to droop, AS. swogan to sough, sigh; cf. geswogen senseless, swooned, geswowung a swooning. Cf. Sough.

OE. swopen, usually, to sweep, As. swapan to sweep, to rush; akin to G. schweifen to rove, to ramble, to curve, OHG. sweifan to whirl, Icel. sveipa to sweep; also to AS. swifan to move quickly. Cf. Sweep, Swift, a. & n., Swipe, Swivel.
OE. swerd, AS. sweord; akin to OFries. swerd, swird, D. zwaard, OS. swerd, OHG. swert, G. schwert, Icel. sver, Sw. svärd, Dan. sværd; of uncertain origin.
L. sycomorus, Gr. sycomore. Cf. Mulberry.
Said to be from a Chinese word, se-tze or se-sze, meaning, fine silk, and to be so called because if pure it may be drawn out into fine threads.
Gr. (Min.) Defn: A nodule of flint, or a pebble, which resembles a fig. [Obs.

Cf. F. symbolique. See Symbolic, a. | L. symbolicus, Gr. symbolique.

F. symphonie (cf. It. sinfonia), L. symphonia, Gr. Phonetic.
NL. symphysis pubis + Gr. (Surg.) Defn: The operation of dividing the symphysis pubis for the purpose of facilitating labor; -- formerly called the Sigualtian section. [Written also symphysotomy.
Gr. Defn: Coalescence; a growing into one with another word. [R.
L., fr. Gr. sympo`sion a drinking party, feast; sy`n with + po`sis a drinking. See Syn-, and cf. Potable.

NL. synacme. See Syn-, and Acme.
NL. synacme. See Syn-, and Acme.

Gr. Defn: Joint rule or sovereignity. [R.
NL., fr. Gr. Defn: A fastening or knitting together; the state of being closely jointed; close union. [R.
Pref. syn- + Gr. Defn: Concurrence of starry position or influence; hence, similarity of condition, fortune, etc., as prefigured by astrological calculation. [R.

NL., fr. Gr. Syn-, and Heresy.
NL., from Gr. (Med.) Defn: A continuous fever. [Obs.
L. synodus, Gr. sino, seno, F. synode, both from the Latin.

NL., perhaps fr. Gr. ovum egg: cf. F. synovie.

L., a mixture, properly, a putting together, Gr. Thesis.
Cf. Gr. Defn: To combine; to unite in regular structure. [R.
L. Syriacus, from Syria: cf. F. syriaque.
F. seringue (cf. Pr. siringua, Sp. jeringa, It. sciringa, scilinga), fg. Gr. svar to sound, and E. swarum. Cf. Syringa.

L. tactio, from tangere, tactum, to touch.

F. taffetas, It. taffetà, from Per. taftah, originally, twisted, woven, from taftan to twist, to spin.

Cf. F. & Sp. tafia, It. taffia; fr. Malay tafia a spirit distilled from molasses. Cf. Ratafia.

F. tailler to cut. See Tail a limitation.
OE. tein, teyne; cf. Icel. teinn a twig, akin to AS. tan, Goth. tains.

Pg. tajaç\'a3, from Braz. tayaç\'a3 a hog or swine.

G. talken to speak indistinctly; or OD. tolken to interpret, MHG. tolkan to interpret, to tell, to speak indistinctly, Dan. tolke to interpret, Sw. tolka, Icel. t to interpret, t an interpreter, Lith. tulkas an interpreter, tulkanti, tulkoti, to interpret, Russ. tolkovate to interpret, to talk about; or perhaps fr. L. torpidus, fr. torpere to be stiff, numb, or torpid; of uncertain origin.
L., from torpere, to be torpid.

L. torridus, fr. torrere to parch, to burn, akin to E. Thist: cf. F. torride. See Thirst.
OF., fr. OF. & F. tors, torse, twisted, wreathed, p. p. of tordre to twist, L. torquere. See Torture.
F., fr. LL. torsio, fr. L. torquere, tortum, to twist. See Torture.
Dan.; akin to Icel. þorskr a codfish, G. dorsch.
It. torso, probably fr. L. thyrsus a stalk, stem, thyrsus, Gr. torso, turso, a stalk, stem, G. dorsche a cabbage stalk. Cf. Thyrsus, Truss.

Of. torteau, tortel, from L.tortus twisted. See Tort.
F. toricolis; L. torquere, tortum, to twist + collum the neck.
L. tortilis, fr. torquere, tortum, to twist: cf. F. tortile.
L. tortus, p.p. of torquere to twist, wind.

OE. tortuce, fr. OF. tortis crooked, fr. L. tortus isted, crooked, contorted, p.p. of torquere, tortum, to wind; cf. F. tortue tortoise, LL. tortuca, tartuca, Pr. tortesa crookedness, tortis crooked. so called in allusion to its crooked feet. See Torture.
NL., fr. L. torquere, tortum, to twist.
OE. tortuos, L.tortuosus, fr.tortus a twisting, winding, fr. torquere, tortum, to twist: cf. F. tortueux. See Torture.

F.,fr.L. tortura, fr. torquere, tortum, to twist, rack, torture; probably akin to Gr. tre`pein to turn, G. drechsein to turn on a lathe, and perhaps to E. queer. Cf. Contort, Distort, Extort, Retort, Tart, n., Torch, Torment, Tortion, Tort, Trope. | Cf. F. Torturer.
NL., dim. of L. torus a semicircular molding.

L., a round, swelling, or bulging place, an elevation. Cf. 3d Tore.

Properly used of the Irish bogtrotters who robbed and plundered during the English civil wars, professing to be in sympathy with the royal cause; hence transferred to those who sought to maintain the extreme prerogatives of the crown; probably from Ir. toiridhe, tor, a pursuer; akin to Ir. & Gael. toir a pursuit.
Cf. OF. tonce shorn, clipped, and E. tonsure.

F. toucher, OF. touchier, tuchier; of Teutonic origin; cf. OHG. zucchen, zukken, to twitch, pluck, draw, G. zukken, zukken, v. intens. fr. OHG. ziohan to draw, G. ziehen, akin to E. tug. See Tuck, v. t., Tug, and cf. Tocsin, Toccata. | Cf. F. touche. See Touch, v.

OF. tornei, tornoi, F. tournoi, fr. OF. torneier, tornoier, tournoier, to tit, to tourney, F. tournoyer to turn round and round. See Turn, v. t. | Cf.OF. torneier. See Tourney, n.

OE. tow, AS. tow, akin to OD. touw, Icel. taw, v.t. | OE. towen, totoga to pull about, OHG. zogon, Icel. toga, AS. tohline a towline, and AS.teón to draw, p.p. getogen. See Tug | Cf. Icel.taug a rope, from the same root as E.tow, v. t.
AS. To, and -ward, wards. | AS. Toward, prep.

OE.towaille, towail, F. touaille, LL. toacula, of Teutonic origin; cf. OHG. dwahila, swahilla, G. zwehle, fr. OHG. dwahan to wash; akin to D. dwaal a towel, AS. þweán to wash, OS. thwahan, Icel. þva, Sw. två, Dan. toe, Goth. þwahan. Cf. Doily.
OE. tour,tor,tur, F. tour, L. turris; akin to Gr. twr a tower, Ir. tor a castle, Gael. torr a tower, castle. Cf. Tor, Turret.
AS. tohline. See Tow, v. t., and Line.

OE. toun, tun, AS. tun inclosure, fence, village, town; akin to D. tuin a garden, G. zaun a hadge, fence, OHG. zun, Icel. tun an inclosure, homestead, house, Ir. & Gael. dun a fortress, W. din. Cf. Down, adv. & prep., Dune, tine to inclose.
L. toxicum poison, originally, a poison in which arrows were dipped, Gr. Intoxicate.
L. toxicum poison, originally, a poison in which arrows were dipped, Gr. Intoxicate.

D. tuid tools, implements, stuff, trash, speeltuig playthings, toys; akin to G. zeug stuff, materials, MNG. zuic, Icel. tygi gear; all ultimately from the root of E. tug, v.t.; cf.G. zeugen to beget, MHG.ziugen to beget, make ready, procure. See Tug, v. t.
L.trabs, trabis, a beam, a timber.

NL.,from L. trachia, Gr. trachei^a (sc. trachée.

Abbrev.fr. tractate. | L. tractus a drawing, train, track, course, tract of land, from trahere tractum, to draw. Senses 4 and 5 are perhaps due to confusion with track. See Trace,v., and cf. Tratt.
L. tractabilis, fr, tractare to draw violently, to handle, treat. See Treat, v. t.

NL., from L. trahere, tractum, to draw.

L. tradere, traditum, to transmit, give up: cf. F. traditif.
L., fr. tradere, traditum. See Traitor.

L. traducere, traductum, to lead across, lead along, exhibit as a spectacle, disgrace, transfer, derive; trans across, over + ducere to lead: cf. F. traduire to transfer, translate, arraign, fr. L. traducere. See Duke.
L. traducens, p. pr. of traducere. See Traduce.
L. traductio a transferring: cf. F. traduction translation. See Traduce.

F. trafiquer; cf. It. trafficare, Sp. traficar, trafagar, Pg. traficar, trafegar, trafeguear, LL. traficare; of uncertain origin, perhaps fr. L. trans across, over + -ficare to make (see -fy, and cf. G. übermachen to transmit, send over, e. g., money, wares); or cf. Pg. trasfegar to pour out from one vessel into another, OPg. also, to traffic, perhaps fr. (assumed) LL. vicare to exchange, from L. vicis change (cf. Vicar). | Cf. F. trafic, It. traffico, Sp. tráfico, tráfago, Pg. tráfego, LL. traficum, trafica. See Traffic, v.

OE. trailen, OF. trailler to trail a deer, or hunt him upon a cold scent, also, to hunt or pursue him with a limehound, F. trailler to trail a fishing line; probably from a derivative of L. trahere to draw; cf. L. traha a drag, sledge, tragula a kind of drag net, a small sledge, Sp. trailla a leash, an instrument for leveling the ground, D. treilen to draw with a rope, to tow, treil a rope for drawing a boat. See Trace, v. t.
OF. trahiner, traïner,F. traîner, LL. trahinare, trainare, fr. L. trahere to draw. See Trail. | F. train, OF. traïn, trahin; cf. (for some of the senses) F. traine. See Train, v.

F., fr. L. tractus, fr. trahere to draw. See Trace, v., and cf. Tract a region, Trace a strap, Tret.

OE. traitour, OF. traïtor, traïteur, F. treître, L. traditor, fr. tradere, traditum, to deliver, to give up or surrender treacherously, to betray; trans across, over + dare to give. See Date time, and cf. Betray,Tradition, Traditor, Treason.
L. trajectus, p. p. of trajicere to throw across; trans across + jacere to throw. See Jet a shooting forth. | L. trajectus, fr. trajicere: cf. F. trajet, OF. traject. See Traject, v. t.
L. trajectio a crossing over, transposition.
L. tralatitius, translatitius, tralaticius, translaticius. See Tralation.
L. trans across + linea a line: cf. It tralineare, tralignare.
L. tralucens, translucens, p. pr. See Translucent.
Prov. E. tram a coal wagon, the shaft of a cart or carriage, a beam or bar; probably of Scand, origin; cf. OSw. tråm, trum, a beam, OD. drom, Prov. & OHG. tram. | Sp. trama weft, or F. trame.
F. tramail, trémail, a net, LL. tremaculum, tremacle, a kind of net for taking fish; L. tres three + macula a mesh. See Three, and Mail armor.
OF. tramontain, It. tramontano, L. transmontanus; trans across, beyond + mons, montis, mountain.

OE. trampen; akin to LG. trampen, G. trampeln, LG. & D. trappen, Dan. trampe, Sw. & Icel. trampa, Goth. anatrimpan to press upon; also to D. trap a step, G. treppe steps, stairs. Cf. Trap a kind of rock, Trape, Trip, v. i., Tread.
OE. trampelen, freq. of trampen. See Tramp, v. t.
L. tranare, transnare, to swim over; trans across, over + nare to swim.

F. transe fright, in OF. also, trance or swoon, fr. transir to chill, benumb, to be chilled, to shiver, OF. also, to die, L. transire to pass over, go over, pass away, cease; trans across, over + ire to go; cf. L. transitus a passing over. See Issue, and cf. Transit.
OE. trangrain a strange thing, trangame a toy. See Tangram.
L. tranquillus; probably fr. trans across, over + a word akin to quietus quiet: cf. F. tranquille. See Quiet.
L. transactus, p. p. of transigere. See Transaction.
L. transactio, fr. transigere, transactum, to drive through, carry through, accomplish, transact; trans across, over + agere to drive; cf. F. transaction. See Act, Agent.
L. transalpinus; trans across, beyond + Alpinus Alpine, from Alpes the Alps: cf. F. transalpin.
Pref. trans- + Atlantic: cf. F. transatlantique.
Pref. trans- + L. calens, p. pr. of calere to grow warm.

L. transcendens, -entis, p. pr. of transcendere to transcend: cf. F. transcendant, G. transcendent.
Pref. trans- + L. colare, colatum, to filter, to strain.
L. transcribere, transcriptum; trans across, over + scribere to write. See Scribe.
L. transcriptum, neut. of transcriptus, p. p. transcribere. See Transcribe.
Cf. F. transcription, L. transcriptio a transfer.
L. transcurrere, transcursum; trans across, over + currere to run.
L. transcurrens, p. pr. of transcurrere.
Cf. L. transcursio a passing over. See Transcur.
L. transducere, traducere, -dictum, to lead across or over. See Traduce.
Pref. trans- + L. septum an inclosure. See Septum.
L. transferre; trans across, over + ferre to bear: cf. F. transférer. See Bear to carry.
F. transfigurer, L. transfigurare, transfiguratum; trans across, over + figurare to form, shape. See Figure, v. t.
L. transfixus, p. p. of transfigure to transfix; trans across, through + figere to fix, fasten. See Fix.
L. transforatus, p. p. of transforare to pierce through; trans through + forare to bore.
L. transformare, transformatum; trans across, over + formare to from: cf. F. transformer. See Form, v. t.
L. transfretare; trans across, over + fretum a strait: cf. OF. transfreter.
L. transfuga; trans across, over + fugere to flee.
L. transfuga; trans across, over + fugere to flee.
L. transfundere; trans over, across + fundere to pour, pour out. See Found to cast, and cf. Transfuse.
L. transfusus, p. p. of transfundere: cf. F. transfuser. See Transfund.

L. transgressio a going across, going over, transgression of the law, from transgredi, transgressus, to step across, go over; trans over, across + gradi to step, walk: cf. F. transgression. See Grade.
Cf. L. transgressivus passing over into another class. F. transgressif.
L. transiens, -entis, p. pr. of transire, transitum, to go or pass over. See Trance.
L. transiliens, p. pr. of transilire to leap across or over; trans across, over + salire to leap.
L. transiliens, p. pr. of transilire to leap across or over; trans across, over + salire to leap.
L. transire to pass through or across, to pass.
L. transitus, from transire to go over: cf. F. transit. See Transient.
L. transitio: cf. F. transition. See Transient.
L. transitivus: cf. F. transitif. See Transient.
L. transitorius: cf. F. transitoire. See Transient.
f. translatus, used as p. p. of transferre to transfer, but from a different root. See Trans-, and Tolerate, and cf. Translation.
F. translation, L. translatio a transferring, translation, version. See Translate, and cf. Tralation.
L. translativus that is to be transferred: cf. F. translatif.
Pref. trans- + L. litera, littera letter.
L. translucens, -entis, p. pr. of translucere to shine through; trans across, through = lucere to shine. See Lucid.
L. translucidus; trans across, through + lucidus lucid: cf. F. translucide. See Translucent.
L. transmarinus; trans beyond + marinus marine: cf. F. transmarin. See Marine.
L. transmeatus, p. p. of transmeare to pass across; trans across, over + meare to go.
F. transmuer, L. transmutare. See Transmute.
L. transmigrans, p. pr. See Transmigrate.
L. transmigrare, transmigratum; trans across + migrare to migrate. See Migrate.
L. transmissio; cf. F. transmission. See Transmit.
L. transmittere, transmissum; trans across, over + mittere to send: cf. F. transmettre. See Missile.
F. transmutation, L. transmutatio. See Transmute.
L. transmutare, transmutatum; trans across + mutare to change. See Mutable, and cf. Transmew.
L. transnatare to swim over; trans across, over + natare to swim.
Probably fr. L. transtrum a crossbeam, transom, from trans across. Cf. Trestle.
L. transpadanus; trans across + Padus the Po.
F., from LL. transparens, -entis, p. pr. of transparere to be transparent; L. trans across, through + parere to appear. See Appear.
Pref. trans- + pass: cf. LL. transpassare. Cf. Trespass.
L. transpicere to see or look through + specere, spicere, to see. Cf. Conspicuous.
Pref. trans- + pierce: cf. F. transpercer.
F. transpirer; L. trans across, through + spirare to breathe. See Spirit.
F. transplanter, L. transplantare; trans across, over + plantare to plant. See Plant.
F. transporter, L. transportare; trans across + portare to carry. See Port bearing, demeanor. | F. See Transport, v.
F. transposer; pref. trans- (L. trans across) + poser to put. See Pose.
F. transposition, from L. transponere, transpositum, to set over, remove, transfer; trans across, over + ponere to place. See Position.
LL. transubstantiatus, p. p. of transubstantiare to transubstantiate; L. trans across, over + substantia substance. See Substance.
Pref. trans- + L. sudare to sweat: cf. F. transsuder.
L. transumere, transsumere, to take from one to another; trans across + sumere to take.
L. transumere, transumptum, to take from one to another, in LL., to transcribe. See Transume.
Pref. trans- + L. vas, vasis, vessel.
L. transvectio, from transvehere to carry across; trans across + vehere to carry.
L. transverberatus, p. p. of transverberare to strike or pierce through.
Cf. F. transversal. See Transverse. | Cf. F. transversale.
L. transversus, p. p. of transvertere to turn on direct across; trans across + vertere to turn: cf. F. transverse. See Verse, and cf. Traverse. | Pref. trans- + verse, n. Cf.Transpose.
L. transvolare to fly over or across; trans across + volare to fly.
Cf. OD. tranten to walk slowly, LG. & D. trant walk, pace.

Akin to OE. trappe trappings, and perhaps from an Old French word of the same origin as E. drab a kind of cloth. | Sw. trapp; akin to trappa stairs, Dan. trappe, G. treppe, D. trap; -- so called because the rocks of this class often occur in large, tabular masses, rising above one another, like steps. See Tramp. | OE. trappe, AS. treppe; akin to OD.trappe, OHG. trapo; probably fr. the root of E. tramp, as that which is trod upon: cf. F. trappe, which is trod upon: cf. Cf. F. trappéen. See Trap a kind of rock.

Cf. Icel. tros rubbish, leaves, and twigs picked up for fuel, trassi a slovenly fellow, Sw. trasa a rag, tatter.

Gr. Defn: A stammering or stuttering. [Obs.

F. travail; cf. Pr. trabalh, trebalh, toil, torment, torture; probably from LL. trepalium a place where criminals are tortured, instrument of torture. But the French word may be akin to L. trabs a beam, or have been influenced by a derivative from trabs (cf. Trave). Cf. Travel. | F. travailler, OF. traveillier, travaillier, to labor, toil, torment; cf. Pr. trebalhar to torment, agitate. See Travail, n.
Through French, fr. L. trabs, trabis, a beam; cf. OF. tref a beam, also F. travail a frame to confine a horse, OE. trave, trevys, travise, It. travaglio, F. travée the space between two beams.
Properly, to labor, and the same word as travail.
F. travers, breadth, extent from side, à travers, en travers, de travers, across, athwart. See Traverse, a.
OF. travers, L. transversus, p. p. of transvertere to turn or direct across. See Transverse, and cf. Travers. | F. traverse. See Traverse, a. | Cf. F. traverser. See Traverse, a.
F. travertin, It. travertino, tiburtino, L. lapis Tiburtinus, fr. Tibur an ancient town of Latium, now Tivoli.
F. travesti, p. p. of travestir to disguise, to travesty, It. travestire, fr. L. trans across, over + vestire to dress, clothe. See Vest.
OF. trauler, troller, F. trôter, to drag about, to stroll about; probably of Teutonic origin. Cf. Troll, v. t.
OF. traïr, F. trahir, L. tradere. See Traitor. | OE. treye, AS. treg. Cf. Trough.
OE. trichour, trichur, OF. tricheor deceiver, traitor, F. tricheur a cheat at play, a trickster. See Treachery.
OE. trecherïe, trichere, OF. trecherie, tricherie, F. tricherie trickery, from tricher to cheat, to trick, OF. trichier, trechier; probably of Teutonic origin. See Trickery, Trick.

OE. triacle a sovereign remedy, theriac, OF. triacle, F. thériaque (cf. Pr. triacla, tiriaca, Sp. & It. triaca, teriaca), L. theriaca an antidote against the bite of poisonous animals, Gr. qhri`on a beast, a wild beast, dim. of qh`r a beast. Cf. Theriac.

OE. treden, AS. tredan; akin to OFries. treda, OS. tredan, D. & LG. treden, G. treten, OHG. tretan, Icel. tro, Sw. tråda, träda, Dan. træde, Goth. trudan, and perhaps ultimately to F. tramp; cf. Gr. dram to run. Cf. Trade, Tramp, Trot.
OE. tredyl a step, AS. tredel. See Tread.
It. tregua; of Teutonic origin, and akin to E. true.
OE. tresun, treisun, traisoun, OF. traïson, F. trahison, L. traditio a giving up, a delivering up, fr. tradere to give up, betray. See Traitor, and cf. Tradition.
OE. tresor, tresour, F. trésor, L. thesaurus, Gr. Thesis, and cf. Thesaurus.
Treasure + OF. trové, F. trouvé, p. p. of OF. trover to find, F. trouver. See Trover.
OE. treten, OF. traitier, F. traiter, from L. tractare to draw violently, to handle, manage, treat, v. intens. from trahere, tractum, to draw. See Trace, v. t., and cf. Entreat, Retreat, Trait.
OE. tretable, F. traitable, L. tractabilis. See Treat, and cf. Tractable.
OE. tretis, OF. treitis, traitis, well made. See Treat.
OE. tretee, F. traité, LL. tractatus; cf. L. tractatus a handling, treatment, consultation, tractate. See Treat, and cf. Tractate.
OE. treble threefold, OF. treble, treible, L. triplus. See Triple. | " It has been said to be a corruption of triplum [Lat.
OF. trebuchet, trebukiet, an engine of war for hurling stones, F. trébuchet a gin, trap, a kind of balance, fr. OF. trebuchier, trebuquier, to stumble, trip, F. trébucher.
OF. trebuchet, trebukiet, an engine of war for hurling stones, F. trébuchet a gin, trap, a kind of balance, fr. OF. trebuchier, trebuquier, to stumble, trip, F. trébucher.
D. trekschuit; trekken to draw + schuit a boat. Cf. Trackscout.

OE. tree, tre, treo, AS. treó, treów, tree, wood; akin to OFries. tr, OS. treo, trio, Icel. tr, Dan. træ, Sw. trä, träd, Goth. triu, Russ. drevo, W. derw an oak, Ir. darag, darog, Gr. dru tree, wood, daru wood. Dryad, Germander, Tar, n., Trough.

Defn: A white crystalline nitrogenous substance present in small amount in the pancreas and spleen, and formed in large quantity from the decomposition of proteid matter by various means, -- as by pancreatic digestion, by putrefaction as of cheese, by the action of boiling acids, etc. Chemically, it consists of oxyphenol and amidopropionic acid, and by decomposition yields oxybenzoic acid, or some other benzol derivative. A dialectic form for fat, OE. fat, AS. fæt; akin to D.vat, OS. fat, G. fass, OHG. faz, Icel. & Sw. fat, Dan.fad, Lith. p a pot, and probably to G. fassen to seize, to contain, OHG. fazz, D. vatten. Cf. Fat a vat.
L. Vaticanus, mons, or collis, Vaticanus, the Vatican hill, in Rome, on the western bank of the Tiber: cf. F. Vatican, It. Vaticano.
L. vates a prophet + caedere to kill.
L. vaticinatus, p. p. of vaticinari to prophesy, fr. vaticinus prophetical, fr. vates a prophet.
F., fr. Vau-de-vire, a village in Normandy, where Olivier Basselin, at the end of the 14th century, composed such songs.

OE. voute, OF. voute, volte, F. voûte, LL. volta, for voluta, volutio, fr. L. volvere, volutum, to roll, to turn about. See Voluble, and cf. Vault a leap, Volt a turn, Volute. | OE. vouten, OF. volter, vouter, F. voûter. See Vault an arch. | Cf. OF. volter, F. voltiger, It. volt turn. See Vault, n., 4.
F. vanter, LL. vanitare, fr. L. vanus vain. See Vain. | F. avant before, fore. See Avant, Vanguard. | See Avant, Advance.
F. avant-mur. See Vanguard, and Mure.
So called after the French chemist Vauquelin, who died in 1829: cf. F. vauquelinite.
OE. vavasour, OF. vavassor, vavassour, F. vavasseur, LL. vavassor, probably contr. from vassus vassorum vassal of the vassals. See Vassal.
For vanward, equivalent to vanguard. See Vanguard, Ward guard.
OE. veel, OF. veel, F. veau, L. vitellus, dim. of vitulus a calf; akin to E. wether. See Wether, and cf. Vellum, Vituline.
L. vectio, from vehere, vectum, to carry.
L. vectitatus bornve, v. intens. fr. vehere, vectum, to carry.
L., a bearer, carrier. fr. vehere, vectum, to carry.
L. vectura, from vehere, vectum, to carry. Cf. Vettura, Voiture.
Skr. v, properly, knowledge, from vid to know. See Wit.
F. vedette, It. vedetta, for veletta (influenced by vedere to see, L. videre), from It. veglia watch, L. vigilia. See Vigil.
F. virer (cf. Sp. virar, birar), LL. virare; perhaps fr. L. vibrare to brandish, vibrate (cf. Vibrate); or cf. L. viriae armlets, bracelets, viriola a little bracelet (cf. Ferrule). Cf. Environ.
Ar. w, properly, falling: cf. F. Wéga.

F. végétable growing, capable of growing, formerly also, as a noun, a vegetable, from L. vegetabilis enlivening, from vegetare to enliven, invigorate, quicken, vegetus enlivened, vigorous, active, vegere to quicken, arouse, to be lively, akin to vigere to be lively, to thrive, vigil watchful, awake, and probably to E. wake, v. See Vigil, Wake, v.
L. vegetatus, p. p. of vegetare to enliven. See Vegetable.
Cf. F. végétation, L. vegetatio an enlivening. See Vegetable.
L. vehemens, the first part of which is perhaps akin to vehere to carry, and the second mens mind: cf. F. véhément. Cf. Vehicle, and Mental.
L. vehiculum, fr. vehere to carry; akin to E. way, wain. See Way, n., and cf. Convex, Inveigh, Veil, Vex.
G. vehm, fehm, fehme, a secret tribunal of punishment, MHG. veime, veme: cf. F. vehmique.

OE. veile, OF. veile, F. voile, L. velum a sail, covering, curtain, veil, probably fr. vehere to bear, carry, and thus originally, that which bears the ship on. See Vehicle, and cf. Reveal. | Cf. OF. veler, F. voiler, L. velarc. See Veil, n.
OE. veine, F. veine, L. vena.
L. velatus, p. p. of velare to veil. See Veil.
NL., dim. from L. velum a veil, a sail.
L. velifer; velum a sail + ferre to bear.
NL., fr. L. velum a veil + gerere bear.
L. velitatio, fr. velitari, velitatus, to skirmish, from veles, -itis, a light-armed soldier.
L. velivolans; velum a sail + volare to fly.
Cf. L. vellus the skin of a sheep with the wool on it, a fleece, a hide or pelt, or E. fell a hide. | Cf. Vell, n.
F. velléité (cf. It. velleità), fr. L. velle to will, to be willing.
L. vellicatus, p. p. of vellicare to twitch, fr. vellere to pluck, pull.
OE. velim, F. vélin, fr. L. vitulinus of a calf, fr. vitulus a calf. See Veal.
L. velox, -ocis, swift + pes, pedis, a foot. See Velocity, and Foot.
L. velocitas, from velox, - ocis, swift, quick; perhaps akin to v to fly (see Volatile): cf. F. vélocité.
L., an awning, a veil. See Veil.
F. velours, OF. velous, from L. villosus hairy. See Velvet.

OE. velouette, veluet, velwet; cf. OF. velluau, LL. velluetum, vellutum, It. velluto, Sp. velludo; all fr. (assumed) LL. villutus shaggy, fr L. villus shaggy hair; akin to vellus a fleece, and E. wool. See Wool, and cf. Villous.
Cf. Sp. venado a does, stag.
L. vena a vein. | L. venalis, from venus sale; akin to Gr. vasna: cf. F. vénal.
NL., fr. L. venans, p. pr. of venari to hunt.
LL. venarius, fr. L. venari, p. p. venatus, to hunt.
L. venaticus, fr. venatus hunting, fr. venari, p. p. venatus, to hunt.
L. venaticus, fr. venatus hunting, fr. venari, p. p. venatus, to hunt.
L. vena a vein. | L. venatio, fr. venari, p. p. venatus, to hunt. See Venison.
F. vendre, L. vendere, from venum dare; venus sale + dare to give. See 2d Venal, Date, time.
From Vend: cf. F. vendeur, OF. vendeor. Cf. Vendor.
L. vendibilis: cf. OF. vendible, F. vendable.
L. venditatio, fr. venditare, venditatum, to offer again and again for sale, v. freq. of vendere. See Vend.
OF. vendue, from F. vendre, p. p. vendu, vendue, to sell.
G. furnieren, fourniren, fr. F. fournir to furnish. See Furnish. | Cf. G. furnier or fournier. See Veneer, v. t.
L. veneficium, fr. veneficus poisoning; venenum poison + facere to make: cf. F. vénéfice.
L. veneatus, p. p. venenare to poison, from venenum poison. Cf. Venom.
L. venenosus, fr. venenum poison. Cf. Venomous.
L. veneratus, p. p. of venerari to venerate; akin to Venus Venus, Skr. van to like, to wish, and E. winsome. See Winsome.
L. venereus, venerius, fr. Venus, Veneris, Venus, the goddess of love. See Venerate.
L. Venus, Veneris, the goddess of love. | OE. venerie, F. vénerie, fr. OF. vener to hunt, L. venari. See Venison.
NL. venaesectio; L. vena vein + sectio section.
F. venue, lit., an arrival, from venir, p. p. venu, venue, to come. See Venue.

F. vengeance, fr. venger to avenge, L. vindicare to lay claim to, defend, avenge, fr. vindex a claimant, defender, avenger, the first part of which is of uncertain origin, and the last part akin to dicere to say. See Diction, and cf. Avenge, Revenge, Vindicate.
L. veniabilis, fr. venia forgiveness, pardon.
OF. venial, F. véniel, L. venialis, from venia forgiveness, pardon, grace, favor, kindness; akin to venerari to venerate. See Venerate.
L., make, or cause, to come.

OE. veneison, veneson, venison, OF. veneison, F. venaison, L. venatio hunting, the chase, game, fr. venari, p. p. venatus, to hunt; perhaps akin to OHG. weidin, weidenen, to pasture, to hunt, G. weide pasturage. Cf. Gain to acquire, Venation.
L., come, imperative 2d person pl. So called from its opening word in the Latin version.
OE. venim, OF. venim, F. venin, L. veneum. Cf. Venenate. | OE. venimen, OF. venimer, L. venenare. See Venom, n.
OE. venemous, venimous, F. venimeux, L. venenosus, fr. venenum poison. See Venom, and cf. Venenose.
L. venosus, from vena a vein. See Vein.

F. vente, fr. L. vendere, -itum, to sell; perh. confused with E. vent an opening. See Vend. | Sp. venta a poor inn, sale, market. See Vent sale. | Cf. F. venter to blow, vent wind (see Ventilate); but prob influenced by E. vent an opening. | OE. fent, fente, a slit, F. fente a slit, cleft, fissure, from fendre to split, L. findere; but probably confused with F. vent wind, L. ventus. See Fissure, and cf. Vent to snuff.
OF. ventaille, F. ventail. See Ventilate, and cf. Aventail.
L. ventus wind + ductus a leading, conduit, fr. ducere, ductum, to lead.
L. ventilatus, p. p. of ventilare to toss, brandish in the air, to fan, to winnow, from ventus wind; akin to E. wind. See Wind rushing air.
Cf. F. ventilateur, L. ventilator a winnower.
L. ventosus windy. See Ventilate. | F. ventôse. See Ventose, a.
L. ventositas: cf. F. ventosité. See Ventose, n.
L. ventralis, fr. venter the belly; perhaps akin to G. wanst: cf. F. ventral.
L. ventriculus the stomach, a ventricle, dim. of venter the belly: cf. F. ventricule. See Ventral.
NL. ventricosus, fr. L. venter belly.
NL. ventricosus, fr. L. venter belly.
L., belly, dim. fr. venter belly.
L. ventriloquus a ventriloquist; venter the belly + loqui, p. p. locutus, to speak. See Ventral, and Loquacious.
Aphetic form of OE. aventure. See Adventure.
Aphetic form of OE. aventurous. See Adventurous, Venture, n.
F. venue a coming, arrival, fr. venir to come, L. venire; hence, in English, the place whither the jury are summoned to come. See Come, and cf. Venew, Veney.
L. venula, dim. from vena vein.
L. Venus, -eris, the goddess of love, the planet Venus.
L. venustus, from Venus the goddess of love.
L. verax, -acis, fr. verus true. See Very.
A word brought by the English from India; of uncertain origin; cf. Skr. vara, Pg. varanda, Sp. baranda, Malay baranda.
F. verbe, L. verbum a word, verb. See Word.
F., fr. L. verbalis. See Verb.
L. verbenatus crowned with a wreath of sacred boughs. See Verbena.
L. verberatus, p. p. of verberare to beat, from verber a lash, a whip.
F. verbiage, from OF. verbe a word. See Verb.
L. verbosus, from verbum a word. See Verb.
F. vert antique a kind of marble; verd, vert, green + antique ancient: cf. It. verde antico.

F. verdoyant, p. pr. of verdoyer to be verdant, to grow green, OF. verdoier, verdeier, fr. verd, vert, green, fr. L. viridis green, fr. virere to be green: cf. OF. verdant verdant, L. viridans, p. pr. of viridare to make green. Cf. Farthingale, Verjuice, Vert.
F. verdier, LL. viridarius, fr. L. viridis green.
F. verdier, LL. viridarius, fr. L. viridis green.
OE. verdit, OF. verdit, veirdit, LL. verdictum, veredictum; L. vere truly (fr. verus true) + dictum a saying, a word, fr. dicere, dictum, to say. See Very, and Dictum.

F. vert-de-gris, apparently from verd, vert, green + de of + gris gray, but really a corruption of LL. viride aeris (equivalent to L. aerugo), from L. viridis green + aes, aeris, brass. See Verdant, and 2d Ore.
Cf. Sp. verdino bright green, F. verdin the yellow-hammer.
F. vert-de-terre, literally, green of earth.
F. verdoyer to become green. See Verdant.
F., fr. L. viridis green. See Verdant.
L. verecundus, fr. vereri to feel awe.
L., dim. of veretrum the private parts.
F. verge, L. virga; perhaps akin to E. wisp. | L. vergere to bend, turn, incline; cf. Skr. v to turn.
F. verger, from verge a rod. See 1st Verge.
L. veridicus; verus true + dicere to say, tell.
F. vérifier, LL. verificare, from L. verus true + -ficare to make. See Very, and -fy.
L. verisimilis; verus true + similis like, similar. See Very, and Similar.
L. verisimilitudo: cf. OF. verisimilitude. See Verisimilar.
F. vérité, L. veritas, fr. verus true. See Very.
OE. vergeous, F. verjus, that is, the juice of green fruits; verd, vert, green + jus juice. See Verdant, and Juice.
F., vermilion, fr. LL. vermiculus, fr. L. vermiculus a little worm, the coccus Indicus, from vermis a worm. See Worm, and cf. Vermicule.
L. vermes, pl. of vermis a worm.
It., pl. of vermicello, literally, a little worm, dim. of verme a worm, L. vermis. See Worm, and cf. Vermicule, Vermeil.
L. vermis a worm + caedere to kill.
L. vermiculus a little worm, dim. of vermis a worm: cf. F. vermiculaire. See Vermicelli.
L. vermiculatus inlaid so as to resemble the tracks of worms, p. p. of vermiculari to be full of worms, vermiculus a little worm. See Vermicular.
L. vermiculus, dim. of vermis a worm. See Vermicular.
L. vermiculus, dim. of vermis worm.
L. vermis a worm + fugare to drive away, fr. fugere to flee. See Worm, and Fugitive.
NL., fr. L. vermis worm + lingua tongue.
OE. vermine, F. vermine, from L. vermis a worm; cf. LL. vermen a worm, L. verminosus full of worms. See Vermicular, Worm.
L. verminare to have worms, fr. vermis a worm.
L. verminatio the worms, a disease of animals, a crawling, itching pain.
L. verminosus, fr. vermis a worm: cf. F. vermineux.
L. vermis a worm + parere to bring forth.
L. vermis a worm + vorare to devour: cf. F. vermivore.
L. vernaculus born in one's house, native, fr. verna a slave born in his master's house, a native, probably akin to Skr. vas to dwell, E. was.
L. vernalis, fr. vernus vernal, ver spring; akin to Gr. vasanta, Icel. var, and E. Easter, east.
L. vernans, p. pr. vernare to flourish, from ver spring.
F. vernation: cf. L. vernatio the sloughing of the skin of snakes.
So named after the inventor, Pierre Vernier.
L. verrucosus, fr. verruca a wart.
L. verrucula, dim. of verruca a wart.
L. versabilis: cf. F. versable. See Versatile.
L. versans, p. pr. versare to turn abound frequently, to turn over in the mind, to meditate. See Versatile. | F.
L. versatilis, fr. versare to turn around, v. freq. of vertere: cf. F. versatile. See Verse.

OE. vers, AS. fers, L. versus a line in writing, and, in poetry, a verse, from vertere, versum, to turn, to turn round; akin to E. worth to become: cf. F. vers. See Worth to become, and cf. Advertise, Averse, Controversy, Convert, Divers, Invert, Obverse, Prose, Suzerain, Vortex.
Cf. F. versé, L. versatus, p. p. of versari to turn about frequently, to turn over, to be engaged in a thing, passive of versare. See Versant, a. | L. versus turned, p. p. vertere. See 1st Versed.
L. versiculus, dim. of versus. See Verse.
L. versicolor; versare to change + color color.
L. versicolor; versare to change + color color.
OE. versifien, F. versifier, L. versificare; versus a verse + -ficare to make. See Verse, and -fy.
F., from L. vertere, versum, to turn, to change, to translate. See Verse.
L. versus, p. p. of vertere to turn: cf. F. verso.
NL., fr. L. vertere, versus, to turn. See Version.
L., toward, turned in the direction of, from vertere, versum, to turn. See Verse.
L. versutus, fr. vertere, versum, to turn.
F., green, from L. viridis. See Verdant, and cf. Verd.
L. vertebra, fr. vertere to turn, change. See Verse.
L. vertex, -icis, a whirl, top of the head, top, summit, from vertere to turn. See Verse, and cf. Vortex.
L. verticillus, dim. of vertex a whirl: cf. F. verticille. See Vertex.
NL., fr. L. verticillus a whirl + aster a star.
L. vertiginosus, fr. vertigo a whirling around, giddiness: cf. F. vertigineux. See Vertig.
L., fr. vertere to turn. See Verse.
OE. verveine, F. verveine, fr. L. verbena, pl. verbenae sacred boughs of laurel, olive, or myrtle, a class of plants; cf. verbenaca vervain. Cf. Verbena.

OE. verai, verray, OF. verai, vrai, F. vrai, (assumed) LL. veracus, for L. verax true, veracious, fr. verus true; akin to OHG. & OS. war, G. wahr, D. waar; perhaps originally, that is or exists, and akin to E. was. Cf. Aver, v. t., Veracious, Verdict, Verity.
NL., from L. Vesuvius, contr. Vesbius, Vesuvius.
L. vesica blister: cf. F. vésicant.
L. vesicula, dim. of vesica a bladder, blister; akin to Skr. vasti bladder: cf. F. vésicule.
L., the evening, the evening star, the west; akin to Gr. west. Cf. Hesperian, Vespers.
OF. vespres, F. vêpres, LL. vesperae, fr. L. vespera evening. See Vesper, n.
OF. vessel, veissel, vaissel, vaissiel, F. vascellum, dim. of vasculum, dim. of vas a vessel. Cf. Vascular, Vase.
F. vessigon, fr. L. vesica a bladder, blister.
F. vessigon, fr. L. vesica a bladder, blister.

L. vestis a garment, vesture; akin to Goth. wasti, and E. wear: cf. F. veste. See Wear to carry on the person, and cf. Divest, Invest, Travesty. | Cf. L. vestire, vestitum, OF. vestir, F. vêtir. See Vest, n.
L. Vesta, akin to Gr. ush to burn (see East), or perhaps to Skr. vas to dwell, and E. was.
L. Vestalis belonging to Vesta, vestal. See Vesta. | L. Vestalis (sc. virgo): cf. F. vestale. See Vestal, a.
L. vestibulum, of uncertain origin: cf. F. vestibule.
L. vestigatus, p. p. of vestigare. See Vestige.
F., from L. vestigium footprint, trace, sign; the last part (-stigium) is probably akin to E. sty, v. i. Cf. Investigate.
OE. vestement, vestiment, OF. vestement, vestiment, F. vêtement, fr. L. vestimentum, fr. vestire to clothe, fr. vestis a garment, clothing. See Vest.
OE. vestrye, F. vestiaire, L. vestiarium, fr. vestiarius belonging to clothes, fr. vestis a garment. See Vest, n., and cf. Vestiary.
OF. vesture, vesteure, F. vêture, LL. vestitura, from L. vestire to clothe, dress. See Vest, v. t., and cf. Vestiture.
Cf. F. Vésuvien, It. Vesuviano. | G. vesuvian. See Vesuvian, a.
Also fitch; OE. ficche, feche, for veche, OF. veche, vecce, vesche, vesce, F. vesce, fr. L. vicia.
L. veteranus, from vetus, veteris, old; akin to Gr. vatsara. See Wether. | L. veteranus (sc. miles): cf. F. vétéran.
L. veterinarius of or belonging to beasts of burden an draught, fr. veterinus, probably originally, of or pertaining to yearlings: cf. F. vétérinaire. See Veteran, Wether.
It. vettura, fr. L. vectura conveyance. Cf. Vecture.
F. vexer, L. vexare, vexatum, to vex, originally, to shake, toss, in carrying, v. intens. fr. vehere, vectum, to carry. See Vehicle.
Cf. F. vexillaire, L. vexillarius a standard bearer.
Cf. F. vexillaire, L. vexillarius a standard bearer. | L. vexillarius: cf. F. vexillaire.
L. See Way. | L., ablative of via way. See Way.
F., from vie life, L. vita. See Vital.
L. via a way + -duct, as in aqueduct: cf. F. viaduc. See Via, and Aqueduct.
OE. viole, fiole, F. fiole. See Phial.
F. viande meat, food, LL. vianda, vivanda, vivenda, properly, things to live on, fr. L. vivere to live; akin to vivus living. See Vivid, and cf. Victualis.
L. viarius, fr. via a way, road.
L. via way + -tecture, as in architecture.
L. viaticus, fr. via a way. See Voyage.
L., from viaticus, a. See Viatic.
L., pl. of vibex, -icis, the mark of a blow.
NL., dim. from L. vibrare to vibrate.
L. vibrans, p. pr.: cf. F. vibrant. See Vibrate.
L. vibratus, p. p. of vibrare, v. t. & v. i., to snake, brandish, vibrate; akin to Skr. vip to tremble, Icel. veifa to wave, vibrate. See Waive and cf. Whip, v. t.
NL., fr. L. vibrare to vibrate, to move by undulations.
L. vibrissae, pl., the hairs in the nostrils of man, fr. vibrare to vibrate; -- so called because touching them tickles a person, and causes him to shake his head.
OE. vicar, viker, vicair, F. vicaire, fr. L. vicarius. See Vicarious.

L. vicarius, from vicis change, alternation, turn, the position, place, or office of one person as assumed by another; akin to Gr. wechsel a change, and probably also to E. weak. See Weak, and cf. Vice, prep.
F., from L. vitium. | See Vise. | L., abl. of vicis change, turn. See Vicarious. | Cf. F. vice-. See Vice, prep.
Vice, a + gerent: cf. F. vicegérant. | Vice, a. + gerent: cf. F. vicegérant.
L. vicenarius, fr. viceni twenty each; akin to viginti twenty.
L. vicennium a period of twenty years; viceni twenty + annus year.
F. vice-roi; pref. vice- in the place of (L. vice) + roi a king, L. rex. See Vice, prep. and Royal.
OF. veisinage, F. voisinage, from OF. veisin, F. voisin, neighboring, a neighbor, L. vicunus. See Vicinity.

L. vicinitas, from vicinus neighboring, near, from vicus a row of houses, a village; akin to Gr. v a house, vi to enter, Goth. weihs town: cf. OF. vicinité. Cf. Diocese, Economy, Parish, Vicinage, Wick a village.
OF. vicious, F. vicieux, fr. L. vitiosus, fr. vitium vice. See Vice a fault.
L. vicissitudo, fr. vicis change, turn: cf. F. vicissitude. See Vicarious.
From OE. vicounte a viscount. See Viscount.
L. victimatus, p. p. of victimare to sacrifice.
L. victor, fr. vincere, victum, to vanquish, to conquer. See Vanquish.
L. victoriosus: cf. F. victorieux. See Victory.
OE. victorie, OF. victorie, victoire, F. victoire, L. victoria. See Victor.

OE. vitaille, OF. vitaille, F. victuaille, pl. victuailles, fr. L. victualia, pl. of. victualis belonging to living or nourishment, fr. victus nourishment, from vivere, victum, to live; akin to vivus living. See Vivid.
F., fr. LL. vice-dominus, fr. L. vice instead of + dominus master, lord.
L., contr. fr. videre licet, literally, it is easy to see, one may or can see.
Cf. Pg. vidonho the quality of grapes, Sp. veduño.
L. vidualis, fr. vidua a widow, fr. viduus widowed. See Widow.
OE. vien, shortened fr. envien, OF. envier to invite, to challenge, a word used in gambling, L. invitare to invite; of uncertain origin. Cf. Invite, Envie.
OF. veue, F. vue, fr. OF. veoir to see, p. p. veu, F. voir, p. p. vu, fr. L. videre to see. See Vision, and cl. Interview, Purview, Review, Vista.
L. vigesimus twentieth, from viginti twenty.
L. vigesimus quartus twenty-fourth. Cf. Duodecimo.
OE. vigile, L. vigilia, from vigil awake, watchful, probably akin to E. wake: cf. F. vigile. See Wake, v. i., and cf. Reveille, Surveillance, Vedette, Vegetable, Vigor.
L. vigilans, -antis, p. pr. of vigilare to watch, fr. vigil awake: cf. F. vigilant. See Vigil.
L. vigintiviratus, fr. vigintiviri; viginti twenty + vir a man.
F. vignette, fr. vigne a vine. See Vine, and cf. Vinette.
Cf. F. vigogne vicuña. See Vicuña.
OE. vigour, vigor, OF. vigor, vigur, vigour, F. vigueur, fr. L. vigor, fr. vigere to be lively or strong. See Vegetable, Vigil.
Cf. OF. vigoros, F. vigoureux, LL. vigorosus.
Icel. vikingr, fr. vik a bay, inlet.
As if the p. p. of a verb to vile. See Vile, a.
OE. vil, F. vil, from L. vilis cheap, worthless, vile, base.
L. vilis vile + -fly; cf. L. vilificare to esteem of little value.
L. vilipendere; vilis vile + pendere to weigh, to value: cf. F. vilipender.
L. vilitas: cf. F. vileté, vilité, OF. vilté.
OF. ville, vile, a village, F. ville a town, city. See Villa.
L. villa, LL. also village, dim. of L. vicus a village: cf. It. & F. villa. See Vicinity, and cf. Vill, Village, Villain.
F., fr. L. villaticus belonging to a country house or villa. See Villa, and cf. Villatic.
OE. vilein, F. vilain, LL. villanus, from villa a village, L. villa a farm. See Villa. | F. vilain.
OE. vilanie, OF. vilanie, vilainie, vileinie, vilanie, LL. villania. See Villain, n.
Dim. of villa; formed on the analogy of the French.
L. villaticus belonging to a country house. See Village.
L. villosus: cf. F. villeux. Cf. Velvet.
L., shaggy hair, a tuft of hair.
L. viminalis pertaining to osiers, fr. vimen a pliant twig, osier.
L. vimineus, fr. vimen pliant twig.
L. vincibilis, fr. vincere to vanquish, conquer: cf. F. vincible. See Victor.
L. vinctura, fr. vincire, vinctum, to bind.
L., from vincire, vinctum, to bind.
L. vindemialis, fr. vindemia a vintage. See Vintage.
L. vindicatus, p. p. of vindicare to lay claim to, defend, avenge. See Vengeance.
L. vindicatio a laying claim, defense, vindication. See Vindicate.
For vindicative, confused with L. vindicta revenge, punishment, fr. vindicare to vindicate. Cf. Vindicative.
F. vigne, L. vinea a vineyard, vine from vineus of or belonging to wine, vinum wine, grapes. See Wine, and cf. Vignette.
OE. vinegre, F. vinaigre; vin wine (L. vinum) + aigre sour. See Wine, and Eager, a.
For OE. winyard, AS. wingeard; influenced by E. vine. See Wine, and Yard an inclosure.
L. vinosus, fr. vinum wine: cf. F. vineux. See Wine.

Corrupted by influence of vintner, vintry, from OE. vindage, vendage, for vendange, OF. vendenge, F. vendange, from L. vindemia; vinum wine, grapes + demere to take off; de + emere, originally, to take. See Wine, Redeem, and cf. Vindemial.
OE. vintener, viniter, OF. vinetier, vinotier, LL. vinetarius, fr. L. vinetum a vineyard, fr. vinum wine. See Wine.
OE. viniterie, from OF. vinotier, vinetier, wine merchant. See Vintner.

F. viole; cf. Pr. viola, viula, Sp., Pg., & It. viola, LL. vitula; of uncertain origin; perhaps from L. vitulari to celebrate a festival, keep holiday, be joyful, perhaps originally, to sacrifice a calf (vitulus; cf. Veal). Cf. Fiddle, Vielle, 2d Viola, Violin.
L., a violet. See Violet. | It. See Viol.
L. violabilis: cf. F. violable. See Violate.
L. violaceus, fr. viola a violet.
L. violatus, p. p. of violare to violate, fr. vis strength, force. See Violent.
F., fr. L. violentia. See Violent.
F. violette a violet (cf. violet violet-colored), dim. of OF. viole a violet, L. viola; akin to Gr. Iodine. | Cf. F. violet. See Violet, n.
It. violino, dim. of viola. See Viol.
Cf. F. violiniste, violoniste, It. violonista.
It. violoncello, dim. of violone a bass viol. See Violone.
It. violone, augment. of viola a viol. See Viol.

F. vipère, L. vipera, probably contr. fr. vivipera; vivus alive + parere to bring forth, because it was believed to be the only serpent that brings forth living young. Cf. Quick, a., Parent, Viviparous, Wivern, Weever.
L. virago, -intis, from vir a man. See Virile.
OF. vire, fr. virer to turn. Cf. Veer, Vireton.
F. virelai; virer to turn + lai a song, a lay.
L. virens, p. pr. of virere to be green.
L. virescens, p. pr. of virescere to grow green, verb incho. fr. virere to be green.
L. virgatus made of twigs, fr. virga a twig, rod. See Verge a rod. | LL. virgata, virgata terrae, so much land as virga terrae, a land measure, contains, fr. L. virga a twig, rod.
L. virgatus striped. See Virgate, a.
L. virgo, -inis: cf. OF. virgine, virgene, virge, vierge, F. vierge.
L. virginalis: cf. F. virginal. | Cf. F. virginale; -- probably so called from being used by young girls, or virgins.
OE. virgintee, F. virginité, L. virginitas.
L. virgo a virgin, the constellation Virgo in the zodiac. See Virgin.
F. virgouleuse, from the village of Virgoulée, near Limoges.
From. L. virgula a small rod.
F. virgule, fr. L. virgula, dim. of virga. See Verge a rod.
L. viridescens, p. pr. of viridescere to grow green.
L. viriditas, fr. viridis green: cf. F. viridité. See Verdant.
L. virilis, fr. vir a man; akin to AS. wer: cf. F. viril. See Werewolf, World, and cf. Decemvir, Virago, Virtue.
L. vir man + potens fit for.
It. virtù virtue, excellence, from L. virtus. See Virtue.
OE. vertu, F. vertu, L. virtus strength, courage, excellence, virtue, fr. vir a man. See Virile, and cf. Virtu.
OE. vertuous, OF. vertuos, vertuous, F. vertueux, fr. L. Virtuous. See Virtue, and cf. Virtuoso.
Cf. F. virulence, L. virulentia an offensive odor, a stench.
Cf. F. virulence, L. virulentia an offensive odor, a stench.
L. virulentus, fr. virus poison: cf. F. virulent. See Virus.
L., a slimy liquid, a poisonous liquid, poison, stench; akin to Gr. visha. Cf. Wizen, v. i.
F. visage, from L. visus a seeing, a look, fr. videre, visum, to see. See Vision.
L. viscidus, fr. viscum the mistletoe, birdlime made from the berries of the mistletoe; akin to Gr. viscide.
OE. vicounte, OF. visconte, vescunte, F. vicomte, LL. vicecomes; L. vice (see Vice, a.) + comes a companion, LL., a count. See Count.
L., perhaps akin to E. viscid.
F. vis a screw, winding stairs, OF. vis, viz, fr. L. vitis a vine; probably akin to E. withy. | F. visé, p. p. of viser to put a visa to, fr. L. visus seen, p. p. of videre to see.
Skr. Vish, from vish to pervade., to extend through nature.
L. visibilis, fr. videre, visum, to see: cf. F. visible. See Vision.
L. Visegothae, pl. Cf. West, and Goth.
OE. visioun, F. vision, fr. L. visio, from videre, visum, to see: akin to Gr. wit. See Wit, v., and cf. Advice, Clairvoyant, Envy, Evident, Provide, Revise, Survey, View, Visage, Visit.
F. visiter, L. visitare, fr. visere to go to see, to visit, fr. videre, visum to see. See Vision. | Cf. F. visite. See Visit, v. t., and cf. Visite.
L. visitans, -antis; p. pr.: cf. F. visitant.
Cf. LL. visitator a bishop temporarily put in place of another.
Cf. F. visif, LL. visivus. See Vision.
OF. visné, veisiné, visnet, neighborhood, LL. vicinatus, fr. L. vicunus neighboring, a neighbor. See Vicinity.
OE. visere, F. visière, fr. OF. vis. See Visage, Vision.
It., sight, view, fr. vedere, p. p. visto, veduto, to see, fr. L. videre, visum. See View, Vision.
L. visualis, from visus a seeing, sight: cf. F. visuel. See Vision.
F., fr. L. vitalis, fr. vita life; akin to vivere to live. See Vivid.
L. vitellus a little calf, the yolk of an egg.
L. vitellus the yolk of an egg.
L., the yolk of an egg.
L. vitiatus, p. p. vitiare to vitiate, fr. vitium a fault, vice. See Vice a fault.
L. viticula, dim. of vitis vine.
L., a kind of tetter, fr. vitium blemish, vice.
L. vitilitigare to quarrel disgracefully; vitium vice + litigare to quarrel.
NL., dim. of L. vitrum glass.
L. vitreous, from vitrum glass; perhaps akin to videre to see (see Vision). Cf. Varnish.
L. vitrum glass + facere, factum, to make.
F. vitrifier; L. vitrum glass + -ficare to make. See Vitreous, -fy.
F. vitriol; cf. Pr. vitriol, vetriol, Sp. & Pg. vitriolo, It. vitriuolo; fr. L. vitreolus of glass, vitreus vitreous. See Vitreous.
L. vittatus bound with a fillet, fr. vitta fillet.
L. vitulinus, fr. vitulus a calf. See Veal.
L. vituperatus, p. p. of vituperare to blame, vituperate; vitium a fault + parare to prepare. See Vice a fault, and Pare, v. t.
L. vituperatio: cf. OF. vituperation. See Vituperate.
L. vívax, -acis, fr. vivere to live. See Vivid.
L., fr. vivarius belonging to living creatures, fr. vivus alive, living. See Vivid.
F., imperative sing. pres. fr. vivre to live, L. vivere. | L. vivus: cf. F. vif. See Vivid.
L. vivens, p. pr. of vivere to live.
F. vivres, pl. of vivre, orig., to live.
OF. vives, F. avives (cf. Sp. abivas, adiva) fr. Ar. ad-dhiba. Cf. Fives vives.
So called by Werner after the English mineralogist F. G. Vivian.
L. vividus, from vivere to life; akin to vivus living. See Quick, a., and cf. Revive, Viand, Victuals, Vital.
L. vivificus: cf. F. vivifique. See Vivify.
L. vivificus: cf. F. vivifique. See Vivify.
L. vivificatus, p. p. vivificare. See Vivify.
F. vivifier, L. vivificare. See Vivid, -fy; cf. Vivificate.
L. viviparus; vivus alive + parere to bear, bring forth. Cf. Viper.
L. vivus alive + E. section: cf. F. vivisection. See Vivid, and Section.
AS. fixen a she-fox, for fyxen, fem. of fox. See Fox.
Ar. wezir, wazir, properly, a bearer of burdens, a porter, from wazara to bear a burden: cf. F. vizir, visir. Cf. Alguazil.
L. vocabulum an appellation, designation, name, fr. vocare to call, fr. vox, vocis, a voice, a word: cf. F. vocable. See Voice.
LL. vocabularium, vocabularius: cf. F. vocabulaire. See Vocable.
L. vocalis, fr. vox, vocis, voice: cf. F. vocal. See Voice, and cf. Vowel. | Cf. F. vocal, LL. vocalis.
L. vocalis (sc. littera) a vowel. See Vocal, a.
L. vocatio a bidding, invitation, fr. vocare to call, fr. vox, vocis, voice: cf. F. vocation. See Vocal.
L. vocativus, fr. vocare to call. | L. vocativus (sc. casus): cf. F. vocatif.
L. vociferatus, p. p. vociferari to vociferate; vox, vocis, voice + ferre to bear. See Voice, and Bear to carry.
L. vocula, dim. of vox, vocis, voice.
Cf. Icel ver sea, vöar a fenced-in landing place.
F. vogue a rowing, vogue, fashion, It. voga, fr. vogare to row, to sail; probably fr. OHG. wag to move, akin to E. way. Cf. Way.
OE. vois, voys, OF. vois, voiz, F. voix, L. vox, vocis, akin to Gr. vac to say, to speak, G. erwähnen to mention. Cf. Advocate, Advowson, Avouch, Convoke, Epic, Vocal, Vouch, Vowel.

OE. voide, OF. voit, voide, vuit, vuide, F. vide, fr. (assumed) LL. vocitus, fr. L. vocare, an old form of vacare to be empty, or a kindred word. Cf. Vacant, Avoid. | OF. voidier, vuidier. See Void, a.
OF., to say the truth, fr. L. verus true + dicere to say.
F., fr. L. vectura a carrying, conveying. Cf. Vettura.
L. volans, -antis, p. pr. of volare to fly: cf. F. volant.
L. vola the palm of the hand, the sole of the foot.
F. volatil, L. volatilis, fr. volare to fly, perhaps akin to velox swift, E. velocity. Cf. Volley. | Cf. F. volatile.
So named after Volborth, who first discovered it.
It. volcano, vulcano, fr. L. Vulcanus Vulkan, the god of fire. See Vulkan.
F. volerie a flying, volière a large bird cage, fr. voler to fly, L. volare. See Volatile.
L. volitare, volitatum, to fly to and fro, v. freq. from volare to fly.
F., fr. L. volo I will, velle to will, be willing. See Voluntary.
F. volée; flight, a volley, or discharge of several guns, fr. voler to fly, L. volare. See Volatile.
From the answer, Volo I will, in the baptismal service. Richardson (Dict.).
F. volte; cf. It. volta. See Vault. | After Alessandro Volta, the Italian electrician.
It. volta a turn, turning, a time. See Volt a tread.
It., fr. voltare to turn. See Volt a tread.
F., fr. voltiger to vault, It. volteggiare. See Volt a tread.
So named in honor of Voltz, a French engineer.
L. volubilis, fr. volvere, volutum, to roll, to turn round; akin to Gr. welle a wave: cf. F. voluble. Cf. F. Well of water, Convolvulus, Devolve, Involve, Revolt, Vault an arch, Volume, Volute.
F., from L. volumen a roll of writing, a book, volume, from volvere, volutum, to roll. See Voluble.

L. voluntarius, fr. voluntas will, choice, from the root of velle to will, p. pr. volens; akin to E. will: cf. F. volontaire, Of. also voluntaire. See Will, v. t., and cf. Benevolent, Volition, Volunteer.
L. voluptuarius or voluptarius, fr. voluptas pleasure.
F. voluptueux, L. voluptuosus, fr. voluptas pleasure, volup agreeably, delightfully; probably akin to Gr. velle to wish. See Voluntary.
Cf. F. volupté pleasure. See Voluptuous.
L., a spiral scroll. See Volute.
L. volutatio, from volutare to roll, wallow, verb freq. volvere, volutum, to roll.
F. volute (cf. It. voluta), L. voluta, from volvere, volutum, to roll. See Voluble.
Cf. LL. volutio an arch, vault.
NL., fr. L. volvere to turn about, to roll.
L., fr. vomere to throw up, vomit.
Cf. L. vomere, vomitum, and v. freq. vomitare. See Vomit, n. | L. vomitus, from vomere, vomitum, to vomit; akin to Gr. vam, Lith. vemiti. Cf. Emetic, Vomito.
Sp. vómito, fr. L. vomitus. See Vomit, n.
Probably (through Creole French vaudoux a negro sorcerer) fr. F. Vaudois Waldensian, because the Waldenses were accused of sorcery.
L. vorax, -acis, fr. vorare to devour; akin to Gr. gar. Cf. Devour.
